Lesson 1.1/Accounting Foundations

Why Accounting Matters for Deals

20 min readPrimer
In brief

Why accounting is the language of every deal conversation, how accrual accounting differs from cash accounting (with a worked example), and what question each of the three financial statements answers.

  1. 1.1.1The language of business — and of every deal
  2. 1.1.2Cash accounting: the intuitive (and wrong) starting point
  3. 1.1.3Worked example: same business, two very different pictures
  4. 1.1.4The three statements at a glance
  5. 1.1.5Why deal teams care so much
  6. 1.1.6What's coming in this module

§1.1.1The language of business — and of every deal

Every private equity deal is, at its core, a bet expressed in numbers. When a deal team says "we're paying 8x EBITDA for a business doing £10m", every word except "we're paying" is an accounting concept. When an investment committee asks "what's the cash conversion?" or "how much of that margin is real?", they are asking accounting questions. You cannot follow a deal discussion — let alone contribute to one — without being fluent in how businesses keep score.

That score is kept in three documents, produced by every company of any size, on a regular rhythm (monthly for management, annually for statutory filing):

  • the income statement (also called the P&L, for "profit and loss"),
  • the balance sheet, and
  • the cash flow statement.

Together they are "the financial statements" or just "the financials". Almost everything in this course — valuation multiples, leverage ratios, quality of earnings, returns math — is built on top of them. If you work in a PE data team, these statements are the schema behind most of the data you will ever be asked to analyse.

Here is the thing that surprises people coming from a data background: the financials are not raw data. They are the output of a model — a set of rules and judgements applied to raw transactions. Two accountants can look at the same business and produce legitimately different numbers. Understanding the model, and where its outputs can bend, is the entire game.

§1.1.2Cash accounting: the intuitive (and wrong) starting point

The naive way to measure a business is to track money in and money out — like your bank statement. Money arrives, count it as income; money leaves, count it as a cost. This is cash accounting, and it is genuinely how very small businesses and sole traders often think.

The problem: cash timing and economic activity are different things. A business can do the work in March, invoice in April, and get paid in June. A business can buy a year of insurance in January that covers it through December. A business can buy a machine today that will produce goods for a decade. Cash accounting smears or spikes all of this in ways that make performance unreadable.

Accrual accounting — the system every real company uses — fixes this with two core ideas:

  1. Recognise revenue when it is earned, not when cash is received. Deliver the goods or perform the service, and you have revenue — even if the customer pays 60 days later.
  2. Match costs to the revenue they generate (the matching principle). The cost of goods you sold this period is this period's cost, even if you bought the stock last period. A machine that lasts ten years is spread over ten years of P&Ls, not dumped into one.

Accrual accounting answers the question "how did the business perform this period?" Cash accounting answers "what happened to the bank balance this period?" Both questions matter — which is exactly why there are separate statements for each.

§1.1.3Worked example: same business, two very different pictures

Meet a tiny fictional business: a consultancy that signs one project in January. The facts of the year:

  • January: signs a £120k project; the client pays a £30k deposit upfront.
  • January–March: does the work, paying £20k of contractor costs per month (£60k total, paid in cash as incurred).
  • March: delivers and invoices the remaining £90k, on 90-day payment terms.
  • June: the client pays the £90k.

What did the first quarter (Jan–Mar) look like?

£k, Q1 (Jan–Mar) Cash view Accrual view
Revenue / cash in 30 (deposit) 120 (work delivered)
Costs / cash out (60) (60)
Result (30) — a loss? 60 profit

On a cash basis, Q1 looks like a disaster: £30k went out the door more than came in. On an accrual basis, Q1 was excellent: the firm earned £120k of revenue, incurred £60k of matched costs, and made £60k of profit. The £90k it is owed sits as a receivable — an asset — until June.

Now look at Q2 (Apr–Jun): no work happens, but £90k of cash arrives.

£k, Q2 (Apr–Jun) Cash view Accrual view
Revenue / cash in 90 0
Costs / cash out 0 0
Result 90 "profit"? 0

Cash accounting says Q2 was the best quarter ever, when in reality nobody did anything. Accrual accounting correctly says the performance happened in Q1 and the cash caught up in Q2. Over the full half-year both views agree — £120k in, £60k out, £60k surplus — because over long enough periods, profit and cash converge. Within any given period, they can diverge wildly, and that divergence is one of the most important things deal teams scrutinise.

Hold onto this example. It contains, in miniature, the single most important idea in this module: profit is an opinion about performance; cash is a fact about the bank account. You need both, and the gap between them is where the interesting questions live.

§1.1.4The three statements at a glance

Each statement answers one question. Learn the questions first; the mechanics come in the next three lessons.

Statement The question it answers Type of measure
Income statement (P&L) "How did the business perform over the period?" Flow — covers a period (a year, a quarter)
Balance sheet "What does the business own and owe right now?" Stock — a snapshot at a single date
Cash flow statement "Where did cash actually come from and go to over the period?" Flow — covers a period

A useful analogy for the data-minded: the balance sheet is a table of current state; the P&L and cash flow statement are aggregations over an event log between two snapshots. And exactly as you would expect from that framing, the statements must reconcile: the profit for the year (P&L) explains part of the change in the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement explains the movement in the cash line from one balance sheet to the next. Lesson 5 traces those links in detail — they are what makes the three statements a closed, self-checking system rather than three unrelated reports.

The income statement starts with revenue at the top (hence "top line"), subtracts costs in layers, and ends with net profit at the bottom (hence "bottom line"). The layers matter: deal teams rarely talk about net profit and constantly talk about intermediate lines like gross profit and EBITDA.

The balance sheet lists everything the business owns (assets: cash, amounts owed by customers, stock, machinery, brands) and sets it against how those assets were funded — either by borrowing (liabilities) or by the owners' money and accumulated profits (equity). By construction, assets = liabilities + equity, always.

The cash flow statement reconciles profit back to cash movements, split into three buckets: cash from running the business (operating), cash spent on or received from long-term assets (investing), and cash raised from or returned to lenders and shareholders (financing).

§1.1.5Why deal teams care so much

Everything a PE fund does maps onto these statements:

  • Pricing the deal. Valuations are usually quoted as a multiple of EBITDA — a P&L-derived number. "8x £10m" means an £80m enterprise value. Get the EBITDA wrong by £1m and the price moves by £8m. This is why so much diligence effort goes into testing whether reported EBITDA is real (lesson 6, and the whole due diligence module).
  • Funding the deal. LBOs are funded substantially with debt, and lenders size that debt off EBITDA and cash flow. The balance sheet shows what debt already exists and what assets support it.
  • Servicing the debt. After the deal closes, the company's cash — not its profit — pays the interest. A profitable company that generates no cash is a company that defaults. The cash flow statement is where that risk shows up first.
  • Judging the business. Margins, working capital behaviour, capital intensity, cash conversion — every quality signal a deal team looks for is computed from the statements.

What looks good: profit that turns into cash reliably; clean, simple statements; numbers that reconcile across the three statements without gymnastics. What looks bad: profit growing while cash stagnates; a widening gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow; frequent "one-off" items. What deal teams actually ask, over and over: "is the profit real, and does it convert to cash?" By the end of this module you will understand precisely what that question means and how the statements answer it.

§1.1.6What's coming in this module

The next three lessons build each statement from scratch using one consistent fictional company — Bramley Foods Ltd, a UK speciality food manufacturer with £50m of revenue — so that every number carries across and you can see the statements as one connected system. Lesson 5 then traces a single transaction (a £5m machine bought with debt) through all three statements over two years. Lesson 6 closes with the uncomfortable truth: many of these numbers involve judgement, judgement can be stretched, and that is why diligence teams never take reported numbers at face value.

One mindset to carry through: whenever you meet a number in this course, ask which statement does it live on, and is it a flow or a snapshot? That one habit prevents most of the confusion beginners experience — and it is exactly the discipline you already apply when you ask whether a column is an event or a dimension.

Lesson 1.2/Accounting Foundations

The Income Statement: From Revenue to EBITDA

25 min readPrimer
In brief

Builds a full P&L line by line for a fictional £50m-revenue company — revenue recognition, COGS vs opex, gross/operating/net profit, D&A, EBIT and EBITDA — and explains why EBITDA dominates PE conversations and where it misleads.

  1. 1.2.1The shape of a P&L
  2. 1.2.2Revenue: recognised, not received
  3. 1.2.3COGS vs opex: direct costs vs overheads
  4. 1.2.4Building the P&L: Bramley Foods Ltd
  5. 1.2.5EBITDA and EBIT: the deal world's favourite acronyms
  6. 1.2.6The limitations — where EBITDA misleads
  7. 1.2.7Margins: the P&L as percentages

§1.2.1The shape of a P&L

The income statement is a subtraction ladder. Start with everything the business earned in the period, subtract costs in a deliberate order, and each rung of the ladder is a named profit measure. The order is not arbitrary — each rung strips out a different kind of cost, so each profit line answers a different question:

Line What has been deducted so far Question it answers
Revenue Nothing How much did we sell?
Gross profit Direct costs of what was sold (COGS) Is the core product profitable?
EBITDA + all operating overheads (opex) How profitable are operations, before asset and funding costs?
EBIT / operating profit + depreciation & amortisation How profitable are operations, after wearing out the assets?
Profit before tax + interest What's left after paying the lenders?
Net profit + tax What's left for the shareholders?

Read from top to bottom: first the product, then the operation, then the assets, then the funding, then the taxman. Everything below EBIT depends on how the company is financed and taxed; everything above it depends on how the business actually runs. That split is why deal teams live in the top half.

§1.2.2Revenue: recognised, not received

The top line is revenue (British accounts often say "turnover"). Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when the performance obligation is satisfied — when goods are delivered or the service is performed — not when cash arrives.

Three patterns cover most businesses:

  • Point-in-time delivery (a manufacturer ships pallets of goods): recognise on delivery. Invoice paid 60 days later? Still this period's revenue; the unpaid amount is a receivable.
  • Over-time services (a 12-month £1.2m support contract billed upfront): recognise £0.1m per month as the service is delivered. The cash received but not yet earned sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue — a liability, because the company still owes the customer eleven months of service.
  • Long projects (construction, big consulting engagements): recognise in proportion to progress, which requires estimating percentage completion — a judgement, and therefore a place numbers can bend (lesson 6).

Quick check of the over-time logic: a company with a 31 December year end signs that £1.2m annual contract on 1 October and bills it all immediately. Revenue this year is 1.2×312=£0.3m1.2 \times \tfrac{3}{12} = £0.3\text{m}1.2×123​=£0.3m, and £0.9m is deferred revenue. Recognising the full £1.2m would overstate this year's performance by £0.9m — this is one of the classic revenue games.

§1.2.3COGS vs opex: direct costs vs overheads

Costs split into two families, and the split drives the two most-quoted margins.

Cost of goods sold (COGS) — also "cost of sales" — is what it directly cost to produce the things sold this period: raw materials, direct production labour, factory running costs. Key property: COGS scales roughly with volume. Sell 10% more units, incur roughly 10% more COGS.

Operating expenses (opex) are the overheads of running the business regardless of exactly how much shipped this month: sales and marketing, distribution, head-office salaries, rent, IT, insurance. Opex is stickier — it steps up as the business grows, but not sale by sale.

Why the split matters: gross profit (revenue − COGS) tells you the underlying economics of the product; growth in a high-gross-margin business drops most of each incremental pound through to profit ("operating leverage"). A business with 60% gross margins and heavy opex can scale beautifully; a business with 15% gross margins has almost no room for anything else, however lean its overheads. Deal teams check the gross margin trend first: eroding gross margin means pricing pressure or input-cost inflation the company cannot pass on — a structural problem opex cuts cannot fix.

§1.2.4Building the P&L: Bramley Foods Ltd

Bramley Foods Ltd is our running fictional company: a UK speciality food manufacturer selling premium sauces and condiments to supermarkets and food-service distributors. Here is its FY24 P&L, built line by line. (We use a 20% tax rate throughout the module to keep the arithmetic round; the actual UK corporation tax main rate is 25%.)

Bramley Foods — FY24 P&L (£m) % of revenue
Revenue 50.0 100%
Cost of goods sold (30.0) 60%
Gross profit 20.0 40%
Distribution costs (4.0)
Sales & marketing (3.5)
Administrative expenses (4.5)
EBITDA 8.0 16%
Depreciation (1.8)
Amortisation (0.2)
EBIT (operating profit) 6.0 12%
Interest expense (1.0)
Profit before tax 5.0 10%
Tax (20%) (1.0)
Net profit 4.0 8%

Walk the ladder:

  • Revenue £50.0m: goods delivered to customers during FY24, whether or not yet paid for.
  • COGS £30.0m: ingredients (£18m), direct factory labour (£8m), factory energy and running costs (£4m). Gross margin = 20.0 / 50.0 = 40% — healthy for premium food manufacturing, where 25–40% is a typical range.
  • Opex £12.0m in three buckets: getting product to customers (£4.0m), winning and keeping customers (£3.5m), and running the company (£4.5m).
  • EBITDA £8.0m = 20.0 − 12.0. Margin 16%.
  • D&A £2.0m: the factory's machines wear out (£1.8m depreciation) and some purchased software and brand assets are written down over their lives (£0.2m amortisation). These are real economic costs but involve no cash leaving this period — the cash left when the assets were bought. Lesson 3 covers the mechanics.
  • EBIT £6.0m = 8.0 − 2.0. Margin 12%.
  • Interest £1.0m: Bramley has £15m of bank debt (lesson 3); this is the cost of it.
  • Tax £1.0m = 20% × 5.0, leaving net profit of £4.0m — an 8% net margin. This is the number that flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet (lesson 5).

Sanity-check habit worth building: every profit line should equal the line above minus the deductions between them. 50.0 − 30.0 = 20.0; 20.0 − 12.0 = 8.0; 8.0 − 2.0 = 6.0; 6.0 − 1.0 = 5.0; 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0. If a P&L you are handed doesn't foot like this, something is being hidden between the lines — it happens more often than you'd think.

§1.2.5EBITDA and EBIT: the deal world's favourite acronyms

EBIT — Earnings Before Interest and Tax — is operating profit: what the business earned from operations before anyone asks how it is financed. EBITDA — Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation — goes one step further and adds back the non-cash asset charges:

EBITDA=EBIT+Depreciation+Amortisation\text{EBITDA} = \text{EBIT} + \text{Depreciation} + \text{Amortisation}EBITDA=EBIT+Depreciation+Amortisation

For Bramley: EBITDA = 6.0 + 2.0 = £8.0m. In practice you'll compute it both ways — down from gross profit, or up from EBIT — and they must agree.

Why does EBITDA dominate PE conversations?

  1. It approximates operating cash generation. By excluding non-cash D&A, EBITDA is a rough proxy for the cash the operations throw off — the pool available to pay interest, fund capex, and reward shareholders. Rough is the operative word; see below.
  2. It is capital-structure-neutral. A PE buyer will replace the company's financing anyway, so a profit measure before interest lets you compare targets regardless of how their current owners funded them.
  3. It irons out asset-accounting differences. Two identical businesses can show different EBIT purely because of depreciation policies or acquisition accounting. EBITDA strips that noise, making cross-company comparison cleaner.
  4. It is the market's pricing and lending unit. Deals are priced as EV/EBITDA multiples; leverage is quoted as debt/EBITDA; loan covenants are written against EBITDA. When everyone transacts in a currency, you learn the currency.

§1.2.6The limitations — where EBITDA misleads

Every deal professional can recite the famous warning that EBITDA is not cash flow. Concretely, EBITDA ignores four real cash demands:

  • Capex. Depreciation is non-cash, but the machines still have to be replaced with cash. A haulage firm and a software firm can post identical EBITDA while one must plough half of it back into trucks every year. EBITDA treats them as equals; free cash flow (lesson 4) does not.
  • Working capital. A growing business ties up cash in stock and unpaid invoices before a penny of EBITDA becomes bankable. Lesson 4's worked example shows a profitable company running out of cash exactly this way.
  • Interest and tax. Real, contractual, non-optional cash outflows. A company leveraged at 6x EBITDA lives a very different life from one at 1x, and EBITDA can't see the difference.
  • Definitional games. Because EBITDA is not a statutory measure, sellers present "adjusted EBITDA" with add-backs of allegedly one-off costs. Some add-backs are legitimate; some are fiction. Lesson 6 opens this can of worms properly.

What looks good: EBITDA margins stable or rising, and operating cash flow tracking EBITDA closely year after year. What looks bad: EBITDA growing while cash conversion deteriorates, or an adjusted-EBITDA bridge with many small add-backs that all conveniently push the number up. What deal teams actually ask: "what's the bridge from reported EBITDA to adjusted EBITDA, and how much of it would survive diligence?" — because at an 8x multiple, every £1m of contested EBITDA is £8m of contested price.

§1.2.7Margins: the P&L as percentages

Divide each profit line by revenue and you get margins — the P&L in comparable, size-free form:

Margin Bramley FY24 Formula
Gross margin 40% Gross profit / revenue = 20.0 / 50.0
EBITDA margin 16% EBITDA / revenue = 8.0 / 50.0
EBIT margin 12% EBIT / revenue = 6.0 / 50.0
Net margin 8% Net profit / revenue = 4.0 / 50.0

Margins are how you compare a £50m business to a £500m one, and how you spot drift over time: a gross margin sliding 40% → 37% → 34% over three years is a story about pricing power that no amount of top-line growth should distract you from. The financial statement analysis module turns margin analysis into a full toolkit; for now, the discipline is simply to always look at the percentage next to the pound number.

One closing reframe for the data-minded: the P&L is a period aggregation with a fixed rollup hierarchy — revenue at the root, cost categories as deductions, profit measures as subtotals at each level. Once you see it that way, "EBITDA" stops being jargon and becomes just a named subtotal: the one taken after operating costs but before asset and funding costs. The next lesson moves from the flow to the snapshot: the balance sheet.

Lesson 1.3/Accounting Foundations

The Balance Sheet: What a Business Owns and Owes

25 min readPrimer
In brief

Derives assets = liabilities + equity from first principles, explains working capital items, PP&E and depreciation, intangibles and goodwill, and debt vs equity funding — then builds Bramley Foods' full two-year balance sheet.

  1. 1.3.1The equation from first principles
  2. 1.3.2A snapshot, sorted by time
  3. 1.3.3Working capital: the operating engine's float
  4. 1.3.4PP&E and depreciation: spreading the cost of long-lived assets
  5. 1.3.5Intangibles and goodwill
  6. 1.3.6Debt vs equity: the two flavours of funding
  7. 1.3.7Bramley Foods: the full balance sheet

§1.3.1The equation from first principles

Strip a business down to its simplest possible form. On day one, two founders put £100k into a company bank account and a bank lends it another £50k. The company now has £150k of cash. But that cash isn't free-floating — every pound of it is claimed by someone: £50k belongs, in an economic sense, to the bank (it must be repaid) and £100k to the founders (it's their stake).

That is the entire balance sheet idea. Everything a company has (assets) was funded by someone, and the funding came from exactly two kinds of source: money that must be paid back (liabilities) or the owners' money and accumulated profits (equity). So, always and by construction:

Assets=Liabilities+Equity\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}Assets=Liabilities+Equity

This isn't an empirical observation that might occasionally fail — it's an identity, like a ledger that double-enters every transaction. Buy a £20k van with cash: assets rearrange (−£20k cash, +£20k van), totals unchanged. Buy it on credit: assets rise £20k and liabilities rise £20k. Make £10k of profit: assets rise (say, cash) and equity rises via retained earnings. Every transaction moves at least two lines and preserves the equation. If a balance sheet doesn't balance, someone has made an error — the format is self-checking, which is precisely why accountants love it.

Equity is therefore best understood as a residual: Equity = Assets − Liabilities. It's what would notionally be left for the owners if the assets were sold at book value and all liabilities repaid. This residual nature is also why equity holders sit at the bottom of the queue — and why, in leveraged deals, small changes in asset value produce large swings in equity value. That lever is the beating heart of the LBO module later.

§1.3.2A snapshot, sorted by time

Unlike the P&L, the balance sheet is a snapshot at a single date — typically the last day of the financial year. Its convention is to sort both sides by time horizon:

  • Current assets: cash, or things expected to become cash within 12 months — customer receivables, inventory, prepayments.
  • Non-current assets: things held to operate with, not to sell — property, plant & equipment (PP&E), intangible assets, goodwill.
  • Current liabilities: due within 12 months — supplier payables, accrued expenses, tax owed.
  • Non-current liabilities: due later — principally long-term debt.

The current/non-current split is what lets you ask liquidity questions ("can it pay its bills this year?") separately from solvency questions ("is it worth more than it owes overall?").

§1.3.3Working capital: the operating engine's float

Three current items deserve special attention because they arise directly from running the business, and together they form (trade) working capital:

  • Trade receivables (debtors): sales delivered and invoiced but not yet paid for. You have effectively lent your customers this money.
  • Inventory (stock): raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods waiting to be sold. Cash converted into things sitting in a warehouse.
  • Trade payables (creditors): what you owe suppliers. They have effectively lent you this money.

Working capital=Receivables+Inventory−Payables\text{Working capital} = \text{Receivables} + \text{Inventory} - \text{Payables}Working capital=Receivables+Inventory−Payables

Positive working capital means the business has cash tied up in its operating cycle: it pays for ingredients, holds stock, delivers, and waits for customers to pay — funding that whole pipeline itself. The crucial dynamic consequence: when the business grows, working capital grows, and that growth consumes cash. A company doubling revenue roughly doubles its receivables and inventory, and the cash to fund that has to come from somewhere before the profit arrives. This single mechanic explains most stories of profitable companies hitting cash crises (lesson 4 works one through).

What deal teams actually ask: "how much working capital does £1 of growth consume?" — because it directly determines how much of EBITDA growth turns into distributable cash.

§1.3.4PP&E and depreciation: spreading the cost of long-lived assets

When Bramley buys a £3m filling line that will run for ten years, expensing £3m against one year's profit would be absurd — the machine serves a decade of revenue. Instead:

  1. The purchase is capitalised: it lands on the balance sheet as PP&E, not in the P&L.
  2. Each year, a slice of the cost is charged to the P&L as depreciation. Straight-line over ten years with no residual value: £0.3m per year.
  3. The balance sheet carries the asset at net book value = original cost − accumulated depreciation. After year 4: 3.0 − 1.2 = £1.8m.

If an asset has an expected salvage value, depreciate cost minus salvage: a £12m asset with £2m residual value over five years is (12−2)/5=£2.0m(12-2)/5 = £2.0\text{m}(12−2)/5=£2.0m per year.

Note what depreciation is not: it is not cash. The cash left when the machine was bought (that's capex, on the cash flow statement). Depreciation is the P&L's way of matching that past cash cost to the periods that benefit. This is why it gets added back to reach EBITDA, and why it appears on all three statements — a linkage lesson 5 makes explicit.

Useful lifetimes and methods are choices (is a van's life five years or eight?), which makes depreciation one of the softer numbers in the accounts — another entry on lesson 6's list.

§1.3.5Intangibles and goodwill

Not all long-term assets are physical. Intangible assets — purchased software, licences, patents, acquired brands and customer relationships — sit on the balance sheet and are amortised (the intangible-asset word for depreciated) over their useful lives.

Goodwill is the strangest line on any balance sheet, and in PE you will meet it constantly. When one company buys another for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets, the excess is recorded as goodwill. Buy a company for £30m when its identifiable net assets are worth £22m, and £8m of goodwill appears. It represents everything you paid for that can't be separately listed: the workforce, the reputation, the expected synergies — and, sometimes, simple overpayment.

Two things to know now: goodwill is not amortised under modern accounting (IFRS); instead it is tested annually for impairment — written down if the acquired business underperforms. And a big goodwill impairment is a public confession of having overpaid. Since PE deals are acquisitions, post-deal balance sheets are full of goodwill; learn to read past it to the operating assets underneath.

§1.3.6Debt vs equity: the two flavours of funding

The right-hand side of the balance sheet answers "whose money funded all this?", and the two answers have profoundly different characters:

Debt Equity
Obligation Contractual — interest and repayment on schedule None — dividends discretionary
Cost to company Interest (tax-deductible) Share of all future value
Risk to provider Lower — paid first, often secured Higher — paid last, can be wiped out
Upside to provider Capped at interest Unlimited
If things go wrong Can enforce, appoint administrators Absorbs the loss

Debt is cheaper (lower risk to the lender, and interest is tax-deductible) but rigid; equity is expensive but forgiving. Private equity's core trick is deliberately loading a company with far more debt than it would naturally carry, precisely because debt's fixed claim concentrates all the upside into a small equity slice. The number to start tracking now: net debt = total debt − cash, usually quoted as a multiple of EBITDA.

§1.3.7Bramley Foods: the full balance sheet

Here is Bramley's balance sheet at the last two year ends — the same company whose FY24 P&L we built in lesson 2 (revenue £50.0m, EBITDA £8.0m, net profit £4.0m).

Bramley Foods — Balance sheet (£m) FY23 FY24
Cash 2.5 3.0
Trade receivables 7.0 8.0
Inventory 5.5 6.0
Prepayments 1.0 1.0
Current assets 16.0 18.0
PP&E (net) 18.8 20.0
Intangible assets 2.2 2.0
Goodwill 5.0 5.0
Non-current assets 26.0 27.0
Total assets 42.0 45.0
Trade payables 6.5 7.0
Accruals 2.0 2.0
Tax payable 1.0 1.0
Current liabilities 9.5 10.0
Bank debt 16.0 15.0
Total liabilities 25.5 25.0
Share capital 5.0 5.0
Retained earnings 11.5 15.0
Total equity 16.5 20.0
Total liabilities + equity 42.0 45.0

Check the identity both years: 25.5 + 16.5 = 42.0 ✓ and 25.0 + 20.0 = 45.0 ✓.

Now read it like a deal person:

  • Working capital (FY24): 8.0 + 6.0 − 7.0 = £7.0m, up from 6.0 + 5.5... careful — FY23 is 7.0 + 5.5 − 6.5 = £6.0m. Growth consumed £1.0m of cash this year; remember that number for the cash flow statement.
  • PP&E rose from 18.8 to 20.0: Bramley spent £3.0m of capex and charged £1.8m of depreciation (18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0). Intangibles fell 2.2 → 2.0 via £0.2m amortisation.
  • Goodwill of £5.0m dates from Bramley's acquisition of a smaller sauce brand years ago — it just sits there unless impaired.
  • Net debt = 15.0 − 3.0 = £12.0m, i.e. 12.0 / 8.0 = 1.5x EBITDA. Modest — a PE buyer would see substantial unused debt capacity here.
  • Equity rose 16.5 → 20.0, an increase of £3.5m: net profit of £4.0m came in via retained earnings and £0.5m went out as a dividend (11.5 + 4.0 − 0.5 = 15.0). That equity roll-forward is one of the key statement links in lesson 5.

What looks good: working capital growing slower than revenue; net debt comfortably low relative to EBITDA; equity building steadily through retained profits. What looks bad: receivables or inventory ballooning faster than sales (cash quietly leaking into the operating cycle — or worse, revenue being booked that customers aren't paying for); goodwill dwarfing tangible assets; debt creeping up to fund ordinary operations. What deal teams actually ask: "what's normalised working capital, and what's the real net debt?" — because both numbers move pounds directly in the purchase price, as the structuring module will show.

One final framing: the P&L told you how Bramley performed; the balance sheet shows the position that performance left behind. The third statement — next lesson — explains the one line here that nothing so far fully accounts for: why cash moved only from 2.5 to 3.0 in a year when the company "made" £4.0m.

Lesson 1.4/Accounting Foundations

The Cash Flow Statement: Where the Money Actually Went

25 min readPrimer
In brief

The three sections of the cash flow statement, the indirect method walked line by line using Bramley Foods' numbers, free cash flow, and a worked example of a profitable company that runs out of cash.

  1. 1.4.1Why a third statement exists at all
  2. 1.4.2The three sections
  3. 1.4.3The indirect method, line by line
  4. 1.4.4Free cash flow
  5. 1.4.5Why profit ≠ cash: a company that profits itself to death
  6. 1.4.6What deal teams look for

§1.4.1Why a third statement exists at all

Lesson 3 ended on a puzzle: Bramley Foods made £4.0m of profit in FY24, yet its cash rose by only £0.5m (2.5 → 3.0). Neither the P&L nor the balance sheet explains that gap — the P&L deliberately ignores cash timing, and the balance sheet only shows the end points. The cash flow statement is the bridge: it reconciles the profit for the period to the actual movement in cash, item by item.

For deal teams this is arguably the most important statement of the three, for a blunt reason: debt is serviced with cash, not profit. An LBO's leverage is sized against cash generation; covenant headroom is measured in cash; a portfolio company dies when it runs out of cash, never when it runs out of profit. Profit is also the easier number to flatter (lesson 6) — cash is harder to fake, which is why "does the profit convert to cash?" is the standard first-pass quality check on any target.

§1.4.2The three sections

Every cash flow statement sorts the period's cash movements into three buckets, by why the cash moved:

Section Question Typical contents
Operating (CFO) Did the day-to-day business generate cash? Profit, add back non-cash charges, working capital movements
Investing (CFI) What was spent on the long-term asset base? Capex, acquisitions, disposal proceeds
Financing (CFF) What moved between the company and its funders? Debt drawn/repaid, dividends, share issues

The signature of a healthy mature business: CFO strongly positive, CFI moderately negative (reinvestment), CFF modestly negative (repaying debt, paying dividends). Variations tell stories — a startup shows negative CFO funded by positive CFF; a business in decline sometimes shows positive CFI (selling the family silver). Reading the three signs together is a 30-second diagnostic worth internalising.

§1.4.3The indirect method, line by line

There are two ways to build the operating section. The direct method lists actual cash receipts and payments — intuitive but rarely used. The indirect method, which virtually every company publishes, starts from profit and adjusts away everything non-cash. It looks odd at first and then becomes second nature. Here is Bramley's FY24 statement, then the logic of each line:

Bramley Foods — FY24 cash flow statement (£m)
Net profit 4.0
Add back: depreciation & amortisation 2.0
(Increase) in trade receivables (1.0)
(Increase) in inventory (0.5)
Increase in trade payables 0.5
Cash from operating activities 5.0
Capital expenditure (3.0)
Cash used in investing activities (3.0)
Repayment of bank debt (1.0)
Dividends paid (0.5)
Cash used in financing activities (1.5)
Net movement in cash 0.5
Opening cash 2.5
Closing cash 3.0

Walk it:

  • Start with net profit (£4.0m) — the accrual measure of the period, which we now convert to cash by undoing its non-cash content.
  • Add back D&A (£2.0m). Depreciation reduced profit but no cash left the building this year — so add it back. (The cash cost of assets shows up below, as capex, in the year of purchase.)
  • Subtract the increase in receivables (£1.0m). Receivables rose 7.0 → 8.0 (lesson 3's balance sheet). That means £1.0m of the revenue counted in profit is still sitting in customers' hands, not Bramley's bank account. Profit overstates cash by that amount.
  • Subtract the increase in inventory (£0.5m). Stock rose 5.5 → 6.0: cash was spent filling the warehouse, but nothing hit the P&L because the goods haven't been sold yet.
  • Add the increase in payables (£0.5m). Payables rose 6.5 → 7.0: Bramley took £0.5m of costs into the P&L that it hasn't yet paid suppliers for. Free short-term funding.

The three working capital lines net to −£1.0m — exactly the working capital increase (6.0 → 7.0) we computed from the balance sheet. That is the general rule worth memorising: an increase in working capital is a cash outflow; a decrease is an inflow. The sign convention trips everyone up once; the fix is to ask "did this tie cash up, or release it?"

  • Operating cash flow: £5.0m = 4.0 + 2.0 − 1.0 − 0.5 + 0.5. Against £8.0m of EBITDA, that's the "cash conversion" a deal team would immediately compute.
  • Investing: capex of £3.0m — the filling-line investment that also explains the PP&E movement (18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0).
  • Financing: −£1.5m — £1.0m of scheduled debt repayment (debt 16.0 → 15.0) and the £0.5m dividend from the equity roll-forward.
  • Net movement +£0.5m, closing cash £3.0m — matching the balance sheet to the penny. Puzzle solved: of the £4.0m profit, £2.0m was offset by capex net of the D&A add-back (3.0 − 2.0), £1.0m got absorbed into working capital, and £1.5m went to funders, leaving £0.5m.

Notice the deep structural point: apart from opening/closing cash, every line came from the other two statements — profit and D&A from the P&L, working capital and debt movements from balance sheet deltas. The indirect-method cash flow statement is derived, which is why a three-statement model always builds it last, and why lesson 5 can treat the three statements as one machine.

§1.4.4Free cash flow

Deal teams compress the statement into one number: free cash flow (FCF) — the cash the business generates after the reinvestment needed to keep it running, i.e. the cash genuinely free to pay lenders and owners. The simplest common definition:

FCF=Operating cash flow−Capex\text{FCF} = \text{Operating cash flow} - \text{Capex}FCF=Operating cash flow−Capex

For Bramley: 5.0 − 3.0 = £2.0m. Definitions vary (before or after interest and tax — be precise about which you're using; the valuation module formalises the variants), but the idea is constant: EBITDA of £8.0m is the headline, and £2.0m is what actually landed. The ratio of the two — here 25% — is the single most revealing quality-of-earnings statistic there is. A business converting 80% of EBITDA to free cash is a compounding machine; one converting 20% is running hard to stand still. Same EBITDA, completely different deals.

§1.4.5Why profit ≠ cash: a company that profits itself to death

Now the promised cautionary tale. Growfast Trading Ltd (fictional) distributes electronic components. It buys stock, holds it, sells on 60-day credit terms, and it is growing ferociously: revenue up 60% this year, from £20.0m to £32.0m. The P&L looks great — net profit of £1.6m (a 5% margin), with £0.4m of depreciation. Champagne?

Look at what growth did to the balance sheet:

Growfast (£m) Opening Closing Cash effect
Trade receivables 3.0 5.0 (2.0)
Inventory 2.5 4.5 (2.0)
Trade payables 2.0 3.0 1.0
Working capital 3.5 6.5 (3.0)

Sixty percent more sales means sixty-ish percent more invoices outstanding and a much bigger warehouse of stock, only partly offset by stretching suppliers. Now assemble the cash flow statement:

Growfast — cash flow (£m)
Net profit 1.6
Add back: depreciation 0.4
Working capital increase (3.0)
Operating cash flow (1.0)
Capex (0.6)
Free cash flow (1.6)
Debt repayment due (0.5)
Net cash movement (2.1)
Opening cash 1.5
Closing cash (0.6)

A company that just reported £1.6m of profit finishes the year £0.6m overdrawn. Nothing fraudulent happened; nothing even went wrong operationally. The profit is real — it is simply trapped in stock and unpaid invoices, while the wage bill, the suppliers and the bank all demand actual cash on actual dates. Unless Growfast raises new funding, slows its own growth, or squeezes its working capital cycle, it will bounce payments while its P&L glows. Insolvency practitioners have a name for this: overtrading. It kills growing companies with real products and real customers.

The general law: profit and cash differ by (i) non-cash charges like D&A, (ii) working capital movements, and (iii) things that hit cash but not profit — capex, debt principal, dividends. Fast growth maximises (ii) and often (iii), which is why growth is a use of cash long before it is a source of it.

§1.4.6What deal teams look for

What looks good: operating cash flow consistently at or above 80–90% of EBITDA; capex comfortably covered; the cash flow statement "boring" — the same shape every year. What looks bad: a widening EBITDA-to-cash gap (classic early warning of aggressive revenue recognition or stock problems); chronic negative operating cash flow dressed up as "investment in growth"; one-off working capital releases flattering a single year (squeeze payables in December, look great at year end, pay for it in January). What deal teams actually ask: "show me EBITDA to free cash flow, line by line, for the last three years" — the so-called cash conversion bridge. If you remember one exhibit from this lesson, make it that one: it is the P&L's claims, audited by the bank account.

Next, lesson 5 ties everything together: one transaction, traced through all three statements over two years, so the linkages stop being rules to memorise and become mechanics you can see.

Lesson 1.5/Accounting Foundations

How the Three Statements Link

25 min readPrimer
In brief

Traces a £5m debt-funded machine purchase through all three statements over two years, and makes the standing linkages explicit — net income to retained earnings, depreciation's triple appearance, and working capital movements.

  1. 1.5.1One machine, three statements, two years
  2. 1.5.2Day one: nothing hits the P&L
  3. 1.5.3Year 1: the costs begin to flow
  4. 1.5.4Year 2: the pattern repeats
  5. 1.5.5The standing linkages
  6. 1.5.6Why this matters beyond exams

§1.5.1One machine, three statements, two years

The fastest way to stop thinking of the statements as three separate reports is to push a single transaction through all of them and watch every statement react. Our test transaction: on the first day of Year 1, a company buys a £5.0m production machine, funded entirely by a new £5.0m bank loan. Assumptions, kept deliberately clean:

  • The machine is depreciated straight-line over 10 years, no residual value → £0.5m depreciation per year.
  • The loan carries 6% interest (£0.3m per year), interest-only for now — no principal repayments in our window.
  • Tax rate 20%, paid in the year incurred.
  • We isolate only this transaction's effects — as if everything else in the company held still. (In reality the machine would earn revenue too; we'll note that at the end.)

This is the classic interview drill — "walk me through a £5m capex funded by debt" — and it is asked precisely because you cannot answer it correctly without understanding every linkage in this lesson.

§1.5.2Day one: nothing hits the P&L

The day the machine is bought, the company has spent £5.0m — and reports zero profit impact. That feels wrong to newcomers and is exactly right: the machine isn't a cost of this period; it's an asset that will serve ten periods. The purchase is capitalised.

  • P&L: no effect. Nothing was consumed yet.
  • Cash flow statement: two entries that cancel — capex of (5.0) in investing, loan drawdown of +5.0 in financing. Net cash movement: nil.
  • Balance sheet: PP&E +5.0 (asset), bank debt +5.0 (liability). The equation grows by £5m on each side and stays balanced. Equity: untouched.

Already the division of labour is visible: the cash flow statement recorded the event, the balance sheet recorded the position, and the P&L correctly stayed silent.

§1.5.3Year 1: the costs begin to flow

Over Year 1 the machine wears (depreciation) and the loan costs money (interest).

P&L impact, Year 1 (£m):
Depreciation (0.50)
Interest expense (0.30)
Profit before tax (0.80)
Tax saving at 20% 0.16
Net income impact (0.64)

Note the tax line: because depreciation and interest are deductible, an £0.8m pre-tax cost reduces the tax bill by £0.16m — the "tax shield". This shield, especially on interest, is one of the quiet subsidies that makes leveraged structures attractive; the LBO module returns to it.

Cash flow statement, Year 1 (£m): start from net income and undo the non-cash items.
Net income impact (0.64)
Add back: depreciation (non-cash) 0.50
Operating cash flow impact (0.14)
Investing 0.00
Financing 0.00
Cash impact (0.14)

Only £0.14m of actual cash left in Year 1: interest of £0.30m paid out, minus £0.16m of tax genuinely saved. The £0.5m depreciation charge cost nothing this year — its cash left on day one.

Balance sheet at end of Year 1 (changes vs. the day before purchase):

Δ £m
PP&E (5.0 cost − 0.5 accumulated depreciation) +4.50
Cash (0.14)
Assets +4.36
Bank debt +5.00
Retained earnings (0.64)
Liabilities + equity +4.36

It balances: +4.36 = +4.36. Every one of those four deltas came from one of the flows above — nothing was plugged.

§1.5.4Year 2: the pattern repeats

Year 2 is a carbon copy of Year 1's flows: depreciation (0.50), interest (0.30), tax saving 0.16, net income impact (0.64), cash impact (0.14). The balance sheet simply accumulates another year of it:

End of Year 2 (cumulative Δ, £m)
PP&E (5.0 − 1.0 accumulated depreciation) +4.00
Cash (2 × 0.14) (0.28)
Assets +3.72
Bank debt +5.00
Retained earnings (2 × 0.64) (1.28)
Liabilities + equity +3.72

Balanced again. Run the film forward mentally: after ten years PP&E reaches zero, cumulative depreciation of £5.0m has flowed through the P&L, and the total P&L cost equals the cash spent on day one — just spread over the machine's life. Accrual accounting never changes what things cost, only when the cost is recognised. (And in real life, of course, the machine would be generating revenue all along — a machine that only appears in a model as costs is a machine that shouldn't have been bought. The point of isolating the costs is to see the plumbing.)

It is worth pausing on where each statement did its distinctive job across the two years. The cash flow statement told the truth about timing: a £5.0m outflow on day one, then only £0.14m a year. The P&L told the truth about economics: no cost on day one, then £0.64m a year of after-tax burden as the machine wears and the loan accrues interest. The balance sheet kept the running score: an asset shrinking by £0.5m a year, a debt sitting unchanged until repaid, and equity quietly absorbing the accumulated after-tax cost. Ask any one statement alone and you get a misleading answer — "we spent £5m and made no profit impact" (cash view, day one) or "this machine only costs £0.64m a year" (P&L view, ignoring the capital tied up). Ask all three and the picture is complete. That is the design: the statements are not three opinions but three projections of one underlying event log.

§1.5.5The standing linkages

The machine story used every major connection between the statements. Here they are as a reusable checklist — these hold for every company, every period:

1. Net income → retained earnings. The P&L's bottom line doesn't vanish at year end; it rolls into equity:

Closing RE=Opening RE+Net income−Dividends\text{Closing RE} = \text{Opening RE} + \text{Net income} - \text{Dividends}Closing RE=Opening RE+Net income−Dividends

Bramley Foods (lessons 2–3): 11.5 + 4.0 − 0.5 = 15.0 ✓. This is the bridge from P&L to balance sheet, and the reason a profitable, dividend-light company shows steadily compounding equity.

2. Depreciation appears three times. The most-tested linkage in every modelling interview:

  • P&L: an expense, reducing EBIT and net income.
  • Cash flow statement: added back to net income in the operating section (non-cash).
  • Balance sheet: accumulates against PP&E, reducing net book value.

One economic event, three coordinated appearances. If you change depreciation in a model and only one statement moves, the model is broken.

3. Working capital links balance sheet deltas to operating cash flow. Every change in receivables, inventory and payables between two balance sheets appears — with the sign flipped for assets — in the operating section. Bramley's receivables +1.0, inventory +0.5, payables +0.5 became (1.0), (0.5), +0.5 in CFO.

4. Capex links CFI to PP&E; D&A closes the loop. Closing PP&E=Opening PP&E+Capex−Depreciation\text{Closing PP\&E} = \text{Opening PP\&E} + \text{Capex} - \text{Depreciation}Closing PP&E=Opening PP&E+Capex−Depreciation. Bramley: 18.8 + 3.0 − 1.8 = 20.0 ✓. Given any three of those numbers, you can solve for the fourth — a standard diligence cross-check on data-room numbers.

5. Financing flows link CFF to debt and equity. Debt drawn/repaid moves the debt balance (Bramley: 16.0 − 1.0 = 15.0); dividends and share issues move equity alongside retained earnings.

6. The cash flow statement's bottom line is the balance sheet's cash line. Opening cash + net cash movement = closing cash (Bramley: 2.5 + 0.5 = 3.0). This is the master check: if a three-statement model balances and the cash reconciles, every flow has been accounted for somewhere.

§1.5.6Why this matters beyond exams

The linked system is self-auditing, and deal teams exploit that constantly:

  • Models are built on it. Every LBO model is a three-statement machine: P&L drives cash flow, cash flow pays down debt, debt sets next year's interest, which feeds back into the P&L. The linkages aren't a nicety — they're the simulation loop.
  • Inconsistencies expose problems. If a management pack shows EBITDA up 20% but debt creeping upward and cash flat, the linkages say the profit isn't converting — something (working capital? capitalised costs? optimistic revenue?) is absorbing it. You don't need to be told where to look; the system tells you.
  • Data work depends on it. When you reconcile portfolio-company reporting into a warehouse, the linkages are your integrity constraints: retained earnings roll-forwards, PP&E roll-forwards, cash reconciliation. A monthly pack that fails them is a data quality incident with a financial name.

What looks good: statements that tie out exactly, with roll-forwards you can reproduce from the disclosed flows. What looks bad: "adjusted" figures that can't be reconciled back to any statement, or balance sheet movements with no corresponding flow (the polite term is "other"). What deal teams actually ask: "does the model balance?" — and, of an analyst, "walk me through £5m of capex funded by debt." You now can, to the decimal.

One lesson remains in this module, and it changes register: so far we've treated the rules as mechanical. In practice, several of the numbers you've just learned to trace — depreciation lives, revenue timing, what counts as an asset — are chosen, not observed. Lesson 6 is about who chooses them, how they bend, and why diligence exists.

Lesson 1.6/Accounting Foundations

Accounting Judgement & Where Numbers Bend

25 min readPrimer
In brief

Where reported numbers involve judgement — accruals and provisions, capitalisation vs expensing, revenue recognition games, one-offs and exceptionals — and why diligence teams adjust reported figures before pricing a deal.

  1. 1.6.1The uncomfortable truth about "the numbers"
  2. 1.6.2Accruals and provisions: profit by estimate
  3. 1.6.3Capitalisation vs expensing: the EBITDA machine
  4. 1.6.4Revenue recognition games
  5. 1.6.5One-offs, exceptionals, and the adjusted-EBITDA bridge
  6. 1.6.6The instinct to carry forward

§1.6.1The uncomfortable truth about "the numbers"

Everything in this module so far has treated accounting like arithmetic: rules in, statements out. Time to complicate that. Accounting standards are a framework, not a formula — they require estimates (how long will this machine last?), judgements (is this project 60% or 80% complete?), and classifications (is this cost an asset or an expense?). Reasonable people can answer these differently, and the answers move profit.

Most of the time, management makes these calls in good faith. But notice the incentives: bonus schemes pay on profit targets, covenants are tested on EBITDA, and — most relevantly for us — companies being sold are valued at a multiple of EBITDA. At an 8x multiple, every £1m of extra EBITDA a seller can present is £8m of extra price. Nobody needs to commit fraud for numbers to drift optimistic; the drift is built into the situation. This is the reason financial due diligence exists: not to re-add columns, but to re-make the judgements from the buyer's side. This lesson is your first tour of the four places numbers bend most. The due diligence module goes much deeper; here we build the instinct.

§1.6.2Accruals and provisions: profit by estimate

Accrual accounting requires estimating costs that haven't been billed yet. An accrual is a cost recognised before the invoice arrives (December's electricity, unbilled bonuses). A provision is a bigger, more uncertain cousin: a liability of uncertain timing or amount — warranty claims, a lawsuit, restructuring costs, doubtful receivables.

Every accrual and provision is an estimate, and estimates have a dial. Worked example: a machinery manufacturer sells £40.0m of equipment with two-year warranties. History says warranty costs run at about 3% of sales, so prudent accounting books a £1.2m provision, charging it against this year's profit. But suppose management, in a year they're being measured on, decides "quality has improved" and books 1.5% instead: the charge is £0.6m and profit is £0.6m higher — with no change whatsoever in the business. The claims will arrive regardless; next year's P&L will absorb the shortfall.

Provisions also enable the opposite game. Overprovide in a bad year (the market has written the year off anyway), then quietly release the excess provision into profit in a later year when the target needs hitting. Releases boost profit with no cash and no performance behind them — this smoothing is sometimes called "cookie-jar accounting".

What deal teams actually ask: how have provision balances moved over three years, and were releases booked into EBITDA? A provision that only ever moves in profit-friendly directions is a red flag with a paper trail.

§1.6.3Capitalisation vs expensing: the EBITDA machine

Recall the boundary from lessons 3 and 5: spend that creates a long-term asset is capitalised (balance sheet, then depreciated/amortised over years); spend that is consumed now is expensed (P&L, immediately). The boundary is genuinely fuzzy — and it sits directly on top of EBITDA.

Worked example. A software company spends £3.0m a year on developers. Two defensible treatments:

£m Expense it all Capitalise £2.0m as development
Revenue 20.0 20.0
Staff costs in P&L (3.0) (1.0)
Other opex (12.0) (12.0)
EBITDA 5.0 7.0
Amortisation of capitalised dev (over 4 years) — (0.5)

Same company, same cash out the door, and EBITDA is 40% higher under the second treatment — because the capitalised £2.0m re-enters the P&L only as amortisation, which sits below the EBITDA line and gets added straight back. At an 8x multiple, that treatment choice is worth £16m of headline price. (In steady state amortisation catches up — by year 4 there's £2.0m of annual amortisation from four overlapping cohorts — but EBITDA never sees it, and EBITDA is what the deal is priced on.)

Capitalising development costs can be entirely legitimate — standards permit it when specific criteria are met. The diligence questions are: is the policy stable or did capitalisation rates creep up before the sale? What happens to "EBITDA minus capitalised development" — the cash-honest version? A rising capitalisation rate in the two years before a sale process is one of the most reliable tells in the book.

§1.6.4Revenue recognition games

Revenue is the biggest number on the P&L, the first thing every buyer looks at, and — because recognition depends on judgements about delivery, completion and contract terms — the most consequential place to be aggressive. The classic moves:

  • Pulling revenue forward. Shipping heavily in the last week of the period (helped by discounts — "channel stuffing"), invoicing ahead of delivery, or recognising an annual contract upfront instead of over its life. Lesson 2's example: booking a £1.2m October-to-September contract entirely in this financial year overstates revenue by £0.9m. The tell: a receivables or deferred-revenue balance that's drifted out of line with revenue.
  • Optimistic percentage-of-completion. Long-contract businesses recognise revenue by estimated progress. Nudge a project from 60% to 75% complete and revenue appears from thin air; reality arrives later as a loss-making final phase. The tell: contract assets ("accrued income" — earned-but-not-yet-billed) growing faster than revenue.
  • Gross vs net presentation. An intermediary handling £100m of bookings on which it earns a 10% commission can present revenue as £100m (gross) or £10m (net). Profit is identical; scale, growth optics, and revenue multiples are wildly different.
  • Bill-and-hold and side letters. Recognising sales for goods still sitting in your own warehouse, or granting undisclosed return rights that make "sales" reversible.

The unifying diagnostic — and the reason lesson 4 matters so much: aggressive revenue makes profit grow faster than operating cash flow, because the fictional-or-early revenue piles up in receivables and contract assets instead of arriving as cash. Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. When the two diverge for more than a year, diligence teams start pulling contracts.

§1.6.5One-offs, exceptionals, and the adjusted-EBITDA bridge

Companies present items as exceptional or "one-off" to argue they don't reflect underlying performance: restructuring costs, a flood at the warehouse, deal fees, a discontinued product line. The logic is fair — you shouldn't price a business off a year distorted by a fire. The abuse is systematic, in one direction: costs are forever one-off; gains are somehow always underlying. Some businesses report "exceptional" restructuring charges every single year for a decade — at which point they are not exceptional, they are the business model.

In a sale process this crystallises into the adjusted EBITDA bridge — the seller's walk from reported to "underlying" EBITDA. A typical one:

Project Orchard — adjusted EBITDA (£m) FY24
Reported EBITDA 6.0
Add: restructuring costs 0.8
Add: aborted-deal professional fees 0.4
Add: flood damage (uninsured portion) 0.3
Add: pro-forma synergies from new site 0.7
Add: normalised owner remuneration 0.3
Adjusted EBITDA 8.5

Reported £6.0m becomes marketed £8.5m — a 42% uplift — and at 8x the adjustments alone are asking for £20m. A diligence team would take each line on its merits: the aborted-deal fees are probably a fair add-back (genuinely non-recurring, verifiable); the restructuring is suspect if one happens every year; the flood add-back needs the insurance file; the "pro-forma synergies" are a forecast wearing an add-back's clothes and usually get struck out or heavily discounted; the owner-remuneration adjustment cuts both ways (what will a market-rate replacement actually cost?). Also note what bridges rarely contain: deductions — the one-off gain on a property sale, the under-accrued bonuses, the R&D that stopped being expensed. A one-directional bridge is itself evidence.

What looks good: a short bridge, each item large, documented, and genuinely non-recurring, with add-backs and deductions. What looks bad: many small add-backs, "one-offs" recurring across years, synergies presented as adjustments. What deal teams actually ask: "rebuild the bridge — what EBITDA would we defend to our investment committee and our lenders?"

§1.6.6The instinct to carry forward

Pull the four sections together and you get the mental posture of a good diligence analyst — and a good data person in PE:

  1. Reported numbers are a starting point, never an answer. They embed estimates made by people with incentives. The question is not "what is EBITDA?" but "whose EBITDA, under whose judgements?"
  2. Cash is the audit of profit. Nearly every game in this lesson — early revenue, skinny provisions, capitalised costs — shows up as a gap between profit and operating cash flow, or as a balance sheet line (receivables, contract assets, capitalised development, provision balances) drifting out of proportion. The three-statement linkages from lesson 5 are your lie detector.
  3. Trends beat snapshots. A single year's judgement calls are hard to assess; three years of capitalisation rates, provision movements, and one-off frequencies tell you whether the dial has been turned. This is genuinely a data problem, which is why data teams get pulled into diligence.
  4. Materiality is priced in multiples. Every contested £1m of EBITDA is £6–10m of price at typical multiples. That is why sellers polish, why buyers commission quality-of-earnings reports, and why this module ends here rather than with the mechanics.

None of this means accounts are fiction — audited statements are mostly reliable, and the self-checking structure you've learned makes gross manipulation hard to sustain. It means the last 10–20% of any reported profit number is soft, the softness is usually optimistic, and deals are won and lost in exactly that band. The financial statement analysis module sharpens the tools; the due diligence module weaponises them. You now speak the language they're written in.

Lesson 2.1/Financial Statement Analysis

Reading Statements Like an Analyst

22 min readPrimer
In brief

How analysts actually read a P&L: common-size and trend analysis, plus the five questions (growth, margin, quality, trajectory, comparability) worked through a fictional company's three-year income statement.

  1. 2.1.1From bookkeeping to judgement
  2. 2.1.2Common-size analysis: divide everything by revenue
  3. 2.1.3Trend analysis: growth rates line by line
  4. 2.1.4The five questions to ask of any P&L
  5. 2.1.5Applying the five questions to Bramley
  6. 2.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.1.1From bookkeeping to judgement

Module 1 taught you what the three statements are. This module teaches you what deal teams do with them. The difference matters: an accountant asks "is this recorded correctly?"; an analyst asks "what is this business really like, and is it getting better or worse?"

When a deal team receives a target's financials — usually a three-year historical P&L plus a budget — nobody reads it top to bottom like a novel. They convert it into two standard views (common-size and trend), then interrogate it with a handful of stock questions. The whole exercise takes twenty minutes and tells you 80% of what a first meeting needs. This lesson walks through exactly that process on a fictional company, Bramley Foods Ltd, a maker of branded chilled ready-meals.

Here is Bramley's summary P&L as it might arrive in an information pack:

£m FY23 FY24 FY25
Revenue 80.0 92.0 100.0
Cost of goods sold (48.0) (56.4) (62.0)
Gross profit 32.0 35.6 38.0
Operating expenses (20.0) (22.0) (23.0)
EBITDA 12.0 13.6 15.0
Depreciation & amortisation (3.0) (3.2) (3.5)
EBIT 9.0 10.4 11.5
Interest (1.0) (1.2) (1.5)
Profit before tax 8.0 9.2 10.0
Tax (2.0) (2.3) (2.5)
Profit after tax 6.0 6.9 7.5

At first glance: everything grows, every subtotal is bigger each year. A seller would call this "a consistent record of profitable growth". Our job is to look harder.

§2.1.2Common-size analysis: divide everything by revenue

Common-size analysis restates every P&L line as a percentage of revenue. It strips out the effect of the company simply getting bigger, so you can see whether the shape of the business is changing. It also makes companies of different sizes directly comparable — a £80m business and a £800m business can sit side by side.

Bramley common-sized:

% of revenue FY23 FY24 FY25
Revenue 100.0% 100.0% 100.0%
COGS 60.0% 61.3% 62.0%
Gross margin 40.0% 38.7% 38.0%
Opex 25.0% 23.9% 23.0%
EBITDA margin 15.0% 14.8% 15.0%
EBIT margin 11.3% 11.3% 11.5%
Net margin 7.5% 7.5% 7.5%

Suddenly the story changes. EBITDA margin looks flat at ~15%, but that flatness is hiding two opposing forces:

  • Gross margin is eroding: 40.0% → 38.7% → 38.0%. Bramley loses two full points of gross margin over two years. On FY25 revenue of £100.0m, two points is £2.0m of EBITDA — real money. Is it input-cost inflation they can't pass on? Price pressure from supermarket customers? A mix shift towards lower-margin products? We don't know yet, but this is now question one for management.
  • Opex is falling as a % of revenue: 25.0% → 23.0%. That could be healthy operating leverage (fixed costs spread over more revenue — more on this in Lesson 2), or it could be under-investment: cutting marketing, delaying hires, skimping on maintenance. Cost discipline that flatters the year before a sale is one of the oldest tricks in the book.

What looks good: stable or rising gross margin with opex leverage on top. What looks bad: exactly Bramley's pattern — gross margin decline masked by opex cuts. The headline margin is flat but the quality of the margin has deteriorated, because gross margin reflects the fundamental economics of what you sell, while opex cuts are finite and often reversible.

§2.1.3Trend analysis: growth rates line by line

The second standard view is year-on-year growth for each line. The rule of thumb: in a healthy business, profit lines grow faster than revenue (margins expanding), and no cost line grows persistently faster than revenue without a good reason.

YoY growth FY24 FY25
Revenue +15.0% +8.7%
COGS +17.5% +9.9%
Gross profit +11.3% +6.7%
Opex +10.0% +4.5%
EBITDA +13.3% +10.3%

Two observations. First, COGS grows faster than revenue in both years (+17.5% vs +15.0%, then +9.9% vs +8.7%) — the arithmetic mirror of the gross margin erosion we saw above, and a pattern that compounds badly if it continues. Second, revenue growth is decelerating: +15.0% then +8.7%. Deceleration isn't fatal, but a buyer paying a growth multiple needs to know where it settles. If FY26 comes in at +4%, this is a different business — and a different price.

A useful companion number is the CAGR (compound annual growth rate):

CAGR=(End valueStart value)1/n−1\text{CAGR} = \left(\frac{\text{End value}}{\text{Start value}}\right)^{1/n} - 1CAGR=(Start valueEnd value​)1/n−1

Bramley's two-year revenue CAGR is (100.0/80.0)1/2−1=11.8%(100.0/80.0)^{1/2} - 1 = 11.8\%(100.0/80.0)1/2−1=11.8%. Sellers love quoting CAGR because it smooths the deceleration into one flattering number. Always look at the year-by-year path behind any CAGR: "11.8% CAGR" and "15% fading to 9%" describe the same data but imply very different futures.

§2.1.4The five questions to ask of any P&L

Common-size and trend views are mechanical. The judgement comes from five questions every analyst should be able to answer after reading any P&L. Commit these to memory.

1. Growth — how fast, and where from? Not just the rate, but the source: volume or price? Existing customers or new? Organic or acquired? £10m of growth from a price rise on captive customers is worth more than £10m from a one-off contract win. If the pack doesn't split volume from price, ask — it's one of the first data requests any deal team sends.

2. Margin — how profitable, and is that normal? Compute gross and EBITDA margin, then benchmark against the sector (Lesson 2 gives you the reference table). A 15% EBITDA margin is excellent for a food distributor, ordinary for a manufacturer, and alarming for a software business. A margin far above sector norms needs as much explanation as one far below — outperformance has a cause, and if you can't find it, suspect the accounting.

3. Quality — is the profit real and repeatable? Are there one-off items in the numbers? Does EBITDA convert to cash (Lessons 3–4)? Is revenue recurring or won deal-by-deal? A P&L alone can't fully answer this — that's what Lesson 6 and, later, quality of earnings work are for — but you should form a first view of how much you trust the reported numbers.

4. Trajectory — which direction is each line heading? Buyers buy the future. A business at a 14% margin and rising is more attractive than one at 16% and falling. For Bramley: growth decelerating, gross margin falling, EBITDA margin held flat by opex cuts. The trajectory read is cautious even though every absolute number went up.

5. Comparability — are the years measured the same way? Trend analysis assumes FY23, FY24 and FY25 are like-for-like. They often aren't: accounting policy changes, acquisitions mid-year, a 53-week year, reclassifications between COGS and opex, a change in revenue recognition. Before trusting any trend, check the basis of preparation. A margin "trend" that's really a reclassification is noise, and worse, it's noise that usually flatters.

§2.1.5Applying the five questions to Bramley

Run Bramley through the framework and write down what you'd actually say in a deal-team meeting:

  • Growth: 15.0% then 8.7%, decelerating; two-year CAGR 11.8%. Need the volume/price split — with food inflation in the period, much of this could be pass-through pricing with flat or falling volumes, which is far less valuable than it looks.
  • Margin: 38.0% gross / 15.0% EBITDA in FY25. For branded chilled food, a 15% EBITDA margin is towards the top of the normal range — good, but check it's earned honestly.
  • Quality: unknown from the P&L alone. Flag for later: does the £15.0m EBITDA turn into cash, and is any of it one-off?
  • Trajectory: the worrying one. Gross margin down 2.0 points in two years; EBITDA margin only flat because opex fell from 25.0% to 23.0% of revenue. If opex cuts have run out and gross margin keeps sliding, FY26 EBITDA margin drops below 14% even with decent growth.
  • Comparability: to verify. Any change in how COGS and opex are split? Any change in depreciation policy (which wouldn't hit EBITDA but would hit EBIT)? Same 52-week years?

Notice how different this is from "revenue and profits grew every year". Same numbers, completely different conversation.

§2.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When this analysis lands in a meeting, the questions it generates are concrete. For a Bramley-shaped business, expect: "What's driving the gross margin decline — input costs, pricing, or mix?", "How much of FY25's opex reduction is sustainable versus deferred spend?", "Give us the volume/price bridge for revenue growth", and "Were there any changes in accounting policy or cost classification across the period?"

Three habits to build from day one. First, always common-size and trend a P&L before forming any view — never react to absolute numbers. Second, be suspicious of flat lines: a suspiciously stable margin often means two offsetting movements, and you need to know what both are. Third, write your five answers down. The discipline of committing to "growth: decelerating; margin: top of range; trajectory: negative" forces clarity, and it's exactly the format an investment committee summary uses.

The rest of this module builds out the toolkit: margin benchmarks and returns ratios (Lesson 2), working capital (Lesson 3), cash conversion (Lesson 4), leverage (Lesson 5), and a first pass at earnings quality (Lesson 6). Every one of them is ultimately in service of the same five questions.
