Lesson 2.2/Financial Statement Analysis

Margins and Profitability Ratios

24 min readPrimer
In brief

The margin ladder (gross, EBITDA, operating, net) with typical ranges by sector, returns ratios (ROCE and ROE), and operating leverage — including a worked example of what a 10% revenue drop does to EBITDA in fixed-cost versus variable-cost businesses.

  1. 2.2.1The margin ladder
  2. 2.2.2What "normal" looks like by sector
  3. 2.2.3ROCE: the quality-of-business ratio
  4. 2.2.4ROE, and why PE treats it carefully
  5. 2.2.5Operating leverage: fixed costs cut both ways
  6. 2.2.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.2.1The margin ladder

Every P&L gives you a ladder of margins, each answering a different question:

  • Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue. What's left after the direct cost of what you sell. This is the purest read on the economics of the product: pricing power, input costs, and mix. It's also the hardest margin to improve — you can cut overheads in a quarter, but improving gross margin means changing what you sell, to whom, at what price.
  • EBITDA margin = EBITDA ÷ revenue. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The lingua franca of PE: it approximates the operating cash profitability of the business before financing choices and capex policy. Almost every deal is priced as a multiple of EBITDA, which is why so much of this course is about whether reported EBITDA can be trusted.
  • Operating (EBIT) margin = EBIT ÷ revenue. EBITDA minus depreciation and amortisation. The honest margin for capital-intensive businesses: a haulier's EBITDA margin ignores the trucks wearing out; its EBIT margin doesn't. When EBITDA and EBIT margins are far apart, the gap is the capital intensity.
  • Net margin = profit after tax ÷ revenue. Everything including financing and tax. Useful for listed-company screens; less used in deals, because a buyer will replace the capital structure anyway.

A worked ladder on Bramley Foods' FY25 (from Lesson 1): revenue £100.0m, gross profit £38.0m, EBITDA £15.0m, EBIT £11.5m, profit after tax £7.5m. Margins: 38.0% gross, 15.0% EBITDA, 11.5% operating, 7.5% net. The 3.5-point EBITDA-to-EBIT gap tells you Bramley carries meaningful fixed assets (factories, chilled logistics) — worth remembering when we get to capex in Lesson 4.

§2.2.2What "normal" looks like by sector

Margins only mean something against a benchmark. A 6% EBITDA margin is a disaster for a software company and a perfectly good result for a distributor. Typical ranges for established mid-market businesses:

Sector Gross margin EBITDA margin
Enterprise software / SaaS 75–90% 20–40%
Business & professional services 30–50% 10–20%
Healthcare services 25–45% 15–25%
Specialist manufacturing 25–40% 10–18%
Consumer brands 35–55% 10–20%
Distribution / wholesale 15–30% 4–8%
Food retail / grocery 20–30% 3–6%
Construction / contracting 10–20% 3–6%

Three ways deal teams use this table. First, placement: is the target at the top, middle or bottom of its range, and why? A distributor at 8% EBITDA margin either has a genuinely differentiated niche (value-added services, exclusive lines) or flattering accounting — find out which. Second, headroom: a services business at 11% when peers make 18% is a value-creation thesis in one line. Third, suspicion: a company above the top of its sector range is a red flag until proven otherwise. Outperformance is possible, but it has a nameable cause; "our margins are just better" is not an answer.

Note also that low-margin sectors are unforgiving: a grocer at a 4% EBITDA margin loses half its profit if costs move 2 points against it. That fragility feeds directly into how much debt such a business can carry (Lesson 5).

§2.2.3ROCE: the quality-of-business ratio

Margins ignore how much capital it takes to earn them. Return on capital employed fixes that:

ROCE=EBITCapital employed,Capital employed=Equity+Net debt\text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Capital employed}}, \qquad \text{Capital employed} = \text{Equity} + \text{Net debt}ROCE=Capital employedEBIT​,Capital employed=Equity+Net debt

(Equivalently: total assets minus current liabilities. Use EBIT, not EBITDA — capital employed includes the fixed assets, so the return should be after the cost of wearing them out.)

Worked example: Bramley has EBIT of £11.5m, shareholders' equity of £40.0m and net debt of £20.0m. Capital employed = £60.0m, so ROCE = 11.5 ÷ 60.0 = 19.2%.

Is that good? Rules of thumb: ROCE below ~10% is a mediocre business (barely covering its cost of capital); 15–20% is solid; 25%+ is genuinely good and usually signals some moat. The power of ROCE is comparing businesses with identical margins: two companies each earning £11.5m of EBIT, but one employs £60.0m of capital (19.2% ROCE) and the other £130.0m (8.8%). The first compounds value; the second treads water. High-ROCE businesses also need less capital to grow — every £1 of extra revenue drags in less investment — which is exactly the cash-generative profile PE pays up for.

§2.2.4ROE, and why PE treats it carefully

Return on equity = profit after tax ÷ shareholders' equity. Bramley: 7.5 ÷ 40.0 = 18.8%.

ROE has a trap: it rises with leverage. Refinance Bramley with £40.0m of net debt and only £20.0m of equity, and (after higher interest) profit after tax might fall to say £6.3m — but ROE jumps to 6.3 ÷ 20.0 = 31.5%. Nothing about the business improved; the equity cheque just got smaller and riskier. Since PE deliberately runs high leverage, ROE mostly measures the financial structure, not the company.

So the working rule: judge the business on ROCE, judge the deal on equity returns (IRR and MOIC — Module 7), and treat ROE as a number that needs decomposing before it tells you anything. If someone quotes a high ROE, your first question is how much of it is leverage.

§2.2.5Operating leverage: fixed costs cut both ways

Operating leverage describes how sensitive profit is to revenue, and it's driven by the cost structure. Costs split into variable (move with revenue: materials, freight, sales commissions) and fixed (don't, at least in the short run: rent, salaried staff, IT, insurance). The more fixed the cost base, the more a change in revenue is amplified into profit.

Compare two businesses, both with £100.0m revenue and £15.0m EBITDA:

£m FlexCo FixCo
Revenue 100.0 100.0
Variable costs (75.0) (45.0)
Fixed costs (10.0) (40.0)
EBITDA 15.0 15.0
EBITDA margin 15.0% 15.0%

Identical P&L headline. Now let revenue fall 10% to £90.0m. Variable costs fall proportionately; fixed costs don't move:

£m FlexCo FixCo
Revenue 90.0 90.0
Variable costs (67.5) (40.5)
Fixed costs (10.0) (40.0)
EBITDA 12.5 9.5
EBITDA change −16.7% −36.7%

A 10% revenue decline costs FlexCo 16.7% of its EBITDA but costs FixCo 36.7% — over a third of profit gone. The shortcut for this sensitivity is the degree of operating leverage:

DOL=%ΔEBITDA%ΔRevenue=Contribution marginEBITDA margin\text{DOL} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{EBITDA}}{\%\Delta \text{Revenue}} = \frac{\text{Contribution margin}}{\text{EBITDA margin}}DOL=%ΔRevenue%ΔEBITDA​=EBITDA marginContribution margin​

where contribution margin = (revenue − variable costs) ÷ revenue. FlexCo: 25% ÷ 15% = 1.7×. FixCo: 55% ÷ 15% = 3.7×. Check: 3.7 × (−10%) ≈ −37% — matches the table.

The same maths runs in reverse: if revenue grows 10%, FixCo's EBITDA jumps 36.7% to £20.5m. Operating leverage is why growing fixed-cost businesses show expanding margins "for free" — and why Lesson 1 told you to ask whether opex leverage is structural or just the good half of a cycle.

A related number worth computing is break-even revenue — the level at which EBITDA hits zero, found by dividing fixed costs by the contribution margin:

Break-even revenue=Fixed costsContribution margin %\text{Break-even revenue} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs}}{\text{Contribution margin \%}}Break-even revenue=Contribution margin %Fixed costs​

FlexCo breaks even at 10.0 ÷ 0.25 = £40.0m of revenue — it could lose 60% of its sales and still not lose money. FixCo breaks even at 40.0 ÷ 0.55 = £72.7m — a 27% revenue decline puts it underwater. Two businesses with identical revenue and identical EBITDA, and one is roughly twice as far from the cliff edge as the other. When you later size debt against these businesses (Lesson 5), that distance to break-even is precisely the cushion the lender is relying on, which is why cost-structure questions appear in every lender due diligence pack.

§2.2.6What deal teams actually ask

Margins and operating leverage come together in diligence questions like these:

  • "Give us the margin bridge." Explain the change in EBITDA margin year over year, split into price, volume, mix, input costs, and opex. If management can't produce this, they don't understand their own business — itself a finding.
  • "What's the fixed/variable split of the cost base?" This drives the downside case. A lender and an IC will both want to know what EBITDA looks like at revenue −10% and −20%. With FixCo's cost structure, revenue −20% means EBITDA of £4.0m — down 73% — which caps how much debt the deal can safely carry.
  • "Why is your margin above/below the sector?" Placement in the benchmark table, with a named cause: niche, scale, contract structure, or — the wrong answer — accounting.
  • "Where does the margin go from here?" Operating leverage plus the growth outlook gives the trajectory. A 15% margin with DOL of 3.7× and decelerating revenue is fragile; the same margin with DOL of 1.7× is robust.

Two habits to take forward. First, always compute the full ladder — gross, EBITDA, EBIT — because divergences between them (gross falling while EBITDA holds; EBITDA fine while EBIT sags) are where the real story hides. Second, never quote a margin without its benchmark and its trajectory. "15% EBITDA margin" is data; "15%, top quartile for the sector, held flat only by opex cuts" is analysis.

Lesson 2.3/Financial Statement Analysis

Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle

24 min readPrimer
In brief

Net working capital and the cash conversion cycle from first principles: DSO, DIO and DPO computed on a worked example, why growth consumes cash, negative working capital businesses, and how seasonality distorts year-end balance sheets.

  1. 2.3.1Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact
  2. 2.3.2DSO, DIO, DPO: a worked example
  3. 2.3.3Why growth consumes cash
  4. 2.3.4Negative working capital: growth that pays you
  5. 2.3.5Seasonality: the year-end is not the year
  6. 2.3.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.3.1Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact

A business can report profit every year and still run out of money. The usual culprit is working capital: the cash tied up in the day-to-day operating cycle. Money goes out to buy stock and pay staff before money comes in from customers, and that timing gap has to be financed by someone — the company, its bank, or its suppliers.

Net working capital (NWC), for analysis purposes, is:

NWC=Trade receivables+Inventory−Trade payables\text{NWC} = \text{Trade receivables} + \text{Inventory} - \text{Trade payables}NWC=Trade receivables+Inventory−Trade payables

(plus smaller items like accruals and prepayments, which matter more than you'd think — Lesson 6 and the case study will show you why). Receivables are sales you've made but not been paid for; inventory is stock you've paid for but not sold; payables are purchases you've made but not yet paid for. Receivables and inventory absorb cash; payables are free credit from suppliers that provides cash.

The single most important sentence in this lesson: an increase in NWC is cash flowing out of the business, even though nothing about it appears in the P&L. A company that books £5m more revenue but collects none of it yet has £5m more profit and £5m less cash than it appears.

A word on those "smaller items". Accruals are costs incurred but not yet invoiced — staff bonuses earned but unpaid, utilities used but unbilled; they behave like payables and should grow roughly in line with the cost base. Prepayments are the mirror image (insurance or rent paid in advance) and behave like receivables. Deferred income is cash collected before the work is done — a liability, and a big one in subscription businesses. Analysts watch accruals particularly closely: an accrual balance that falls while revenue and headcount grow usually means costs are being under-recognised, which inflates profit directly. Hold that thought for this module's case study.

§2.3.2DSO, DIO, DPO: a worked example

Raw NWC balances are hard to interpret — £23m of working capital means nothing without scale. So we convert each component into days, which are comparable across time and across companies. Take Fenwick Trading, a distributor of plumbing supplies:

£m FY25
Revenue 120.0
COGS 90.0
Trade receivables 20.0
Inventory 18.0
Trade payables 15.0

DSO (days sales outstanding) — how long customers take to pay:

DSO=ReceivablesRevenue×365=20.0120.0×365=60.8 days\text{DSO} = \frac{\text{Receivables}}{\text{Revenue}} \times 365 = \frac{20.0}{120.0} \times 365 = 60.8 \text{ days}DSO=RevenueReceivables​×365=120.020.0​×365=60.8 days

DIO (days inventory outstanding) — how long stock sits before selling. Note the denominator is COGS, not revenue, because inventory is held at cost:

DIO=InventoryCOGS×365=18.090.0×365=73.0 days\text{DIO} = \frac{\text{Inventory}}{\text{COGS}} \times 365 = \frac{18.0}{90.0} \times 365 = 73.0 \text{ days}DIO=COGSInventory​×365=90.018.0​×365=73.0 days

DPO (days payables outstanding) — how long the company takes to pay suppliers (also on COGS):

DPO=PayablesCOGS×365=15.090.0×365=60.8 days\text{DPO} = \frac{\text{Payables}}{\text{COGS}} \times 365 = \frac{15.0}{90.0} \times 365 = 60.8 \text{ days}DPO=COGSPayables​×365=90.015.0​×365=60.8 days

The cash conversion cycle chains these together: the number of days between paying for stock and getting paid for the finished sale.

CCC=DSO+DIO−DPO=60.8+73.0−60.8=73.0 days\text{CCC} = \text{DSO} + \text{DIO} - \text{DPO} = 60.8 + 73.0 - 60.8 = 73.0 \text{ days}CCC=DSO+DIO−DPO=60.8+73.0−60.8=73.0 days

Fenwick finances 73 days of its operating cycle out of its own pocket. Sanity-check against the balances: NWC = 20.0 + 18.0 − 15.0 = £23.0m, which is 23.0 ÷ 120.0 = 19.2% of revenue — a fairly typical level for a stockholding distributor. Both views (days and % of revenue) are standard; deal teams tend to quote NWC as % of revenue for the headline and use days to diagnose which component moved.

What looks good / bad: stable or gently improving days over time. A rising DSO means customers paying slower (or worse — disputed invoices, or aggressive revenue recognition booking sales that customers haven't accepted). Rising DIO means stock building up (demand softening, or obsolete stock not written off). A suddenly rising DPO looks like free cash but usually means the company is leaning on suppliers — which reverses, and which we'll see planted in this module's case study.

§2.3.3Why growth consumes cash

Here's the counterintuitive bit that catches people out: growth makes the working capital problem worse, not better. If NWC runs at a stable percentage of revenue, then every pound of new revenue drags new working capital with it.

Fenwick again: NWC is 19.2% of revenue. Suppose revenue grows 20% next year, from £120.0m to £144.0m. At a constant 19.2%, NWC grows from £23.0m to about £27.6m — an outflow of £4.6m that never touches the P&L. If Fenwick's EBITDA is, say, £8.4m (a 7% margin), more than half the year's EBITDA is swallowed by funding its own growth. Fast-growing, working-capital-heavy businesses can be profitable on paper and cash-starved in fact; "overtrading" — growing faster than your working capital funding allows — kills more healthy-looking companies than losses do.

The multiplication to internalise:

Cash absorbed by growth≈Revenue growth (£)×NWC as % of revenue\text{Cash absorbed by growth} \approx \text{Revenue growth (£)} \times \text{NWC as \% of revenue}Cash absorbed by growth≈Revenue growth (£)×NWC as % of revenue

£24.0m of growth × 19.2% ≈ £4.6m. This is why lenders and deal models always carry a working capital line tied to revenue growth, and why a buyer of a growing distributor needs a revolving credit facility sized for it.

§2.3.4Negative working capital: growth that pays you

Now flip every sign. Some business models collect from customers before paying suppliers, so NWC is negative and the operating cycle generates cash rather than consuming it.

Worked example — a grocery retailer: revenue £200.0m, COGS £150.0m, receivables £1.0m (customers pay at the till: DSO = 1.0/200.0 × 365 = 1.8 days), inventory £10.0m (DIO = 10.0/150.0 × 365 = 24.3 days), payables £20.0m (DPO = 20.0/150.0 × 365 = 48.7 days).

CCC=1.8+24.3−48.7=−22.6 days\text{CCC} = 1.8 + 24.3 - 48.7 = -22.6 \text{ days}CCC=1.8+24.3−48.7=−22.6 days

NWC = 1.0 + 10.0 − 20.0 = −£9.0m. The retailer sells the stock roughly 24 days before paying for it. Every new store releases cash on opening; growth funds itself and then some. Classic negative-working-capital models: food retail, insurance (premiums up front, claims later), and any business collecting subscriptions or deposits in advance — SaaS businesses with annual up-front billing carry large deferred revenue balances that work the same way.

PE finds these models attractive for obvious reasons — cash arrives early and reliably, supporting more debt — but note the sting in the tail: negative working capital reverses viciously in decline. If the grocer's revenue shrinks, payables unwind faster than stock, and the model that funded growth now drains cash exactly when the business can least afford it. Same for a subscription business losing customers: the deferred revenue it already spent has to be delivered anyway.

§2.3.5Seasonality: the year-end is not the year

Working capital breathes. A toy distributor builds stock from June, peaks in October, and collects cash in January. A December year-end balance sheet catches it near its best-looking moment (stock sold, cash in); a September balance sheet would show peak inventory and stretched payables. Neither single date is "the" working capital of the business.

Practical consequences:

  • Use monthly data, not year-end snapshots. Any serious analysis asks for 24–36 months of month-end NWC balances and looks at the average and the peak, not just the year-end. The gap between average and year-end NWC is itself informative: a company whose year-end is always its low point may have chosen its year-end for that reason.
  • The peak sets the funding need. Facilities must cover the worst month, not the average. A business with average NWC of £15m and a seasonal peak of £26m needs ~£11m of headroom just for the cycle.
  • In deals, seasonality drives the "working capital peg". Acquisitions complete on a cash-free, debt-free basis with an agreed normal level of working capital; completing in the low month without an adjustment would hand the seller a windfall. You'll meet the mechanics in Module 8 — for now, know that "what is normalised working capital?" is a standard, and often contentious, diligence question.
  • Watch for window dressing. Companies can flatter a single date: delay paying suppliers for two weeks, run a collections blitz, hold off purchases. Monthly data makes this visible; a year-end DPO that's 15 days above every other month-end is a tell.

§2.3.6What deal teams actually ask

The stock questions on working capital, all answerable with this lesson's tools:

  • "What are DSO, DIO and DPO, and how have they trended over three years?" — compute them per year; a stable CCC with growing revenue is the good answer.
  • "What's NWC as a % of revenue, and how much cash does the growth plan absorb?" — the 19.2% × growth calculation above, straight into the deal model.
  • "What does monthly working capital look like — average, peak, trough?" — seasonality, funding needs, and the peg.
  • "Has the company stretched payables or accelerated collections recently?" — because a seller preparing for exit can 'generate' one-off cash and even flatter apparent conversion by squeezing working capital, and it always unwinds on the buyer's watch.

Working capital is where accounting profit and cash reality diverge first, which is exactly why the next lesson builds the full bridge from EBITDA down to free cash flow — with working capital as the first and most volatile step.

Lesson 2.4/Financial Statement Analysis

Cash Conversion and Capex

24 min readPrimer
In brief

The bridge from EBITDA to free cash flow with a full worked table, maintenance versus growth capex, and cash conversion ratios — what "good" looks like by business type and why PE prizes 85%+ conversion in asset-light businesses.

  1. 2.4.1EBITDA is where the analysis starts, not ends
  2. 2.4.2The EBITDA-to-FCF bridge: full worked table
  3. 2.4.3Maintenance vs growth capex
  4. 2.4.4Cash conversion ratios
  5. 2.4.5What "good" looks like
  6. 2.4.6What deal teams actually ask

§2.4.1EBITDA is where the analysis starts, not ends

Deals are priced off EBITDA, but debt is repaid with cash. Between the two sits a series of very real claims: working capital, capex, tax, and eventually interest. Cash conversion measures how much of each £1 of EBITDA survives the journey to become spendable cash — and it varies enormously. Two businesses with identical £15.0m EBITDA can throw off £13m and £6m of cash respectively, and they are worth very different amounts.

This lesson builds the standard bridge, line by line, on Marlow Instruments, a fictional specialist manufacturer with £100.0m revenue and £15.0m EBITDA.

§2.4.2The EBITDA-to-FCF bridge: full worked table

£m FY25 Notes
EBITDA 15.0 Reported, pre any adjustments
Change in net working capital (1.2) Growth absorbing cash (Lesson 3)
Maintenance capex (2.0) Keeping existing kit running
Operating free cash flow 11.8 "Pre-tax operating FCF"
Growth capex (1.5) New capacity — discretionary
Cash exceptionals (0.3) Restructuring costs actually paid
Cash tax (2.4) Tax paid, not the P&L charge
Free cash flow (pre-financing) 7.6 Cash available to all capital providers
Cash interest (1.5)
FCF after interest 6.1 Cash available for debt paydown

Read it top to bottom. Of £15.0m EBITDA, £1.2m goes into working capital just to fund growth, £3.5m in total goes on capex, £0.3m pays for last year's restructuring promises, and £2.4m goes to HMRC. What's left before financing is £7.6m — about half the headline EBITDA. After interest, £6.1m remains: this is the number that actually pays down debt in an LBO, which is why lenders build exactly this bridge before offering a single pound.

Three technical notes. First, every line is the cash amount, not the P&L amount — cash tax and the P&L tax charge differ (timing differences, instalments), and "exceptional" costs are only relevant here when actually paid. Second, ΔNWC is a flow: the year-on-year change in the balance, not the balance itself. Third, notice what's absent: depreciation. It's non-cash — capex is the cash reality it approximates, which is the whole reason the bridge replaces one with the other.

Always rebuild this bridge yourself from the audited cash flow statement rather than accepting the version in a sale pack. The cash flow statement is the hardest of the three statements to flatter — cash either arrived or it didn't — so it acts as the truth serum for the other two. If the pack's bridge shows £9m of free cash flow but the cash flow statement shows net debt flat year on year, something in the bridge is a definition game: a "pre-exceptional" line here, an "underlying working capital" adjustment there. Tracing every bridge line to a statutory cash flow line item is twenty minutes of work that regularly pays for itself.

§2.4.3Maintenance vs growth capex

The single most argued-about split in the bridge. Maintenance capex keeps today's revenue running: replacing worn machines, van fleets, routine IT refresh, safety work. Growth capex creates tomorrow's revenue: a new production line, a new warehouse, a major systems build. The distinction matters because maintenance capex is a compulsory deduction from earnings power — a business that "makes" £15.0m but must spend £2.0m every year just to stand still really makes £13.0m — while growth capex is discretionary and should come with a return attached.

Sellers know this, so information packs habitually label as much capex as possible "growth". Three cross-checks deal teams run:

  • Compare capex to depreciation. Over time, maintenance capex should roughly track depreciation (you replace assets at about the rate they wear out). Marlow's D&A is £3.5m against claimed maintenance capex of £2.0m — a gap worth probing. Persistent total capex below depreciation is the classic sign of an under-invested business: the P&L looks fine while the asset base quietly rots, and the buyer inherits the catch-up bill.
  • Look at capex/revenue over 5+ years. The long-run average through a cycle is a better estimate of true ongoing capex than any single year or any management label.
  • Ask for the capex register. Project-by-project detail makes the split auditable: "replacement CNC machine" is maintenance whatever the pack calls it.

A sudden drop in capex in the year or two before a sale is a standard red flag: it flatters free cash flow at the cost of asset condition, and it reverses on the buyer.

Remember too that capex is naturally lumpy. A distributor might spend £0.8m a year for four years and then £4m in year five when the warehouse racking, fleet and ERP all come due together. A single low-capex year proves nothing about the ongoing requirement — which is why every capex ratio in this lesson should be computed on a multi-year average, and why "last year's capex" is never the number that goes into a model.

§2.4.4Cash conversion ratios

Several ratios compress the bridge into one number; be precise about which one is being quoted, because they differ a lot:

  • Lender's conversion = (EBITDA − total capex) ÷ EBITDA. Marlow: (15.0 − 3.5) ÷ 15.0 = 76.7%.
  • Underlying conversion = (EBITDA − maintenance capex) ÷ EBITDA. Marlow: (15.0 − 2.0) ÷ 15.0 = 86.7%. Flattering, and dependent on that contestable capex split.
  • Operating cash conversion = (EBITDA − ΔNWC − total capex) ÷ EBITDA. Marlow: (15.0 − 1.2 − 3.5) ÷ 15.0 = 10.3 ÷ 15.0 = 68.7%. The toughest test, and the one closest to cash reality year to year.

The trap to avoid: quoting the flattering ratio and benchmarking it against the tough one. "90% cash conversion" from a seller usually means EBITDA-minus-maintenance-capex in a year when working capital happened to be flat. Always ask: which definition, over which period? — and recompute it yourself from the cash flow statement.

§2.4.5What "good" looks like

Rules of thumb for operating cash conversion (EBITDA − ΔNWC − capex, as a % of EBITDA), averaged over a few years:

Business type Typical conversion Why
Asset-light services / software 85–100%+ Minimal capex, low or negative NWC
Distribution 60–80% Modest capex, but NWC grows with revenue
Manufacturing 55–75% Real capex plus stock and debtors
Capital-intensive (plants, fleets, infra) 30–60% Heavy, lumpy, non-negotiable capex

85%+ is the magic number for asset-light businesses, and it's why PE gravitates to them. The reason is mechanical, and it's worth spelling out. An LBO's returns come substantially from paying down debt out of the company's own cash (Module 7 does the full maths). A £15.0m-EBITDA business converting at 90% generates roughly £13.5m a year before tax and interest to service and repay debt; the same EBITDA converting at 50% generates £7.5m. The first business can safely borrow far more, deleverages faster, and is less likely to hit trouble if trading dips — every one of which improves equity returns. High conversion also validates the EBITDA itself: profit that reliably turns into cash is much harder to fake than profit that doesn't (Lesson 6 picks this thread up).

Contrast Marlow with an asset-light peer, Ashworth Advisory: same £15.0m EBITDA, but ΔNWC of only (0.5) and capex of (0.8). Operating FCF = 15.0 − 0.5 − 0.8 = £13.7m — conversion of 91.3% versus Marlow's 68.7%. If both trade at 8× EBITDA, the buyer of Ashworth is paying 8.8× its operating free cash flow while the buyer of Marlow is paying 11.7×. Same EBITDA multiple, very different cash multiple — which is the sense in which "PE loves asset-light" is not a style preference but arithmetic.

What looks bad: conversion persistently below ~50%, conversion that swings wildly between years (usually working capital games or lumpy under-managed capex), and — worst — conversion declining while EBITDA grows. That last pattern means each incremental pound of profit brings less cash with it, and it's the signature of aggressive revenue recognition or stuffed inventory. Growing EBITDA with falling conversion is one of the highest-yield red flags in all of financial analysis.

§2.4.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show us the EBITDA-to-FCF bridge for the last three years." Not one year — three, because ΔNWC and capex are lumpy and a single year can flatter or slander.
  • "Split capex into maintenance and growth, and reconcile to depreciation." With the register, not just management's labels. Expect the maintenance number to be argued over in every deal you'll ever see.
  • "Why did conversion dip in FY24?" There's usually a story — a stock build, a big debtor, a capex project — and whether it's one-off or structural changes the model.
  • "What's normalised capex through the cycle?" The number that goes into the model is a through-cycle estimate, not last year's (possibly starved) actual.

Habit to build: whenever someone shows you an EBITDA number, mentally append "…of which how much is cash?" Lessons 3 and 4 give you the two big leakages — working capital and capex. The next lesson takes the output of this bridge and asks the lender's question: how much debt can this cash flow support?

Lesson 2.5/Financial Statement Analysis

Leverage and Coverage Ratios

22 min readPrimer
In brief

Net debt/EBITDA, interest cover and fixed charge cover with worked examples, a table of normal versus stretched leverage by context, and the intuition for how much debt a given cash flow profile can support.

  1. 2.5.1Why leverage ratios exist
  2. 2.5.2Net debt / EBITDA: the headline leverage ratio
  3. 2.5.3What's normal vs stretched: context is everything
  4. 2.5.4Interest cover: can the P&L afford the debt?
  5. 2.5.5Fixed charge cover: the fuller test
  6. 2.5.6Debt capacity: the intuition
  7. 2.5.7What deal teams actually ask

§2.5.1Why leverage ratios exist

Debt is central to private equity — it's the "leveraged" in leveraged buyout — so you need a compact way to answer two questions about any company: how much debt is it carrying relative to its size? and can it comfortably afford the payments? The first is a leverage ratio; the second is a coverage ratio. Between them they determine whether a balance sheet is conservative, efficient, or an accident waiting for a downturn.

Our worked company throughout: Whitmore Group, with EBITDA of £15.0m, gross debt of £65.0m, and cash of £5.0m.

§2.5.2Net debt / EBITDA: the headline leverage ratio

Leverage=Net debtEBITDA,Net debt=Gross debt−Cash\text{Leverage} = \frac{\text{Net debt}}{\text{EBITDA}}, \qquad \text{Net debt} = \text{Gross debt} - \text{Cash}Leverage=EBITDANet debt​,Net debt=Gross debt−Cash

Whitmore: net debt = 65.0 − 5.0 = £60.0m, so leverage = 60.0 ÷ 15.0 = 4.0×. Read as "four turns of EBITDA": if every pound of EBITDA went to repayment (it can't — tax, capex and working capital take their cut first, as Lesson 4 showed), it would take four years to clear the debt.

Two definitional traps that deal teams check before quoting the ratio:

  • What counts as debt? Bank loans and bonds obviously; but lease liabilities, unpaid earn-outs from past acquisitions, pension deficits and stretched-beyond-terms supplier balances are all debt-like claims. Buyers and lenders typically add these; sellers typically don't. The gap can be a full turn of EBITDA. (These "debt-like items" return with a vengeance in the equity bridge in Module 4.)
  • Which EBITDA? Reported, adjusted, run-rate, or "pro-forma with synergies"? Leverage quoted on an optimistic EBITDA understates risk by construction — a big part of why Lesson 6's quality-of-earnings toolkit matters. Leverage of 4.0× on trustworthy EBITDA and 4.0× on flattered EBITDA are entirely different risks wearing the same number.

§2.5.3What's normal vs stretched: context is everything

There is no universally "safe" leverage number — it depends on how stable and cash-generative the EBITDA is. Typical ranges:

Context Normal Stretched
Investment-grade listed corporate 1.0–2.5× above 3.0×
Cyclical / project-based business 1.5–2.5× above 3.5×
Mid-market LBO 3.5–4.5× above 5.0×
Large-cap LBO, stable sector 4.5–6.0× above 6.5×
Software / contracted recurring revenue 6.0–7.0× above 7.5×

The pattern behind the table: leverage capacity tracks EBITDA stability and cash conversion. A software business with 95% recurring revenue and 90% cash conversion can carry 6.5× because its EBITDA barely moves and mostly turns into cash. A housebuilder at the same leverage would be reckless: its EBITDA can halve in a downturn, at which point 6.5× becomes 13× overnight. Note that the "same" company can sit in different rows at different times — leverage taken on at the cycle peak is the classic way LBOs die.

Whitmore at 4.0× is normal for a mid-market buyout of a decent business, aggressive for a cyclical, and conservative for contracted software. Placement, again, not the raw number.

§2.5.4Interest cover: can the P&L afford the debt?

Interest cover=EBITDACash interest\text{Interest cover} = \frac{\text{EBITDA}}{\text{Cash interest}}Interest cover=Cash interestEBITDA​

Whitmore pays roughly 8% on its £65.0m gross debt: cash interest ≈ £5.2m. Cover = 15.0 ÷ 5.2 = 2.9×. Rules of thumb: above 3× is comfortable, 2–3× is tight (normal in fresh LBOs, which start tight by design and improve as debt amortises), below 2× is a flashing light, and below 1.5× means the company is working mostly for its lenders. Some analysts use EBIT instead of EBITDA in the numerator for capital-intensive businesses — harsher and arguably more honest, since depreciation foreshadows compulsory capex.

Notice the useful identity linking the two ratios: interest as a share of EBITDA ≈ leverage × interest rate. At 4.0× and 8%, interest eats roughly 4.0 × 8% = 32% of EBITDA before anything else is paid. At 6× and 10% money, that's 60% — which is why leverage appetite falls when rates rise, independent of anyone's risk tolerance.

§2.5.5Fixed charge cover: the fuller test

Interest isn't the only unavoidable payment. Rent behaves exactly like interest — miss it and you lose the premises — and scheduled debt amortisation is contractual too. Fixed charge cover (FCC) widens the lens:

FCC=EBITDA+RentCash interest+Rent\text{FCC} = \frac{\text{EBITDA} + \text{Rent}}{\text{Cash interest} + \text{Rent}}FCC=Cash interest+RentEBITDA+Rent​

(Rent is added back on top because EBITDA is already stated after deducting it; variants also add scheduled amortisation to the denominator.) Suppose Whitmore also pays £2.0m of rent. FCC = (15.0 + 2.0) ÷ (5.2 + 2.0) = 17.0 ÷ 7.2 = 2.4× — meaningfully tighter than the 2.9× interest cover suggested. For rent-heavy businesses — retail, leisure, gyms, restaurants — FCC is the ratio: a retailer can look modestly levered on net debt/EBITDA while an enormous off-balance-sheet-feeling rent roll makes its true fixed charges crushing. Lenders to such businesses covenant on FCC (healthy is roughly 1.5×+; below 1.2× is danger territory) precisely because interest cover flatters them.

§2.5.6Debt capacity: the intuition

Turn the ratios around and you get the question every deal team actually asks: how much debt will this business support? Two ways to triangulate:

Top-down (market convention): debt capacity ≈ sustainable EBITDA × the leverage multiple lenders will offer for this sector and quality. If lenders do 4.0–4.5× for mid-market businesses like Whitmore, capacity is roughly 4.25 × 15.0 ≈ £60–68m. This is how deals are actually sized day-to-day.

Bottom-up (cash flow): debt capacity is whatever the free cash flow can service and repay with headroom. Recall Whitmore-like cash flows from Lesson 4: after working capital, capex and tax, roughly £7.6m of pre-interest free cash flow. At 8% interest, £60.0m of debt costs £4.8m — leaving under £3m a year for repayment, so meaningful deleveraging takes years and depends on EBITDA growth. Push leverage to £75m (5.0×) and interest of £6.0m consumes nearly 80% of free cash flow, with nothing left for bad luck.

The structure of the debt matters too. Amortising debt has a contractual repayment schedule, so the free cash flow must cover interest and the instalments every year; bullet debt repays only at maturity, easing annual cash demands but betting the refinancing on conditions years away. Most LBO structures mix the two, and the more bullet-heavy the stack, the more the deal depends on exit or refinancing markets being open when the music stops.

Then stress it, because lenders will: EBITDA −20% takes Whitmore to £12.0m. Leverage becomes 60.0 ÷ 12.0 = 5.0× and interest cover 12.0 ÷ 5.2 = 2.3× — the same balance sheet now reads "stretched" on the table above. A structure is only sound if it survives the downside case, and the fixed/variable cost analysis from Lesson 2 tells you how bad that downside is: high operating leverage plus high financial leverage is the combination that turns a 10% revenue dip into a covenant breach.

What looks good: leverage in the normal band on conservative EBITDA, cover above 3×, headroom in the downside case, and cash conversion strong enough to deleverage a turn every 18–24 months. What looks bad: leverage justified only by adjusted EBITDA, cover below 2×, FCC ignored in a rent-heavy model, or capacity sized off peak-cycle earnings.

These same ratios live on after the deal closes, as covenants — contractual promises in the loan agreement that leverage will stay below, and cover above, agreed levels, typically tested quarterly. A deal levered at 4.0× might carry a leverage covenant at 5.0×, giving Whitmore about 20% EBITDA headroom before a breach: EBITDA below 60.0 ÷ 5.0 = £12.0m trips the test. Breaching a covenant doesn't usually mean instant insolvency — it means the lenders gain the right to renegotiate, take fees, raise pricing, or in bad cases take the keys. That's why deal teams quote "covenant headroom" as a percentage of EBITDA and treat anything under ~15% as uncomfortable: a structure with thin headroom hands control of the company's bad quarter to its lenders. When you read that a portfolio company "reset its covenants", the ratios in this lesson are exactly what was reset.

§2.5.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's leverage through the cycle?" Net debt against trough EBITDA, not just current. 4.0× on £15.0m is 5.0× if EBITDA reverts to £12.0m.
  • "What's in net debt?" The debt-like items hunt: leases, earn-outs, pension deficits, factored receivables (debt dressed as working capital), and payables stretched beyond terms — the case study in this module plants exactly that one.
  • "What does the downside case do to covenants?" Model EBITDA −15–20% and check leverage and cover against the covenant levels; the gap is "headroom" and ICs want it quantified.
  • "How fast does it deleverage?" Free cash flow after interest ÷ net debt gives a crude annual deleveraging rate; Whitmore's ~£3m on £60.0m (~5% a year) means the deal's returns must lean on EBITDA growth instead — a genuinely different investment thesis.

You now have the full statement-analysis chain: what the P&L says (Lessons 1–2), what cash it really produces (Lessons 3–4), and what obligations sit against it (this lesson). The last step is the sceptic's question underneath all of it: can you trust the EBITDA in the first place? That's Lesson 6.

Lesson 2.6/Financial Statement Analysis

First Look at Quality of Earnings

25 min readPrimer
In brief

What makes reported EBITDA trustworthy or not: run-rate versus reported, one-off adjustments, customer concentration, related-party items, and the recurring / re-occurring / one-time revenue quality hierarchy.

  1. 2.6.1The question underneath every deal
  2. 2.6.2Run-rate vs reported: which year are you actually buying?
  3. 2.6.3One-offs: the adjusted EBITDA bridge
  4. 2.6.4Customer concentration: earnings held hostage
  5. 2.6.5Related-party items: transactions that aren't at arm's length
  6. 2.6.6Revenue quality: recurring, re-occurring, one-time
  7. 2.6.7The trustworthiness checklist

§2.6.1The question underneath every deal

Everything in this module so far — margins, conversion, leverage — takes the reported numbers as inputs. This lesson asks the prior question: should you believe them? In deal-speak this is quality of earnings (QoE): how well reported EBITDA represents the true, sustainable, cash-backed earning power of the business.

The stakes are mechanical. Deals price at a multiple of EBITDA. At 8×, every £1m of overstated EBITDA is £8m of overpayment — and because the debt was sized off the same number, the overpaid deal is also over-levered. Full QoE work is a specialist workstream you'll meet in Module 9; this lesson gives you the first-pass toolkit, which catches a surprising fraction of the problems.

The mindset: reported EBITDA is a claim, made by a seller with every incentive to maximise it, in the one year when it matters most. Your job is to work out what the number would be if it were computed the way a sceptical owner would compute it for themselves.

§2.6.2Run-rate vs reported: which year are you actually buying?

Reported EBITDA describes the last twelve months. But a buyer owns the next twelve, so the number that matters is run-rate EBITDA: what the business earns on a going-forward basis, given everything already known to have changed.

Run-rate adjustments cut both ways:

  • Upwards ("annualisation"): a price rise implemented in month 7 only benefited half the year; a full year of it adds the missing half. A signed new contract starting next quarter isn't in reported numbers at all. Cost savings already actioned (a closed office, completed redundancies) get a full-year credit.
  • Downwards: a customer that gave notice mid-year still contributed months of profit to the reported figure but will contribute nothing next year. A rent review, a lapsed subsidy, an input-cost rise locked in for next year — all reduce run-rate.

Sellers, unsurprisingly, present every upward annualisation and forget the downward ones. The discipline is simple: for every adjustment, ask would this survive being computed in both directions by the same rule? If mid-year price rises get annualised, so do mid-year customer losses.

§2.6.3One-offs: the adjusted EBITDA bridge

Between reported and run-rate sits the land of "adjustments" — items management argues are one-off, non-recurring, or non-operational. A worked example. Hollins Media reports EBITDA of £10.0m and presents this bridge:

£m Legitimate?
Reported EBITDA 10.0
Add back: legal settlement paid +0.6 Probably — if genuinely isolated
Add back: owner's excess salary +0.4 Yes — if a market-rate MD costs £0.4m less
Annualise: mid-year price rise +0.5 Yes — if churn didn't follow it
Deduct: customer lost in September (0.8) Required — sellers rarely volunteer it
Deduct: below-market related-party rent (0.3) Required — see next section
Adjusted run-rate EBITDA 10.4

Note the shape: the seller's own version of this bridge would likely have shown £11.5m (reported plus all the add-backs, minus none of the deductions). The honest number is £10.4m — and at 8×, that gap is £8.8m of price.

Tests for whether an add-back deserves to live:

  • Frequency: "one-off" restructuring costs appearing three years running are just costs. Sum the exceptionals over five years; if the total is large and steady, the business simply has a lower margin than claimed.
  • Direction: does the pack contain only favourable one-offs? Genuine one-offs are random; a list where every item increases EBITDA has been curated. A one-off gain (property disposal, insurance recovery, provision release) sitting quietly inside EBITDA is the mirror image, and must come out.
  • Cash: was it actually paid/received, and does the cash flow statement agree?
  • Evidence: each material add-back should trace to invoices or contracts, not to a spreadsheet cell labelled "normalisation".

§2.6.4Customer concentration: earnings held hostage

EBITDA of £10m means something different when one customer generates £4m of it. Customer concentration is a quality issue, not just a risk footnote, because concentrated earnings are (a) fragile — one procurement decision away from disappearing — and (b) low-bargaining-power — the big customer eventually learns to price accordingly.

First-pass checks, all doable from a data pack:

  • Revenue share of the top 1, 5 and 10 customers, over three years. Rules of thumb: top customer above ~15% of revenue needs explaining; above 25–30% it dominates the deal conversation and usually the price. (Watch for the sneaky version: five "different" customers that are all subsidiaries of one group.)
  • Profit concentration, which is usually worse than revenue concentration: big customers negotiate hard, but they also absorb fixed costs. If the top customer is 30% of revenue at thin margins, losing it doesn't remove 30% of overheads — contribution maths (Lesson 2) says EBITDA can fall by far more than the customer's "share" of it.
  • Contract cover: is the relationship contracted, for how long, with what notice and termination-for-convenience terms? Revenue with a 90-day notice clause is barely more secure than uncontracted revenue.
  • Trajectory: a top customer growing its share flatters growth while quietly concentrating risk — growth quality and revenue quality can move in opposite directions.

§2.6.5Related-party items: transactions that aren't at arm's length

Private companies tangle with their owners: the founder owns the warehouse and charges the company rent; a sibling's firm supplies logistics; family members are on the payroll. None of this is necessarily improper — but it means reported costs aren't market costs, and the buyer's future costs will be.

The adjustment logic is always the same: restate the P&L as if every related-party transaction happened at market rates. In the Hollins bridge above, the company pays the owner's property company £0.2m rent for premises that would cost £0.5m on the open market — so run-rate EBITDA loses £0.3m, because the buyer will pay market rent from day one. Below-market owner salaries work the same way (the £0.4m add-back only stands if a market CEO genuinely costs less than the departing owner). Also look for: sales to related parties (are they real, at real prices, actually paid?), assets used but not owned, and services provided free by a parent (group IT, insurance, treasury) that a standalone buyer must replace — a big theme in corporate carve-outs.

Red flag hierarchy: disclosed and quantified related-party items are a pricing question; undisclosed ones found by accident are an integrity question, and integrity questions kill deals.

§2.6.6Revenue quality: recurring, re-occurring, one-time

Not all revenue is equal, and the standard taxonomy has three tiers:

  • Recurring: contractually committed and automatically continuing — subscriptions, maintenance contracts, rent. The customer must act to stop it. Highest quality; supports the highest multiples and the most debt.
  • Re-occurring: repeats reliably in practice but without contractual commitment — the plumber's merchant a builder uses every week, annual audit work, refill purchases. The customer must act to continue it, but habitually does. Good quality, but the evidence is behavioural (retention and repeat-purchase data), not contractual.
  • One-time: projects, installations, one-off sales. Every year starts from zero. Lowest quality — the revenue may recur, but the customer relationship has to be re-won each time.

Worked example: two consultancies each report £20.0m revenue and £4.0m EBITDA. Alpha's revenue is 70% multi-year retainers, 20% repeat clients, 10% one-off projects. Beta's is 10% / 30% / 60%. Alpha enters next year with ~£14m contractually in the bag; Beta with £2m. Same P&L, radically different risk — Alpha might trade at 10× and Beta at 6×, and the gap is pure revenue quality. Deal packs know this, so treat labels sceptically: "recurring revenue" claims should be tested against contracts and churn — genuinely recurring revenue comes with a measurable retention rate, and if management can't produce one, the revenue is re-occurring at best.

§2.6.7The trustworthiness checklist

Pulling the module together — reported EBITDA deserves trust when:

  1. It converts to cash at a rate that makes sense for the sector (Lesson 4). Profit that never becomes cash is the master red flag; most manipulations (early revenue recognition, under-accrual, capitalised costs) leave profit up but cash behind.
  2. The margin is explicable — within sector norms, or above them for a nameable reason, with a margin bridge that adds up (Lessons 1–2).
  3. Adjustments are few, evidenced, and two-directional. A one-page bridge with items in both directions reads honest; three pages of favourable add-backs reads like a negotiating position.
  4. Accounting policies are stable. Changes to capitalisation, revenue recognition, depreciation or provisioning in the run-up to a sale are guilty until proven innocent — this module's case study turns on exactly this.
  5. Working capital behaves — days stable, accruals growing with the business, no year-end payables stretch manufacturing fake cash flow (Lesson 3).
  6. Earnings aren't hostage to one customer, one contract, one subsidy, or one related party.

The reflex to build: whenever you see "Adjusted EBITDA", reach for three numbers — reported EBITDA, cash generated, and your own run-rate estimate — and make the pack reconcile them. In the case study that follows, you'll do precisely that for a distributor whose margins improved suspiciously well in the year before its sale.

Lesson 3.1/Business Models & Unit Economics

How Businesses Make Money — Revenue Models

22 min readPrimer
In brief

The six revenue models you will meet in deal work — transactional, subscription, usage, licensing, marketplace, and distribution — what each one's P&L looks like, and why the revenue model, not the revenue number, drives the valuation multiple.

  1. 3.1.1Why the revenue model matters more than the revenue number
  2. 3.1.2Transactional revenue: sell it once, sell it again
  3. 3.1.3Recurring / subscription revenue: sell it once, get paid forever
  4. 3.1.4Usage-based revenue: the meter is running
  5. 3.1.5Licensing revenue: selling permission
  6. 3.1.6Marketplace / take-rate revenue: clipping the ticket
  7. 3.1.7Distribution / resale revenue: buy at 100, sell at 118
  8. 3.1.8Why the revenue model drives the valuation multiple

§3.1.1Why the revenue model matters more than the revenue number

Two companies each report £20m of revenue and £5m of EBITDA. One might sell for £30m, the other for £90m. The difference is almost never accounting — it is the revenue model: how the money arrives, how predictable it is, and how much of it comes back next year without anyone lifting a phone.

When a deal team opens a CIM, one of the first questions is "how does this business actually make money?" Not the sector, not the product — the mechanics. Does a customer pay once or forever? Does revenue arrive in £5 increments a million times, or in £2m increments ten times? Does the company own the customer relationship or just clip a fee as money passes through?

This lesson walks through the six models you will meet constantly. For each: how it works, a realistic example, what the P&L looks like, and how buyers think about it. Learn to classify a business within the first five pages of a CIM — everything else in this module builds on it.

§3.1.2Transactional revenue: sell it once, sell it again

The oldest model: a customer pays for a discrete product or service, and the relationship ends until they choose to come back. A kitchen fitter, a corporate law firm billing by the matter, an M&A boutique, a retailer selling sofas.

Example. Hartwell Kitchens sells fitted kitchens at £12,000 average order value. Last year: 1,500 orders, £18m revenue. Materials and installation labour cost £10.8m (60%), so gross profit is £7.2m (40%). Marketing, showrooms and overheads eat £5.4m, leaving £1.8m EBITDA — a 10% margin.

The P&L shape: revenue resets to zero on 1 January. Every year Hartwell must find 1,500 new buyers, and a kitchen is a once-a-decade purchase, so repeat business is minimal. Marketing spend is high and permanent — it is the engine, not an investment that compounds.

What deal teams ask: what fraction of revenue is repeat or referral? Is there an order book giving even 3–6 months of visibility? How did revenue behave in the last downturn? Transactional businesses can be excellent — high ROCE, cash-generative, capex-light — but buyers price the uncertainty. Typical multiples sit well below recurring-revenue peers: often 4–7x EBITDA where a comparable recurring business gets 10–15x.

§3.1.3Recurring / subscription revenue: sell it once, get paid forever

The customer signs up and pays a fixed amount per period — monthly or annually — until they cancel. Software-as-a-service is the canonical case, but the model is everywhere: alarm monitoring, testing and certification contracts, gym memberships, managed IT services.

Example. Brindle HR sells payroll software at £500 per client per month. With 3,000 clients that is £1.5m MRR, or £18m ARR. Hosting and support cost £3.6m (80% gross margin). Sales and marketing run at £5.4m, R&D £3.6m, G&A £1.8m — EBITDA £3.6m, a 20% margin.

The P&L shape: next year's revenue is mostly already sold. If Brindle retains 92% of clients, it starts the year with £16.6m of the £18m banked before the sales team makes a single call. Costs split into serving existing customers (cheap) and acquiring new ones (discretionary). That split is why subscription businesses can dial profitability up or down at will — cut new-customer spend and EBITDA jumps, at the cost of growth.

What looks good: retention above 90%, contracts with auto-renewal, revenue billed annually in advance (which also means customers fund working capital — deferred revenue is a liability that never has to be repaid in cash). What looks bad: "recurring" revenue that is really re-occurring — repeat but uncontracted. Deal teams always test the definition. Lesson 3 goes deep here.

§3.1.4Usage-based revenue: the meter is running

The customer pays per unit consumed: per API call, per kWh, per parcel shipped, per test processed. Cloud infrastructure, payment processors charging per transaction, and lab-testing businesses all run meters.

Example. Ferrocourier charges e-commerce sellers £2.50 per parcel. A seller shipping 4,000 parcels a month generates £10,000; one shipping 400 generates £1,000. Revenue is the sum of thousands of meters, each tied to the customer's activity.

The P&L shape: revenue is repeatable but variable — it grows automatically when customers grow (a free tailwind no salesperson earned) and shrinks automatically in a downturn. Gross margin depends on how much marginal cost each unit carries: near-100% for an API call, maybe 25% for a parcel with a driver behind it.

What deal teams ask: is usage tied to customers' revenue (resilient — payments volume) or to their discretionary spend (fragile — ad impressions)? What are minimum-commitment floors? A usage business with contracted minimums covering 70% of revenue prices closer to subscription; one with no floors prices closer to transactional. The honest classification is usually "hybrid", and the diligence job is to size each layer.

§3.1.5Licensing revenue: selling permission

The company owns intellectual property — software, a brand, a patented process, content — and sells the right to use it. Two flavours matter:

  • Perpetual licence: a one-off fee for indefinite use, usually with a separate annual maintenance contract at 15–22% of the licence price. Old-school enterprise software.
  • Royalty / term licence: an ongoing fee, often a percentage of the licensee's sales. Think of a character brand licensed to a toymaker at a 10% royalty.

Example. Calderbrook Systems sells factory-scheduling software: £400k perpetual licences plus 20% annual maintenance (£80k per customer per year). In a good year it closes 25 licence deals (£10m) on top of a £6m maintenance base from past sales: £16m revenue, and because the marginal cost of a licence is near zero, EBITDA margin hits 35%.

The P&L shape: gross margin is spectacular, but the licence line is lumpy. Slip three deals from December into January and the year's revenue drops £1.2m with no warning. The maintenance base is the genuinely valuable part — it behaves like subscription revenue. Buyers routinely split a licensing P&L in two: maintenance priced like recurring revenue, new-licence revenue priced like transactional revenue. The Module 3 case study turns exactly on this split.

§3.1.6Marketplace / take-rate revenue: clipping the ticket

The company operates a platform matching buyers and sellers and keeps a percentage — the take rate — of each transaction. Property portals, freelance platforms, food-delivery apps, ticket exchanges.

The key distinction is GMV versus revenue. Gross merchandise value is everything transacted on the platform; revenue is only the slice the platform keeps. A marketplace boasting "£500m of transactions" at a 6% take rate is a £30m-revenue business. CIMs love to headline GMV; deal teams immediately convert to revenue.

Example. TradeYard connects builders with reclaimed-materials sellers: £200m GMV at a 7.5% take rate is £15m revenue. Payment processing and support cost £3m (80% gross margin); marketing to keep both sides liquid costs £7m; EBITDA is £2m.

The P&L shape: tiny marginal cost per transaction, so contribution margins are superb at scale — but scale is everything. A subscale marketplace burns cash acquiring both sides at once. And take rates face constant pressure: if the platform adds little value, buyers and sellers meet once and then transact off-platform ("disintermediation"). Deal teams ask: what stops leakage? Is the take rate rising or falling? Does the platform hold the money flow (payments integration is the strongest lock-in)?

§3.1.7Distribution / resale revenue: buy at 100, sell at 118

The company buys products from manufacturers and resells them — adding logistics, availability, credit, range, and technical support. Pharmaceutical wholesalers, electrical distributors, food-service suppliers, IT value-added resellers.

Example. Kembrey Electrical distributes cabling and switchgear to contractors: £120m revenue at an 18% gross margin (£21.6m gross profit). Warehouses, vans and salespeople cost £16.8m; EBITDA is £4.8m — a 4% EBITDA margin on revenue, but a much healthier 22% margin on gross profit.

The P&L shape: huge revenue, thin margins, real working capital. Inventory and receivables soak up cash as the business grows. The revenue line is almost meaningless for comparison — a distributor "growing revenue 10%" may just be passing through copper-price inflation. Deal teams analyse distributors on gross profit, treating it as the real top line, and watch two threats: suppliers going direct, and customers consolidating their purchasing.

Not a glamorous model — but predictable demand (much of it repair and maintenance, not projects), fragmented customers, and density economics make good distributors quietly excellent LBO candidates, which is why PE keeps buying them.

§3.1.8Why the revenue model drives the valuation multiple

A multiple is shorthand for a DCF: it embeds growth, risk, and reinvestment needs. The revenue model moves all three, which is why classification is a valuation act, not a taxonomy exercise.

Model Predictability Marginal economics Typical pricing attitude
Subscription Very high — revenue is contracted forward High gross margin Premium; often priced on revenue, not EBITDA
Usage (with floors) High, but cyclical with customers Varies Premium if tied to non-discretionary volumes
Marketplace at scale High Excellent Premium — if take rate and liquidity defensible
Licensing (maintenance base) High on maintenance, low on new licences Excellent Sum-of-parts: base premium, licence line discounted
Distribution Moderate — repeat but uncontracted Thin, working-capital-heavy Modest EBITDA multiple, judged on gross profit
Transactional Low — resets each year Varies Discounted; buyers cap what they'll pay for hope

Same arithmetic from the buyer's chair: with £5m EBITDA that is 90% pre-sold via contracts, next year's downside is narrow, a lender will happily lend 4–5x against it, and the exit buyer in five years will pay up for the same predictability. With £5m EBITDA that must be re-won from scratch every January, one bad year can halve it, lenders cap leverage at 2–3x, and the exit is harder. Less debt, more risk, worse exit — every driver of the LBO return is weaker, so the entry multiple must be lower to compensate.

Practical takeaways for deal work:

  • Classify before you value. "£20m revenue software company" is meaningless until you know the recurring/licence/services split.
  • Reported revenue is not homogeneous. Split every target's revenue into layers by model and quality; value the layers, not the total.
  • Beware relabelling. Sellers know recurring revenue prices higher, so CIMs stretch the definition. "Recurring and repeat revenue: 78%" is a phrase designed to blur contracted subscriptions with habitual re-ordering. Diligence separates them — and the price moves when it does.

Lesson 3.2/Business Models & Unit Economics

Unit Economics — Contribution Margin, CAC and LTV

25 min readPrimer
In brief

How to judge a business one unit at a time: contribution margin, customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, and payback periods — with a full worked SaaS example, cohort thinking, and the situations where unit economics actively mislead.

  1. 3.2.1Why deal teams think in units
  2. 3.2.2Contribution margin: the first cut
  3. 3.2.3CAC: what a customer costs to acquire
  4. 3.2.4LTV: what a customer is worth
  5. 3.2.5Full worked example: Brindle HR
  6. 3.2.6Payback period: the cash-flow lens
  7. 3.2.7Cohort thinking: the honest view
  8. 3.2.8When unit economics mislead

§3.2.1Why deal teams think in units

A P&L tells you what happened to the whole company last year. Unit economics answer a sharper question: does the business make money on each incremental customer, and how fast? If the answer is yes, growth creates value and losses today may be investment. If the answer is no, growth destroys value and the losses are just losses — "we lose money on every unit but make it up on volume" is the oldest joke in finance because people keep doing it.

The "unit" depends on the model: a customer (SaaS), an order (e-commerce), a site (gyms, dental practices), a vehicle (logistics), a project (consulting). Pick the unit that decisions are actually made at. For most of this lesson the unit is a customer, because that is where PE spends its time.

§3.2.2Contribution margin: the first cut

Contribution margin = revenue per unit − variable costs per unit. It is what each unit contributes towards fixed costs and profit. The discipline is deciding what is truly variable: costs that scale one-for-one with the unit (materials, payment fees, delivery, per-seat hosting), not allocated overhead.

Worked example — an e-commerce order:

Per order £
Average order value 80.00
Product cost (36.00)
Packaging and delivery (8.00)
Payment fees and returns provision (4.00)
Contribution before marketing 32.00 (40%)
Marketing cost per order (18.00)
Contribution after marketing 14.00 (17.5%)

Two readings of the same business. At £32 contribution before marketing, every order helps cover the £2m of fixed costs. But if £18 of paid advertising is needed to cause each order, the real per-order economics are £14 — and if a rising share of orders needs paid traffic, the business is weaker than its gross margin suggests. Deal teams always compute both lines and ask which orders come "free" (repeat customers, organic search) versus bought.

Contribution margin also sets the operating leverage story: high-contribution businesses (software at 80%+) convert incremental revenue to profit rapidly once fixed costs are covered; low-contribution businesses (distribution at 18%) need volume and cost discipline forever.

§3.2.3CAC: what a customer costs to acquire

Customer acquisition cost = total sales & marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired in the period. Use fully loaded S&M — salaries, commissions, ad spend, events, sales tooling — not just the ad budget. Sellers quote CAC on ad spend alone; diligence rebuilds it fully loaded, and the number often doubles.

Two subtleties that matter in practice:

  • New customers only. Marketing that serves existing customers (retention campaigns, account management) belongs in the cost of retention, not CAC. Most companies can't split it cleanly; make a reasonable allocation and state it.
  • Time lag. This quarter's spend produces next quarter's customers in long-sales-cycle B2B. For a business with a 6-month cycle, divide this period's new customers into prior period S&M, or CAC looks artificially good during a slowdown (spend falls first, signings later).

§3.2.4LTV: what a customer is worth

Lifetime value = the contribution a customer generates over their whole life. For a subscription business with steady churn, the workhorse formula:

LTV=ARPU×gross marginchurn rate\text{LTV} = \frac{\text{ARPU} \times \text{gross margin}}{\text{churn rate}}LTV=churn rateARPU×gross margin​

with ARPU and churn measured over the same period (both monthly or both annual). The logic: average customer lifetime = 1/churn. At 2% monthly churn, expected lifetime is 50 months.

Note the gross margin term. LTV on revenue flatters every business; only gross profit can repay acquisition cost. And strictly, future contribution should be discounted — at a 50-month lifetime, undiscounted LTV overstates value meaningfully. Simple LTV is a screening tool, not a valuation.

§3.2.5Full worked example: Brindle HR

Take the payroll-software business from Lesson 1 and run its unit economics end to end.

Input (per customer, monthly) Value
Subscription price (ARPU) £500
Gross margin 80%
Monthly gross churn 1.5%
Fully loaded S&M last year £5.4m
New customers acquired 450

Step 1 — CAC. £5,400,000 ÷ 450 = £12,000 per customer.

Step 2 — monthly contribution. £500 × 80% = £400 per month.

Step 3 — expected lifetime. 1 ÷ 1.5% = 66.7 months (about 5.6 years).

Step 4 — LTV. £400 × 66.7 = £26,700 (equivalently £500 × 0.80 ÷ 0.015).

Step 5 — LTV/CAC. £26,700 ÷ £12,000 = 2.2x.

Step 6 — CAC payback. £12,000 ÷ £400 = 30 months to recover acquisition cost from gross profit.

Now the judgement, which is the whole point:

  • LTV/CAC of 2.2x is thin. The folk benchmark for a healthy SaaS business is 3x+; below ~1.5x, growth is value-destructive once you discount and add doubt to the churn estimate. Brindle creates some value per customer, but not much cushion.
  • 30-month payback is slow. Good B2B SaaS pays back in 12–18 months. At 30 months, every new customer is a 2.5-year loan the company makes to itself — growth consumes cash, and if churn ticks up from 1.5% to 2.5%, lifetime drops to 40 months, LTV falls to £16,000 and the ratio to 1.3x. The model is fragile to a one-point churn move.
  • What would fix it: raise price (ARPU £600 at the same churn → LTV £32,000, payback 25 months), cut CAC (more inbound, channel partners), or reduce churn (see Lesson 3 — by far the highest-leverage lever, because churn sits in the denominator).

A deal team seeing these numbers doesn't walk away — it reprices the growth story. The CIM's "double the sales team and double growth" plan only works if the unit economics deserve the fuel.

§3.2.6Payback period: the cash-flow lens

LTV/CAC compresses everything into one ratio, but it leans on the churn estimate — the softest number in the room. CAC payback = CAC ÷ monthly gross-profit contribution needs no lifetime assumption at all, which is why many investors trust it more:

  • Under 12 months: excellent. The business can grow fast on its own cash flow.
  • 12–24 months: normal for B2B; growth needs funding but the maths works.
  • Over 24 months: growth is expensive; the company is betting heavily on retention, and the balance sheet must carry the bet.

Payback also frames the classic PE conversation with a loss-making but healthy SaaS company: losses equal to this year's S&M spend are a choice. If payback is 14 months and retention is strong, cutting growth spend would reveal a profitable core — which is exactly the value-creation case some software deals are built on.

§3.2.7Cohort thinking: the honest view

Blended averages hide everything interesting. A cohort is the set of customers acquired in the same period, tracked over time. Cohort tables answer the questions averages dodge: do customers actually stay as long as the churn rate implies? Do they spend more or less over time? Are recent vintages better or worse than old ones?

Example — annual revenue retained per cohort (each row indexed to 100 at acquisition):

Cohort Yr 0 Yr 1 Yr 2 Yr 3
2022 100 88 82 79
2023 100 84 76 —
2024 100 78 — —

Blended churn might still look stable, because a growing base of young customers masks decay. But read down the Yr 1 column: 88 → 84 → 78. Each vintage is worse than the last — perhaps the company has exhausted its best-fit market and newer customers are poorer matches. This is one of the most valuable patterns diligence can find, because it says the future unit economics are worse than the historic ones the CIM is selling. The reverse pattern (improving vintages) is a genuine buy signal.

Deal teams ask for cohort data in every subscription diligence. A seller who "can't produce it" either has weak systems (an operational finding) or unflattering cohorts (a pricing finding). Either way, you learned something.

§3.2.8When unit economics mislead

Unit economics are a lens, not the truth. The classic failure modes:

1. Average masks mix. A blended LTV/CAC of 3x can be one segment at 8x and another at 0.5x. If the growth plan pours money into the second segment, the blended history is irrelevant. Always segment — by size, channel, product, geography — before trusting a ratio.

2. The churn assumption does the work. LTV divides by churn, so small errors explode: moving assumed monthly churn from 1.5% to 1.0% inflates LTV by 50% with one keystroke. Young companies have little churn history, and CIM LTVs routinely assume best-ever retention persists for a decade. Prefer payback, which assumes nothing.

3. Marginal versus average CAC. The first customers came cheap — founders' networks, early adopters, free press. The next 1,000 cost more, because channels saturate and each new audience converts worse. Historic CAC understates the CAC embedded in the growth plan; look at the trend by quarter, not the average.

4. Fixed costs exist. Contribution-positive units can still add up to a loss-making company if the fixed base is too big for realistic volume. Unit economics say whether growth is worth buying; they say nothing about whether the overhead is affordable. A business "profitable on a unit basis" for ten straight years is running a scale it cannot support.

5. Units that aren't repeatable. In lumpy project businesses, "average project margin" is not a unit economic — projects are heterogeneous, and one bad fixed-price contract can wipe out twenty good ones. Unit economics need many similar units to mean anything.

6. Bought loyalty. Discounts, free months and paid incentives make acquisition-period cohorts look sticky while they're being paid to stay. Check what retention looks like after promotional pricing rolls off — that step-down is where the truth lives.

The deal-team habit: compute the units, then attack your own computation with these six questions. What survives is usually the real investment case.
