Lesson 3.3/Business Models & Unit Economics

Recurring Revenue and Retention

25 min readPrimer
In brief

ARR and MRR properly defined, gross versus net revenue retention with a worked cohort table, why small monthly churn numbers compound into catastrophe, what actually makes revenue sticky, and how PE prices recurring versus transactional revenue.

  1. 3.3.1ARR and MRR: the vocabulary, precisely
  2. 3.3.2Gross versus net revenue retention
  3. 3.3.3Churn maths: why 2% monthly churn is catastrophic
  4. 3.3.4What actually makes revenue sticky
  5. 3.3.5How PE prices recurring versus transactional revenue

§3.3.1ARR and MRR: the vocabulary, precisely

MRR (monthly recurring revenue) is the sum of all contracted, subscription revenue normalised to a monthly figure. ARR (annual recurring revenue) is MRR × 12, or the sum of annual contract values. Both are run-rate snapshots — "if nothing changed, what would we bill over the next year?" — not accounting revenue. A company can have £12m ARR on 31 December but only £10.5m of recognised subscription revenue for the year, because ARR was added along the way and only earned for part of it.

What belongs in ARR: contracted subscription fees, committed minimums on usage contracts, maintenance contracts with renewal terms. What does not: one-off implementation fees, overage billing above committed minimums, "customers who always come back" without a contract, and non-refundable but one-time licence sales. Sellers stretch this constantly. The single most common diligence adjustment in software deals is redefining ARR downwards — stripping out re-occurring services and uncommitted usage — and the price adjusts with it, because buyers pay recurring-revenue multiples only for revenue that is genuinely contracted to recur.

Related vocabulary you will meet: bookings (new contract value signed in a period), billings (what was invoiced), and recognised revenue (what accounting rules let you count). They differ by timing; bridging them is a standard QoE exercise.

§3.3.2Gross versus net revenue retention

Take all customers who existed at the start of the period and ask what their revenue looks like one year later. Two answers:

  • Gross revenue retention (GRR) counts only losses — cancellations and downgrades. It can never exceed 100%. GRR isolates the question: how leaky is the bucket?
  • Net revenue retention (NRR) adds back expansion — upsells, price rises, seat growth — from those same customers. It can exceed 100%. NRR asks: does the existing book grow on its own?

Crucially, both metrics exclude new customers. That is the point: they measure the quality of the installed base, uncontaminated by sales effort.

Worked cohort table — one customer book over FY25 (£000, ARR):

Movement in the FY24 customer base £000
Opening ARR (1 Jan) 10,000
Churned customers (full losses) (700)
Downgrades (kept customers, smaller contracts) (300)
Retained ARR 9,000
Upsell and cross-sell to retained customers 900
Price increases on renewal 300
Closing ARR from the opening cohort 10,200
GRR=10,000−700−30010,000=90%NRR=10,20010,000=102%\text{GRR} = \frac{10{,}000 - 700 - 300}{10{,}000} = 90\% \qquad \text{NRR} = \frac{10{,}200}{10{,}000} = 102\%GRR=10,00010,000−700−300​=90%NRR=10,00010,200​=102%

If the company also signed £1.3m of new-logo ARR, total closing ARR is £11.5m — but that £1.3m appears in neither retention metric.

Reading the pair together is the skill:

  • NRR 102% / GRR 90% (this table): the base grows, but by patching a real leak with expansion. Ask whether expansion can outrun churn forever.
  • NRR 115% / GRR 95%: elite. Growth is nearly free; the sales team is a bonus.
  • NRR 105% / GRR 78%: a red flag dressed as a green one. A third of customers leave within eighteen months while a few whales expand hard. Concentration risk is building inside a healthy-looking NRR — always ask how much of the expansion comes from the top five accounts.
  • NRR 88% / GRR 85%: the bucket leaks and nobody upgrades. The company must sprint (new sales) just to stand still.

What deal teams actually ask for: the GRR/NRR calculation by cohort and by segment, the definition used (logo vs revenue, annualised vs monthly), and whether price rises are doing all the NRR work — pricing-led NRR is real money but tests customer goodwill and can't repeat forever.

§3.3.3Churn maths: why 2% monthly churn is catastrophic

Small monthly percentages hide brutal compounding. Monthly churn ccc gives annual retention (1−c)12(1-c)^{12}(1−c)12:

Monthly churn Annual retention Annual churn Implied avg. customer life
0.5% 94.2% 5.8% 200 months (~17 yrs)
1.0% 88.6% 11.4% 100 months (~8 yrs)
2.0% 78.5% 21.5% 50 months (~4 yrs)
3.0% 69.4% 30.6% 33 months (~3 yrs)
5.0% 54.0% 46.0% 20 months

"Only 2% a month" means losing more than a fifth of the book every year. A £10m-ARR company at 2% monthly churn must sign £2.15m of new ARR annually before growing at all. Over a five-year PE hold, the original book shrinks to 0.7855≈30%0.785^5 \approx 30\%0.7855≈30% of itself — the company you bought has mostly evaporated and been replaced, at full CAC, twice over.

Now the flywheel in reverse. Cut monthly churn from 2% to 1% and average customer life doubles from 50 to 100 months; LTV doubles with it; every pound of CAC buys twice the value; and the new-sales treadmill slows by half. This is why churn reduction is the highest-leverage operating initiative in any subscription portfolio company — worth more than most growth plans, and much cheaper.

One more trap: churn compounds off a growing denominator. Fast-growing companies quote low blended churn because the base is full of new customers who haven't had time to leave yet. Always ask for churn by tenure: if customers churn heavily at month 13 (first renewal), a company that doubled last year hasn't met its own churn rate yet.

§3.3.4What actually makes revenue sticky

Retention is an output. The inputs — stickiness drivers — are what diligence tests, because they predict whether historic retention persists under new ownership and higher prices:

  • Workflow embedment. The product is where work happens daily (payroll, practice management, ERP). Ripping it out means retraining everyone and migrating data. Contrast a reporting tool that one analyst opens monthly.
  • Data gravity. Years of records live in the system and export badly. Switching means losing history or paying for a painful migration.
  • Integration depth. The product is wired into five other systems via APIs. Each integration is a switching cost someone else would have to rebuild.
  • Multi-stakeholder usage. Ten departments use it; no single person can decide to leave. Products with one internal champion die when the champion changes jobs.
  • Mission criticality vs pain of failure. Software running a factory or a payroll cannot be allowed to fail; a 3% price rise is not worth the risk of change. This is why boring, critical software carries 95%+ GRR and premium prices.
  • Contract mechanics. Multi-year terms, auto-renewal, annual advance billing, and contractual price escalators (CPI+2% clauses) all harden revenue — cheap to add, valuable at exit, and a standard 100-day-plan item.

What looks bad: discretionary "nice-to-have" products, single-champion sales, month-to-month terms, heavy discounting at renewal (retention that is being bought), and support tickets trending up (the leading indicator of churn, 6–12 months early).

§3.3.5How PE prices recurring versus transactional revenue

The market pays radically different prices for the same pound of profit depending on how it recurs. Stylised, for a decent mid-market business:

Revenue type Typical pricing lens
Contracted recurring (GRR 90%+) 10–15x EBITDA, or 3–6x+ revenue for growers
Repeat / re-occurring (uncontracted) 7–9x EBITDA
Transactional / project 4–7x EBITDA
One-off licences in a software mix Often valued near 1x revenue — barely more than this year's sales

Why the gap is rational rather than fashion:

  1. Debt capacity. Lenders size leverage off downside cash flow. Contracted revenue supports 4–5x leverage; lumpy revenue maybe 2–3x. More cheap debt mechanically lifts equity IRR, so buyers can pay more and hit the same return.
  2. Downside distribution. A 90%-GRR book has a hard floor; a project book can halve. Equity in a leveraged structure is an option on the downside — narrower downside is worth paying for.
  3. Exit reliability. The next buyer applies the same logic, so the multiple is likelier to hold or expand. Multiple risk is lower even if multiple level were the same.
  4. Compounding without effort. An NRR-105% base grows 5% a year with zero sales cost. Embedded growth is the cheapest growth there is.

Two practical consequences for deal work. First, mixed businesses get sum-of-parts pricing: a £20m-revenue software company with £12m maintenance and £8m licences/services is priced as a premium multiple on the first part and a modest one on the second — which is why sellers fight to reclassify revenue upwards and buyers fight back. Second, mix shift is a value-creation lever in itself: converting licence customers to subscription, adding contracts to handshake relationships, or attaching monitoring contracts to equipment sales can re-rate the whole company at exit even with flat EBITDA. Some buy-and-build theses are essentially "buy transactional multiples, sell recurring multiples".

A quick sanity check you can run on any target in five minutes: take reported "recurring" revenue, multiply by GRR, and compare the result to next year's budgeted revenue from existing customers. If the budget assumes more than ARR×NRR\text{ARR} \times \text{NRR}ARR×NRR from the installed base, someone is planning on retention improving — ask why. If reported recurring revenue at 93% GRR somehow fell 15% last year, the "recurring" label is doing more work than the contracts are. These are thirty-second calculations that regularly reprice deals.

The one-line summary a deal partner would give you: revenue quality is priced, not just revenue quantity — and retention is the single best proxy for quality.

Lesson 3.4/Business Models & Unit Economics

Moats and Competitive Position

24 min readPrimer
In brief

The five moat types — switching costs, network effects, scale economies, brand, and regulatory barriers — how to use Porter's five forces as a practical checklist rather than a diagram, and why fragmented market structures attract buy-and-build strategies.

  1. 3.4.1Why moats are a pricing question
  2. 3.4.2Switching costs: the PE favourite
  3. 3.4.3Network effects, scale economies, brand, regulation
  4. 3.4.4Porter's five forces, used practically
  5. 3.4.5Market structure: fragmented versus consolidated
  6. 3.4.6Why fragmentation attracts buy-and-build

§3.4.1Why moats are a pricing question

A moat is anything that lets a company sustain above-normal returns without competitors eroding them. In public-market investing, moats are about compounding for decades. In PE, the horizon is a 4–6 year hold, so the question is sharper and more practical: will this company's margins and retention survive the hold period, plus long enough for the next buyer to believe in them?

That matters because an LBO price capitalises today's EBITDA at a multiple. If competition can compress margins from 25% to 18% over five years, the buyer overpaid regardless of how good the diligence spreadsheets looked. Every commercial due diligence report is fundamentally a moat assessment wearing a suit.

The test for any claimed moat is always the same: what specifically happens when a competitor cuts price 20% or a customer threatens to leave? If the answer involves real costs, lost data, retraining, regulatory approval, or an inferior alternative, there's a moat. If the answer is "our service is great", there isn't.

§3.4.2Switching costs: the PE favourite

Switching costs make leaving painful even when alternatives are cheaper. They come in flavours:

  • Procedural: retraining staff, migrating data, re-integrating systems. A vet-practice management system touches booking, clinical records, billing and stock — replacing it disrupts the whole practice for months.
  • Financial: unamortised setup fees, lost volume discounts, early-termination clauses.
  • Relational: an account manager who knows the client's quirks; certification of a supplier that took 18 months of audits (common in aerospace and pharma supply chains).
  • Risk-based: the strongest of all. If the current product works and failure is catastrophic (payroll, air-traffic parts, lab accreditation), the risk of switching outweighs any saving. Nobody gets fired for renewing.

Worked micro-example: a customer pays £40k/yr for software; a rival offers £30k. Switching costs: £25k migration, £15k of internal project time, and six months of disruption risk. Payback on switching is 4+ years of savings — so the incumbent keeps the customer and can push a 5% annual price rise. That pricing headroom, discovered in diligence, is a value-creation lever; PE loves switching-cost businesses precisely because modest price increases drop straight through to EBITDA at ~100% margin.

What looks bad: switching costs that cut the other way (the target's suppliers or channel hold the relationship), or low switching costs masked by long contracts — when the contracts roll, the truth arrives.

§3.4.3Network effects, scale economies, brand, regulation

Network effects — the product improves as more people use it. Marketplaces (more buyers attract more sellers), exchanges, social platforms, and data networks (each customer's data improves the product for all). Powerful but rare in mid-market PE, and often local: a freelancer marketplace can dominate one vertical while being irrelevant next door. Diligence question: does liquidity actually concentrate, or do users multi-home across two or three platforms? Multi-homing (drivers on two apps, sellers on three marketplaces) guts the effect.

Scale economies — unit costs fall with volume: purchasing power, route density in distribution, fixed-cost amortisation (one R&D budget over more customers), and data scale. The mid-market version is usually density, not size: a waste collector with 80% of the bins on a street earns structurally more per bin than a rival with 20%, whatever the national market shares say. This is the quiet engine behind many buy-and-build strategies — bolt-ons buy density, and density buys margin.

Brand — a moat only when it changes behaviour: commands a price premium, wins the default choice, or reduces perceived risk ("no one ever got fired for buying…"). In B2B, "brand" is usually better described as reputation and accreditation — a testing house whose certificates customers' own clients demand. Be sceptical of consumer brand moats in diligence: ask for evidence of price premium versus peers and repeat-purchase rates, not awareness surveys. A brand that is only a marketing budget is a cost, not a moat.

Regulatory and licence moats — permits, accreditations, and compliance regimes that take years or are simply no longer granted (landfill permits, certain care licences, aviation approvals). These create hard supply constraints and grandfathered positions. The flip side is regulatory risk: the same state that grants the moat can reprice it — pharmacy reimbursement rates, energy tariffs, and government-funded care fees can move against you in one budget statement. A moat granted by the payer is also a dependency on the payer; diligence treats single-payer exposure as concentration risk.

§3.4.4Porter's five forces, used practically

Porter's framework earns its keep as a checklist of questions about who captures the value in an industry — not a diagram for page 4 of the IC deck. The practical version a deal team runs on every target:

  1. Supplier power — who do they buy from, and could those suppliers squeeze or bypass them? One-brand distributors die when the brand goes direct. Check: supplier concentration, exclusivity terms, how gross margin has trended (drifting down = someone upstream is winning).
  2. Customer power — can buyers squeeze? Check the top-10 customer concentration, whether customers run procurement/tender processes, contract lengths, and realised price increases over five years. A company that hasn't raised prices since 2019 either has no power or unused power — diligence must find out which, because one is a red flag and the other is the upside case.
  3. Rivalry — how do competitors actually behave? Count them, but more importantly ask how they compete: on price (bad — someone is always desperate) or on service, spec and relationships (survivable)? Win/loss data and quote-to-win rates tell you more than market share charts.
  4. New entrants — what does it cost to credibly enter? Capital, accreditation, reference customers, density. If a competent team with £2m could take share in 18 months, margins are on borrowed time. If entry needs 10 years of certifications, sleep well.
  5. Substitutes — not rival vendors, but different ways of solving the problem: in-house teams instead of outsourcing, software instead of services, doing nothing at all. Substitutes are the force CIMs never mention and the one that kills industries rather than companies.

The output that matters is not five scores but one sentence: where does the value settle in this chain, and is the target on the right side of it? A business can grow revenue for a decade while suppliers and customers capture every pound of the growth.

§3.4.5Market structure: fragmented versus consolidated

Beyond firm-level moats, the shape of the market drives PE strategy:

  • Consolidated (top 3 players hold 60%+): stable pricing and fat margins if behaviour is rational, but targets are big, expensive, and often already efficient. The moat question is whether the oligopoly holds.
  • Fragmented (hundreds of local operators, no player above ~5%): dental practices, vet clinics, accountancy firms, HVAC services, testing labs. Individually small and often owner-managed, priced cheaply because small businesses trade at small multiples.

Fragmentation usually persists for a reason — local relationships matter, the service is physical and local, owner-operators accept low returns. The PE insight is that some of those reasons dissolve under shared ownership: back-office, procurement, systems and compliance can centralise even when delivery stays local.

§3.4.6Why fragmentation attracts buy-and-build

Buy-and-build (a "platform" acquisition followed by many "bolt-on" acquisitions) is the single most common mid-market PE playbook, and fragmented markets are its habitat. The value creation stacks four layers:

  1. Multiple arbitrage. Small businesses trade cheaply; big ones dearly. Buy a £3m-EBITDA platform at 7x, buy ten £1m-EBITDA bolt-ons at 4x, and the combined £13m-EBITDA group exits at 9x. The bolt-on EBITDA was bought at 4x and sold at 9x — £5 of value per £1 of EBITDA before any operational improvement at all. Worked numbers: total invested = £21m + 10×£4m = £61m; exit = £13m × 9 = £117m — before synergies, and ignoring leverage, which amplifies it.
  2. Synergies. Central procurement, one finance function, shared systems, cross-selling. Even 1–2 margin points across the group compounds the arbitrage.
  3. Density and scale moats. Each local bolt-on adds route density, purchasing power, and recruiting reach — the group builds the scale moat the fragments never had.
  4. Exit story. A professionalised, systemised group of 30 sites is buyable by a larger fund or trade buyer in a way no individual site ever was. Liquidity itself is manufactured.

What deal teams check before believing a buy-and-build thesis: is there a real pipeline of willing sellers at sane prices (bolt-on multiples inflate quickly once two or three sponsors work the same space)? Does integration actually work here, or does value walk out of the door with the selling owner-operator and their client relationships? And is the platform's own operating model strong enough to absorb ten acquisitions — a mediocre platform plus ten bolt-ons is just a bigger mediocre business with integration debt.

The moat connection closes the loop: the end state of a good buy-and-build is a company with moats — density, brand/accreditation, systems — in a market that used to have none. You are not just buying EBITDA cheaply; you are constructing the competitive position that justifies the exit multiple. When the IC asks "why will the exit buyer pay 9x for what you bought at 4x?", the answer had better be a moat, not a spreadsheet.

moatsfive-forcesbuy-and-buildmarket-structure

Lesson 3.5/Business Models & Unit Economics

Sector Archetypes PE Loves (and Avoids)

25 min readPrimer
In brief

The six sectors that dominate mid-market PE — business services, software, healthcare services, industrials, distribution, and consumer — with typical margins, capex intensity, cyclicality, and key KPIs for each, plus the classic value traps that catch new analysts.

  1. 3.5.1Reading a sector like a deal team
  2. 3.5.2Business services: the workhorse of mid-market PE
  3. 3.5.3Software: the multiple champion
  4. 3.5.4Healthcare services: demographics with a payer problem
  5. 3.5.5Industrials and niche manufacturing: cash flow with a cycle
  6. 3.5.6Distribution: unglamorous, dense, and quietly excellent
  7. 3.5.7Consumer: brands, baskets, and fashion risk
  8. 3.5.8The classic value traps

§3.5.1Reading a sector like a deal team

By the end of this module you can classify a revenue model, run unit economics, judge retention, and assess a moat. Sectors are where it all lands: each PE-favoured sector is really a bundle of recurring characteristics — a typical margin structure, capex appetite, cyclicality, and a short list of KPIs the deal team lives in.

Knowing the archetypes does two things. First, speed: when a teaser says "tech-enabled compliance services business, 60% recurring revenue", you should already have a prior on margins, multiple range, and the three risks to probe. Second, calibration: you spot deviations from the archetype — a distributor with 30% EBITDA margins or a software company with 60% churn is either a gem or a fiction, and both deserve immediate attention.

Margins below are typical mid-market EBITDA ranges — priors to be updated, not laws.

§3.5.2Business services: the workhorse of mid-market PE

Testing and inspection, facilities management, compliance services, IT managed services, professional training, waste — companies paid to do something businesses must do but don't want to do themselves.

  • Margins: wide range, 10–25% EBITDA; accreditation-led niches at the top, contract cleaning and generic outsourcing at the bottom.
  • Capex: low — people businesses; capex often <2% of revenue. Cash conversion is excellent when working capital is managed.
  • Cyclicality: low for compliance-driven services (regulation doesn't check the FTSE), moderate for discretionary ones (consulting, marketing services).
  • Key KPIs: contract retention rate, revenue per employee, staff attrition (the real capacity constraint), % revenue under contract, net pricing achieved vs wage inflation.

Why PE loves it: recurring or repeat revenue from must-do spend, low capex, fragmented markets ripe for buy-and-build, and margins that respond quickly to pricing and mix work. The classic risk: the assets go home at night. If margins depend on paying people below market, wage inflation and attrition will collect eventually — diligence always tests whether pricing can outrun wages. Avoid the sub-archetype where "services" means bodies on client sites at thin markups with no contract; that is staffing, and it prices like staffing (low).

§3.5.3Software: the multiple champion

Covered heavily in Lessons 1–3, so briefly through the sector lens:

  • Margins: 25–40%+ EBITDA at maturity; gross margins 70–85%. Growth-stage companies show lower EBITDA by choice (S&M spend).
  • Capex: minimal — though watch capitalised development costs, which shift R&D from the P&L to the balance sheet and flatter EBITDA. QoE work always looks at EBITDA minus capitalised dev.
  • Cyclicality: low for mission-critical vertical software; higher for discretionary tools bought seat-by-seat, where downturns bring seat reductions ("downgrade churn").
  • Key KPIs: ARR growth, GRR/NRR, CAC payback, Rule of 40 (revenue growth % + EBITDA margin % ≥ 40), logo concentration, % revenue truly contracted.

Why PE loves it: the best revenue quality money can buy — contracted, compounding, 90%+ gross-retained — plus pricing power from switching costs. Why PE hesitates: entry multiples are the highest in the market (often 12–20x EBITDA, or revenue multiples for growers), so the margin for error is thin; and product/technology risk is real — a platform one architecture generation behind needs re-investment the CIM will not volunteer. The mid-market sweet spot is boring vertical market software — pharmacy systems, plant maintenance, legal practice management — small markets big tech ignores, dominant local share, brutal switching costs.

§3.5.4Healthcare services: demographics with a payer problem

Dental and vet groups, care homes, clinics, pharmacies, staffing, at-home care.

  • Margins: 15–25% EBITDA at site level; group margins lower after central costs.
  • Capex: moderate to high — sites need fit-outs, clinical kit, maintenance capex that is genuinely non-deferrable. Care homes are near-real-estate businesses.
  • Cyclicality: demand is nearly acyclical (teeth and pets ignore GDP). The volatility comes from the payer, not the patient.
  • Key KPIs: occupancy/utilisation, fee rate vs cost inflation, payer mix (self-pay vs government vs insurer), clinician vacancy and agency-staff usage, regulatory ratings.

Why PE loves it: demographic tailwinds, fragmented supply, acyclical demand — the classic buy-and-build habitat (vets and dentistry were the textbook examples). Why PE gets burned: reimbursement risk — where government sets the fee, one budget decision can compress every site's margin simultaneously; staff cost inflation with fee rates lagging; and regulatory or reputational blow-ups that impair the whole platform. The payer-mix line in the CIM is the single most important table in a healthcare services deal: 80% self-pay dentistry and 80% government-funded care are different asset classes wearing the same scrubs.

§3.5.5Industrials and niche manufacturing: cash flow with a cycle

Specialty components, engineered products, flow control, packaging, aerospace supply chain.

  • Margins: 10–20% EBITDA for decent niche players; 25%+ for genuine spec-in monopolies.
  • Capex: the real cost — maintenance capex 3–6% of revenue, and "one-off" machine purchases that recur suspiciously often. PE analyses these businesses on EBITDA minus capex, not EBITDA; a 15%-margin manufacturer with 5% capex intensity is a 10% business.
  • Cyclicality: the defining risk. End-market exposure decides everything — aftermarket parts and consumables are resilient; original-equipment sales into construction or autos swing hard.
  • Key KPIs: order book/backlog and book-to-bill ratio, aftermarket vs OE revenue split, capacity utilisation, raw-material pass-through ability, customer/platform concentration.

Why PE likes the right ones: niche leaders with spec-in positions (the part is designed into the customer's product and re-qualification is painful) have quiet moats and pricing power, plus a valuable aftermarket annuity. The discipline: never pay a mid-cycle multiple on peak-cycle EBITDA. The classic industrial deal failure is buying at the top of the cycle at 7x "current" EBITDA that was really 10x normalised EBITDA. Diligence builds a through-cycle view — what did FY09 or FY20 look like, and what would this cost base do to covenants in a 20%-volume-down year?

§3.5.6Distribution: unglamorous, dense, and quietly excellent

Covered as a revenue model in Lesson 1; as a sector:

  • Margins: gross margins 15–30%; EBITDA margins just 3–8% of revenue — but judge them as a % of gross profit, where 20–30% is healthy.
  • Capex: low (warehouses often leased, fleets leaseable) — but working capital is the real capital: inventory plus receivables can be 15–25% of revenue, so growth consumes cash.
  • Cyclicality: follows end markets, softened where revenue is repair/maintenance ("break-fix") rather than new projects. MRO-weighted distributors are prized for exactly this.
  • Key KPIs: gross margin %, gross profit per employee, inventory turns, share of own-brand product (a margin lever), customer and supplier concentration, % revenue from MRO vs projects.

Why PE loves it: repeat purchasing from fragmented customers, density economics, proven buy-and-build maths, and self-help levers (pricing discipline, own-brand mix, warehouse consolidation) that reliably add 100–200bps of margin. The two existential questions: does the internet/manufacturer-direct channel erode the value-add, and could a key supplier terminate? A distributor is structurally a middleman; diligence must prove the middle is where some value genuinely settles — technical advice, availability, credit, range — or the margin is on loan from the supply chain.

§3.5.7Consumer: brands, baskets, and fashion risk

Food and beverage brands, personal care, leisure operators, e-commerce, multi-site restaurant or gym rolls-outs.

  • Margins: brands 10–20% EBITDA; retail/leisure operators 8–15% (pre-rent economics matter — always check whether "EBITDA" is quoted before or after rent/IFRS 16).
  • Capex: high for site roll-outs (each new site is a mini-project with a payback case); low for asset-light brands that outsource manufacturing.
  • Cyclicality: discretionary spend is the first thing households cut; premium and big-ticket segments swing hardest. Staples and value positioning are more resilient.
  • Key KPIs: like-for-like (same-store) sales growth, repeat purchase rate, new-site payback period, channel mix and retailer concentration, marketing as % of sales, price vs volume split of growth.

Why PE is selective: winners are spectacular (brand compounding plus roll-out maths), but the sector carries fashion risk, channel power (a grocer delisting one SKU can vaporise 15% of a brand's revenue), and the perennial trap of confusing a trend with a franchise. The roll-out question is always the same: are new sites as good as old ones? A concept whose recent cohort of sites pays back in 4 years while the CIM quotes the 2-year average across all vintages is decelerating in plain sight — the same cohort logic as Lesson 2, applied to buildings.

§3.5.8The classic value traps

Traps catch analysts because each one looks like a quality marker at first glance:

1. Project-based revenue dressed as growth. Three years of 20% growth built on ever-larger projects is not a growth business; it is a business that must replace 100% of its revenue every year, currently enjoying a hot streak. The tell: revenue growth with a shrinking or absent order book, "flagship contract" language, and lumpy quarterly phasing. Price it on the sustainable base of repeat revenue, not the headline.

2. Customer concentration. A business with 40% of revenue from one customer is partly a subsidiary of that customer, whatever the margin says. Concentration caps leverage, chills buyers at exit, and hands the customer pricing power at every renewal (they know their own weight). Rules of thumb deal teams carry: top customer >20% needs explaining; >35% reshapes the whole deal (earn-outs, price chips, or walking away). And check contract concentration too — five contracts with one framework body renewing the same year is one risk, not five.

3. Cyclical peak earnings. The most expensive mistake in PE, because leverage magnifies it: paying a full multiple on EBITDA that is cyclically elevated (post-COVID demand surges, commodity windfalls, one-off regulatory deadlines pulling demand forward). The tell: record margins the company can't fully explain, capacity sold out, competitors also at record levels. The discipline: normalise first, then apply the multiple to that.

Honourable mentions: regulatory dependency (the moat that can be repriced by the payer), founder dependency (the moat that retires at completion), and "recurring" revenue that diligence reclassifies (Lesson 3). The common thread of every trap is the same: an earnings number that will not repeat, priced as if it will. The entire discipline of this module — revenue models, unit economics, retention, moats — exists to answer one question: which parts of this year's EBITDA are permanent? Pay for those, and only those.

Lesson 4.1/Valuation

Enterprise Value vs Equity Value: The Bridge

25 min read
In brief

Why every deal has two prices — enterprise value and equity value — how the bridge between them works item by item (net debt, pensions, leases, earn-outs, minorities), and what "cash-free, debt-free" actually means in an SPA.

  1. 4.1.1Two prices for the same company
  2. 4.1.2Net debt: the core of the bridge
  3. 4.1.3Debt-like items: where the arguments live
  4. 4.1.4A worked bridge
  5. 4.1.5Cash-free, debt-free
  6. 4.1.6Why deals price on EV but shareholders receive equity value
  7. 4.1.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.1.1Two prices for the same company

Every deal has two headline numbers, and confusing them is the fastest way to look junior in a deal-team meeting.

Enterprise value (EV) is the value of the business — the operating assets that generate cash flow — regardless of how it happens to be financed today. Equity value is what the shareholders actually receive when they sell. The difference between the two is everyone else with a claim on the business's cash flows: lenders, pension trustees, lessors, minority shareholders, the vendor of a business bought last year on an earn-out.

Think of a house. The house is "worth" £500k — that's the enterprise value. But if there's a £300k mortgage outstanding, the seller walks away with £200k — that's the equity value. Nobody would say the seller "got £500k for the house", and nobody sensible compares houses by what sellers pocketed after their mortgages. You compare houses on the £500k number and you pay sellers the £200k number. Companies work exactly the same way.

The two are linked by the EV-to-equity bridge:

Equity value=EV−Net debt−Debt-like items−Minority interests\text{Equity value} = \text{EV} - \text{Net debt} - \text{Debt-like items} - \text{Minority interests}Equity value=EV−Net debt−Debt-like items−Minority interests

where net debt is gross debt minus cash. Everything in this lesson is about what belongs in that bridge and why deal teams argue about it for weeks.

§4.1.2Net debt: the core of the bridge

The simplest version of the bridge subtracts gross debt (bank loans, bonds, drawn revolving credit facilities, shareholder loans owed to outgoing owners) and adds back cash. A company with £100m of EV, £40m of debt and £8m of cash has net debt of £32m and equity value of £68m.

Why does cash add to equity value? Because the buyer receives it. If you buy the business and there's £8m sitting in the bank account on day one, you could in principle pay yourself an £8m dividend the next morning. The seller knows this, so they charge you for it. Symmetrically, you inherit the obligation to repay the £40m of debt, so you pay the seller £40m less than the business is worth.

Two practical wrinkles deal teams always probe:

  • Is the cash really free? Cash trapped in overseas subsidiaries with repatriation costs, regulatory or ring-fenced cash (client money, insurance reserves), and a minimum level of operating cash needed to run tills and pay wages are not freely distributable. Buyers argue for treating trapped and operating cash as not cash — reducing what they pay for it. A retailer that "has £10m of cash" but needs £6m in tills and in transit really has £4m.
  • Is the debt really all the debt? The audited balance sheet is a starting point, not the answer. That's what the rest of the bridge is for.

§4.1.3Debt-like items: where the arguments live

Between clean bank debt and clean cash sits a long list of items that behave like debt — fixed or near-fixed claims that the buyer will have to settle with cash that would otherwise belong to shareholders. The most common:

  • Pension deficits. A defined-benefit scheme that is underfunded is a promise to pay cash into the scheme over future years. Buyers treat the deficit (usually post-tax, because contributions are tax-deductible) as debt. A £10m deficit with 25% tax relief is roughly a £7.5m debt-like item. Sellers argue for the lower "technical provisions" number; buyers argue for the higher buy-out cost. The gap can be enormous — this is a diligence workstream in itself, not a footnote.
  • Leases. Under IFRS 16, lease liabilities sit on the balance sheet and EBITDA excludes rent, which flatters EBITDA. You must be consistent: either use EV including lease liabilities against IFRS 16 EBITDA, or strip leases from both sides and use pre-IFRS 16 ("frozen GAAP") EBITDA with rent deducted. Mixing conventions — an IFRS 16 EBITDA multiplied by a comps multiple built on pre-IFRS 16 numbers — silently misprices the deal. Finance leases on genuinely debt-financed kit are almost always treated as debt either way.
  • Earn-outs and deferred consideration. If the target bought a business last year and still owes the vendor £5m contingent on performance, that £5m (or its probability-weighted value) is a debt-like item — the buyer inherits the obligation.
  • Tax liabilities. Overdue corporation tax, disputed assessments, deferred payroll taxes.
  • Other favourites: dilapidations provisions, legal settlements, customer prepayments significantly above normal levels (you've been paid for work you still have to do), bonuses accrued but unpaid, dividends declared but unpaid, derivative liabilities.

Minority interests (non-controlling interests) are subtracted for a different reason: consistency. If the target owns 80% of a subsidiary, consolidated EBITDA includes 100% of that subsidiary's earnings, so the EV you compute off that EBITDA includes value that partly belongs to the 20% outside shareholders. Subtract their share to get to the equity value of your shareholders. Symmetrically, stakes in associates (where you own 30% and don't consolidate) are added — they're value the EBITDA doesn't capture.

§4.1.4A worked bridge

Suppose we've agreed to buy Brindley Engineering at an enterprise value of £100m. Diligence finds the following, in £m:

EV-to-equity bridge £m
Enterprise value 100.0
Less: bank debt (40.0)
Less: finance leases (5.0)
Less: pension deficit (post-tax) (6.0)
Less: minority interest (3.0)
Plus: cash 8.0
Equity value 54.0

The headline in the press release will say "£100m deal". The sellers' bank accounts will show £54m between them. Both numbers are true; they answer different questions.

Notice the leverage in the arithmetic — not financial leverage, negotiating leverage. The EV was agreed at "8x EBITDA of £12.5m". Nobody moves that headline now; it was set in the competitive phase of the auction. But every £1m the buyer's diligence adds to debt-like items comes straight out of the sellers' £54m. A pension actuary who moves the deficit from £6m to £10m just cost the sellers £4m — a 7.4% haircut to their proceeds from a 4% quibble on a £100m deal. This is why bridge items are fought over line by line in the SPA, and why "what's in net debt" is a defined term running to several pages.

§4.1.5Cash-free, debt-free

Most private M&A is done on a cash-free, debt-free (CFDF) basis: the price is quoted as an enterprise value, and the mechanism says "the sellers keep or repay the cash and debt; we're buying the operating business only". At completion, the EV is adjusted by actual net debt and debt-like items on the completion date to compute the cash that changes hands.

CFDF almost always travels with a second adjustment: normalised working capital. The buyer needs the business to come with a normal level of stock, debtors and creditors — otherwise a seller could quietly harvest cash before completion by not paying suppliers (creditors up, cash up) or aggressively collecting receivables. So the SPA sets a target working capital (usually a 12-month average, itself heavily negotiated) and adjusts the price pound-for-pound for any difference at completion. If normal working capital is £10m and the business completes with £7m, the buyer pays £3m less — they'll have to fund that £3m themselves in the first weeks of ownership.

The alternative mechanism, a locked box, fixes the equity price off a historical balance sheet date and prohibits "leakage" (dividends, fees to sellers) between that date and completion — simpler, faster, and seller-friendly, which is why sellers in competitive auctions increasingly insist on it. Either way, the intellectual structure is the same: agree value on EV, deliver equity value through a bridge.

§4.1.6Why deals price on EV but shareholders receive equity value

Why not just negotiate the equity number directly? Three reasons, all worth being able to recite:

  1. Comparability. EV is capital-structure-neutral. Two identical businesses, one financed with 60% debt and one debt-free, are worth the same EV but wildly different equity values. Multiples of EBITDA or EBIT (which are pre-interest measures) only make sense against EV — pairing an equity value with a pre-interest earnings measure is a category error. That's why comps, precedent transactions and headline deal announcements all speak in EV.
  2. The capital structure changes at completion anyway. In a buyout, the buyer repays the existing debt and installs a new structure. The seller's financing choices are irrelevant to what the business is worth to the buyer; they only determine how the EV is split between the seller's lenders and the seller's shareholders.
  3. Timing. Cash and debt balances move daily; the operating business's value doesn't. You agree the stable number early (EV) and true-up the volatile part (net debt, working capital) at completion.

But shareholders can only ever receive equity value — the rest of the EV goes to repaying lenders and settling debt-like claims. When a founder says "I sold my company for £100m", the deal team's first question is always: "was that EV or equity?" The answer changes the story by nearly half in the Brindley example.

§4.1.7What deal teams actually ask

When a bridge lands on the table, experienced eyes go straight to a few places:

  • "What's in 'cash'?" Trapped cash, client money, till floats, uncleared cheques. What looks good: clean, onshore, unrestricted cash. What looks bad: a third of "cash" sitting in a Chinese subsidiary or held against customer deposits.
  • "Is that the full pension picture?" Which deficit measure, which discount rate, what the trustees will demand on a change of control. A change-of-control clause can let trustees reopen the funding schedule at the worst possible moment.
  • "IFRS 16 — are the multiple and the EBITDA on the same basis?" The single most common technical error in junior models. Leases in the bridge and rent added back to EBITDA is double counting in the buyer's favour; leases nowhere is a gift to the seller.
  • "Any debt-like items hiding in working capital?" Stretched creditors, factored receivables (debt dressed as a working-capital movement), deferred capex.
  • "Who gets the equity value?" With institutional sellers there's usually a waterfall — loan notes, preference shares, sweet equity — so even the equity value isn't shared pro rata. That's a later module, but the bridge is where it starts.

The bridge is arithmetic a spreadsheet does in one column. The judgement — what counts as debt, what cash is real, which measure of a pension deficit is fair — is where deals are won, lost, and repriced. Get fluent in it: every subsequent lesson in this module quotes multiples of EV, and every multiple is only as good as the bridge behind it.

Lesson 4.2/Valuation

Valuation Multiples: What Each One Really Tells You

25 min read
In brief

EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, EV/Sales and P/E — what each captures and distorts, when each fits, LTM vs NTM conventions, how to adjust multiples for growth, margin and capex differences, and how multiple arbitrage generates (and flatters) PE returns.

  1. 4.2.1A multiple is a compressed DCF
  2. 4.2.2The four workhorses
  3. 4.2.3LTM vs NTM: which year's earnings?
  4. 4.2.4Adjusting multiples for growth, margin and capex
  5. 4.2.5Multiple arbitrage
  6. 4.2.6What deal teams actually ask

§4.2.1A multiple is a compressed DCF

A valuation multiple looks like the opposite of a discounted cash flow: quick, crude, no forecasts. It isn't. A multiple is a DCF with the assumptions hidden. Pay 8x EBITDA and you are implicitly making claims about growth, margins, capex needs and risk — you just haven't written them down. The perpetuity maths makes this explicit: if free cash flow is a stable proportion of EBITDA and grows at ggg forever, then

EVEBITDA=FCF/EBITDAWACC−g\frac{EV}{EBITDA} = \frac{FCF/EBITDA}{WACC - g}EBITDAEV​=WACC−gFCF/EBITDA​

A business converting 50% of EBITDA to free cash flow, with a 10% discount rate and 2% growth, is "worth" 0.5/0.08=6.25x0.5 / 0.08 = 6.25x0.5/0.08=6.25x. Raise conversion to 70% (low capex, negative working capital) and the same formula gives 8.75x. Nothing about the business changed except the quality of its cash conversion — and the "fair" multiple moved by 40%. Keep this formula in your head: every argument about why one company deserves a higher multiple than another is an argument about one of those three inputs.

The corollary: multiples from companies with different cash conversion, growth or risk are not comparable without adjustment. "The sector trades at 10x" is the beginning of an analysis, not the end of one.

§4.2.2The four workhorses

EV/EBITDA is the default currency of private markets. Numerator and denominator are both capital-structure-neutral (EBITDA is before interest, EV is before the bridge), so it compares companies regardless of leverage. It also neutralises depreciation policy differences. What it distorts: it treats capex as free. Two businesses with £20m EBITDA look identical at 8x, even if one must spend £10m a year on machinery and the other £1m on laptops. EBITDA is not cash — Module 2 made that point; here it becomes a pricing error worth millions.

EV/EBIT partially fixes that: depreciation is a rough long-run proxy for capex, so EBIT gets you closer to sustainable pre-tax operating cash flow. It fits capital-intensive sectors — manufacturing, transport, rental businesses — where EBITDA flatters aggressively. Its weaknesses: depreciation is an accounting estimate (useful lives, revaluations, and acquired intangibles amortisation muddy it), and it diverges from capex whenever a company is growing or shrinking its asset base.

Worked contrast, £m: Alpha and Beta both have EBITDA of 20 and are both offered at EV 160 — 8.0x EBITDA. Alpha depreciates 10 (heavy kit, capex to match); Beta depreciates 2. Alpha's EBIT is 10, Beta's is 18. On EV/EBIT, Alpha is at 16.0x and Beta at 8.9x. Beta is dramatically cheaper for the same headline multiple, because more of its EBITDA survives contact with the capex line. Whenever two comps show similar EV/EBITDA but very different EV/EBIT, capital intensity is the reason — and EBITDA is the wrong lens.

EV/Sales ignores profitability entirely, which is precisely when you need it: loss-making or sub-scale businesses (early SaaS, turnarounds) where EBITDA is negative or meaningless. It only works between companies with similar margin potential — 2x sales for a business that can reach 30% EBITDA margins is cheap; 2x sales for one structurally stuck at 5% is ruinous. A useful bridge: EV/Sales = EV/EBITDA × EBITDA margin. A 10x EBITDA business at a 20% margin trades at 2.0x sales; at a 10% margin, 1.0x sales. Quoting EV/Sales without quoting margin is quoting half a number.

P/E (price/earnings — equity value over net income) is the odd one out: it's an equity multiple, after interest and tax. That makes it the natural tool for banks and insurers (where leverage is the business, not the financing) and for public-market investors buying shares. In M&A it's dangerous, because it entangles operating performance with capital structure: gear a business up and its P/E falls with no change in the enterprise. Never pair an equity-side numerator with an enterprise-side denominator or vice versa — EV/earnings and price/EBITDA are both category errors, and both appear depressingly often in first drafts.

Rule of thumb for choosing: EBITDA for most PE deals and services businesses; EBIT where capex is structural; Sales where profits haven't arrived; P/E where the analysis is genuinely about equity (listed shares, financials).

§4.2.3LTM vs NTM: which year's earnings?

A multiple needs a time period. The two standards:

  • LTM (last twelve months): actual, audited-ish, real. But backward-looking — you're buying the future, not the past.
  • NTM (next twelve months) / forward: matches price to what you'll actually own, but relies on forecasts — and management forecasts in a sale process have a well-documented optimism problem.

For a growing company, NTM EBITDA is bigger than LTM, so the NTM multiple is lower. EV of £200m on LTM EBITDA of £20m is 10.0x; if EBITDA grows 25% to £25m, the same price is 8.0x NTM. Sellers therefore quote NTM ("only 8x!"), buyers quote LTM ("a full 10x!"), and both are describing the same deal. In comps work the cardinal rule is consistency: every company in the set on the same basis, and the multiple you apply to your target on the same basis as the comps that produced it. Applying a comps-set NTM multiple to your target's LTM EBITDA understates value for a grower; the reverse overstates it. This sounds too obvious to mention until you see it in a live IC paper.

Precedent transactions bring a third basis: EBITDA as disclosed at announcement, which is usually LTM at signing — worth remembering when precedent multiples look rich against today's trading comps.

§4.2.4Adjusting multiples for growth, margin and capex

The compressed-DCF formula tells you what to adjust for. In practice, three moves:

Growth. Faster growth justifies a higher multiple — but how much higher? A quick tool is the growth-adjusted multiple (EV/EBITDA ÷ expected EBITDA growth, analogous to the equity market's PEG ratio). Two comps at 12x and 8x look far apart; if the first grows EBITDA at 15% and the second at 5%, the growth-adjusted picture (0.8 vs 1.6) reverses the ranking. Cruder but effective: run the comps on NTM or NTM+1 numbers, which lets growth "catch up" into the denominator.

Margin. For EV/Sales especially, regress or simply scatter EV/Sales against EBITDA margin across the comps set — the relationship is usually strong, and your target should be priced on the line, not at the set's median. A 25%-margin business priced at the median EV/Sales of a 15%-margin comps set is being given away.

Capex. Where capital intensity differs across the set, switch to EV/EBIT, or better, compute EV/(EBITDA − maintenance capex) for each comp. This is the closest a multiple gets to a cash flow lens and it is what many PE ICs actually want to see. In the Alpha/Beta example above: Alpha at EV/(20−10) = 16.0x, Beta at EV/(20−2) = 8.9x — same answer as EV/EBIT here, but the measure keeps working even when depreciation and capex diverge.

What looks bad in a comps page: a single median multiple applied to a target that sits at the extreme of the set on growth, margin or capex. What looks good: an explicit "why our target deserves a premium/discount to the median" argument tied to those three drivers.

§4.2.5Multiple arbitrage

Multiple arbitrage (or multiple expansion) is selling at a higher multiple than you paid. Buy at 8x EBITDA of £20m (EV £160m), sell five years later at 10x EBITDA of £25m (EV £250m): of the £90m EV gain, £40m came from EBITDA growth at the entry multiple (5 × 8) and £50m came purely from the multiple moving — arbitrage. With leverage amplifying equity returns, multiple expansion has historically been a very large share of PE value creation, which is exactly why ICs treat it with suspicion.

Where does legitimate expansion come from?

  • Size: bigger businesses trade at higher multiples (more on this in Lesson 6). Growing a £10m-EBITDA business to £25m can move it into a different buyer universe.
  • Buy-and-build: acquiring bolt-ons at 5-6x and selling the assembled group at 9x — the arbitrage is earned through integration work.
  • Quality improvement: shifting the revenue mix to recurring contracts, diversifying customers, professionalising the finance function.
  • Re-rating of the sector or market: luck, dressed as skill.

The IC discipline that follows: base cases generally assume exit multiple = entry multiple (or a modest step-down for conservatism), so the underwritten return depends on EBITDA growth and deleveraging — things the fund controls. Multiple expansion is upside, not plan. When a deal only reaches its target return with exit at 11x against entry at 9x, the model is telling you the price is too high and someone has hidden the problem in the last row of the assumptions page.

§4.2.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's the multiple of?" Reported EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, run-rate EBITDA including synergies? A "7x deal" on aggressively adjusted EBITDA can be a 9x deal on real earnings. The denominator is negotiated as fiercely as the multiple (Lesson 6 and Module 9 pick this up as quality of earnings).
  • "LTM or NTM, and is the basis consistent with the comps?"
  • "Pre- or post-IFRS 16?" Lesson 1's warning, applied: rent-heavy businesses can move a full turn of EBITDA between bases.
  • "What does the multiple imply?" Invert the compressed DCF: at 12x with 50% cash conversion and a 10% discount rate, the implied perpetual growth is 10%−0.5/12=5.8%10\% - 0.5/12 = 5.8\%10%−0.5/12=5.8% — forever. Is that believable for this business? Implied-assumption checks kill more bad deals than any comps page.
  • "Would we be happy holding at this multiple if we can't sell higher?" The multiple arbitrage question, asked honestly.

Multiples are how the market talks, so you must be fluent. Just remember what fluency means here: not reciting the sector median, but knowing what any given multiple assumes, what it hides, and when it's the wrong tool entirely. The next lesson puts this to work building a comps set properly.

Lesson 4.3/Valuation

Comparable Companies and Precedent Transactions

25 min read
In brief

How to build a comps set properly — screening, calendarisation, spreading, outlier handling — the difference between trading comps and precedent transactions, where control premia come from, and why "the comps say 10x" always deserves scepticism.

  1. 4.3.1What comps are actually for
  2. 4.3.2Screening: choosing the set
  3. 4.3.3Spreading and calendarisation
  4. 4.3.4A worked mini comps set
  5. 4.3.5Trading comps vs precedent transactions
  6. 4.3.6Why "the comps say 10x" deserves scepticism
  7. 4.3.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.3.1What comps are actually for

Comparable company analysis ("trading comps") answers a simple question: what is the market paying today for businesses like this one? You take a set of listed companies resembling your target, compute their multiples, and apply a chosen multiple to your target's earnings. Precedent transaction analysis ("deal comps") does the same with prices actually paid in M&A.

Both methods are relative valuation: they tell you what something is worth compared with what similar things fetch, not what it's intrinsically worth. That's a feature and a bug. Feature: markets aggregate enormous amounts of information, and any buyer who ignores what the market pays will systematically lose auctions or overpay. Bug: if the market is wrong — a bubble, a panic, a sector temporarily in fashion — comps import the error straight into your valuation with a spurious air of objectivity. Comps tell you the price of comparable assets; whether that price is value is your problem, not the spreadsheet's.

The craft is almost entirely in building the set. The multiplication at the end takes seconds; a defensible set takes days.

§4.3.2Screening: choosing the set

Start wide, then cut with explicit criteria. Deal teams screen on:

  • Business model, not SIC code. Industry classifications lump together companies that make their money completely differently. A "software" screen returns licence-and-maintenance dinosaurs and 130%-net-retention SaaS; their multiples differ by 3x for good reason. Read the annual reports; screen on how revenue is actually earned (recurring vs project, asset- light vs asset-heavy, B2B vs B2C).
  • Size. A £2bn company is not a comp for a £100m company, however similar the product — scale changes margins, customer concentration, funding costs and, crucially, the multiple itself (Lesson 6). Common practice: within roughly 0.3x–3x of the target's revenue or EBITDA where the universe allows.
  • Geography and end-markets. A UK contractor exposed to public-sector spend is not priced like a US peer exposed to data-centre capex.
  • Growth and margin profile. Lesson 2's point: a comp growing at three times your target's rate belongs in the appendix, not the median.
  • Liquidity and coverage. Illiquid micro-caps with no analyst coverage produce stale, noisy multiples.

Expect to land on 5–10 names. Fewer than five and the median is fragile; more than a dozen and you've stopped screening. There is never a perfect comp — the honest output is a set where you can articulate, for each name, how it differs from the target and in which direction that should push the multiple.

§4.3.3Spreading and calendarisation

"Spreading comps" means building each company's numbers to a common standard, because reported figures aren't comparable off the shelf:

  • EV built properly. Market capitalisation (fully diluted — options and convertibles in-the-money) plus the full Lesson 1 bridge: debt, leases on a consistent basis, pensions, minorities, less cash and associates. A comp's EV taken lazily from a data vendor can be wrong by a full turn of EBITDA.
  • Clean earnings. Strip one-offs from each comp's EBITDA — restructuring charges, disposals, impairments — the same way you'd want your target's EBITDA cleaned. Consistent treatment of IFRS 16 across every comp.
  • Calendarisation. Companies have different year-ends; multiples must be for the same twelve months. The standard fix is a weighted blend. A June-year-end comp with FY-Jun-24 EBITDA of £28m and FY-Jun-25 forecast of £32m has calendar-2024 EBITDA of 0.5×28+0.5×32=£30m0.5 \times 28 + 0.5 \times 32 = £30m0.5×28+0.5×32=£30m. A March year-end blends 3/12 and 9/12. Skipping calendarisation in a growing sector systematically misstates every off-cycle comp.

§4.3.4A worked mini comps set

Our target is Tarn Instruments, a UK testing and certification business with LTM EBITDA of £25m. The screened set (all £m, calendarised LTM):

Company EV EBITDA EV/EBITDA Net debt/EBITDA EBITDA growth
Halden Testing plc 450 50 9.0x 1.8x +6%
Wrekin Labs plc 240 30 8.0x 2.0x +4%
Girton Analytics plc 1,800 150 12.0x 1.5x +15%
Pennine Inspection plc 130 20 6.5x 5.5x +2%
Solent Certification plc 285 30 9.5x 2.2x +7%
Mean 9.0x
Median 9.0x

Mean and median both say 9.0x. Case closed? Look closer:

  • Girton at 12.0x is six times the size of the next-largest name and growing at twice the set's rate. Its multiple embeds scale and growth your £25m-EBITDA target doesn't have. Including it drags the mean up for reasons that don't transfer.
  • Pennine at 6.5x carries net debt of 5.5x EBITDA. Its equity is a sliver of the EV, its shares trade like an option, and its depressed multiple reflects distress and forced-seller dynamics, not the value of testing businesses. Its 6.5x drags the mean down — again for reasons that don't transfer.

Excluding both, the core set (Halden, Wrekin, Solent) runs 8.0–9.5x, median 9.0x. The answer didn't move much this time — but the reasoning did, and next time the outliers won't happen to cancel. Outlier handling should be explicit and symmetric: state the exclusion rule (distress, scale, pending takeover, accounting restatement), apply it both directions, and show the set with and without. Quietly deleting the names that hurt your answer is the oldest trick in the book, and an IC that catches it once will re-check your work forever.

For Tarn: 8.5–9.5x on £25m gives an EV range of £212.5m–£237.5m, with a case for the lower half (smallest name in the peer group, growth in line with the slower names).

§4.3.5Trading comps vs precedent transactions

Precedent transactions apply the same machinery to M&A deals: EV paid over the target's EBITDA at announcement. They answer a different question — not "what does the market pay for minority stakes in listed peers?" but "what have buyers paid for control of whole companies?"

Precedents typically print higher than trading comps, for reasons worth separating:

  • Control premium. Buying control lets you replace management, change strategy, releverage, and capture the whole benefit — worth paying for. Public-to-private premia have historically averaged around 25–40% over the undisturbed share price.
  • Synergies. Strategic buyers can pay for cost overlaps a financial buyer can't. A deal at 11x to a trade consolidator taking out £5m of duplicated overhead may be 8x on a post-synergy basis — that multiple is unavailable to you unless you have the same synergies.
  • Competitive dynamics. Auction heat is baked into every precedent print by construction: the recorded price is the winning bid, i.e. the most optimistic buyer's number.

Precedents also have data problems trading comps don't: private-deal terms are patchily disclosed (the EBITDA behind a rumoured multiple may be adjusted, run-rate, or invented); structures muddy the headline (earn-outs, rollover, vendor loans); and deals are stale — a 2021 print at 12x tells you about 2021's debt markets, not today's. Standard practice: last 3–5 years, flag the cycle context of each print, and never let one trophy deal set your range.

Use both, for what each is: trading comps for today's market level, precedents for what control of the whole business has cost. A PE buyer paying "trading comps plus a control premium" with no synergies should hear alarm bells — that premium has to be earned back by someone, and it's them.

§4.3.6Why "the comps say 10x" deserves scepticism

When someone quotes a single comps number in a meeting, run this checklist in your head:

  1. 10x what? LTM or NTM? Reported or adjusted EBITDA? Pre- or post-IFRS 16? Each choice moves the answer; combinations move it a lot.
  2. Whose set? A seller's banker built a set to maximise the number; the buyer's to minimise it. Both will describe theirs as "the comps".
  3. Mean, median, or cherry? With five names, one outlier moves a mean a full turn. Median with disclosed outlier policy, always.
  4. Is the target actually mid-set? Applying the median assumes the target is a median business. Smaller, slower-growing, more concentrated than the set → it belongs below the median, and a private company usually deserves a further illiquidity discount against listed peers.
  5. Multiple of which metric? If the set's EV/EBITDA range is tight but EV/EBIT is all over the place, capital intensity differs and EBITDA is hiding it (Lesson 2).
  6. When? Comps are a snapshot. Sector re-ratings of ±2 turns within a year are routine.

None of this makes comps useless — it makes the headline useless without the workings. What looks good in a comps page: explicit screen, calendarised numbers, both bases shown, outliers handled openly, and a recommended multiple with a stated premium/discount to the median tied to the target's characteristics. What looks bad: a naked median, a set of four, and a footnote saying "source: broker research".

§4.3.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Walk me from the raw set to your number." They're testing whether the set was screened or reverse-engineered from the answer.
  • "Why is [obvious name] not in the set?" Have a one-line reason ready for every exclusion.
  • "What were these names trading at a year ago?" Level vs history matters: 9x might be the set's five-year low (market-wide de-rating — opportunity?) or its all-time high.
  • "Which precedent is most like our deal, and what did the buyer achieve?" One deeply understood precedent beats ten rows of vendor-database multiples.
  • "If we paid the comps median, what does the LBO return?" The PE punchline — comps propose, the LBO model disposes. Lesson 6 takes this up properly.

Comps are the most-used and most-abused tool in valuation. Used well, they discipline a valuation with market evidence. Used lazily, they launder one number through five tickers. The difference is the workings.

Lesson 4.4/Valuation

DCF Fundamentals: Cash Flows, WACC and Terminal Value

30 min read
In brief

The mechanics of a discounted cash flow: projecting unlevered free cash flow, building a WACC from its parts (risk-free rate, ERP, beta, size premium, cost of debt), terminal value by Gordon growth and exit multiple, a full worked mini-DCF for a fictional company, and a WACC-growth sensitivity table.

  1. 4.4.1The idea, stripped bare
  2. 4.4.2Projecting free cash flow
  3. 4.4.3Building a WACC from parts
  4. 4.4.4Terminal value
  5. 4.4.5The full mini-DCF
  6. 4.4.6The sensitivity table
  7. 4.4.7What deal teams actually ask

§4.4.1The idea, stripped bare

A business is worth the cash it will hand its capital providers over its life, discounted back to today at a rate reflecting the risk of actually receiving it. That's the whole theory of a DCF. Everything else — the tabs, the betas, the terminal value formulas — is implementation.

EV=∑t=1nFCFt(1+WACC)t+TV(1+WACC)nEV = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{FCF_t}{(1+WACC)^t} + \frac{TV}{(1+WACC)^n}EV=t=1∑n​(1+WACC)tFCFt​​+(1+WACC)nTV​

Two design choices define the standard version. First, we discount unlevered free cash flow — cash generated by operations before any financing — so the answer is an enterprise value, independent of capital structure, exactly parallel to Lesson 1. (Get to equity value through the bridge, as always.) Second, because we can't forecast forever, we project explicitly for 5–10 years and collapse everything after into a single terminal value.

A DCF is the only mainstream method that values the business from its own economics rather than from other people's prices. That independence is its point — and, as Lesson 5 will show, its danger, because nothing external disciplines the inputs.

§4.4.2Projecting free cash flow

Unlevered FCF for each forecast year:

FCF=EBIT×(1−tax)+D&A−Capex−ΔNWCFCF = EBIT \times (1 - tax) + D\&A - Capex - \Delta NWCFCF=EBIT×(1−tax)+D&A−Capex−ΔNWC

Start from EBIT, not EBITDA, so tax is computed on the right base; add back the non-cash D&A; subtract the two real cash drains earnings ignore — capex and growth in net working capital. Note what's absent: interest (financing, not operations) and dividends (distribution, not generation).

Let's build year 1 for Kestrel Foods, a fictional ambient-foods producer (£m):

Year 1 build £m
Revenue 100.0
EBITDA (20% margin) 20.0
Less: D&A (6.0)
EBIT 14.0
Less: tax at 25% (3.5)
NOPAT 10.5
Add back: D&A 6.0
Less: capex (6.0)
Less: increase in NWC (0.5)
Unlevered FCF 10.0

Running the same logic across a five-year plan (revenue growing ~5%, stable margin, capex tracking D&A, working capital consuming ~10% of each year's revenue growth) gives, rounded: FCF of 10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 13.0, 14.0.

The projection is where the value really lives, so the quality checks live here too: does the revenue growth imply believable market share? Does the margin expand for a reason (mix, pricing, operating leverage) or just because the spreadsheet drags right? Is capex consistent with the growth — you cannot grow volumes 5% a year on maintenance-only capex? Does working capital scale with revenue? A DCF inherits every sin of its forecast; Lesson 5 catalogues them.

§4.4.3Building a WACC from parts

The discount rate is the weighted average cost of capital — the blended return the company's investors require:

WACC=EE+D×ke+DE+D×kd×(1−tax)WACC = \frac{E}{E+D} \times k_e + \frac{D}{E+D} \times k_d \times (1 - tax)WACC=E+DE​×ke​+E+DD​×kd​×(1−tax)

Debt is cheaper than equity (lenders get paid first, so they bear less risk) and interest is tax-deductible — hence the (1−tax)(1-tax)(1−tax) shield. Weights should be target long-run weights at market values, not today's accident of a balance sheet.

Cost of equity comes from CAPM plus, in practice, adjustments:

ke=rf+β×ERP+size premiumk_e = r_f + \beta \times ERP + \text{size premium}ke​=rf​+β×ERP+size premium

Build one for Kestrel:

Component Value Where it comes from
Risk-free rate rfr_frf​ 4.0% Long-dated government bond yield (10–20yr gilt)
Equity risk premium 5.0% Long-run excess return of equities over bonds; practitioner consensus ~4.5–6%
Beta β\betaβ 1.2 Sector betas from listed comps, unlevered then re-levered to the target structure
CAPM cost of equity 10.0% 4.0%+1.2×5.0%4.0\% + 1.2 \times 5.0\%4.0%+1.2×5.0%
Size premium 2.0% Empirically, small companies return more / are riskier; ~1–3% for mid-market
Cost of equity 12.0%

Beta measures how the sector's returns move with the market — food producers below 1 (defensive), housebuilders above it (cyclical); 1.2 reflects Kestrel's private-label exposure. The size premium is the practitioner's patch for CAPM's best-documented failure: small-company risk (illiquidity, key-person dependence, concentration) that beta doesn't capture. It is also, frankly, a judgement dial — which Lesson 5 returns to.

Cost of debt: what the company would pay to borrow today — say 7.0% pre-tax, or 7.0%×(1−0.25)=5.25%7.0\% \times (1-0.25) = 5.25\%7.0%×(1−0.25)=5.25% after tax.

Weights: target 70% equity / 30% debt.

WACC=0.70×12.0%+0.30×5.25%=8.4%+1.6%≈10.0%WACC = 0.70 \times 12.0\% + 0.30 \times 5.25\% = 8.4\% + 1.6\% \approx 10.0\%WACC=0.70×12.0%+0.30×5.25%=8.4%+1.6%≈10.0%

A mid-market UK company in 2026 typically lands somewhere in the 9–13% range. Hold the intuition, not just the formula: WACC is the return the money could earn elsewhere at the same risk. Discounting at 10% says "£1 of Kestrel cash next year is worth 91p today, because 10% is what this risk must pay."

§4.4.4Terminal value

The explicit forecast stops at year 5; the business (we hope) doesn't. Two standard ways to value everything beyond:

Gordon growth treats year-5 FCF as growing at a constant rate ggg forever:

TV=FCF5×(1+g)WACC−gTV = \frac{FCF_5 \times (1+g)}{WACC - g}TV=WACC−gFCF5​×(1+g)​

For Kestrel with g=2%g = 2\%g=2%: TV=14.0×1.020.10−0.02=14.280.08=178.5TV = \frac{14.0 \times 1.02}{0.10 - 0.02} = \frac{14.28}{0.08} = 178.5TV=0.10−0.0214.0×1.02​=0.0814.28​=178.5.

Discipline on ggg: it is perpetual growth, so it cannot exceed long-run nominal GDP growth (~3.5–4%) — a company growing faster than the economy forever eventually is the economy. Typical range 1.5–2.5%. Note the mechanics of the denominator: as ggg approaches WACC, TV explodes toward infinity. Small changes in either input move TV violently — which matters, because TV is most of the answer.

Exit multiple instead asks what the business would sell for in year 5 at a comps-style multiple: terminal-year EBITDA of £24.3m at, say, 7.5x gives TV ≈ £182m. This is more intuitive for deal people but smuggles relative valuation into your "intrinsic" method — your DCF is now partly a comps page in disguise.

Best practice: use one, cross-check with the other. Our Gordon TV of £178.5m against year-5 EBITDA of £24.3m implies an exit multiple of 178.5/24.3=7.3x178.5 / 24.3 = 7.3x178.5/24.3=7.3x — below today's sector multiples, i.e. mildly conservative. If your Gordon TV had implied 14x, the terminal assumptions would be doing something the market doesn't believe.

§4.4.5The full mini-DCF

Discounting at WACC = 10%:

£m Y1 Y2 Y3 Y4 Y5
Unlevered FCF 10.0 11.0 12.0 13.0 14.0
Discount factor @10% 0.909 0.826 0.751 0.683 0.621
PV of FCF 9.1 9.1 9.0 8.9 8.7
Valuation build £m
Sum of PV of explicit FCF (Y1–Y5) 44.8
Terminal value at Y5 (Gordon, g = 2%) 178.5
PV of terminal value (× 0.621) 110.8
Enterprise value 155.6

Two observations before anyone gets excited about the precision. First, EV of £155.6m on year-1 EBITDA of £20m is an implied multiple of ~7.8x — a number you can now sanity-check against comps, which is exactly how the methods should talk to each other. Second, the terminal value contributes 110.8/155.6=71%110.8 / 155.6 = 71\%110.8/155.6=71% of the entire answer. Five carefully-built forecast years drive under a third of the value; a two-line perpetuity formula drives the rest. Sit with that — it is the central fact about DCFs and the subject of the next lesson.

To get equity value, apply Lesson 1: if Kestrel carries net debt and debt-like items of £35m, equity value is £120.6m.

§4.4.6The sensitivity table

Because TV dominates and its formula is hair-trigger, no DCF should ever be presented as a single number. The standard exhibit is a two-way sensitivity of EV to WACC and terminal growth:

EV (£m) g = 1.5% g = 2.0% g = 2.5%
WACC 9% 169.1 178.6 189.5
WACC 10% 148.6 155.6 163.6
WACC 11% 132.4 137.7 143.8

Read what it's telling you: across entirely defensible input combinations — nobody can prove 10% right and 9% wrong, or 2.0% right and 2.5% wrong — the valuation spans £132m to £190m, a 43% range. The DCF hasn't given you a number; it has given you a map from assumptions to numbers. That is genuinely useful (it shows which assumptions matter and prices them), but only if you present the map rather than pointing at your favourite cell.

§4.4.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "What's TV as a percentage of EV?" Above ~75% and the explicit forecast is decoration.
  • "What exit multiple does your Gordon TV imply?" The single fastest sanity check.
  • "Why is your WACC 10% and not 9%?" If you can't defend each component, the table above says that's a £23m question.
  • "Does capex support the growth?" Growth in the revenue line with maintenance capex in the cash flow line is the most common way DCFs flatter.
  • "What does the DCF say at management's case vs our case?" A DCF is run on someone's forecast; always know whose.

You now have the machine. The next lesson is about the judgement — where the machine misleads, and how experienced teams use it anyway.
