Lesson 4.5/Valuation

DCF Judgement and Pitfalls

25 min read
In brief

Where DCFs go wrong and how professionals use them anyway: terminal value dominance, hockey-stick forecasts, the false precision of WACC, the mid-year convention, when DCF beats multiples and vice versa, and triangulating methods on a football-field chart.

  1. 4.5.1The uncomfortable truth about DCFs
  2. 4.5.2Terminal value dominance: what to do about it
  3. 4.5.3Hockey sticks: the forecast pathology
  4. 4.5.4WACC: precise, and false
  5. 4.5.5The mid-year convention
  6. 4.5.6When DCF beats multiples — and vice versa
  7. 4.5.7Football fields and triangulation
  8. 4.5.8What deal teams actually ask

§4.5.1The uncomfortable truth about DCFs

Lesson 4 ended on the number that should reframe how you see every DCF: in a completely standard model, terminal value was 71% of enterprise value. That's typical — 60–80% is the normal range for a five-year explicit period. The implication is blunt: a DCF is mostly a perpetuity formula wearing a five-year forecast as a disguise. The forecast tab gets weeks of work and the IC's attention; two cells — WACC and terminal growth — quietly decide the answer.

This doesn't make DCFs useless. It makes them a different kind of tool than they appear. A DCF is at its best not as a valuation oracle but as an assumptions X-ray: it forces every belief about growth, margins, capex and risk into the open, prices each one, and shows you which beliefs the valuation actually turns on. Teams that use DCFs well spend their time interrogating the map — the sensitivity table — rather than defending a favourite cell of it. Teams that use them badly present EV to one decimal place. Kestrel is "worth £155.6m" only in the sense that a dart is "at treble twenty" while still in your hand.

§4.5.2Terminal value dominance: what to do about it

You can't eliminate TV dominance — it's mathematics, not sloppiness; most of any long-lived asset's value genuinely lies beyond year 5. You can stop it hiding:

  • Report TV% of EV on the face of the output. Above ~75%, say so and treat the DCF as a supporting method, not the lead.
  • Cross-check the implied exit multiple (Lesson 4's habit). A Gordon TV implying 12x for a business trading peers price at 8x means your terminal assumptions — not your forecast — are the entire investment thesis.
  • Check the terminal year is steady-state. The perpetuity extrapolates year 5 forever, so year 5 must be a representative year: margins at sustainable (not peak) levels, capex ≈ D&A plus a growth allowance, working capital growing in line with revenue, no expiring one-offs. Capitalising a peak year into perpetuity is the most expensive single error a DCF can make: at an 8% capitalisation rate, £1m of overstated terminal FCF adds £12.5m of TV.
  • Lengthen the explicit period for businesses mid-transition (10 years, with fade of growth and margins toward steady state) rather than asking the perpetuity to do transition work it can't.

§4.5.3Hockey sticks: the forecast pathology

Every sell-side plan you will ever see shows the same shape: flat or bumpy history, then a smooth upward sweep starting — always — next year. The hockey stick. Management forecasts in sale processes are systematically optimistic because everyone's incentives point the same way: the vendor wants price, management often has sale bonuses, and the CIM is a marketing document.

Concrete tells, with the numbers you'd actually see:

  • Margin ramps without a mechanism. EBITDA margin 12% for five years of history, then 12% → 20% over the plan. On £100m of revenue that ramp manufactures £8m of EBITDA which, capitalised into terminal value at 12.5x (8% cap rate), fabricates ~£100m of DCF value. Demand the bridge: which contracts, which price rises, which cost lines.
  • Growth with no cost. Revenue +8% p.a. while headcount, marketing and capex are held flat. Operating leverage is real but bounded; unbounded operating leverage is a typo.
  • "Year 1 is already secured." Check the order book actually covers it, and check what last year's plan said about this year — the single most powerful diligence question is plan-vs-actual for the last three plans. A management team that has missed three straight budgets by 20% has told you the discount to apply to this one.
  • The base year is flattered. The stick starts from an adjusted, run-rate, pro-forma-for-everything base (Module 9's territory). A hockey stick from an inflated base compounds two frauds.

The professional response is not cynicism but re-underwriting: build your own case (usually "management minus" — haircut growth, slower margin ramp, realistic capex), run the DCF on both, and know which case you're being asked to pay for.

§4.5.4WACC: precise, and false

Open any valuation textbook and WACC arrives with decimal places. Now recall its parts, each a judgement wearing a formula: which risk-free rate (spot or average? 10- or 20-year?); an ERP that respectable sources put anywhere from 4% to 6.5%; a beta estimated by regression (over what period, against what index, unlevered how?) whose standard error is often half its value; a size premium of 0–3% depending on which study you cite. Stack the defensible-high choices and you get 9%; stack the defensible-low and you get 12.5% — for the same company. On Kestrel's sensitivity table, that spread is worth roughly £60m of EV, and it comes entirely from methodology, before anyone has an opinion about the business.

So treat WACC honestly:

  • A range, not a point. Present 9–11%, sensitised, and resist any output that flips sign or verdict inside that band.
  • Consistency beats precision. Nominal cash flows with nominal rates; same currency in flows and rate; tax in the flows or the shield, not double-counted; leverage in the re-levered beta consistent with the weights. Most real-world WACC errors are consistency errors, not estimation errors.
  • Watch for the dial being used as a dial. When a deal's DCF "works" at 9.0% WACC and 2.75% terminal growth and at no neighbouring cell, someone solved for the answer. ICs know this move; auditors know it; you should be able to spot it at fifty paces.

§4.5.5The mid-year convention

One genuine mechanical refinement, worth knowing because it's standard and because it shows up in diffs between models. Discounting year-1 FCF by a full year assumes all cash arrives on 31 December; in reality it arrives roughly evenly, on average mid-year. The mid-year convention discounts year ttt at (1+WACC)t−0.5(1+WACC)^{t-0.5}(1+WACC)t−0.5 instead of (1+WACC)t(1+WACC)^t(1+WACC)t.

Effect: every discount factor shrinks by half a year, scaling the whole valuation up by (1+WACC)0.5(1+WACC)^{0.5}(1+WACC)0.5 — at 10% WACC, a factor of 1.049, so Kestrel's £155.6m becomes ~£163.2m. Call it a ~5% uplift. It is more accurate for evenly-spread cash flows; it is also, in practice, a small seller-friendly button. The things to check: is it applied consistently to the terminal value (it should be), disclosed, and matched to reality (a business that collects everything in a year-end season shouldn't use it). If a banker's model is 5% above yours for no visible reason, look here first.

§4.5.6When DCF beats multiples — and vice versa

Neither method is "better"; they fail in different situations.

DCF earns its keep when:

  • There are no good comps — unusual business models, hybrid companies, niche infrastructure. Relative valuation needs relatives.
  • Cash flows are contracted or highly visible — concessions, PPAs, long-term leases, subscription books with known churn. Here the forecast is genuinely knowable, TV dominance shrinks (the asset may even be finite-life, killing TV entirely), and DCF is close to the answer.
  • The business is changing shape — heavy investment now, payoff later. Multiples on today's depressed earnings punish transition; a DCF can price it, if you believe the plan.
  • You suspect the whole market is mispriced. Comps import the market's mood; only an intrinsic method can disagree with it. (2007 vintage buyers who "validated" prices against each other's deals learned this expensively.)

Multiples win when:

  • Comparability is rich — mature sectors with many traded peers and frequent transactions. The market's aggregated judgement beats your spreadsheet's.
  • Forecasts are unreliable — cyclicals, early-stage, anything where year 3 is a guess. A DCF on garbage forecasts is garbage with more steps.
  • You need to transact. Deals clear at market prices. A DCF that says a business is worth 6x when every auction clears at 9x is an interesting essay, not a bid strategy.
  • Speed and communication matter. "8x EBITDA" travels through an IC, a bank, and an SPA in a way a 40-tab model doesn't.

§4.5.7Football fields and triangulation

Since every method is flawed differently, professionals run several and look for overlap. The standard exhibit is the football field: a chart with one horizontal bar per method, each bar spanning that method's value range, all on a common EV axis.

A typical field for a UK mid-market target:

Method Low (£m) High (£m)
Trading comps (8.0–9.0x LTM EBITDA) 160 180
Precedent transactions (9.0–10.5x) 180 210
DCF (WACC 9–11%, g 1.5–2.5%) 165 215
LBO ability-to-pay (target 2.5x MoM) 150 175

Reading it is the skill. Where do the bars overlap? Here roughly £165–180m — a credible central range. Which bar is the outlier and why? Precedents sit high (control premia and synergy-rich strategic deals — do those conditions apply to us?). The LBO bar sits low, as it usually does — it's a constraint, not an opinion (Lesson 6). What would you have to believe to pay £200m? Only the DCF's optimistic half and strategic-buyer precedents support it; if you're a financial buyer without synergies, the field is telling you £200m is someone else's price.

Triangulation is not averaging. Averaging four numbers launders judgement into arithmetic. The field is an argument: each bar is evidence with known biases, and the valuation conclusion is the range you can defend after weighing them — written down, with the weighing shown.

§4.5.8What deal teams actually ask

  • "TV percentage? Implied exit multiple?" — the two-question DCF audit, every time.
  • "Whose forecast, and what's their plan-vs-actual record?"
  • "Show me the deal at WACC +1% and growth −0.5%." If the recommendation dies, it was never alive.
  • "Mid-year convention on or off, and is theirs?" when reconciling to a counterparty's number.
  • "Where do the methods disagree, and why?" Disagreement between bars is information — usually about control, synergies, or market mood — not noise to be averaged away.

Carry Lesson 4's machine and this lesson's scepticism together, and a DCF becomes what it should be: the most honest way to have an argument about assumptions. The final lesson turns to how PE actually sets the number it will pay.

Lesson 4.6/Valuation

Valuation in a PE Context: What Can We Pay?

25 min read
In brief

How PE actually sets price: LBO ability-to-pay ("what can we pay and still make 2.5x"), entry multiple discipline, quality-of-earnings adjustments to the multiple base, comparing the methods' outputs, and rule-of-thumb multiple ranges by sector and size — including why small companies trade cheaper.

  1. 4.6.1PE asks a different question
  2. 4.6.2LBO ability-to-pay: the reverse valuation
  3. 4.6.3Entry multiple discipline
  4. 4.6.4Quality of earnings: fighting over the multiple base
  5. 4.6.5Comparing the methods' outputs
  6. 4.6.6Rule-of-thumb ranges by sector and size
  7. 4.6.7Why small companies trade cheaper
  8. 4.6.8What deal teams actually ask

§4.6.1PE asks a different question

Everything so far answered "what is this business worth?" A PE fund asks something subtly and importantly different: "what can we pay and still make our return?" The fund has promised its LPs a target — call it 2.5x money and a 20%+ IRR over a ~5-year hold — and every deal must underwrite to it. Valuation in PE is therefore a constraint satisfaction exercise: comps and DCF describe the market's price and the business's intrinsic worth, but the number that decides the bid comes out of the LBO model, run backwards.

This is why PE professionals can seem weirdly uninterested in DCFs. It's not that intrinsic value doesn't matter — it's that the fund's economics impose a harder test. A business can be genuinely worth 10x and still be a bad PE deal at 10x, if leverage, growth and exit assumptions can't turn 10x into 2.5x money.

§4.6.2LBO ability-to-pay: the reverse valuation

The mechanics — full detail in Module 7 — run like this. Fix the things you can defend, then solve for the entry price.

Worked example, £m. Target: industrial services, EBITDA today £15.0.

  1. Exit assumptions. Credible plan grows EBITDA to £20.0 by year 5. Exit multiple disciplined to entry — assume 8.0x (no expansion assumed; Lesson 2's rule). Exit EV = £160.0.
  2. Debt. Lenders will provide 4.0x EBITDA at entry = £60.0. Cash generation pays this down to £40.0 by exit. Exit equity = 160.0 − 40.0 = £120.0.
  3. Required return. Fund target 2.5x money. Maximum entry equity = 120.0 / 2.5 = £48.0.
  4. Ability to pay. Max entry EV = entry equity + entry debt = 48.0 + 60.0 = £108.0, i.e. 7.2x today's EBITDA.

If the auction is clearing at 8.5x (£127.5m), this fund is £19.5m short. Its options are exactly four, and every live deal discussion is some mix of them: believe more growth (EBITDA to £23m+ — can the plan really support it?); pay up and accept ~2.2x (does the IC bend?); find more leverage or cheaper capital (structuring, Module 8); or walk. What it cannot do is discover, in week six, that the multiple was never LBO-able. Running ability-to-pay before the first bid is the whole point.

Notice what this machine really is: a DCF where the discount rate is the fund's required return and the terminal value is the exit. All the Lesson 5 scepticism applies — the two assumptions doing the heavy lifting are EBITDA growth and the exit multiple, and the model rewards optimism in both. Discipline lives in the IC's standard challenges: exit ≤ entry multiple, leverage the debt market will actually provide, base case without multiple expansion.

§4.6.3Entry multiple discipline

Because returns decompose (Module 7) into EBITDA growth, deleveraging and multiple change, the entry multiple is the one lever fixed irreversibly on day one. Overpay by a turn and you spend the whole hold running to stand still: at £15m EBITDA, one turn is £15m — roughly a third of the equity cheque in the example above.

What discipline looks like in practice:

  • A house view on the multiple, independent of the auction. The comps range (Lesson 3) and ability-to-pay set a ceiling before price discovery starts; the auction then tests willpower, not analysis.
  • Underwriting the base, not the story. The multiple applies to adjusted EBITDA — see below — and to this year's, not a run-rate of a hoped-for year.
  • Paying for what exists, optioning what doesn't. Upside cases (new market entry, the big contract) are why you do the deal, not what you pay for. If the seller insists on being paid for the plan, structure it — earn-outs move price into the contingent future (Module 8).
  • Knowing when the discipline says walk. Funds are remembered for the deals they didn't do in 2007 and 2021. "We were outbid" is a fine sentence in an annual meeting; "we won it at 13x" often is not.

§4.6.4Quality of earnings: fighting over the multiple base

At 8x, every £1m of EBITDA is £8m of price — so the definition of EBITDA is worth exactly eight times as much argument as you'd naively expect. This is the quality of earnings (QoE) battleground, previewed here and fought properly in Module 9.

The seller presents "Adjusted EBITDA" — reported earnings plus add-backs for everything one-off, and strangely, the adjustments almost always point up. The buyer's QoE work re-cuts the base. A typical exchange, £m:

EBITDA bridge £m
Reported EBITDA (LTM) 15.0
Seller add-back: "one-off" legal costs +0.6
Seller add-back: pro-forma new contract at full run-rate +0.9
Seller's Adjusted EBITDA 16.5
Buyer: legal costs recur every year of the last three (0.6)
Buyer: run-rate contract not yet delivered a full quarter (0.9)
Buyer: one-off grant income in the base (0.8)
Buyer: under-market owner salary normalised (0.2)
Buyer's QoE-adjusted EBITDA 14.0

Same business, 18% apart on the base. At 8.0x that's the difference between £132m and £112m — £20m, likely more than the fee of every adviser on the deal combined. The practical rules: every add-back needs evidence (three years of history for "one-off" is a contradiction); run-rate credit needs delivery, not signature; and adjustments must be symmetric — a seller who normalises costs up must normalise windfalls down. When you hear "7.5x" and "8.5x" quoted for the same deal, the two sides are usually quoting the same price over different denominators.

§4.6.5Comparing the methods' outputs

From the PE seat, the Lesson 5 football field gets read with a specific grammar:

Method Range (£m) What it means to a PE buyer
Trading comps 8.0–9.0x on £14.0m QoE EBITDA 112–126 Where the market prices peers — context, and the seller's anchor
Precedent transactions 9.0–10.0x 126–140 What control has cost others — mostly strategics with synergies; a warning about the auction, not a target
DCF (9–11% WACC) 110–140 Sanity check on intrinsic worth; wide, TV-dominated
LBO ability-to-pay at 2.5x 100–115 The bid range

The LBO bar sits lowest, as it almost always does — a financial buyer with no synergies, paying with expensive equity and disciplined leverage, should have the lowest willingness-to-pay in the room. The deal is doable where the LBO bar overlaps the price the auction will clear: here, only at the bottom of the comps range, which tells you this deal is won on angle (a bolt-on thesis, an operational plan, a proprietary relationship) or not at all. When the LBO bar sits above comps, either you've found genuine mispricing — or, far more often, your model believes something the market doesn't. Re-check the model first.

§4.6.6Rule-of-thumb ranges by sector and size

Calibration matters: you should flinch at "14x for a contractor" before opening a spreadsheet. Indicative UK/European EV/EBITDA ranges for decent mid-market assets (moods shift with cycles; treat as anchors, not gospel):

Sector archetype Typical EV/EBITDA Why
Contract-backed software / SaaS 12–20x+ (often EV/ARR) Recurring revenue, ~90%+ retention, low capex
Healthcare services, pharma services 10–15x Non-cyclical demand, regulatory moats
Tech-enabled / professional services 8–12x Sticky clients, people risk
Industrial / testing / route-based services 7–10x Contracted but competitive, some cyclicality
Manufacturing / distribution 5–8x Capex-hungry, cyclical, low differentiation
Construction / project contracting 3–6x Lumpy, low-margin, working-capital sinks, tail risk

Within every sector, a size gradient: a £3m-EBITDA business might fetch 5–6x while a £30m-EBITDA peer in the same trade fetches 9x. This is the size discount, and it's the engine behind buy-and-build: acquire at small-company multiples, sell the aggregate at mid-market ones (Lesson 2's earned arbitrage; Module 10's playbook).

§4.6.7Why small companies trade cheaper

The size discount is rational, not a market inefficiency to be "captured" naively. Small companies carry more of everything bad:

  • Key-person risk. The founder is sales, the CFO is a bookkeeper, and the customer relationships live in two heads that may leave at completion.
  • Concentration. Three customers at 60% of revenue is normal at £3m EBITDA and would be a scandal at £30m. One loss and the equity story is over.
  • Data and controls. Unaudited accounts, no monthly management pack, QoE surprises positively correlated with time spent looking.
  • Financing. Lenders offer smaller businesses less leverage at wider margins, mechanically reducing every buyer's ability to pay (the £108m machine above, with worse inputs).
  • Buyer universe and liquidity. Fewer funds cover the size; exit routes are thinner; the eventual exit multiple carries the same discount unless the business has grown out of it.
  • Resilience. One bad quarter, one lost contract, one departed rainmaker — small businesses have no shock absorbers.

The professional summary: small companies are cheaper because their earnings deserve a lower multiple — riskier pounds, capitalised. The buy-and-build magic only works when integration genuinely fixes the risks (diversified customers, professional management, real reporting), so the assembled group has earned the bigger multiple. Stapling five key-person businesses together and calling the bundle institutional is the version that ends badly.

§4.6.8What deal teams actually ask

  • "What does the LBO say we can pay — and at what leverage and exit assumptions?" The first question on any new opportunity, usually answered on one page before an NDA is signed.
  • "What's the real EBITDA?" Reported, seller-adjusted, and QoE views, with the multiple quoted on each.
  • "Where does our number sit against comps and precedents — and if we're below the market, what's our angle for winning anyway?"
  • "Are we paying for the plan or the actuals?" If price only works on the forecast, structure the gap.
  • "What has to be true?" The IC's favourite: invert the model, list the beliefs the price requires — EBITDA to £20m, 8x exit, 4x leverage — and ask which you'd bet carry on.

That question — what has to be true — is where this module lands. Bridges, multiples, comps, DCFs and LBO models are all machines for turning beliefs into prices and back. The valuation skill PE actually pays for is running them in both directions: given a price, extract the beliefs it implies; then judge, with evidence, whether those beliefs are ones you'd own.

Lesson 5.1/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

What Private Equity Is

20 min readPrimer
In brief

What the private equity asset class is, the strategy spectrum from venture capital through growth equity to buyouts and special situations, why the model exists at all, and how a PE firm is actually organised from partners down to the ops and data teams.

  1. 5.1.1The asset class in one paragraph
  2. 5.1.2The strategy spectrum
  3. 5.1.3Why private equity exists
  4. 5.1.4How a PE firm is organised
  5. 5.1.5What looks good, what looks bad
  6. 5.1.6Where this module goes next

§5.1.1The asset class in one paragraph

Private equity is investing in companies whose shares do not trade on a public exchange, through funds that lock up investor money for around ten years. A PE firm raises a pool of capital from institutions, buys stakes in (usually) private companies, works on those companies for three to seven years, sells them, and returns the proceeds. The firm is paid a management fee for running the fund and a share of the profits — carried interest — for performing. That is the whole model. Everything else in this module is the machinery that makes it work.

The word "private" does the heavy lifting. Because the shares are illiquid, PE funds can take control, replace management, change strategy, and load the company with debt without a share price punishing them every quarter. Because investors cannot redeem, the fund can hold through a downturn rather than being forced to sell at the bottom. Illiquidity is not a bug the industry tolerates; it is the feature the returns are built on.

Scale check: the global PE industry manages several trillion pounds of assets, and buyout funds alone hold well over £1 trillion of committed-but-uninvested capital ("dry powder", covered in lesson 3). A single large-cap fund can exceed £15bn; a UK lower-mid-market fund might be £150m. The mechanics in this module apply to both — only the number of zeros changes.

§5.1.2The strategy spectrum

"Private equity" covers a spectrum of strategies that differ on three axes: company maturity, ownership stake, and use of leverage. Deal teams place any fund on this spectrum within seconds of hearing its name; you should be able to as well.

Strategy Company stage Typical stake Leverage Return driver Loss rate
Venture capital Pre-profit, often pre-revenue 10–25% minority None A few huge winners (power law) High — many zeros
Growth equity Revenue £10m+, growing 20%+ 20–40% minority Little or none Revenue growth Low-moderate
Buyout (LBO) Profitable, cash-generative 51–100% control 3–6x EBITDA of debt EBITDA growth, debt paydown, multiple Low, but each loss hurts
Special situations / distressed Stressed or broken Varies — often via debt Complex Buying below intrinsic value, fixing Moderate

Venture capital buys minority stakes in early-stage companies. The maths is a power law: a fund makes 25 investments expecting 15 to fail, 7 to return roughly their cost, and 2–3 to return 10–50x and carry the whole fund. No leverage — the companies have no cash flow to service debt.

Growth equity sits in the middle: minority stakes in profitable or near-profitable companies growing fast, where the cheque funds expansion rather than buying out existing shareholders. Downside protection often comes from preference structures (module 8) rather than control.

Buyouts are the centre of gravity of this course. A buyout fund acquires control of a profitable, cash-generative business, funds a large slice of the price with debt secured on the company itself, improves earnings, repays debt, and sells. A typical worked shape: buy a company making £20m EBITDA for 10x = £200m enterprise value, fund it with £110m debt and £90m equity, grow EBITDA to £28m over five years, repay £50m of debt, sell at 10x = £280m EV, so equity = £280m − £60m remaining debt = £220m: roughly 2.4x the £90m invested (220 ÷ 90 = 2.44). Module 7 unpacks that arithmetic properly; here the point is the shape — control, leverage, operational improvement, exit.

Special situations funds buy where something is broken: over-levered balance sheets, distressed sellers, carve-outs nobody wants, litigation-heavy assets. Returns come from buying well below intrinsic value and fixing the specific problem.

What deal teams actually ask when they hear a fund's name: where on the spectrum, what fund size, what cheque size, control or minority? Those four facts predict almost everything about how the firm behaves in a process.

§5.1.3Why private equity exists

A fair question: public markets are cheaper to access and liquid — why does anyone accept a ten-year lock-up and fat fees? Four reasons, in descending order of how much deal teams believe them.

1. Governance and alignment. A PE owner holds a concentrated, controlling stake, sits on the board, and can change the CEO in a week. Management is given meaningful equity (typically 5–15% of the upside via a management incentive plan) so a mediocre outcome hurts them and a great one makes them rich. Compare a FTSE 250 company whose largest shareholder owns 4% and whose board meets eight times a year. Concentrated ownership plus real incentives is the most defensible source of PE outperformance.

2. Leverage. Debt amplifies equity returns (and losses). If a company is bought for £100m with £60m debt and £40m equity and enterprise value rises just 20% to £120m with debt unchanged, equity is now £60m — up 50% on a 20% asset move. Leverage also imposes discipline: cash must go to interest and amortisation, not empire-building.

3. Access and information. PE buyers do months of due diligence with full access to the data room, management, and customers — far more than a public investor can obtain legally. They can buy businesses that are simply not available on exchanges: family successions, corporate carve-outs, founder exits.

4. Time arbitrage. A five-year hold lets an owner make investments that depress year-one earnings — new systems, salesforce build-outs, factory consolidation — that a quarterly-reported company struggles to justify.

Be honest about the counter-case, because sophisticated LPs are: net of fees, average PE funds have delivered returns close to leveraged public equity, and the illiquidity is real. The industry's pitch survives because top-quartile funds persistently outperform, and because the dispersion between good and bad managers is far wider than in public equities — which is exactly why fund selection, and everything in lessons 4–6 about fees and performance measurement, matters so much.

§5.1.4How a PE firm is organised

A PE firm is a surprisingly small business. A firm managing £1bn+ might employ 40–80 people. The hierarchy is steep and the titles are consistent across the industry:

  • Founding / Managing Partners own the management company, sit on the investment committee (IC), and hold the LP relationships. They decide what gets bought and who gets carry.
  • Partners / Managing Directors lead deals end-to-end: originate, negotiate, chair portfolio boards. Typically 8–15 years in.
  • Principals / Directors run deal execution day-to-day and are being tested for partnership.
  • Vice Presidents (VPs) manage the workstreams: coordinating advisers, running the model reviews, drafting IC papers.
  • Associates (usually ex-bankers or ex-consultants, 2–4 years' experience) build the models, crunch the data room, write the first draft of everything.
  • Analysts exist at larger firms; at smaller ones the associate is the bottom rung.

Around the deal ladder sit the functions that have grown fastest in the last decade:

  • Operating partners / portfolio team — former CEOs and functional experts who work inside portfolio companies on pricing, procurement, and 100-day plans (module 10).
  • Investor relations (IR) — runs fundraising and LP reporting.
  • Finance / fund operations — calculates capital calls, distributions, management fees, and the waterfall (lessons 2, 4, 5 are their day job).
  • Data and digital teams — increasingly central: deal-sourcing signals, portfolio KPI pipelines, board-pack automation, DD analytics. If you work in a PE data team, your customers are the deal teams and the portfolio team, and your raw material is everything in module 12.

A worked example of the economics that pay for all this. Take a firm managing two funds: Fund I, £500m, now year 7, with £300m of invested cost remaining at a 1.5% fee; Fund II, £700m, year 2, paying 2.0% on commitments. Annual fee income = (1.5% × £300m) + (2.0% × £700m) = £4.5m + £14m = £18.5m a year. That funds salaries, rent, and dead-deal costs for perhaps 50 people. The real prize is carried interest: if Fund II returns 2.0x on £700m, profit is £700m and the 20% carry pool is £140m, split among perhaps 15–25 carry-holders and paid out over years 6–10. Lesson 4 does this arithmetic properly.

§5.1.5What looks good, what looks bad

You can tell a lot about a firm before seeing a single deal. Deal teams and LPs read the same signals:

Looks good:

  • A stated strategy the track record actually matches — a "UK lower-mid-market buyout" firm whose last ten deals were UK companies at £5–15m EBITDA cheques.
  • Fund sizes growing steadily (£150m → £250m → £400m), not quadrupling — discipline about staying where the returns were earned.
  • Low senior-team turnover and carry shared beyond the founders; departures of the people who made the old track record are the classic hidden red flag.
  • Genuine operating capability, not two "senior advisers" on the website.

Looks bad:

  • Strategy drift: a buyout firm doing minority growth deals, or a £300m fund suddenly writing £80m cheques, usually means the fund was raised bigger than the opportunity set.
  • A track record built by two partners who have since left.
  • "Spray" portfolios of 25+ deals from a small team — nobody is minding the companies.
  • Vague answers about who is on the IC and how decisions are made.

§5.1.6Where this module goes next

You now have the map: an illiquid asset class, a spectrum of strategies with buyouts at the centre, a rationale built on governance, leverage, access, and time, and a small firm with steep hierarchy running the show. The next five lessons follow the money: who supplies the capital and on what terms (lesson 2), how a fund lives and dies over ten-plus years (lesson 3), how the GP gets paid (lesson 4), exactly how profits are split when cash comes back (lesson 5), and how anyone can tell whether the fund was any good (lesson 6). Keep the £500m fund from this lesson in mind — we will reuse it as the running example.

Lesson 5.2/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

LPs and GPs: Who Funds Private Equity and How

25 min read
In brief

Who the limited partners are and why they allocate to PE, the difference between committed and called capital, how capital calls and distributions actually work, the J-curve with a full worked cash-flow table, and the legal architecture of limited partnership, GP entity, and management company.

  1. 5.2.1The two parties: LP and GP
  2. 5.2.2Who the LPs are and why they bother
  3. 5.2.3Commitments, capital calls, and distributions
  4. 5.2.4The J-curve: a worked example
  5. 5.2.5The legal architecture: LP, GP entity, management company
  6. 5.2.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.2.1The two parties: LP and GP

Every PE fund has exactly two kinds of participant. The limited partners (LPs) supply almost all the capital, have limited liability, and — crucially — have essentially no say in investment decisions. The general partner (GP) supplies a small sliver of the capital, makes every decision, and bears unlimited liability (in theory; in practice the GP is a shell entity, as we'll see). "LP" and "GP" are legal terms from limited partnership law, but the industry uses them as shorthand for "the investors" and "the PE firm".

The relationship is governed by the Limited Partnership Agreement (LPA) — a 150-plus-page contract that sets the fund's life, the fee rate, the hurdle, the waterfall, what the GP is and isn't allowed to buy, and what happens if things go wrong. Most of lessons 3–5 is really a tour of the LPA's key clauses. Side letters give large LPs bespoke extras (fee discounts, co-invest rights, extra reporting) — a perennial governance grumble for smaller LPs.

The GP also invests its own money — the GP commitment, typically 1–5% of the fund. On a £500m fund a 2% GP commitment is £10m of the partners' own cash. LPs read this closely: 1% financed by a loan against future fees says one thing; 4% in cash from personal balance sheets says another. Skin in the game is the cheapest diligence signal an LP gets.

§5.2.2Who the LPs are and why they bother

The capital comes overwhelmingly from institutions managing other people's long-dated liabilities:

LP type Why PE fits Typical PE allocation
Public & corporate pension funds 30-year liabilities; can harvest the illiquidity premium 5–15% of assets
Sovereign wealth funds Effectively permanent capital; huge cheques 5–20%
University endowments & foundations Perpetual horizon; pioneered the model (Yale) 15–40%
Insurance companies Long liabilities, though regulation constrains them 2–8%
Funds of funds Aggregate small investors into diversified PE portfolios 100% (it's their product)
Family offices & wealthy individuals Return-seeking, flexible, faster decisions Varies widely

Why accept a ten-year lock-up? Because these investors do not need the money soon, and they believe (with fair evidence for top-quartile managers, weaker evidence on average) that PE returns beat public equities by a few hundred basis points net of fees. A pension fund paying benefits in 2050 gives up little by holding illiquid assets and, in exchange, collects the illiquidity premium plus access to the governance-and-leverage engine from lesson 1. Boards also appreciate that PE valuations move quarterly and smoothly rather than daily — economists call this "volatility laundering", allocators call it convenient.

What an LP diligences before committing: track record (net returns, realised vs unrealised, and whether the people who generated it are still there), strategy discipline, team stability and carry allocation, terms (fees, hurdle, waterfall — lessons 4–5), and operations (fund administration, valuation policy, LP reporting quality).

§5.2.3Commitments, capital calls, and distributions

Here is the mechanic that surprises everyone new to the industry: when an LP commits £10m to a fund, no money moves. A commitment is a contractual promise to wire cash when asked. The GP draws the money in instalments — capital calls (or "drawdowns") — as it needs it, deal by deal, fee payment by fee payment, typically on 10 business days' notice.

  • Committed capital: the total promise (£10m).
  • Called (paid-in) capital: the cumulative amount actually drawn to date.
  • Uncalled commitment (the LP's "unfunded"): committed minus called — still owed.

Worked example: an LP commits £10m. In year 1 the fund calls 25% (£2.5m) across three deals and a fee call. In year 2 it calls another £3.0m. Called capital is now £5.5m; the unfunded commitment is £4.5m. If the fund sells a company in year 3 and sends the LP £0.5m, that is a distribution — and note that (absent recycling, lesson 3) it does not reduce the £4.5m still callable. Distributions and commitments run on separate tracks.

This structure has teeth. An LP that fails to meet a call is in default, and LPAs impose brutal remedies — forfeiting up to the entire existing stake in the fund. So LPs must hold their unfunded commitments in reasonably liquid form, which drags on their overall returns; and in a crisis (2008–09) some LPs found themselves facing calls precisely when everything else in their portfolio was underwater. Managing "commitment pacing" — how much to commit each year so that calls and distributions roughly offset — is a real job in every LP organisation.

For the GP, uncalled capital is firepower. For the LP, the practical return question is not "what did the fund earn on my commitment?" but "what did it earn on my paid-in capital, and when?" — which is exactly what the metrics in lesson 6 (DPI, TVPI, IRR) measure.

§5.2.4The J-curve: a worked example

Plot an LP's cumulative net cash flow (distributions minus calls) over a fund's life and you get the industry's most famous shape: down for years, then (hopefully) up. The J-curve.

Take our LP's £10m commitment through a decent fund's full life:

Year Calls (£m) Distributions (£m) Net flow (£m) Cumulative net (£m) NAV (£m)
1 (2.5) – (2.5) (2.5) 2.2
2 (3.0) – (3.0) (5.5) 5.0
3 (2.5) 0.5 (2.0) (7.5) 7.6
4 (1.5) 1.5 0.0 (7.5) 9.0
5 (0.5) 2.5 2.0 (5.5) 8.5
6 – 3.5 3.5 (2.0) 6.5
7 – 4.0 4.0 2.0 3.5
8 – 3.0 3.0 5.0 1.5
9 – 1.5 1.5 6.5 0.5
10 – 1.0 1.0 7.5 –

Total called: £10.0m. Total distributed: £17.5m — a 1.75x net multiple on paid-in capital. But look at the path: the LP is out of pocket until year 7, hits maximum exposure of £7.5m in years 3–4, and only breaks even in cash terms when the fund is seven years old.

The J-curve is steepest in reported returns early on, for two mechanical reasons. First, management fees are drawn from day one — in year 1 our LP paid £0.2m of fees inside that £2.5m call while the investments were still at cost, so NAV (£2.2m) sits below paid-in capital and the interim IRR is sharply negative. Second, conservative valuation practice holds new deals at cost while any problems are written down promptly, so early marks skew negative. A three-year-old fund with a −5% IRR may be doing perfectly well; lesson 6 returns to why interim IRRs mislead.

What LPs do about the J-curve: commit steadily across vintage years so older funds' distributions fund younger funds' calls (a "self-financing" programme); buy stakes in mature funds on the secondaries market (which also prices the J-curve — buying at year 5 skips the worst of it); and tolerate GPs using subscription credit lines, which flatten the early curve cosmetically (lesson 6 covers the controversy).

§5.2.5The legal architecture: LP, GP entity, management company

"The fund" is not a company — it is a limited partnership, chosen for two properties: it is tax-transparent (profits flow through to investors and are taxed in their hands, vital for pension funds and international LPs), and it hard-wires the passive-LP/active-GP split. Common domiciles: England, Scotland, Delaware, Luxembourg, the Channel Islands and Cayman — Scottish limited partnerships are popular because they have separate legal personality.

Three entities matter, and the distinction is worth keeping straight because fees, carry, and liability each flow to a different one:

  1. The fund (limited partnership) — holds the investments. LPs are the limited partners.
  2. The GP entity — a special-purpose company that serves as the fund's general partner, carries the (theoretically unlimited) liability, and typically receives the carried interest. A fresh GP entity is created for each fund, ring-fencing liability fund by fund.
  3. The management company ("the manager", "the adviser" — the PE firm itself) — employs the people, pays the rent, and receives the management fee under an advisory agreement with the fund. This is the entity the partners own, and the one that persists across funds.

So when we say "the GP earns 2-and-20" (lesson 4): the 2% management fee is management-company revenue that pays salaries; the 20% carry accrues in the GP entity (usually via a "carry partnership" whose members are the individual partners and, at better firms, the wider team). Carry is typically structured to be taxed as capital gain rather than income — a large part of why the structure looks the way it does, and a recurring political football in both the UK and US.

One more layer you will meet in practice: funds often hold each portfolio company through a stack of holding companies (Topco/Midco/Bidco — module 8), and large LPs may invest through feeder vehicles or parallel funds for their own tax or regulatory reasons. The economics are as described here; the org chart on the structure slide is just plumbing.

§5.2.6What looks good, what looks bad

Looks good (through LP eyes): a GP commitment of 2%+ in cash; a diversified, stable LP base with high re-up rates from existing investors (the single strongest external signal — the people with the most information came back); clean pacing of calls; LPA terms close to market (ILPA-aligned); an experienced independent fund administrator.

Looks bad: a GP commitment funded entirely by fee waivers or loans; one LP making up 40% of the fund (concentration risk — if they wobble, the fund fails); heavy reliance on new LPs because past investors quietly declined to re-up; LP defaults in the prior fund; opaque or chronically late capital-call notices — sloppy fund ops is a leading indicator of sloppy everything else.

Next: the fund's timeline — fundraising, the investment period, harvest, and how a GP decides how many deals to do and at what size.

Lesson 5.3/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

The Fund Lifecycle

25 min read
In brief

The ten-plus-year life of a fund — fundraising, the investment period, harvest, and extensions — plus vintage years, dry powder, recycling, and how a GP constructs a portfolio: number of deals, cheque sizes, and reserves, with a worked £500m example.

  1. 5.3.1The shape of a fund's life
  2. 5.3.2Fundraising and closings
  3. 5.3.3The investment period
  4. 5.3.4Portfolio construction: a worked £500m fund
  5. 5.3.5Harvest, extensions, and the end of life
  6. 5.3.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.3.1The shape of a fund's life

A buyout fund is a machine with a timer. The LPA typically sets a ten-year term: roughly years 1–5 to buy companies (the investment period), years 4–10 to improve and sell them (the harvest period, overlapping because early deals exit while late deals are still being made), plus the option of extensions — usually two one-year extensions, the first at the GP's discretion, the second needing LP consent. In practice the average fund takes 12–14 years to fully wind up, a fact LPs grumble about constantly.

Overlay the fundraising cycle and a GP's decade looks like this: raise Fund II while investing Fund I; when Fund II is ~70–80% invested (often the LPA's own threshold before a successor fund may be raised), go to market with Fund III. A healthy firm therefore has two to three funds alive at once, each at a different stage — which is exactly the two-fund fee arithmetic we did in lesson 1. The flywheel only spins if exits from the old fund arrive in time to sell the track record for the new one. When exit markets freeze, fundraising freezes about eighteen months later; the whole industry's rhythm is downstream of the exit environment (module 11).

§5.3.2Fundraising and closings

Fundraising is a 12–24 month sales process run by the IR team and placement agents. The GP issues a private placement memorandum (PPM), LPs run due diligence, and commitments are gathered in stages called closings. At the first close the fund can legally start doing deals; further LPs join at subsequent closes until the final close, capped by the LPA's hard cap. LPs joining late pay an equalisation adjustment plus interest so everyone is treated as if they invested from day one.

Three terms deal teams use loosely but you should use precisely:

  • Target: the number on the cover of the PPM (say £500m).
  • Hard cap: the contractual maximum (say £600m). "Raised at hard cap in one close" is the industry's flex; "extended fundraising, final close below target" is the euphemism for a struggle.
  • Vintage year: the year the fund starts deploying — conventions vary (year of final close, first close, or first capital call), but a fund is benchmarked only against funds of the same vintage (lesson 6). Comparing a 2019-vintage fund with a 2021 vintage tells you about the markets, not the managers.

Vintage diversification matters because entry years dominate outcomes: funds that deployed into 2006–07 prices mostly limped; funds of the 2009–10 vintages, buying cheap into the recovery, were among the best ever. Since nobody can time this, disciplined LPs commit similar amounts every year and let the vintages average out.

§5.3.3The investment period

During the investment period (typically five years, sometimes four or six) the GP may call capital for new platform deals. When it ends — or earlier if the fund becomes fully invested — new-deal investing stops; thereafter capital may usually be called only for follow-on investments in existing companies, fees, and expenses. Two consequences flow from this clock:

Deployment pacing. A £500m fund with a five-year investment period needs to invest roughly £85–100m a year. Too slow, and the fund risks expiry with capital unspent and an IRR clock ticking on nothing; too fast, and the fund concentrates into a single price environment — 2021's frantic deployment into peak multiples is the cautionary tale. LPs scrutinise pacing in every quarterly report; a GP suddenly doing four deals in the final six months of its investment period is chasing the clock, and everyone knows it.

Dry powder. At any moment, committed-but-uncalled capital is the fund's dry powder. If our £500m fund has called £280m so far, dry powder is £220m — regardless of what distributions have been paid out, because (as lesson 2 established) distributions don't refill the uncalled pot. Industry-wide dry powder in the trillions is why competitive auctions stay competitive even in downturns: the money is contractually committed and fee-paying, so it will be spent.

Recycling. LPAs usually let the GP re-invest ("recycle") some early proceeds rather than distributing them — commonly capped at 10–25% of commitments, and often limited to proceeds from investments realised within, say, 18 months, or to recouping amounts used for fees. The point: on a £500m fund paying £68m of lifetime fees, only £432m would otherwise ever reach companies; recycling lets the GP get closer to putting the full £500m to work, which is good for LPs' money-multiple (more capital earning a return) at the price of slightly later cash back.

§5.3.4Portfolio construction: a worked £500m fund

Before the first deal, the GP has already decided the portfolio's shape, and pitched it to LPs. Let's construct our running £500m buyout fund properly.

Step 1 — investable capital. Lifetime fees and expenses (lesson 4 derives this): 2.0% on £500m for five years = £50m, then 1.5% on declining invested cost ≈ £18m, total £68m. Add ~£7m of partnership expenses and assume recycling recovers ~£25m of that; call investable capital £450m.

Step 2 — reserves. Hold back capital for follow-ons: equity injections for add-on acquisitions (module 10's buy-and-build), or defensive top-ups for companies in covenant trouble. Buyout funds typically reserve 10–20% of investable capital; VC funds far more (often ~50%, because winners get multiple rounds). Take 15%: reserves = £68m, leaving £382m for platforms.

Step 3 — number of deals and cheque size.

Design Platforms Avg equity cheque Implication
Concentrated 8 £48m Each deal ~10% of fund; one zero forfeits ~0.25x of expected TVPI
Chosen 12 £32m Each deal ~6–7% of fund; two failures survivable
Diffuse 20 £19m No deal moves the fund; team of 10 can't govern 20 boards

Twelve platforms at an average £32m equity cheque (£382m ÷ 12 ≈ £31.8m) is a classic mid-market shape: enough concentration that good deals matter, enough diversification that a failure doesn't sink the fund. Sanity-check the cheque against strategy: £32m of equity at ~50% loan-to-value buys an enterprise value around £65m — a company making roughly £8m EBITDA at 8x. If the firm's pipeline is actually £3m-EBITDA businesses, the fund is too big for its strategy; that mismatch is the strategy drift red flag from lesson 1.

Step 4 — pacing. Twelve platforms over five years is 2–3 deals a year — comfortably executable for a team of, say, four partners each leading roughly one deal every 18 months.

The failure-tolerance arithmetic LPs run: for the fund to return 2.0x gross, £450m invested must become £900m. If two £32m deals go to zero (£64m lost), the remaining £386m of cost must generate the full £900m — a 2.33x on everything else. Feasible. In the concentrated design, two £48m zeros would leave £354m of cost needing to produce the £900m — a 2.5x on every survivor. Heroic. This is why "how many deals, what cheque size, what reserves?" is the first page of every LP's underwriting.

§5.3.5Harvest, extensions, and the end of life

From roughly year 4, exits begin. The GP's job flips from buying to selling: exit readiness, timing, and route (trade sale, secondary buyout, IPO — module 11). Distributions flow through the waterfall (lesson 5) as each deal realises. A well-run fund is substantially realised by year 10.

Then reality: there are nearly always stragglers — the two companies that missed their plan and won't fetch an acceptable price. Options, in rising order of LP-relations difficulty:

  • Extensions: run the one- or two-year extensions; fees during extensions are typically reduced or zero.
  • Sell anyway: take the disappointing price and return cash. Often the right answer; chronically hard for GPs to do because it crystallises the bad mark.
  • Continuation vehicles: sell the asset(s) from the old fund into a new GP-managed vehicle funded by secondaries investors, giving old LPs a cash-out option. Now mainstream, but conflict-laden — the GP sits on both sides of the price — so expect fairness opinions and LP advisory committee votes.
  • Tail-end liquidation: distribute in kind or sell the rump portfolio to a secondaries buyer.

A "zombie fund" — past year 10, unsold assets, no successor fund coming, fees still trickling — is the worst outcome short of losses: the team has no carry incentive left and the LPs have no exit. LPs diligence a GP's previous fund tails for exactly this pattern.

§5.3.6What looks good, what looks bad

Looks good: steady deployment (roughly level annual investment across the period); cheque sizes consistent with the stated strategy and with the prior fund (adjusted for fund-size growth); reserves actually used for accretive follow-ons; funds substantially realised by year 10–12; successor funds raised on realised — not paper — track records.

Looks bad: a deployment cliff at the end of the investment period; fund size up 2.5x with the same team and strategy ("the fee motive"); repeated extensions with full fees; a continuation vehicle for the good assets priced by the GP itself without competitive tension; dry powder still above 40% in year 4 (either the market or the team isn't working); recycling used aggressively to inflate the invested-capital story.

Lesson 5.4/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Fees and Carried Interest

30 min read
In brief

How the GP gets paid: management fee mechanics including the committed-to-invested step-down, fee offsets, the 8% preferred return, the catch-up, and full worked 2-and-20 economics for a £500m fund showing exactly how a 2.5x gross becomes a 1.93x net.

  1. 5.4.1Two-and-twenty: the headline and the reality
  2. 5.4.2Management fee mechanics: the step-down
  3. 5.4.3Fee offsets and the other fee streams
  4. 5.4.4The hurdle: 8% preferred return
  5. 5.4.5The catch-up
  6. 5.4.6Full worked example: 2-and-20 on the £500m fund
  7. 5.4.7What looks good, what looks bad

§5.4.1Two-and-twenty: the headline and the reality

The famous formula: the GP charges a management fee of ~2% a year and keeps 20% of the profits as carried interest, usually above an 8% preferred return to LPs. "2-and-20" is a fine first approximation and wrong in every detail — the fee base changes over the fund's life, parts of it get offset, the 20% only switches on after a hurdle-and-catch-up mechanism, and the market rates vary by fund size and negotiating power (large buyout funds are often 1.5–1.75%; hot mid-market funds still get 2%; some GPs now offer 25–30% carry in exchange for a higher hurdle). This lesson builds each piece, then assembles the full economics of our £500m fund.

Keep the lesson-2 entity map in mind: the management fee is revenue of the management company (it pays salaries whether or not the fund performs), while carry is profit share flowing to the GP entity (it pays out only on success, usually years after the work). Fee pays the mortgage; carry builds the house.

§5.4.2Management fee mechanics: the step-down

The fee has two regimes, split at the end of the investment period:

  • During the investment period (years 1–5): a percentage of committed capital — the whole £500m, regardless of how little has been invested. Rationale: the team's cost of sourcing and executing scales with the mandate, not with capital deployed to date. Effect: the fee is at its maximum precisely when the fund has done the least, which is the engine of the J-curve from lesson 2.
  • After the investment period: the base steps down to invested capital — usually the cost basis of investments still held (sometimes called net invested capital; realised and written-off deals fall out of the base). Often the rate also drops (2.0% → 1.5–1.75%). Rationale: the job is now minding a shrinking portfolio.

Worked example for our £500m fund at 2.0% stepping to 1.5% on invested cost:

Years Basis Amount (£m) Rate Fee (£m)
1–5 Committed capital 500 2.0% 10.0 × 5 = 50.0
6 Invested cost 400 1.5% 6.00
7 Invested cost 350 1.5% 5.25
8 Invested cost 250 1.5% 3.75
9 Invested cost 150 1.5% 2.25
10 Invested cost 50 1.5% 0.75
Lifetime 68.0

£68m — 13.6% of commitments — goes to fees over the fund's life. That is capital LPs pay in but that never buys a company: only £432m of the £500m reaches deals (recycling can claw some back, lesson 3). When LPs say "fee drag", this is the number they mean, and it is why the step-down exists at all: without it (2% × £500m × 10 years = £100m, a fifth of the fund) the economics would be indefensible. A fund that charges on committed capital for the full term, or whose "invested capital" definition quietly includes realised deals, is taking £10–30m that market-standard terms would not allow — read the LPA definition, not the headline rate.

§5.4.3Fee offsets and the other fee streams

Historically GPs double-dipped: besides the management fee, they charged the portfolio companies transaction fees (1–2% of deal value for doing the deal), monitoring fees (annual "advisory" charges), directors' fees, and break fees on dead deals. Since LPs ultimately own those companies, these fees came out of LPs' pockets into the management company.

The fix is the management fee offset: a percentage of such fees is credited against the management fee. Market standard is now 100% offset (80% at laggards). Worked example: our GP charges a portfolio company a £2.0m transaction fee at closing. With a 100% offset, the next £2.0m of management fee otherwise due from LPs is cancelled — the GP is exactly indifferent, which is the point: offsets kill the incentive to milk portfolio companies. With an 80% offset, the GP keeps £0.4m and offsets £1.6m.

Still borne by LPs outside the fee: organisational expenses (fund set-up legals, typically capped ~£1–2m), partnership expenses (audit, admin, valuation), and broken-deal costs for transactions the fund pursued and lost — these can be material (£5m+ over a fund's life) and LPs increasingly demand disclosure. When you see "Total Expense Ratio" in an LP report, it is trying to capture all of this, not just the 2%.

§5.4.4The hurdle: 8% preferred return

Carry does not switch on at the first pound of profit. First, LPs must receive back their capital plus a preferred return — the hurdle — almost universally 8% a year, compounded, accruing on each drawdown from the date the cash left the LP until it comes back. The logic: 8% approximated what LPs could earn in liquid markets, so the GP should be paid for performance only above that opportunity cost. (Yes, the number has survived every interest-rate regime since the 1980s; it is a Schelling point, not a calculation. Credit funds use 6–7%; some VC funds have no hurdle at all.)

Two flavours matter:

  • Soft hurdle (with catch-up) — the overwhelming standard, described below: once the hurdle is cleared, the GP catches up so that carry ends up at 20% of all profits.
  • Hard hurdle — the GP earns carry only on profits above the hurdle, no catch-up. Much more LP-friendly, much rarer.

Because the pref compounds on actual drawdowns day by day, the entitlement in pounds depends on the fund's cash-flow timing — a fund that returns capital quickly accrues a smaller pref. For worked examples we will state the computed entitlement as an assumption and note the shape: £500m drawn over five years and returned over years 5–10 accrues a pref in the region of £150–200m.

§5.4.5The catch-up

After the pref, the standard waterfall inserts a GP catch-up tier: the GP receives 100% of distributions (an "100% catch-up"; some funds use 50%, which just stretches the tier) until the GP has received 20% of cumulative profits distributed so far. Then the split settles at 80/20.

The arithmetic everyone gets wrong the first time: if LPs have received a pref of £24m, the catch-up is not 20% × £24m = £4.8m. The GP catches up until GP receipts are 20% of total profit distributions. Let the catch-up be ccc: we need c=0.20×(24+c)c = 0.20 \times (24 + c)c=0.20×(24+c), so 0.8c=4.80.8c = 4.80.8c=4.8 and c=£6.0mc = £6.0mc=£6.0m. Check: total profits distributed £30m, GP has £6m — exactly 20%. General shortcut for a 100% catch-up: catch-up = pref ÷ 4 (because pref ÷ 0.8 × 0.2).

The effect of the whole pref-plus-catch-up mechanism: for a fund that comfortably clears the hurdle, the GP ends up with a straight 20% of total profits — the hurdle protects LPs only in mediocre outcomes, where it bites hard (a fund returning just above capital-plus-pref generates almost no carry). This "dead zone then cliff" is worth internalising: around the hurdle, small changes in fund outcome swing carry violently, which is exactly when GPs get creative about valuations and exit timing.

§5.4.6Full worked example: 2-and-20 on the £500m fund

Assemble everything. Assumptions: £500m committed and fully drawn; fees as computed (£68m, so £432m invested, no recycling); the portfolio returns 2.5x gross on invested capital; pref entitlement works out at £180m; 100% catch-up; 20% carry; whole-fund (European) waterfall — lesson 5 contrasts the alternative.

Gross proceeds = 2.5 × £432m = £1,080m. Fund profit over contributions = £1,080m − £500m = £580m.

Tier Rule Amount (£m) To LPs (£m) To GP (£m)
1. Return of capital 100% to LPs until £500m returned 500.0 500.0 –
2. Preferred return 100% to LPs until 8% pref paid 180.0 180.0 –
3. GP catch-up 100% to GP until GP has 20% of profits 45.0 – 45.0
4. 80/20 split Remaining proceeds 355.0 284.0 71.0
Total 1,080.0 964.0 116.0

Checks worth doing by hand every time: catch-up = 180 ÷ 4 = £45m, and after tier 3 the GP holds £45m of the £225m profits distributed = 20% ✓. Residual = 1,080 − 500 − 180 − 45 = £355m, split £284m/£71m ✓. Total carry £116m = 20% × £580m total profit ✓. Distributions total 964 + 116 = £1,080m ✓.

Now the scoreboard:

Measure Calculation Result
Gross multiple on invested capital 1,080 ÷ 432 2.50x
Gross multiple on committed capital 1,080 ÷ 500 2.16x
Net multiple to LPs (TVPI) 964 ÷ 500 1.93x
GP: lifetime management fee £68m
GP: carried interest 20% × 580 £116m
GP: total take 68 + 116 £184m

The one-line summary deal teams carry around: a 2.5x gross became a 1.93x net — roughly 0.6x of multiple, or about a quarter of the LPs' profit, absorbed by fees and carry. In IRR terms the same fund might be ~24% gross and ~17–18% net. The GP's £184m total take on a £500m fund also explains lesson 3's fee-motive warning about fund-size inflation: doubling the fund roughly doubles the fee stream regardless of performance.

§5.4.7What looks good, what looks bad

Looks good (LP lens): 2%/20%/8% with a step-down to invested cost and 100% offsets — boring, market-standard terms; carry spread across the team (retention); GP commitment 2%+ in cash; a GP willing to show net-of-everything track record without being asked.

Looks bad: fees on committed capital for the whole term; "invested capital" defined to include realised investments; offsets below 100% combined with active monitoring-fee charging; management fee waivers recharacterised as GP commitment (the GP contributes foregone fees instead of cash — less skin, plus tax games); no hurdle, or carry above 20% without a matching hurdle increase; heavy undisclosed broken-deal and travel expenses pushed to the fund.

Lesson 5.5/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Distribution Waterfalls

30 min read
In brief

How exit proceeds are split between LPs and GP: the four-tier waterfall, European (whole-fund) vs American (deal-by-deal) mechanics with full numeric tables on the same £100m fund, why the two converge in totals but differ in timing and risk, and how clawback and escrow protect LPs.

  1. 5.5.1What a waterfall is
  2. 5.5.2European (whole-fund) waterfall: worked example
  3. 5.5.3American (deal-by-deal) waterfall: worked example
  4. 5.5.4Clawback: the true-up, with numbers
  5. 5.5.5Escrow and other protections
  6. 5.5.6What looks good, what looks bad

§5.5.1What a waterfall is

When a portfolio company is sold, cash arrives at the fund and must be divided between LPs and the GP. The LPA prescribes the split as a sequence of tiers — each must fill completely before a drop reaches the next, hence waterfall. The standard four tiers, assembled in lesson 4:

  1. Return of capital — 100% to LPs until contributed capital is back.
  2. Preferred return — 100% to LPs until the 8% compounded pref is paid.
  3. GP catch-up — 100% to the GP until the GP holds 20% of profits distributed so far (catch-up = pref ÷ 4 under a 100% catch-up).
  4. Carry split — everything further 80% LPs / 20% GP.

The tiers are settled ground. The fight is over scope: is the waterfall applied to the fund as a whole, or deal by deal? That single choice — European (whole-fund) vs American (deal-by-deal) — determines when the GP first sees carry and who bears the risk of late losses. The names are conventional, not geographic (though European funds do mostly use whole-fund and US funds historically deal-by-deal).

§5.5.2European (whole-fund) waterfall: worked example

Under a whole-fund waterfall, tiers 1 and 2 apply to the entire fund's capital: the GP receives no carry until LPs have received back all contributed capital (every deal, plus fees) and the full preferred return. Early exit proceeds therefore go 100% to LPs.

Worked example. A £100m fund (all called) distributes £250m over its life. Assume the compounded 8% pref entitlement works out at £40m.

Tier Rule Amount (£m) To LPs (£m) To GP (£m)
1. Return of capital 100% LP until £100m 100.0 100.0 –
2. Preferred return 100% LP until pref paid 40.0 40.0 –
3. GP catch-up 100% GP until 20% of profits 10.0 – 10.0
4. 80/20 Balance 100.0 80.0 20.0
Total 250.0 220.0 30.0

Checks: catch-up = 40 ÷ 4 = £10m; after tier 3 the GP holds £10m of £50m profits distributed = 20% ✓. Balance = 250 − 100 − 40 − 10 = £100m ✓. Total carry £30m = 20% of the £150m fund profit ✓. LPs' 220 + GP's 30 = 250 ✓.

The defining feature is when tier 3 arrives. If this fund's exits ran £75m (year 3), £15m (year 4), £50m (year 5), £40m+ (years 6–8)… the first £140m of proceeds — the whole of the first two exits and most of the third — belongs entirely to LPs. The GP's first carry pound arrives around year 5, six-plus years after the work on the first deal began. LPs love this: maximum protection, no over-distribution risk. GPs point out the human consequence: associates and principals promised carry may wait a decade to see any of it, which is a genuine retention problem at younger firms.

§5.5.3American (deal-by-deal) waterfall: worked example

Under a deal-by-deal waterfall, the four tiers apply to each realised investment separately: when deal A exits, LPs get back deal A's capital plus a pref on it, and the GP takes carry on deal A's profit — even though deals B, C, D are still unrealised. Protections bolted on to stop this being a one-way bet: realised losses carry forward (a loss on any realised deal must be netted against later profits before more carry is paid — and prior carry recomputed), unreturned fees and expenses are typically included in the capital tier, and the whole thing is trued up at the end by the clawback (next section).

Same £100m fund, now as four £25m deals. To keep the table readable, assume each profitable deal's pref is met within the figures shown and focus on the loss-netting mechanics:

Exit Cost (£m) Proceeds (£m) Profit/(loss) (£m) Loss b/f applied (£m) Carry basis (£m) GP carry @20% (£m) To LPs (£m)
Yr 3: Deal A 25 75 50 – 50.0 10.0 65.0
Yr 4: Deal B 25 15 (10) – – – 15.0
Yr 5: Deal C 25 50 25 (10) 15.0 3.0 47.0
Yr 7: Deal D 25 40 15 – 15.0 3.0 37.0
Total 100 180 80 80.0 16.0 164.0

Walk it through: Deal A pays the GP £10m of carry in year 3. Deal B's £10m loss earns no carry and carries forward. Deal C's £25m profit is first reduced by B's loss, so carry is 20% × £15m = £3m. Deal D likewise. Total carry £16m — which is exactly 20% of the fund's £80m total profit, the same as a whole-fund waterfall would ultimately pay on these cash flows (run it: capital 100, pref say 30, catch-up 7.5, balance 42.5 → GP 7.5 + 8.5 = £16m).

So in a fund that ends up comfortably successful, the two waterfalls converge on the same total — the loss carryforward and final true-up force it. What differs is timing (here the GP has £10m in year 3 under American vs first carry around year 5 under European — worth millions in present-value terms to the GP) and risk: under American, the GP is holding LP money whenever early winners precede late losers. Which brings us to the clawback.

§5.5.4Clawback: the true-up, with numbers

Re-run the American fund with a worse ending: deals C and D each limp out at cost, £25m of proceeds apiece.

  • Proceeds: 75 + 15 + 25 + 25 = £140m on £100m — fund profit £40m.
  • Carry actually paid along the way: £10m on deal A (year 3); nothing on B, C, D.
  • Final whole-fund test (every American LPA has one): assume the fund-level pref entitlement is £35m. LPs are entitled to 100 + 35 = £135m before carry; above that, the catch-up tier applies. Total distributions were £140m, so the GP's true entitlement is the £5m above £135m (a partial catch-up — a full catch-up would have been 35 ÷ 4 = £8.75m, but only £5m of headroom exists).
  • The GP holds £10m but is entitled to £5m: clawback = £5m, repayable to LPs.

End state: LPs £135m, GP £5m, total £140m ✓. Note how the pref did real work here: without it, GP entitlement would have been 20% × £40m = £8m and the clawback only £2m. Around mediocre outcomes, the hurdle bites (lesson 4's "dead zone").

Why clawbacks are hated in practice, and only partly effective:

  • Tax leakage. Clawback obligations are almost always net of tax the carry-holders paid. If the GP partners paid ~£2.8m of tax on the £10m received, the recoverable amount shrinks toward £7.2m even before arguing. LPs may recover less than the gross over-distribution.
  • Collection risk. By year 12 the individuals who received the carry may have left, retired, divorced, or spent it. LPAs require several (sometimes joint) personal guarantees from carry-holders, but chasing ex-partners through the courts is nobody's plan A.
  • Timing. A clawback tested only at final liquidation can leave LPs out of pocket for years; better LPAs add interim clawback tests (e.g. at the end of the investment period, or whenever NAV coverage deteriorates).

§5.5.5Escrow and other protections

Because clawback is a lawsuit-shaped remedy, LPs prefer prevention:

  • Escrow / holdback: a slice of each carry distribution — commonly 20–50% under deal-by-deal waterfalls — is held in an escrow account until the fund's final numbers are safe. In our clawback example, a 50% escrow would have held £5m back from the deal-A carry, exactly covering the shortfall without touching anyone's bank account.
  • NAV coverage tests: carry may only be distributed if remaining NAV exceeds some multiple (say 125%) of unreturned capital — a live solvency check before each carry payment.
  • The European waterfall itself — the bluntest protection: if carry only flows after all capital plus pref is back, over-distribution is nearly impossible. This is why ILPA (the LP trade body) recommends whole-fund waterfalls as best practice, and why the market has drifted that way since 2008.

The negotiation logic to internalise: the GP wants early carry (American, low escrow, tax-net clawback); LPs want certainty (European, or American with fat escrow, interim tests, and several guarantees). Where a fund lands on this spectrum tells you precisely how much bargaining power the GP had at fundraise — hot funds get GP-friendly waterfalls.

§5.5.6What looks good, what looks bad

Looks good (LP lens): whole-fund waterfall, 8% compounded pref, 100% catch-up only after full capital-plus-pref, escrow on any early carry, interim clawback tests, joint-and-several guarantees, clawback gross of tax where achievable (rare). For the GP's team: carry vesting and allocation documented, so mid-level staff actually benefit — good for LPs too, via retention.

Looks bad: deal-by-deal carry with no loss carryforward on unrealised write-downs (paper losses ignored until crystallised — GPs can delay crystallising); low or no escrow; clawback net of a generously assumed tax rate; carry paid while NAV coverage is thin; "recycled" carry provisions letting the GP re-earn on the same profits. In diligence, LPs ask one killer question: "Has any of your prior funds had a clawback situation, and how was it resolved?" — the answer, and the willingness to answer, are both informative.

Next: measuring whether any of this was worth it — IRR, the multiple family, PME, and the tricks (subscription lines included) that flatter the numbers.
