Lesson 5.6/PE Industry & Fund Mechanics

Fund Performance Measurement

30 min read
In brief

How fund performance is measured and gamed: IRR vs the multiple family (TVPI, DPI, RVPI, MOIC), why interim IRRs mislead, public market equivalent (PME) basics, how LPs benchmark funds by vintage and quartile, and the IRR effect of subscription credit lines with worked numbers.

  1. 5.6.1Two families of metric
  2. 5.6.2The multiple family: TVPI, DPI, RVPI, MOIC
  3. 5.6.3Why interim IRRs mislead
  4. 5.6.4PME: benchmarking against public markets
  5. 5.6.5How LPs benchmark funds
  6. 5.6.6Subscription credit lines and the IRR effect
  7. 5.6.7What looks good, what looks bad

§5.6.1Two families of metric

Every question about fund performance is answered with one of two families:

  • Multiples — "how many times my money?" Simple ratios of cash and value to cash invested. Ignore time completely.
  • IRR — "at what annual rate?" The discount rate that sets the fund's dated cash flows (calls negative, distributions positive, closing NAV as a terminal inflow) to zero net present value. All about time.

Neither is sufficient alone. A 2.0x over four years is excellent (18.9% IRR — since 21/4=1.1892^{1/4} = 1.18921/4=1.189); the same 2.0x over ten years is pedestrian (7.2%). Conversely a 40% IRR on a deal held eight months that returned 1.25x barely moved the fund. LPs therefore always quote the pair: "net TVPI and net IRR", and deal teams keep the doubling table in their heads: 2.0x in 3 years ≈ 26%, in 4 years ≈ 19%, in 5 years ≈ 15%.

Always check gross vs net: gross is before management fees, expenses, and carry (deal-level performance); net is what LPs actually got. Lesson 4's fund ran 2.5x gross / 1.93x net — roughly 24% gross IRR landing at 17–18% net. Any track-record slide that doesn't say which is being quoted is quoting gross.

§5.6.2The multiple family: TVPI, DPI, RVPI, MOIC

All are anchored on paid-in capital (cumulative called capital, including fees). Worked example: a year-8 fund has called £400m, distributed £520m, and holds a residual portfolio at a NAV of £280m.

Metric Formula Calculation Result
DPI ("distributions to paid-in") Cumulative distributions ÷ paid-in 520 ÷ 400 1.30x
RVPI ("residual value to paid-in") NAV ÷ paid-in 280 ÷ 400 0.70x
TVPI ("total value to paid-in") (Distributions + NAV) ÷ paid-in 800 ÷ 400 2.00x

TVPI = DPI + RVPI, always. The decomposition is the point: this fund claims 2.0x, but only 1.3x is realised — cash in LP bank accounts — while 0.7x rests on the GP's own valuation marks. The older the fund, the more DPI should dominate. LP shorthand: "DPI is truth, RVPI is opinion, TVPI is the pitch." A nine-year-old fund boasting 2.2x TVPI with 0.4x DPI is telling you its winners are unsold — or unsellable.

MOIC (multiple of invested capital) is the same idea computed on invested cost rather than paid-in capital, and usually gross — deal teams use MOIC for deals ("a 3.1x MOIC on Project Falcon"), LPs use TVPI/DPI for funds. Because paid-in includes the fee load, net TVPI < gross MOIC for the same portfolio; sloppy decks blur this line, always ask which denominator.

§5.6.3Why interim IRRs mislead

The industry's dirty secret: a fund's IRR in years 1–5 is close to meaningless, yet that is precisely when the GP is fundraising on it. Four mechanical reasons:

  1. The J-curve (lesson 2): early fees on committed capital plus assets at cost push early IRR negative; nothing about final quality is revealed.
  2. Unrealised marks. Interim IRR treats current NAV as a cash inflow today. NAV is a GP-produced fair-value estimate — audited, but with genuine latitude (comparable multiples chosen, budgets believed). The IRR inherits every assumption.
  3. Small-base explosiveness. One early win annualises absurdly. A fund that returns 1.3x on its first small deal in 18 months prints a ~19% IRR (1.31/1.5=1.191.3^{1/1.5} = 1.191.31/1.5=1.19) on tiny capital; that number will drift down for a decade. Early top-quartile IRR has near-zero predictive power for final ranking — funds routinely swing two quartiles between years 3 and 10.
  4. Money-weighting quirks. IRR implicitly assumes interim distributions are reinvested at the IRR itself; a fund that returns capital fast can post a stellar IRR on modest total profit. You cannot eat IRR — a 30%-IRR fund with 1.5x DPI made LPs less money than a 17%-IRR fund at 2.1x.

The discipline LPs apply: judge funds younger than ~6 years mostly on deployment, entry discipline, and portfolio health, not IRR; from year 6, watch DPI converge on TVPI; treat any IRR quoted to one decimal place as false precision.

§5.6.4PME: benchmarking against public markets

An LP's real alternative was an index fund, so the sharpest question is: did this fund beat the public market on the same cash flows? Public Market Equivalent (PME) analyses answer it by replaying the fund's calls and distributions into a public index.

The cleanest version is Kaplan–Schoar PME: future-value every cash flow to today using the index's return, then compute KS-PME=FV(distributions)+NAVFV(contributions)\text{KS-PME} = \frac{FV(\text{distributions}) + \text{NAV}}{FV(\text{contributions})}KS-PME=FV(contributions)FV(distributions)+NAV​ A result above 1.0 means the fund beat the index; below 1.0, the LP paid fees for underperformance.

Worked example. An LP pays £100m into a fund at t=0; the fund distributes £250m at t=5 and holds nothing else. Over the same five years the chosen index returned 2.0x. The £100m contribution, had it gone into the index, would be worth £200m at t=5. KS-PME = 250 ÷ 200 = 1.25 — the fund delivered 25% more wealth than the index on identical timing. Had the index returned 2.6x, PME = 250 ÷ 260 = 0.96: a fund that proudly reported a 2.5x TVPI and ~20% IRR would still have destroyed value versus indexing — entirely possible in strong bull markets, and exactly why LPs run PME.

Practical notes: index choice moves the answer (small-cap or sector indices are fairer than the FTSE 100 for mid-market funds — and flattering index choice is a classic GP trick); variants (PME+, direct alpha) fix technical quirks; and PME on young funds inherits the same NAV-dependence as interim IRR.

§5.6.5How LPs benchmark funds

The standard machinery:

  • Vintage-year peer groups. A fund is ranked against funds of the same vintage, strategy, and geography, using databases such as Burgiss, Cambridge Associates, Preqin, or PitchBook. Quartile boundaries on net IRR and net TVPI are the lingua franca: "top quartile" means above the 25th-percentile boundary of that cohort.
  • Beware quartile arbitrage. With several benchmark providers, multiple metrics (IRR or TVPI), and choice of vintage assignment (first close vs first call), a middling fund can usually find some cut on which it is "top quartile" — which is why a comfortable majority of funds in market claim it. Diligent LPs recompute quartiles themselves on a consistent benchmark, and ask for the full cash-flow tape rather than summary numbers.
  • Persistence. The evidence: performance persistence across a GP's successive funds is real but has weakened over time, and is stronger at the bottom (bad managers stay bad) than the top. Hence the LP mantra: re-up decisions weigh team continuity and strategy discipline as much as the raw track record — the numbers were earned by specific people at a specific fund size.
  • Attribution. Sophisticated LPs decompose returns: how much from leverage, multiple expansion, and EBITDA growth (module 7's value-creation bridge); how concentrated in one or two deals ("take out your best deal, what's the fund?"); realised vs unrealised split.

§5.6.6Subscription credit lines and the IRR effect

A subscription credit line ("sub line") is a bank facility secured not on portfolio companies but on the LPs' uncalled commitments — the bank lends against the enforceability of capital calls. Original purpose: operational convenience — bridge a deal closing for a few weeks, then call capital once, quarterly, instead of pestering LPs deal by deal.

The modern controversy: GPs leave sub lines outstanding for 6–24 months, so LP capital goes in later and the measured IRR clock starts later. Worked example:

  • A deal costs £50m, is held five years, and returns £100m — a 2.0x. If LP capital funds it on day one, LP IRR = 21/5−1=14.9%2^{1/5} - 1 = 14.9\%21/5−1=14.9%.
  • Same deal, but a sub line funds the first 12 months and LP capital is called at the end of year 1: LPs' money is out for four years. LP IRR = 21/4−1=18.9%2^{1/4} - 1 = 18.9\%21/4−1=18.9%.

Four points of IRR conjured from financing mechanics, with the underlying deal identical. Meanwhile the interest cost (say 2–3% on the drawn line for a year, ~£1.2m here) comes out of proceeds, so the multiple falls slightly — LPs receive ~£98.8m, a 1.98x. Sub lines trade TVPI down for IRR up; since headline league tables run on IRR, GPs take that trade.

Second-order effects worth knowing: the 8% pref accrues from capital call dates, so delaying calls shrinks the pref entitlement and gets the GP to carry sooner — a genuine conflict-of-interest, not just cosmetics; early-fund IRRs become spectacular and meaningless (infinite, briefly, if distributions precede any call); and in a crisis a levered fund must still call the capital, into the teeth of LPs' own liquidity stress. ILPA guidance therefore asks GPs to report IRR both with and without the facility, cap size (typically 15–25% of commitments) and duration, and disclose costs. When comparing two funds' IRRs, the first diligence question is now: "what's your sub-line usage?" — an unlevered 16% can be better than a levered 18%.

§5.6.7What looks good, what looks bad

Looks good: net numbers volunteered alongside gross; DPI ≥ 1.0x by around year 7–8 and converging toward TVPI thereafter; returns broad-based across the portfolio rather than one hero deal; KS-PME comfortably above 1.0 on a fair index; conservative marks (exits consistently at or above last carrying value — the cleanest single test of valuation honesty); sub-line use disclosed with with/without IRRs.

Looks bad: TVPI-heavy, DPI-light "performance" late in fund life; IRR quoted gross, levered, and to one decimal; top-quartile claims that survive only on one metric from one provider; exits repeatedly below carrying value (marks were marketing); a track record whose authors have left; refusal to share the cash-flow tape. And the perennial: a GP fundraising on a three-year-old fund's 28% IRR — now you know all four reasons that number is a placeholder, not a result.

That completes the fund-mechanics toolkit: you can now read an LPA's economic terms, trace a pound from capital call to clawback, and interrogate any performance claim a GP makes.

Lesson 6.1/The Deal Lifecycle

Sourcing and Origination

22 min read
In brief

Where deals come from: proprietary vs intermediated origination, how sell-side advisors bring auctions to market, what teasers and CIMs contain and how to read them sceptically, NDAs, and why the quality of a fund's origination engine drives its returns.

  1. 6.1.1Where deals actually come from
  2. 6.1.2Proprietary vs intermediated: what the difference is worth
  3. 6.1.3Sell-side advisors and how auctions come to market
  4. 6.1.4The teaser: one page, no name
  5. 6.1.5NDAs: what you're actually agreeing to
  6. 6.1.6The CIM: what's in one
  7. 6.1.7How to read a CIM sceptically
  8. 6.1.8Why origination quality drives fund returns

§6.1.1Where deals actually come from

Before a deal team ever builds a model, someone had to find the deal. Origination is the top of the funnel, and it shapes everything downstream: the price you pay, the information you get, and the competition you face. Deals reach a PE fund through a handful of channels:

  • Intermediated (auction) deals — a sell-side advisor (an investment bank or M&A boutique) runs a structured sale process and invites multiple buyers. The large majority of mid-market and large-cap deals arrive this way.
  • Limited or targeted processes — the advisor approaches only three to six carefully chosen buyers, trading a little competitive tension for speed and confidentiality.
  • Proprietary deals — the fund finds the company itself: a partner's relationship with a founder, a thesis-driven outreach programme, a buy-and-build platform approaching bolt-on targets directly, or an introduction from an operating partner or portfolio CEO.

The word "proprietary" gets abused. A deal a banker showed to you first is not proprietary — it is early. A genuinely proprietary deal is one where no other buyer is at the table and no advisor is running a price-discovery process. These are rare, perhaps 10–20% of completed mid-market deals depending on the market, and they are prized because competition, not cleverness, is what sets price in an auction.

§6.1.2Proprietary vs intermediated: what the difference is worth

The economics are simple and brutal. In a competitive auction the clearing price is set by the most optimistic (or most desperate) credible bidder. In a proprietary deal the price is a negotiation anchored on the seller's alternatives.

Worked example. Target with £10m EBITDA. In a well-run auction, comparable businesses clear at 9.0x, so you pay £90m EV. Sourced proprietarily, the same business might be agreed at 7.5x — £75m EV — because the founder values certainty, speed, and the relationship, and no rival bid exists to push the price.

Assume both deals are funded 50% debt / 50% equity, EBITDA grows to £13m over five years, and you exit at 9.0x in both cases (exit EV £117m). Ignore cash sweep for simplicity:

Auction entry Proprietary entry
Entry EV £90.0m £75.0m
Entry equity £45.0m £37.5m
Debt (constant) £45.0m £37.5m
Exit EV (9.0x × £13m) £117.0m £117.0m
Exit equity £72.0m £79.5m
MOIC 1.6x 2.1x

Same company, same operational performance, and the proprietary entry adds half a turn of MOIC. That half-turn is why funds invest heavily in origination: sector teams that publish thought pieces to attract founders, dedicated business-development professionals who track thousands of companies, and CRM systems logging every banker meeting. It is also why "angle" matters even inside auctions — a fund with a genuine reason to pay more (synergies with a portfolio company, sector insight that de-risks the plan) or to be chosen at the same price (credibility with management, certainty of funds) wins better deals.

What deal teams actually ask when a new opportunity lands: How did this reach us? Who else is seeing it? Why are we advantaged here? If the honest answers are "broad auction, everyone, we're not", the bar for spending diligence money should be high.

§6.1.3Sell-side advisors and how auctions come to market

When an owner decides to sell — a founder retiring, a corporate divesting a division, or another PE fund exiting — they usually hire a sell-side advisor through a pitch (a "bake-off" between banks). The advisor's job is to maximise price and certainty, and their fee (typically 1–2% of deal value in the mid-market, with incentive ratchets above a target price) aligns them with the seller, not with you.

Before launch, the advisor spends six to twelve weeks on preparation: building the financial model, drafting marketing materials, often commissioning vendor due diligence (VDD) — a sell-side quality of earnings report and sometimes commercial and legal VDD — and grooming the numbers (more on scepticism below). They assemble a buyer list: trade buyers, PE funds, sometimes infrastructure or family offices, usually 30–80 names for a broad process.

The process then launches in a deliberate sequence: teaser out under codename, NDAs signed, CIM distributed, first-round bids, and so on (the full timetable is Lesson 2). Everything about the choreography — simultaneous deadlines, controlled information, codenames like "Project Falcon" — exists to create competitive tension and keep the seller's options open for as long as possible.

§6.1.4The teaser: one page, no name

The teaser is a one-to-two-page anonymous summary sent to the long buyer list before any NDA. It gives you just enough to decide whether to engage: sector, rough geography, a blind description ("a leading UK provider of mission-critical compliance software"), headline financials (revenue ~£40m, EBITDA ~£10m, growth ~15%), and the deal rationale.

Read teasers with a translator's eye. "Leading" means "we found one league table it tops". "Highly cash generative" is doing heavy lifting if capex is capitalised development spend. "Significant white-space opportunity" often means growth has already slowed. The teaser's real information content is: the sector, the size, and the fact that this business is for sale now — timing itself is a signal worth interrogating.

§6.1.5NDAs: what you're actually agreeing to

To get past the teaser you sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA, or confidentiality agreement). Standard terms: keep the information confidential, use it only to evaluate the transaction, and destroy or return it if you withdraw. Three clauses deserve real attention because they constrain your fund beyond this deal:

  • Non-solicitation of employees — typically 12–24 months. Fine in principle, but push for carve-outs for general recruitment advertising, or you have restricted hiring across your whole firm for a company you may never buy.
  • Standstill provisions — mostly relevant to listed targets; they bar you from buying shares or making unsolicited approaches.
  • Team separation / no-club clauses — sellers increasingly prohibit bidders from teaming up (forming consortia) or speaking to financing banks named to other bidders without consent, precisely to preserve competitive tension.

NDAs are negotiated by lawyers but scanned by the deal team; the practical question is always "what does this stop us doing later, and for how long?"

§6.1.6The CIM: what's in one

Once the NDA is signed you receive the Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM, also called the IM or, in Europe, the "info memo") — a 60–150 page marketing document. A typical structure:

  1. Executive summary — the deal in ten pages, always the most polished section.
  2. Investment highlights — six to eight bullet-form reasons to buy.
  3. Market overview — market size, growth, drivers, usually citing a commissioned market study.
  4. Business description — products, customers, operations, technology, sites.
  5. Organisation and management — org chart, leadership bios.
  6. Financials — historical P&L (usually three years), the current-year budget or forecast, a management projection ("the business plan"), and an adjusted EBITDA bridge reconciling statutory numbers to the headline figure.
  7. Transaction overview — what is being sold, process contact details.

Alongside the CIM you may get a financial fact book or the VDD report (sometimes only in round 2), and a model or data pack for larger processes.

§6.1.7How to read a CIM sceptically

A CIM is an advocacy document. Nothing in it is (usually) false — everything in it is selected. Your job is to reconstruct the unvarnished business from a varnished text. The places deal teams probe first:

The adjusted EBITDA bridge. Worked example — the CIM headlines "£12.0m adjusted EBITDA" for a business whose statutory accounts show £9.2m:

Bridge item £m
Statutory EBITDA 9.2
One-off legal dispute +0.8
Owner remuneration above market +0.6
"Run-rate" of price increases implemented in Q4 +0.9
Pro-forma synergies from a recent bolt-on +0.5
Adjusted EBITDA 12.0

At a 9.0x multiple, each £1m of add-backs is £9m of price. The legal cost may genuinely be one-off; owner remuneration is checkable against a market salary; but the run-rate price increase assumes zero volume loss, and pro-forma synergies are a plan, not a result. A sceptical reader banks perhaps £10.0–10.6m of that bridge, not £12.0m — and notes each weak add-back as a future price negotiation point.

Other classic tells:

  • Definitional games — revenue including pass-through costs; "recurring revenue" defined to include repeat-but-uncontracted purchases; gross margin flattered by reclassifying costs below the line.
  • The forecast hockey stick — three years of 6% growth, then a plan showing 15%. Ask what changed, and check whether the current year is tracking budget (ask for year-to-date trading versus budget — the single most revealing early request).
  • Customer concentration buried in an appendix — if the top-10 customer chart shows percentages but not names or contract terms, assume the biggest one is the problem.
  • What's missing — no mention of churn in a subscription business, no capex history in an industrial, no named competitors in the "fragmented market". Silence is data.
  • Why now? — sellers time exits. Selling just after two record years, ahead of a contract renewal, or before a regulatory change is rational for them and dangerous for you.

What looks good in a CIM: reconciliations that tie exactly to audited accounts, add-backs that are few and boring, a forecast the business is already beating, and disclosure of warts (a lost customer, a failed product) — sellers who disclose bad news early usually have less of it hidden.

§6.1.8Why origination quality drives fund returns

Zoom out from the single deal to the fund. A fund's gross return is roughly the average of its deals' MOICs, and entry price is the one lever fully in the fund's control at the moment of investment. Recall the worked example: a 1.5x-of-EBITDA saving at entry (7.5x vs 9.0x) turned a 1.6x deal into a 2.1x deal. Across a ten-deal fund, sourcing even three deals off-auction at that kind of discount moves fund-level gross MOIC by roughly 0.15x — often the difference between a second-quartile and first-quartile fund, and therefore between raising the next fund easily or not.

Origination quality also improves the information you buy with. Proprietary and early-look deals give you months with management instead of four hours; auction deals give you a data room curated by the other side. Funds systematise this: sector coverage models, tracked "priority target" lists reviewed quarterly, banker relationship programmes so they see auction deals early, and post-mortems on lost deals. For a data team, origination is one of the highest-leverage places to work — screening company databases, monitoring trigger events (founder age, fund hold periods of PE-owned targets, covenant stress), and measuring conversion through the funnel.

The judgement to carry into the next lesson: how a deal reached you tells you how to price it. A broad auction means paying close to full value, so returns must come from the plan, not the price — which raises the bar for everything the process now has to prove.

Lesson 6.2/The Deal Lifecycle

The Auction Process End-to-End

24 min read
In brief

The mechanics of a two-round auction: process letters, indicative offers (IOIs) and how binding they are, management presentations, data rooms, final offers and LOIs, and exclusivity — with a timeline of a typical four-month process and the seller-side tactics deployed at each stage.

  1. 6.2.1The shape of an auction
  2. 6.2.2Process letters: the rules of the game
  3. 6.2.3Round 1: the IOI
  4. 6.2.4The shortlist and round 2 access
  5. 6.2.5The data room and Q&A
  6. 6.2.6Round 2: final offers and the LOI
  7. 6.2.7Exclusivity: the buyer's prize, the seller's last card
  8. 6.2.8A typical four-month timetable — and the seller's tactics at each stage
  9. 6.2.9Pre-emption and process judo

§6.2.1The shape of an auction

A standard mid-market sale is a two-round auction. Round 1 filters a long list of interested parties down to a shortlist using cheap, indicative bids. Round 2 gives the shortlist expensive access — management, data room, advisor sessions — and demands near-binding final offers. The seller then picks a winner, grants (or refuses) exclusivity, and negotiates to signing.

Everything in the design serves one goal: keep multiple credible buyers competing for as long as possible while revealing as little as possible. Understanding the choreography from the seller's side is how a buyer avoids being played by it.

§6.2.2Process letters: the rules of the game

At each round the sell-side advisor issues a process letter — a formal letter setting out what bidders must submit, in what form, by when. A first-round process letter typically requires your indicative offer to state:

  • Value: enterprise value or a range, and the key assumptions behind it (cash-free debt-free basis, normalised working capital, the EBITDA figure you priced on).
  • Funding: how you will finance the deal — fund equity available, expected debt quantum, whether financing is a condition.
  • Approvals: your internal process (IC stage reached, what approvals remain) and any regulatory approvals you would trigger.
  • Diligence plan: what confirmatory work you would need and how long it would take.
  • Contact protocol: all contact through the advisor; approaching management or employees directly is grounds for exclusion.

The second-round letter adds the heavier asks: a markup of the seller's draft SPA, debt commitment letters from financing banks, equity commitment confirmation, and confirmation that diligence is complete or nearly so.

Process letters are not contracts — the seller almost always reserves the right to change the process, admit late bidders, or sell to anyone at any time. Read that reservation literally: it is used.

§6.2.3Round 1: the IOI

The first-round submission is an indicative offer or IOI (indication of interest) — usually a 3–8 page letter. Its core content:

Element What good looks like (from the seller's side)
Headline value A tight range, e.g. "£95–105m EV", not "£80–120m"
Basis Cash-free debt-free; states the EBITDA it capitalises, e.g. "9.5x FY25E EBITDA of £10.5m"
Funding Named debt providers already engaged; equity from a fund with dry powder
Conditionality Few conditions; diligence scope defined and short
Approvals "Fully approved by our Investment Committee to submit this offer"
Speed Ability to complete round 2 in 4–6 weeks

How binding is an IOI? It is not. It is expressly non-binding: a statement of intent, subject to diligence, financing, documentation, and internal approvals. No court will make you pay it. Its force is reputational and procedural: bid £105m in round 1 and cut to £88m in round 2 without new facts, and you will be dropped — and remembered by that advisor across future processes. Serial "bid high, chip late" behaviour genuinely damages a fund's deal flow.

That creates the round-1 pricing dilemma. Bid your true maximum and you have nowhere to go and may be overpaying to enter; bid low and you don't make the shortlist. The standard play is to bid at the top of the range your early work genuinely supports, state your EBITDA basis precisely (so any later reduction is attributable to their numbers disappointing, not your gamesmanship), and flag the two or three diligence items your price depends on. That paper trail is what makes a later price chip defensible.

§6.2.4The shortlist and round 2 access

The advisor scores round-1 bids on price, certainty, and credibility, and admits typically three to six parties to round 2. Now the seller starts spending real resources on you — and you on them. A round-2 budget for a £100m deal can easily reach £1.5–2.5m of adviser fees (financial, commercial, legal, tax, insurance diligence plus financing costs), most of it lost if you don't win. Aborted deal costs are why funds are selective about which auctions to enter at all.

Management presentations (MPs) are the set-piece: a half- or full-day session where the CEO and CFO present the business and take questions. What deal teams actually do with an MP: less fact-gathering (facts are in the data room) and more calibration — does the CFO know the numbers cold or defer to the advisor? Do answers to margin questions match the CIM? How does the team respond when challenged? A rehearsed CEO with a shaky CFO is a classic warning sign, because the plan's numbers live with the CFO. You typically also get expert sessions (product demos, site visits) and later, if you're a favoured bidder, smaller-group access.

Remember the seller coached this team for weeks. The MP is theatre with an information layer; treat unprompted disclosures as significant and polished sections as rehearsed.

§6.2.5The data room and Q&A

The virtual data room (VDR) opens with round 2: thousands of documents — statutory accounts, management accounts, contracts, employment terms, IP, litigation, tax. Access is logged; sellers literally monitor which bidders open which documents, and read effort as interest. Alongside it runs a formal Q&A process: written questions submitted through a portal, batched answers, often with per-bidder question limits (say 50 per week).

Practical craft for the buy-side:

  • Prioritise ruthlessly. Question limits mean each question must earn its place. Ask for data (monthly revenue by customer for 36 months), not opinions ("how sticky are customers?").
  • Triangulate. The data room shows what they chose to upload. Cross-check contract terms against the revenue recognition in the accounts; check the top-10 customer list against the debtors ledger.
  • Watch the gaps. A missing major contract, thin board minutes, or an empty "disputes" folder that later turns out to be non-empty — absence of documents is itself a finding, and worth a direct Q&A question ("please confirm no other material litigation exists").

§6.2.6Round 2: final offers and the LOI

The round-2 submission is the final offer — in US practice often wrapped in an LOI (letter of intent). It must be capable of acceptance with little further negotiation:

  • A single number, not a range, on a stated cash-free debt-free basis with a normalised working capital assumption.
  • A marked-up SPA — the seller circulated their draft sale and purchase agreement; your markup shows how much legal risk you are asking them to keep. A light markup is a price tool: fewer changes reads as more certain.
  • Debt commitment letters — financing banks committed on agreed terms ("certain funds" in UK/European practice), so financing is not a condition.
  • Equity commitment and evidence of full IC approval.
  • Remaining conditions: ideally only regulatory/antitrust ones.

Final offers are still formally non-binding until the SPA is signed (except where a process demands executable "sign-here" offers with the SPA agreed), but the space for walking away has narrowed to almost nothing that won't cost you reputationally. The real bid is now three-dimensional: price × certainty × speed. Sellers routinely take a slightly lower price from a bidder with no financing risk and a clean markup — certainty has a price, usually reckoned in low single-digit percentages of EV.

§6.2.7Exclusivity: the buyer's prize, the seller's last card

After final offers, the seller picks a preferred bidder and usually grants exclusivity: a contractual promise not to negotiate with others for a fixed window, typically 2–6 weeks, to let the winner finish confirmatory work and sign. This is the single biggest shift of leverage in the whole process — competitive tension, the seller's only real weapon, is switched off.

So sellers ration it: short windows with extensions only for demonstrated progress; sometimes "soft" exclusivity (a comfort letter, not a binding lock-up); occasionally a dual-track kept warm (a second bidder or an IPO ready if you falter). Buyers push the other way: no exclusivity, no final spend on lawyers and W&I. Once inside exclusivity, the buyer's leverage rises daily — the seller's process has gone cold and restarting it is costly and stigmatising — which is precisely why late, unjustified price chips ("re-trading") happen, and why sellers hate them and remember the funds that do it.

§6.2.8A typical four-month timetable — and the seller's tactics at each stage

Week Stage Seller-side tactic to watch
−8 to 0 Preparation: VDD, CIM drafting, buyer list Numbers groomed; adjusted EBITDA maximised; process timed just after strong results
0–2 Teaser out, NDAs negotiated Broad list creates the impression of deep interest; NDA terms tightened while you have least leverage
2–5 CIM distributed; early Q&A Advisor "guides" bidders on value expectations to anchor round-1 bids upward
5–6 Round 1: IOIs due Deadline pressure; hints that "the round is very competitive" (true or not — you cannot verify)
6–7 Shortlist chosen Ambiguity about how many are through ("a small number of parties") to keep tension
7–11 Round 2: MPs, data room, expert sessions Staged disclosure — sensitive data (customer names, pipeline detail) held back to the end; access rationed to favoured bidders
11–12 Draft SPA issued; W&I process started Seller-friendly draft plus stapled W&I sets the negotiating baseline
12–13 Final offers with SPA markups due "Best and final" that may not be final — a top-two bid-off ("we need you to sharpen your number") is common
13–14 Preferred bidder; exclusivity negotiated Exclusivity kept short; runner-up kept warm as leverage
14–17 Confirmatory diligence, SPA negotiation Time pressure inverted onto buyer: "sign by month-end or we go back to the market"
17 Signing —

Timelines stretch in practice — slippage of two to six weeks is normal, and a process that accelerates usually means a pre-empt is in play (below).

§6.2.9Pre-emption and process judo

The auction structure can be attacked. A confident buyer may offer a pre-emptive bid: a knockout price with full financing and a signable SPA, conditional on immediate exclusivity — paying up to avoid a bid-off at the end. Sellers accept when the price clears their expectations and the certainty is real; the buyer's calculus is that the premium paid is less than the price inflation a full round 2 would generate.

Conversely, when you lack an angle, the honest move is early withdrawal: round 2 costs £1.5m+ and a fund that enters every auction "to learn" burns money and credibility. The questions a deal team asks before committing to round 2 are always the same: Can we win this at a price that works? What is our angle versus the other likely bidders? What would need to be true, and can round 2 actually prove it? The next lesson covers the internal machine — the Investment Committee — that forces those questions to be answered in writing.

Lesson 6.3/The Deal Lifecycle

Inside the PE Firm — the IC Process

22 min read
In brief

How deals are approved inside a PE firm: screening memos and early looks, the structure of a full IC paper (thesis, market, financials, returns, risks), how investment committees challenge deals, staged capital approval tied to spend, and why most deals die — with the funnel numbers showing where.

  1. 6.3.1Why the IC exists
  2. 6.3.2Screening memos and early looks
  3. 6.3.3Staged capital approval: permission to spend, not just to buy
  4. 6.3.4Anatomy of an IC paper
  5. 6.3.5The returns section: what the IC actually stares at
  6. 6.3.6How ICs challenge deals
  7. 6.3.7Why most deals die — and where

§6.3.1Why the IC exists

While the auction runs outside, a parallel process runs inside the fund: the Investment Committee (IC). The IC — typically the firm's senior partners, sometimes with a rotating seat or an independent member — is the body that approves spending LP money, both the diligence budget and the equity cheque itself.

The IC exists because deal teams fall in love. After three months on a deal, the team has sunk cost, personal relationships with management, and a carry incentive to deploy. The IC is the institutional antidote: people with no time invested in this deal, pattern recognition from hundreds of others, and a mandate to ask the questions the team has stopped asking itself. LPs diligence a fund's IC process precisely because it is the firm's quality-control system; a fund where the founder can push deals through a rubber-stamp IC is a fund one bad vintage away from trouble.

The IC also matches the auction clock. Round-1 process letters ask what internal approvals you have; round-2 letters demand proof of full approval. A firm whose IC cadence cannot produce a real approval inside a four-month auction simply cannot compete for good deals.

§6.3.2Screening memos and early looks

Not every teaser deserves a meeting. The first internal artefact is the screening memo (or "one-pager"/"early look memo"): two to five pages produced in days, from the teaser, CIM executive summary, and desk research. It covers:

  • What the business does and its rough size (revenue, EBITDA, growth).
  • Fit with the fund's mandate: sector, cheque size, geography, control.
  • The two or three reasons this could be interesting — the embryonic thesis.
  • The two or three most likely killers — concentration, cyclicality, structural decline, a price expectation the maths can't reach.
  • A back-of-envelope return: entry at the guided multiple, plausible growth, standard leverage — does anything like 2.5x gross MOIC exist here?
  • A recommendation: pass, watch, or work it up.

The corresponding meeting is the early look — often a weekly pipeline meeting rather than the formal IC. Its purpose is to kill fast and cheaply. The most valuable output of a good screening process is a quick, well-reasoned "no": every deal that survives screening will consume partner time and, soon, real money.

What looks good at screening: a thesis you could state in two sentences and test with specific diligence. What looks bad: "attractive market, strong management, multiple levers" — a thesis so generic it fits every CIM ever written, which means the team hasn't found the actual reason to own this business.

§6.3.3Staged capital approval: permission to spend, not just to buy

The IC does not make one decision; it makes a sequence of escalating commitments, each unlocking the spend needed to reach the next. A typical staging for an auction deal:

Stage Auction moment What the IC approves Rough spend at risk
Screening / early look Teaser–CIM Team time to work it up Internal time only
First-round IC Before IOI Submit indicative offer in a price range; small advisor budget £50–150k
Second-round IC Entering round 2 Full diligence budget; engage advisors and financing banks £1.5–2.5m
Final IC Before binding offer Submit final offer up to a price ceiling; approve deal structure The equity cheque
Sign-off / closing approval Before signing Confirm no material adverse findings since final IC; execute —

Two design features matter. First, price discipline is set as a ceiling: the IC approves "up to 9.25x FY25 EBITDA of £10.5m, maximum EV £97m", and any bid above it requires going back. This stops the auction's endgame — the "sharpen your pencil" call at 11pm — from being decided by an adrenalised deal team alone. Second, spend is staged to information: the £2m diligence budget is only committed once the cheap questions have survived, which is what makes a wide funnel affordable.

§6.3.4Anatomy of an IC paper

The full IC paper for a final decision runs 30–80 pages plus appendices. Structures vary by firm, but the canonical skeleton is:

  1. Executive summary and thesis. One page stating the deal — "acquire X at up to £97m EV (9.25x), because A, B, C" — and the two or three beliefs the returns depend on. The best papers state the thesis falsifiably: "we believe churn is structurally below 5% because contracts embed switching costs; commercial DD tested this with 25 customer interviews."
  2. Transaction and process. How the deal arose, the auction dynamics, who else is bidding (as far as known), timetable, exclusivity position.
  3. Market. Size, growth, structure, competitive position — now grounded in the commercial DD findings rather than the CIM's commissioned study.
  4. Business and financials. Historicals with the team's own view of quality of earnings (which CIM add-backs were accepted and rejected), the management plan versus the IC base case — the team's more conservative operating model — and a downside case.
  5. Returns. Entry assumptions, sources and uses, leverage, and returns under each case, usually with a sensitivity grid (see below).
  6. Risks and mitigants. The honest list, each paired with a mitigant and with what diligence did to size it. ICs read this section first and judge the paper by whether the risks are real ones or straw men.
  7. Recommendation and conditions. The ask: approve up to £Xm, subject to the named outstanding confirmations.
  8. Appendices. DD report summaries, model outputs, structure charts, 100-day plan outline.

§6.3.5The returns section: what the IC actually stares at

Worked example of the core exhibit. Deal: entry EV £90m (9.0x × £10.0m EBITDA), funded with £45m debt and £45m equity. IC base case grows EBITDA to £13.0m by year 5 and repays £20m of debt (net debt £25m at exit). Management case reaches £15.0m.

Exit equity = exit multiple × exit EBITDA − net debt. At a 9.0x exit, base case: 9.0 × 13.0 − 25 = £92m equity on £45m invested = 2.0x MOIC, ~15% IRR over five years. The sensitivity grid shows how that survives the two big uncertainties:

MOIC on £45m equity Exit 8.0x Exit 9.0x Exit 10.0x
Exit EBITDA £11.0m 1.4x 1.6x 1.9x
Exit EBITDA £13.0m 1.8x 2.0x 2.3x
Exit EBITDA £15.0m 2.1x 2.4x 2.8x

(Check one cell: 8.0 × 11.0 = £88m EV − £25m net debt = £63m ÷ £45m = 1.4x.) The IC's reading: the plan needs to work (£13m) just to hit 2.0x at a flat exit multiple, and the downside-left cell still returns capital. If the base case already assumed multiple expansion to reach 2.0x, expect the paper to be sent back — paying 9.0x and underwriting a 10.0x exit is buying the return in the market, not the business.

§6.3.6How ICs challenge deals

Good ICs attack the paper's load-bearing assumptions, not its typos. The recurring questions, worth internalising because they are also your checklist as an author or analyst:

  • "Why do we win?" In a broad auction, what do we know or bring that the underbidders don't? "We like it" is not an angle; the winner's curse is the default.
  • "What must be true?" Which two or three assumptions carry the returns, and what evidence — not assertion — supports each?
  • "Why is the base case below the management plan by only 8%?" Haircuts should be justified line by line, not applied as a cosmetic percentage.
  • "What kills it?" Walk the downside: recession year 2, biggest customer lost, covenants — does the structure survive, and do we still get our money back?
  • "What did diligence change?" If £2m of diligence confirmed everything the team already believed, either the deal is unusually clean or the diligence was scoped to confirm rather than test.
  • "Are we the forced buyer?" End-of-fund-life deployment pressure, a sector team needing a deal — the IC polices the incentive problems the firm knows it has.

Mechanically, ICs manage dissent in different ways — some require unanimity, some a majority with the CIO holding a veto, some use devil's-advocate assignments or written pre-votes to stop anchoring on the senior partner's view. The output is rarely a flat yes: it is "yes, subject to" — a price ceiling, a structural requirement (say, a locked-box ticker cap or a specific indemnity), or named confirmatory items.

§6.3.7Why most deals die — and where

The funnel numbers are stark. A representative mid-market fund's year:

Stage Deals Survival to next stage
Opportunities logged (teasers, intros) 500 20%
Screened seriously (memo written) 100 30%
First-round bid submitted 30 40%
Round 2 entered 12 ~42%
Final binding offer made 5 40%
Deals closed 2 —

So roughly 0.4% of logged opportunities close, and even after the fund has spent seven figures in round 2, most of those deals still die. Where and why:

  • At screening (most deaths): mandate misfit, structurally challenged business, or price guidance the maths cannot reach. Cheap deaths — the system working.
  • After round 1: outbid, or early findings (a QofE red flag, a customer issue) break the thesis. Cost so far is small.
  • In round 2 (the expensive deaths): diligence contradicts the CIM — churn is 12% not 5%, the "run-rate" price rises leaked volume, the plan's margin bridge doesn't reconcile. Or the IC caps the price below the level round 2 reveals is needed to win. Losing a final bid-off after full spend is the worst routine outcome in the business.
  • After preferred bidder / in exclusivity (rare, ugly): confirmatory diligence finds something material, financing markets move, or SPA negotiation breaks down over risk allocation. Late deaths burn the most money and the most reputation on both sides.

The discipline to notice: a healthy fund's dead deals die early and for stated reasons. Deal-by-deal post-mortems ("what did we believe at IOI that turned out false?") feed back into screening quality. And a fund that closes everything it takes to final IC isn't disciplined — it is either brilliant at screening or, more likely, its IC has stopped saying no. Next lesson: what happens when the IC says yes and the deal sprints from preferred bidder to a signed SPA.

  3. 6.4.3The SPA: what it actually does
  4. 6.4.4Pricing mechanism 1: the locked box
  5. 6.4.5Pricing mechanism 2: completion accounts
  6. 6.4.6Warranties, indemnities, and W&I insurance
  7. 6.4.7MAC clauses and the signing–closing gap

§6.4.1The sprint: everything in parallel

Winning preferred bidder status starts the most intense phase of the deal: typically four to six weeks in which every workstream runs simultaneously, because exclusivity is short and each week inside it costs money and goodwill. The deal team becomes a project manager of advisors:

Workstream Who runs it Typical output Indicative cost (£100m deal)
Financial / QofE (confirmatory) Accounting firm Confirmed adjusted EBITDA, net debt and working capital analysis £300–500k
Commercial DD (confirmatory) Strategy consultancy Market model, customer references, plan validation £300–600k
Legal DD + SPA Law firm DD report, negotiated SPA and ancillaries £400–800k
Tax structuring Tax advisor Acquisition structure, tax DD report £100–250k
Debt financing Debt advisor + lenders Committed facilities, term sheets to full docs Fees mostly in debt pricing/OID
Insurance / W&I Broker + insurer W&I policy bound at signing Premium £0.5–1.5m
Management terms Deal team + lawyers Rollover and incentive package agreed —

"Confirmatory" is the key word: round 2 diligence built the thesis from data-room material; this phase verifies it — access to the auditors' files, customer calls that were previously forbidden, detailed tax and legal review. The findings feed directly into the SPA: a diligence issue either changes the price, becomes a warranty or indemnity, or is accepted as a risk. That triangle — price, protection, or acceptance — is the entire logic of the documentation phase.

§6.4.2Debt financing: staple vs self-arranged

An LBO needs committed debt at signing (in UK/European practice, "certain funds" — the seller will not sign against financing that can still fall away). Two routes:

Staple financing. The sell-side bank (or a lender it organises) offers a pre-packaged debt facility "stapled" to the deal — any winning bidder can use it. Indicative staple terms might be: 4.5x EBITDA of senior debt at SONIA + 5.5%, 2% arrangement fee. The staple serves the seller: it sets a floor on leverage every bidder can access (supporting price), signals the debt market's appetite, and speeds the process. For a buyer it is a useful benchmark and a fallback — but it is rarely the best available terms, and using the seller's bank as your lender leaks information about your bid economics.

Self-arranged financing. The buyer runs its own process: a debt advisor or the fund's capital markets team sends a financing pack to banks and private credit funds, takes term sheets, and negotiates. A competitive private credit process on the same deal might produce 5.0x at SONIA + 5.25% with cov-lite terms — half a turn more leverage and cheaper margin than the staple, because the lenders are competing for you rather than being handed the deal. The cost is management time and the risk of slower commitment.

In practice buyers do both: engage the staple to keep it honest, run their own track, and pick at commitment-letter time. What the deal team watches: total leverage, margin and fees, covenant package, the flex terms (the arranger's right to worsen pricing to syndicate the debt), and conditionality — the fewer conditions in the commitment letter, the stronger your "certain funds" position and your bid.

§6.4.3The SPA: what it actually does

The sale and purchase agreement (SPA) is the contract that transfers the shares. Its economic core answers three questions:

  1. What exactly is the price, and how does it adjust? (Pricing mechanism: locked box or completion accounts.)
  2. Who bears which risks about the past? (Warranties, indemnities, limitations, W&I insurance.)
  3. What must happen between signing and closing, and who bears risk in that gap? (Conditions precedent, covenants, MAC clauses.)

Everything else — 150 pages of it — is machinery for those three questions.

§6.4.4Pricing mechanism 1: the locked box

Offers are made on a cash-free, debt-free basis with normal working capital: you bid an enterprise value, and the equity price is EV minus net debt, adjusted for any working capital deviation. The mechanisms differ on when that calculation is fixed.

Under a locked box, the price is fixed off a historical balance sheet — the locked-box date — and does not adjust afterwards. Worked example:

  • EV agreed: £100m. Locked-box date: 31 December, using the audited balance sheet.
  • Net debt at 31 December: £30m; working capital at its normal level.
  • Equity price: £70m. Fixed. Completion happens on 30 June — six months later.

From the locked-box date, the business is run for the buyer's economic benefit: profits accrue to the buyer even before completion. Two consequences:

  • Value ticker. Because the buyer gets the profits but the seller waits for the money, the seller charges interest on the equity price — a "ticker" of, say, 8% per annum. Here: £70m × 8% × 6/12 = £2.8m, so the buyer pays £72.8m at completion. A sanity check deal teams run: the ticker rate should roughly match the business's cash generation — if the company will generate £4m of free cash in those six months, a £2.8m ticker still leaves the buyer ahead; a 12% ticker (£4.2m) would not.
  • Leakage. Since the price can't adjust, the seller must promise that no value has left the box since the locked-box date except agreed items. Leakage (dividends, above-market fees to the seller, asset transfers to affiliates) is repayable £ for £. Permitted leakage is the negotiated list of allowed items — e.g. a £0.4m monitoring fee to the exiting sponsor — which the buyer prices in.

Locked box gives price certainty (no post-closing true-up, no argument), favours sellers (they fix the price on numbers they prepared, and PE sellers love distributing clean proceeds with no escrow held back), and works best with an audited, recent balance sheet. Its risk to buyers grows with the gap: a stale locked-box date means months of unverified trading between the numbers you priced and the business you receive — plus more ticker. That is why buyers scrutinise current trading right up to signing, and resist boxes more than ~6–9 months old.

§6.4.5Pricing mechanism 2: completion accounts

Under completion accounts, the price adjusts to the actual balance sheet at completion. Worked example, same deal:

  • EV: £100m. At completion the seller delivers an estimate: net debt £30m, working capital at the agreed target (the "peg", set at normalised level, say £12m).
  • Buyer pays the estimated equity price at completion: £70m.
  • 60–90 days later, completion accounts are drawn up and (if disputed) settled by an independent expert. Actual net debt: £32m (a supplier payment was accelerated — or so the buyer argues). Actual working capital: £11m, i.e. £1m below the peg.
  • Adjustment: buyer overpaid £2m of net debt and received £1m less working capital → seller repays £3m; final equity price £67m.

Completion accounts price the business you actually receive — protection against deterioration and manipulation in the gap — but at the cost of a second negotiation after closing. The definitions become the battleground: is that customer prepayment "debt-like"? Are overdue creditors "working capital" or "debt"? Deal teams and their accountants fight line by line over the net debt and debt-like items schedule and the working capital peg (typically set off a 12-month average to neutralise seasonality). What looks bad: a seller pushing completion accounts and controlling the first draft and proposing loose definitions — that is an invitation to a £5m argument next quarter.

Choosing between them: UK/European PE sellers strongly prefer locked box (certainty, clean exit); US practice and corporate carve-outs lean to completion accounts (no clean historical balance sheet exists for a carve-out). Buyers accept a locked box when the accounts are audited, recent, and diligenced — and demand completion accounts when the box would be stale or the perimeter is being carved out.

§6.4.6Warranties, indemnities, and W&I insurance

Warranties are statements of fact about the business ("the accounts give a true and fair view", "no litigation except as disclosed"). If false and the buyer suffers loss, the buyer claims damages — subject to negotiated limitations: a cap (often 10–30% of price for business warranties in an uninsured deal), a time limit (18–24 months; longer for tax), de minimis and basket thresholds, and the disclosure letter — anything fairly disclosed against a warranty cannot be claimed on. Warranties do double duty: they allocate risk, and they flush out information, because sellers scrub the business to disclose against them.

Indemnities are stronger: a promise to repay a specific, identified loss £ for £ if it materialises ("the ongoing HMRC enquiry"), usually uncapped by the general limits and without needing to prove a warranty was breached. Diligence findings that are real but unquantifiable become indemnities; quantifiable ones become price reductions.

W&I insurance has transformed this market. A buy-side W&I policy means the buyer claims against an insurer, not the seller, for warranty breaches. Typical shape on a £100m deal: policy limit 10–30% of EV (say £20m), premium ~1–1.5% of the limit (£200–300k), an excess/retention around 0.5% of EV, and the seller's own liability capped at a nominal £1. Sellers — especially PE funds, who cannot hold contingent liabilities against a fund they want to wind up — increasingly staple a W&I policy to the process. The buyer's cautions: W&I excludes known issues (anything in the DD reports or disclosure letter — so it never substitutes for diligence), typically excludes forward-looking statements, some tax matters, and fraud; and a nominal seller cap means the warranties may be negotiated lazily ("warranty-light") since the seller no longer stands behind them. A thin policy limit with a £1 seller cap shifts essentially all residual risk to the buyer — which is a price point, and negotiable.

§6.4.7MAC clauses and the signing–closing gap

A material adverse change (MAC) clause lets the buyer walk away (or renegotiate) if something severe happens to the business between signing and closing. Sellers resist fiercely, and courts (especially in Delaware, but the logic travels) set the bar very high — a genuine MAC must be durationally significant and company-specific, with market- and sector-wide events usually carved out. Practical read: a MAC clause is a nuclear option, not a price-adjustment tool; in UK private deals a true MAC condition is relatively rare, and buyers protect the gap instead through pre-completion covenants — the seller must run the business in the ordinary course, not pay dividends (locked box leakage covers this too), not lose key contracts without consultation, etc.

§6.4.8Signing vs closing, and conditions precedent

Signing (exchange) is when the SPA becomes binding. Closing (completion) is when shares and money actually move. They separate whenever something must happen in between — the conditions precedent (CPs):

  • Regulatory: merger control clearance, foreign direct investment approvals (e.g. UK NSIA), sector regulator change-of-control consents (FCA for financial firms).
  • Occasionally: shareholder approvals, a key contract counterparty consent, a carve-out separation step.

Notably absent from a well-negotiated PE deal: financing conditions (certain funds) and diligence conditions (finished before signing). UK practice keeps CPs minimal; a simultaneous sign-and-close happens when no approvals are needed.

Between signing and closing the buyer holds a binding contract but not the company — typically 4–12 weeks, longer with complex antitrust. Risk in the gap is allocated by the CPs, the conduct covenants, any MAC, and sometimes break fees (reverse termination fees if the buyer's approvals fail). Once the last CP is satisfied, a completion date is set — and the deal moves to the mechanics of actually moving the money, which is the next lesson.

The judgement summary for this lesson: every diligence finding must land somewhere — price (chip or mechanism), protection (warranty, indemnity, W&I), or accepted risk (with the IC told explicitly). Deals go wrong when findings land nowhere.

↑ Module 6

Lesson 6.5/The Deal Lifecycle

Close and Beyond

20 min read
In brief

What happens at and after completion: satisfying regulatory conditions, the funds flow on completion day with a worked sources-and-uses table, day-1 readiness, and the handover from deal team to ownership that sets up value creation.

  1. 6.5.1Between signing and closing: clearing the conditions
  2. 6.5.2Completion day: the funds flow
  3. 6.5.3Day-1 readiness
  4. 6.5.4The post-completion tail
  5. 6.5.5The handover into ownership
  6. 6.5.6The deal lifecycle, seen whole

§6.5.1Between signing and closing: clearing the conditions

The SPA is signed; the press release is out; nobody owns anything yet. The weeks between signing and completion are about satisfying the conditions precedent — and almost all of the calendar risk sits with regulators:

  • Merger control. Most regimes are driven by turnover or share thresholds. A UK mid-market deal may need CMA consideration; deals with EU dimension go to the European Commission; a US nexus triggers HSR filing with its waiting period. A straightforward "Phase 1" clearance takes roughly 4–8 weeks from filing; a referral to Phase 2 adds months and real deal risk. PE deals are usually clean (funds rarely own direct competitors — though buy-and-build platforms increasingly do, and regulators have noticed roll-ups).
  • Foreign direct investment / national security. The UK's National Security and Investment Act (NSIA) makes notification mandatory in 17 sensitive sectors (defence, energy, data infrastructure, AI, and others) — closing without clearance where notification was mandatory makes the transaction void. Equivalent regimes exist almost everywhere (CFIUS in the US). Deal teams screen for this early because it catches deals that feel nowhere near "national security".
  • Sector regulators. Change-of-control consent from the FCA for regulated financial firms, Ofgem, Ofcom, the CQC in healthcare — often the slowest condition of all.

While lawyers chase clearances, the deal team runs the completion machine: agreeing the completion steps paper (a numbered choreography of every signature and payment), finalising the funds flow statement, satisfying the lenders' CP checklist (board resolutions, security documents, insurance certificates), and — in a completion accounts deal — receiving the seller's estimated net debt and working capital numbers that set the completion payment.

§6.5.2Completion day: the funds flow

Completion is, mechanically, a series of simultaneous payments executed against a pre-agreed funds flow statement — the single page every party's lawyers check to the penny. Continue the running example from Lesson 4: EV £100m, locked box with equity value £70m plus a £2.8m ticker; the target has £32m of gross bank debt (net debt £30m at the locked-box date after £2m of cash); management rolls £4.0m of its proceeds into the new structure; new senior facilities of £45m fund at close.

Funds flow at completion £m
Sources
Senior term loan (drawn at close) 45.0
Sponsor equity (fund) 60.3
Management rollover (applied to equity, non-cash) 4.0
Total sources 109.3
Uses
Cash to selling shareholders (£72.8m less £4.0m rolled) 68.8
Management rollover into NewCo equity (non-cash) 4.0
Repay existing bank debt (£32.0m) incl. break costs £0.5m 32.5
Debt arrangement fees (2% of £45m) 0.9
Advisory fees (financial, legal, tax, commercial DD) 2.4
W&I insurance premium 0.7
Total uses 109.3

Points a deal team (and its data team, who often build and check this table) verifies:

  • It balances. Sources = uses, exactly. The sponsor equity line is the plug — here £60.3m — and it is what the fund actually draws from LPs, so getting it wrong means an embarrassing same-day capital call correction.
  • The rollover is non-cash. Management's £4.0m never moves: it nets off what they are owed as sellers against what they subscribe as buyers. It appears on both sides of the table so the economics are visible.
  • Existing debt is repaid at completion via payoff letters from the incumbent lenders, who release their security the moment they are paid. The target's £2m of cash stays in the business — the buyer paid for it through the net debt deduction.
  • Fees are real uses of equity. Roughly £4.0m of this table (£0.9m + £2.4m + £0.7m) buys nothing but the deal itself — nearly 7% of the sponsor's cheque, which is why aborted processes hurt and why fee budgets are IC-approved.

The day itself is anticlimactic and tense in equal measure: a completion call, lawyers confirming receipt of each wire, the board resignations and appointments signed in sequence from the steps paper, and — often hours later than planned because a wire is stuck in an intermediary bank — confirmation that completion has occurred. Share transfers are registered, and the fund owns a company.

§6.5.3Day-1 readiness

At 9am the next morning, employees want to know if they still have jobs, customers read the press release, and suppliers wonder about their terms. Day-1 readiness is the workstream — planned in the signing-to-close window — that makes the first day boring:

  • Communications: sequenced announcements to employees (first), customers, suppliers, and press; the CEO's town hall; FAQ scripts for account managers facing customer questions.
  • Control basics: new bank mandates and payment authorities, board composition, delegated authority limits (what can management now spend without sponsor consent — typically formalised in a shareholders' agreement matrix), insurance switched over.
  • Carve-out mechanics where relevant: transitional services agreements (TSAs) live from day 1 — payroll, IT, invoicing still run by the seller for 6–18 months, priced and time-limited.
  • Reporting go-live: the lender reporting clock starts immediately (monthly or quarterly covenant reporting), and the fund's own monitoring cadence begins. For a data team this is the sharpest deadline: the KPI pack the deal team promised the IC has to exist within weeks, built from systems you first saw in a data room.

What looks bad on day 1: silence. Un-communicated ownership change breeds rumour, and the best employees and most nervous customers move first. What looks good: management announcing the deal with the sponsor, a concrete "nothing changes today, here's the plan for the next 90 days" message, and the first sponsor–management meeting already in the diary.

§6.5.4The post-completion tail

Completion does not quite end the transaction; three tails run for months afterwards, and someone has to own each one:

  • The completion accounts true-up (where that mechanism was used). The buyer — who now controls the books — prepares the completion accounts within 60–90 days; the seller reviews; disputes go to an independent expert whose decision is final. The arguments are always about definitions agreed months earlier: recall the Lesson 4 example where £2m of extra net debt and a £1m working capital shortfall moved £3m back from seller to buyer. Under a locked box there is no true-up, but the buyer's finance team still verifies that no leakage occurred — any dividend or non-permitted payment to the seller since the locked-box date is claimable £ for £, and the claim window (often 6–12 months) is short enough that the check must happen in the first close-down of the accounts.
  • Warranty and W&I windows. General warranty claims typically expire 18–24 months after completion, tax warranties after 4–7 years. Issues surfacing in the first two audits — a misstated debtor, an undisclosed dispute — need to be assessed against the disclosure letter and the W&I policy before the clock runs out. In practice most W&I claims are notified in year one, and the most common heads are accounts warranties and tax.
  • Fund mechanics. The equity cheque was drawn from LPs via a capital call shortly before completion; the deal now enters the fund's quarterly valuation cycle at cost, and the deal team writes the first quarterly report LPs will see. Under-drawn or over-drawn amounts (that funds flow plug again) are trued up in the next call.

§6.5.5The handover into ownership

The deal team that fought the auction now hands over to (or becomes part of) the ownership team, and the deal's centre of gravity shifts from buying well to running well. The bridge documents:

  • The IC paper becomes the value creation plan. The thesis, base case, and risk register were promises to the IC; the 100-day plan turns them into owned actions with names and dates — pricing review, procurement quick wins, the finance function upgrade, the first bolt-on pipeline.
  • Diligence reports become the operating manual's first draft. Commercial DD's customer interviews seed the sales strategy; QofE's working capital analysis becomes the cash management agenda; every risk the SPA couldn't price is now a management action.
  • The model becomes the budget. The IC base case is cut into the monthly board pack format: covenant headroom, KPI dashboard, 13-week cash flow if leverage is high.

Two governance artefacts formalise the new world: the shareholders' agreement (board seats, reserved matters, management leaver terms) and the board calendar (monthly packs, quarterly deep dives). The habits set in the first 100 days — reporting discipline, honesty about misses, the working relationship between CEO and sponsor — persist for the whole hold.

§6.5.6The deal lifecycle, seen whole

Step back across the module. A deal is a funnel of decisions under escalating commitment:

Phase Core question Money at risk
Sourcing Is this worth our time — and do we have an angle? Time
Round 1 What is it plausibly worth to us? Tens of £k
Round 2 / IC What must be true, and can we prove it? £1.5–2.5m
Exclusivity to signing Price, protection, or acceptance for every finding? Fees + reputation
Signing to close Clear the CPs, prepare day 1 The equity cheque
Ownership Deliver the plan the IC bought The fund's returns

The recurring discipline at every stage is the same: write down what you believe, attach evidence, and make the price and contract reflect it. Funds that do this lose auctions they should lose and win deals that work. The next module — Value Creation — picks up exactly where the funds flow ends: you own the company, the 100-day plan is on the table, and the return now has to be built rather than bought.

Lesson 7.1/LBOs & Returns Math

The LBO Idea: Buying With Borrowed Money

22 min read
In brief

Why buying a business with borrowed money amplifies equity returns: the house-purchase analogy done properly, a worked 0x vs 4x leverage comparison on the same business, why leverage cuts both ways, and the checklist that makes a business "LBO-able".

  1. 7.1.1The house analogy, done properly
  2. 7.1.2Same business, two capital structures
  3. 7.1.3Where the extra return comes from — and the mirror image
  4. 7.1.4Why targets need stable cash flows
  5. 7.1.5What makes a business "LBO-able"
  6. 7.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§7.1.1The house analogy, done properly

Everyone reaches for the house analogy, so let's do it with numbers and then be honest about where it breaks down.

You buy a house for £500k with a £400k mortgage and £100k of your own money. Five years later you sell it for £600k. The house went up 20% — but you didn't make 20%. After repaying the £400k mortgage you walk away with £200k on £100k invested: you doubled your money. A 20% asset return became a 100% equity return, because the lender's claim was fixed and every pound of upside above it belonged to you.

Now the honest part. The analogy breaks down in two ways, and both matter for LBOs:

  1. You paid the mortgage from your salary. The house didn't generate the cash to service its own debt. In an LBO, the business itself must produce the cash that pays interest and repays principal. That is the single most important difference — it's why LBO targets are screened on cash generation above almost everything else.
  2. The bank could repossess. If the house had fallen to £380k, your £100k would be gone entirely before the lender lost a penny. Leverage amplifies losses exactly as efficiently as it amplifies gains. Equity is the first-loss piece.

A leveraged buyout is precisely this structure applied to a company: a private equity fund buys a business using a large slug of debt (historically 50–70% of the price), secured on the business itself and serviced by the business's own cash flows. The fund's equity cheque covers the rest. At exit — typically 3 to 7 years later — the debt outstanding is repaid from proceeds and the equity keeps everything above it.

§7.1.2Same business, two capital structures

Take one business and buy it twice — once with no debt, once with leverage — and watch what happens to the equity return. The business: £10m EBITDA, bought at 8.0x, so an enterprise value of £80m. Over five years EBITDA grows to £13m and the exit multiple is unchanged at 8.0x, so exit EV is £104m. Same business, same operational outcome, same price discipline.

Case A — all equity. You write an £80m cheque. Case B — 4x leverage. You borrow £40m (4.0x EBITDA) and write a £40m cheque.

First pass: ignore cash generation entirely and assume the £40m of debt is still outstanding at exit (interest paid out of free cash flow, no repayment).

Case A: 0x leverage Case B: 4x leverage, no paydown
Entry EV £80m £80m
Debt — £40m
Equity invested £80m £40m
Exit EV (8.0x × £13m) £104m £104m
Less: debt at exit — (£40m)
Exit equity £104m £64m
MOIC 1.3x 1.6x
IRR (5 years) ~5% ~10%

The EV grew 30% in both cases. But in Case B that £24m of EV growth accrued to a £40m equity base instead of an £80m one — the fixed debt claim concentrated the gain.

Second pass: let the business's cash flow repay debt. Say the business generates roughly £5m a year of free cash flow after interest, all swept to repay principal — £25m over the hold, so debt at exit is £15m:

Case B with debt paydown
Exit EV £104m
Less: debt at exit (£15m)
Exit equity £89m
MOIC (on £40m) 2.2x
IRR (5 years) ~17%

Same business, same exit price. All-equity: 1.3x. Levered with paydown: 2.2x. The difference is the whole thesis of the asset class. (In Case A the cash the business generated would pile up on the balance sheet or be paid out as dividends, which lifts the all-equity return somewhat — but nowhere near enough to close the gap, because that cash isn't being applied against a fixed prior claim.)

§7.1.3Where the extra return comes from — and the mirror image

It's worth being precise about why Case B wins, because "leverage juices returns" is the kind of phrase people repeat without being able to defend in an interview.

  • A fixed claim concentrates upside. The lender's return is capped at interest. Every pound of EV growth above the debt belongs to a smaller equity base.
  • Debt paydown transfers value to equity. Each pound of principal repaid out of the company's cash flow converts enterprise value into equity value, pound for pound, even if the EV never moves. This is the "forced saving" effect — you'll meet it again as deleveraging in returns attribution.
  • Interest is (partly) tax-deductible, so the government subsidises a slice of the cost of debt — a real but second-order effect (and one that tax rules like the UK's corporate interest restriction now cap).

And the mirror image. Rerun the deal with a bad outcome: EBITDA falls to £8m and the buyer at exit only pays 7.0x — exit EV £56m. All-equity: £56m/£80m = 0.7x, a 30% loss, painful but survivable. Levered (assume weak cash flow meant no debt paydown): equity = £56m − £40m = £16m on £40m invested — 0.4x, a 60% loss. And if EV had fallen below £40m, the equity would be worth zero. Leverage doesn't create value; it amplifies whatever happens, in both directions, and it adds a failure mode the unlevered buyer doesn't have: running out of cash to service the debt before you ever get to exit.

§7.1.4Why targets need stable cash flows

Debt service is contractual. EBITDA is not.

A 4–5x levered business might pay 8–10% interest on its debt: on our £40m package that's £3–4m a year of interest before a pound of capex, tax, or working capital. If EBITDA is £10m and steady, that's comfortable. If EBITDA swings between £4m and £16m across a cycle — same average! — there will be years the business cannot cover interest, and the lenders, not the fund, then control what happens next: waived covenants for a fee at best; enforced security and a wiped-out equity cheque at worst.

This is why the LBO screen cares less about growth than about predictability:

  • Recurring or repeat revenue — contracts, subscriptions, maintenance, regulated income — beats project-based or cyclical revenue at the same margin.
  • High cash conversion — EBITDA that turns into cash. Low capex needs, low working capital absorption. A business that converts 80%+ of EBITDA to pre-interest free cash flow can carry far more debt than one at 40%.
  • Demonstrated resilience — what actually happened to revenue in the last downturn is worth more than any management assertion about defensiveness.

§7.1.5What makes a business "LBO-able"

The classic checklist a deal team runs, roughly in order of importance:

  1. Stable, predictable cash flows — see above. The load-bearing criterion.
  2. Strong market position / moat — pricing power and defensible share protect margins over a 5-year hold. Lenders read the same CIM the fund does.
  3. Low capex and working capital intensity — cash must be free to service debt, not trapped in machines and inventory.
  4. A believable value-creation angle — cost-out, pricing, buy-and-build, professionalisation. Leverage amplifies the plan; it isn't the plan.
  5. Deleveraging capacity — can the business plausibly repay a meaningful slug of debt over the hold? Lenders size the package off exactly this.
  6. Exitable — will there be a buyer at a sensible multiple in 5 years (trade, another sponsor, IPO)? A business nobody wants to own next is a bad LBO however cheap.
  7. A management team worth backing (or a clear plan to upgrade it).

What looks bad: heavy cyclicality, customer concentration (one customer = 40% of revenue is a lender's veto), structurally declining end markets, big lumpy capex programmes, businesses whose assets walk out of the door at night (pure people businesses carry less debt for a reason), and heavy existing lease or pension obligations that behave like debt already.

§7.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When a deal team first screens a target for leverage, the questions are concrete:

  • "What's the cash conversion?" — pre-interest free cash flow ÷ EBITDA. Above ~70–80% is attractive; below ~50% caps the debt the deal can carry.
  • "What did FY09/FY20 look like?" — the downturn test. A business that fell 5% in the GFC and recovered in a year supports far more leverage than one that fell 40%.
  • "How much debt will this carry?" — answered in turns of EBITDA (4x? 5x?), and driven by the two questions above plus the credit market's mood that quarter.
  • "Can we underwrite 2x on conservative assumptions?" — i.e. does the deal work with no multiple expansion and sensible growth, with leverage doing its share?

Keep the two-sided intuition from this lesson in your head permanently: leverage multiplies the equity consequences of everything else in the deal. The next lesson gives you the two numbers — MOIC and IRR — that measure those consequences.
