Lesson 8.3/Deal Structuring

Management Rollover and Incentives

25 min read
In brief

Why sellers and managers roll equity into the new deal, market norms for rollover percentages, good and bad leaver provisions, vesting, drag and tag rights, and ratchets — with a worked example of a ratchet kicking in above a 2.5x fund return hurdle.

  1. 8.3.1Why anyone rolls money back into the deal
  2. 8.3.2Leaver provisions: what you keep when you leave
  3. 8.3.3Drag, tag, and who controls the exit
  4. 8.3.4Ratchets: performance-linked equity splits
  5. 8.3.5What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.3.1Why anyone rolls money back into the deal

A rollover is when a seller — a founder, a management team in a secondary buyout, or an exiting sponsor's managers — takes part of their sale proceeds not in cash but in shares and loan notes of the new acquisition vehicle. On paper it looks odd: they just achieved liquidity and are immediately re-risking it. In practice rollover is close to universal wherever the sellers keep running the business, for four reasons:

  1. Alignment the buyer can believe. A founder who takes 100% cash and stays on as CEO is a walking red flag. Rolling 20-40% of proceeds says "I believe the plan I just sold you." Funds routinely make rollover a condition of the deal, not an option.
  2. The second bite of the cherry. Rolled equity participates in the next exit. A founder who rolls £16m into a deal that returns 2.5x turns that £16m into £40m — often comparable to the original cash-out. Sellers who have watched a buyer double the business they built once tend not to want to miss it twice.
  3. Bridging price gaps. Rollover reduces the cash the fund needs at close, which can support a higher headline price. £80m headline with £16m rolled costs the fund £16m less equity than £80m all-cash.
  4. Tax deferral. In the UK, a properly structured share-for-share exchange lets the seller defer capital gains tax on the rolled portion until the eventual exit (high-level framing only — this is specialist advice territory).

Market norms. Founders selling a majority typically roll 10-30% of gross proceeds. Management teams in secondary buyouts often roll 50% or more of their net (post-tax) proceeds — funds push hard here because these managers are the plan. Below ~10% the signalling value evaporates; above ~50% of net proceeds you start hearing legitimate complaints about concentration and personal risk.

The rolled money normally subscribes for the same institutional strip as the fund — 90/10 loan notes and ordinaries, pari passu (Lesson 2). Watch for exceptions: rollover into ordinaries only, or into a junior class of notes, quietly subordinates the seller.

§8.3.2Leaver provisions: what you keep when you leave

Management's equity is not just an investment; it is tied to their employment through leaver provisions, which force a departing manager to sell shares back and set the price. The standard taxonomy:

  • Good leaver — death, serious illness, retirement at plan, sometimes redundancy or departure "through no fault". Typically receives fair market value for vested shares.
  • Bad leaver — dismissal for cause, resignation to a competitor, breach of restrictive covenants. Typically receives the lower of cost and fair market value — i.e. at best their money back, and less if the equity is underwater.
  • Intermediate leaver (increasingly common) — voluntary resignation without aggravating factors. Often gets fair value on vested shares and cost on unvested.

The battleground is where plain resignation sits. Fund-friendly documents make any resignation before exit a bad-leaver event — a manager who serves four years, builds the value, then leaves for family reasons forfeits the upside. Management-friendly documents move resignation to intermediate status after a qualifying period. When you review a structure, read the leaver matrix before the ratchet: it determines whether the equity is really owned or merely dangled.

Vesting interacts with all of this. Sweet equity commonly vests over 3-5 years (straight-line, sometimes with a one-year cliff), or simply "at exit". Unvested shares go back at cost regardless of leaver status. Cliff-vesting everything at exit maximises retention but is brutal in year four; straight-line vesting is fairer but weakens the handcuffs. Note the asymmetry with the fund: the fund's strip never vests — vesting is a discipline applied only to the sweet.

§8.3.3Drag, tag, and who controls the exit

Two transfer provisions appear in every institutional shareholders' agreement:

  • Drag-along: if the fund (usually >50% of shares, sometimes defined as "investor majority") accepts an offer for the company, it can compel all other shareholders to sell on the same terms. Without drag, a 5% management holdout could block or tax a sale. For the fund this is non-negotiable: it must be able to deliver 100% of the company to a buyer.
  • Tag-along: the mirror image. If the fund sells its stake, minorities have the right to sell alongside it on the same terms. This protects management and rollover sellers from waking up with a new controlling shareholder they never chose, while the fund has cashed out.

The judgement points: drag thresholds (can the fund drag at a price where sweet equity gets nothing? usually yes — the waterfall, not the drag, is the protection); whether the drag requires the same form of consideration for everyone (cash for the fund, paper for management is a classic squeeze); and whether tag rights cover partial sales.

§8.3.4Ratchets: performance-linked equity splits

A ratchet adjusts management's share of the ordinary equity based on the fund's realised return. An upside ratchet says: "if the fund clears a hurdle, management's ordinary percentage steps up." It lets a fund concede more upside only in outcomes where it is already winning — a cheap concession at signing, valuable to management precisely in the scenarios they are aiming for.

Worked example. A fund invests £50m in the institutional strip. Management holds 15% of the ordinary shares, ratcheting to 20% if the fund's total return (loan notes plus its ordinary proceeds) reaches at least 2.5x. At exit, the loan notes including accrued PIK are worth £65m. Run two exits:

Exit 1 — equity proceeds £125m. Notes repaid £65m, leaving an ordinary pool of £60m. Test the hurdle at the pre-ratchet split (fund 85%): fund total = 65 + 0.85 × 60 = 65 + 51 = £116m, i.e. 2.32x on £50m. Below 2.5x — no ratchet. Management takes 15% × 60 = £9m; fund takes £116m. (Check: 116 + 9 = 125. ✓)

Exit 2 — equity proceeds £145m. Ordinary pool = 145 − 65 = £80m. Pre-ratchet fund total = 65 + 0.85 × 80 = 65 + 68 = £133m = 2.66x. Above 2.5x — ratchet triggers. Management's share steps up to 20%: management takes 0.20 × 80 = £16m instead of £12m; the fund takes 65 + 0.80 × 80 = £129m = 2.58x, still comfortably over the hurdle. (Check: 129 + 16 = 145. ✓) The ratchet moved £4m from fund to management, and the fund barely felt it — that is the design.

Two technical points deal teams always probe. First, circularity: if the hurdle is tested on the fund's post-ratchet return, the ratchet can pull the fund back below its own trigger. Documents handle this by testing pre-ratchet (as above), or by providing that the ratchet applies only to the extent the fund stays at or above the hurdle. Second, cliff edges: a single-step ratchet creates a discontinuity — here, at the trigger point management's proceeds jump by a third for £1 of extra price. Around the cliff, management and fund have distorted incentives on exit timing and price acceptance. Sliding-scale ratchets (e.g. 15% at 2.0x rising linearly to 20% at 3.0x) cost more drafting but behave far better.

Reverse ratchets exist too — management's percentage falls if performance disappoints — but they are rarer: taking equity off a struggling team mid-hold is usually counterproductive, and the sweet equity's option-like payoff already punishes underperformance.

§8.3.5What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

What looks good: rollover of 20-40% of proceeds by sellers who stay operationally involved, invested pari passu with the fund; a leaver matrix with a genuine intermediate category; vesting that is mostly earned by the expected exit date; drag and tag both present with same-terms, same-consideration language; ratchets that are sliding-scale and tested without circularity.

What looks bad: a departing founder rolling nothing while urging the buyer on; resignation-equals-bad-leaver with repurchase at cost after year four; drag rights exercisable with non-cash consideration for minorities only; single-cliff ratchets set exactly at the fund's base case (maximum incentive distortion at the most likely outcome); rollover sellers in a different, junior instrument to the fund.

What deal teams actually ask: "How much of the seller's net proceeds are going back in, and in what instrument?" and "Show me management's outcome if the CFO resigns in year three." The first question filters signalling from substance. The second forces the leaver matrix, vesting schedule and valuation mechanics to be read together — which is the only way they ever operate in real life.

Next we zoom in on the management incentive plan itself: how big the sweet pot should be, the envy ratio, option pools versus direct equity, and the tax framing that shapes all of it.

Lesson 8.4/Deal Structuring

Management Incentive Plans in Detail

25 min read
In brief

Sizing sweet equity, the envy ratio defined and computed, option pools versus direct equity, high-level UK tax framing (capital vs income), and what separates a MIP that motivates from the classic design mistakes that quietly demotivate a team.

  1. 8.4.1What a MIP is actually for
  2. 8.4.2Sizing the sweet pot
  3. 8.4.3The envy ratio: definition and worked computation
  4. 8.4.4Direct equity vs option pools
  5. 8.4.5Tax framing, at a high level
  6. 8.4.6What a well-designed MIP achieves — and the classic mistakes

§8.4.1What a MIP is actually for

A management incentive plan (MIP) is the package of equity instruments, prices and terms through which the operating team shares in the deal's outcome. Strip away the legal machinery and it has exactly three jobs:

  1. Motivate: make the difference between an average exit and a great one worth life-changing money to the people who determine which one happens.
  2. Retain: make leaving before the exit expensive (vesting, leaver terms — Lesson 3).
  3. Align: ensure management gets rich in the same scenarios the fund does — not in different ones, and not in none.

Everything else — envy ratios, hurdle instruments, pool sizes — is engineering in service of those three. A MIP that is generous but pays out in scenarios the fund doesn't care about has failed. So has one that is beautifully aligned but so stingy, or so far underwater, that the team mentally writes it off in year two. The most expensive MIP is the one nobody believes in.

§8.4.2Sizing the sweet pot

Recall the architecture from Lesson 2: the fund's money goes ~90% into loan notes, and the ordinary shares — the sweet equity — form a small pool that management buys into. Two dials set what management gets:

  • The pool percentage: management's share of the ordinary equity. UK mid-market norm is 10-20% of the ordinaries for the whole team (CEO commonly taking a third to a half of the management allocation), with the fund holding the rest.
  • The price: management subscribes at (or close to) the market value of the shares at completion. Because the ordinaries sit beneath a large loan-note claim, that market value is low — which is exactly what makes the equity "sweet". The cheque should still hurt a little: 0.5-1.5x annual salary per participant is the customary sanity range. Free equity aligns nobody and creates tax problems; equity that costs three years' salary creates resentment and personal-borrowing risk instead of motivation.

§8.4.3The envy ratio: definition and worked computation

The envy ratio is the standard single-number summary of how sweet the sweet equity is. Definition:

Envy ratio=institutional investment/institutional % of ordinary equitymanagement investment/management % of ordinary equity\text{Envy ratio} = \frac{\text{institutional investment} / \text{institutional \% of ordinary equity}}{\text{management investment} / \text{management \% of ordinary equity}}Envy ratio=management investment/management % of ordinary equityinstitutional investment/institutional % of ordinary equity​

In words: how much the fund pays per percentage point of the upside instrument, divided by how much management pays per percentage point. An envy ratio of 1 means management got no structural favour at all; higher numbers mean a sweeter deal for management (the fund "envies" their entry price).

Worked computation. A fund invests £36m in total — £34.8m of loan notes and £1.2m of ordinary shares — ending up with 80% of the ordinaries. Management invests £1.2m of their own cash for the other 20%.

  • Fund: £36m ÷ 80 = £0.45m per point of ordinary equity.
  • Management: £1.2m ÷ 20 = £0.06m per point.
  • Envy ratio = 0.45 / 0.06 = 7.5.

Management is buying upside participation at one-seventh and a half of the fund's effective price. The discount isn't charity — the fund's £34.8m of notes rank ahead and accrue a coupon, so the fund has bought protection while management bought pure risk. The envy ratio simply measures how that trade nets out.

Market norms: UK mid-market envy ratios typically land between 4 and 8, with competitive processes for strong teams pushing higher (10+ happens when a fund is desperate to win a management team's backing) and proprietary deals or nervous credit markets pushing lower. A ratio below ~3 will strike any experienced management adviser as mean; anything in double digits will make the fund's investment committee ask who negotiated it.

One caution: the envy ratio compresses a whole structure into one number and can be gamed. A high envy ratio alongside a 12% PIK coupon and a seven-year hold can leave management worse off than a modest ratio with an 8% coupon. Always run the waterfall (Lesson 2) at base case; never judge a MIP on envy alone.

§8.4.4Direct equity vs option pools

UK buyouts overwhelmingly use direct equity: managers buy real shares at completion with real money. US deals and earlier-stage companies lean more on options or profits interests. The trade-offs:

Direct sweet equity Option pool
Cash from managers Yes — skin in the game No (strike paid at exercise, often net-settled)
UK tax character Capital gains on growth (if structured properly) Unapproved options: gains taxed as income at exercise
Downside for managers Real — can lose the cheque None beyond opportunity cost
Flexibility for joiners Harder — new shares need valuing each time Easy — grant from the pool
Dilution mechanics Fixed at completion Pool overhang, top-ups possible

The UK preference for direct equity is largely tax-driven (next section) but also philosophical: funds want managers to have written a cheque they can lose. The practical weakness of direct equity is mid-hold hires — a CFO joining in year three must buy shares at current market value, which after two good years may be many times the entry price. Well-designed MIPs hold back an unallocated reserve of sweet equity (often 2-5% of the ordinaries, warehoused by the fund or an employee benefit trust) to bring joiners in without renegotiating the whole structure.

§8.4.5Tax framing, at a high level

No detailed tax advice here — every real MIP is structured with specialist advisers — but you cannot read UK structures without knowing the shape of the incentive:

  • Capital vs income is the whole game. Growth on shares a manager genuinely bought at market value is taxed as capital gains; UK CGT rates are materially below the top combined rates of income tax plus employee and employer National Insurance. The same economic gain, recharacterised as employment income, can lose roughly half its value and create employer NIC cost on top. This single distinction explains why UK MIPs are built from purchased shares rather than granted options or bonuses.
  • Entry price must be defensible. Because managers are employees, shares acquired cheap relative to market value are "employment-related securities" and the discount is taxable as income. Hence the ritual of valuing the sweet equity at completion — the thin ordinary slice under a big loan-note stack genuinely is worth little, and the valuation evidences it. Standard practice includes elections (in the UK, under s431) to pay any small income-tax cost upfront so that all future growth is capital.
  • The structure is doing tax work everywhere. The loan-note coupon, the split of rollover between notes and shares, and the leaver valuation mechanics all have tax consequences. When a term looks economically pointless, the explanation is usually tax.

The judgement point for a deal team is not the tax detail — it is noticing when a MIP's tax position is fragile (aggressive entry valuations, ratchets that HMRC might read as disguised bonuses) because fragile tax positions blow up at exit, mid-negotiation with a buyer, at the worst possible moment.

§8.4.6What a well-designed MIP achieves — and the classic mistakes

A good MIP produces sentences like this from the CEO, unprompted, in year two: "If we hit the plan, my equity is worth about £4m, and I check that maths every quarter." Concretely, a well-designed plan has:

  • Sweet equity in the money at the fund's base case with a meaningful margin — the team's realistic effort changes their outcome now, not only in dreamland;
  • cheques that are real but survivable for each participant;
  • an envy ratio and coupon inside market norms, so the plan survives a management adviser's review without poisoning the relationship;
  • a reserve pool for future hires;
  • leaver and vesting terms the team accepts as fair (Lesson 3); and
  • simplicity — the CFO can reproduce the payoff maths on one page.

The classic design mistakes, all field-tested ways to destroy value:

  1. Underwater by construction. A 10-12% PIK coupon on a big note stack plus a slipped exit timetable, and by year five the ordinaries need a stretch-case exit to be worth anything. The team knows it before the fund admits it; effort quietly reallocates to CVs.
  2. Cliff-everything. 100% exit vesting plus resignation-as-bad-leaver reads as distrust, and in year four it retains bodies, not minds.
  3. A pool sized for the org chart, not the plan. Spreading 15% across twenty-five managers gives nobody a motivating stake; concentrating it on three people leaves the next tier — often the operators who actually deliver — with nothing.
  4. No dry powder, so every senior hire triggers a renegotiation with all existing holders.
  5. Complexity as a weapon: multiple ratchets, catch-ups and hurdle instruments that only the fund's lawyers can model. If management needs an adviser to tell them what they'd make at 2.5x, alignment has already failed.

What deal teams actually ask: "What does the CFO personally make at base case, at 1.5x, and at zero — and does she know those numbers?" If the answers are respectively "meaningful", "something", and "loses her cheque", and she knows them cold, the MIP is doing its job. The case study for this module puts you on the other side of exactly that conversation.

Lesson 8.5/Deal Structuring

Earnouts, Deferred Consideration and Vendor Instruments

24 min read
In brief

When earnouts bridge valuation gaps, how to choose metrics and periods, why earnouts go wrong (measurement disputes and control), vendor loan notes and contingent structures in carve-outs — with a worked three-scenario earnout example.

  1. 8.5.1Not all consideration arrives at completion
  2. 8.5.2Earnouts: bridging the valuation gap
  3. 8.5.3A worked earnout
  4. 8.5.4Why earnouts go wrong
  5. 8.5.5Vendor loan notes and deferred consideration
  6. 8.5.6Contingent structures in carve-outs
  7. 8.5.7What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.5.1Not all consideration arrives at completion

So far the seller has been paid in two currencies: cash at close and rollover equity. There is a third family — consideration that is promised rather than paid, and sometimes conditional rather than certain:

  • Deferred consideration: a fixed amount payable later ("£10m on the second anniversary"). Certain in amount, uncertain only in credit — the seller is now an unsecured creditor of the buyer.
  • Earnout: a variable amount payable later, contingent on the business hitting defined targets. Uncertain in amount and credit.
  • Vendor loan notes: the seller formally lends part of the price back to the buyer, on documented terms with a coupon. Deferred consideration with paperwork and interest.

All three exist for the same underlying reason: the buyer and seller disagree about the future, or the buyer can't (or won't) fund the full price today. Structure lets the disagreement be priced instead of argued to a standstill.

§8.5.2Earnouts: bridging the valuation gap

The canonical earnout situation: the seller says "we'll do £10m of EBITDA next year, pay me for it"; the buyer says "you did £7m last year, I'll pay for that". An earnout converts the argument into a bet both sides can accept — the buyer pays for the £10m only if it shows up. Earnouts appear most often where uncertainty is concentrated and near-term: founder-led businesses with customer concentration, businesses mid-way through a big contract win, pharma and services businesses with pipeline risk, and — critically for PE — carve-outs whose standalone economics are unproven.

Metric choice is the central design decision. Revenue is hard to manipulate downward but rewards unprofitable growth; EBITDA measures what the buyer actually bought but is riddled with definitional judgement (which overheads? whose accounting policies? what about the integration costs the buyer chooses to incur?); gross profit sits usefully between the two. Non-financial milestones (regulatory approval, contract renewal) work when they are genuinely binary. The rule: pick the metric the seller can still influence and the buyer cannot easily distort, and define it in an appendix with worked examples, not a one-liner.

Period: one to three years is the norm. Shorter periods keep the numbers attributable to the seller's business; anything longer means the result reflects the buyer's ownership more than the seller's machine, and the seller is taking equity-like risk without equity-like upside.

§8.5.3A worked earnout

Sale of Fernway Ltd: £50m at completion, plus an earnout of £2 for every £1 of FY2 EBITDA above £8m, capped at £10m. (FY2 EBITDA as defined in the SPA schedule — same accounting policies as the locked-box accounts, before buyer integration costs.) Three outcomes:

Scenario FY2 EBITDA Excess over £8m Earnout (2x excess, cap £10m) Total consideration
Miss 7.5 — 0.0 50.0
Partial 9.5 1.5 3.0 53.0
Beat 13.5 5.5 10.0 (11.0 capped) 60.0

Read it from both chairs. The seller's story was "this is a £10m EBITDA business worth £60m"; the buyer's was "it's £8m and worth £50m". The earnout pays the seller's price only on the seller's numbers — at £9.5m of EBITDA the total lands in between, and the marginal price of 2x per incremental £1 of EBITDA is far below the ~6x multiple the headline implies, which is why buyers concede earnout formulas more readily than headline price. Note the cap: without it, the £13.5m blow-out year would cost the buyer £11m, and open-ended earnouts make lenders and investment committees equally nervous.

A modelling habit: always express the earnout's expected cost across scenarios, not just the cap. A buyer who probability-weights these three scenarios at 30/50/20 is really paying 50+0.3(0)+0.5(3)+0.2(10)=£53.5m50 + 0.3(0) + 0.5(3) + 0.2(10) = £53.5m50+0.3(0)+0.5(3)+0.2(10)=£53.5m — that, not £50m or £60m, is the number to compare against other bids.

§8.5.4Why earnouts go wrong

Earnouts have a deserved reputation as litigation machines. The two root causes:

Measurement. The seller's £9.6m and the buyer's £8.9m can both be "FY2 EBITDA", separated by accounting-policy choices, management charges from the new parent, bonus accruals, and the allocation of group overheads. Every one of those is decided after completion, mostly by the buyer. Mitigations: freeze accounting policies by reference to a worked schedule; exclude buyer-controlled costs (integration, management fees) from the definition; give the seller audit and information rights; appoint an independent expert, not a court, for disputes.

Control. The buyer runs the business during the earnout period and can — through entirely defensible commercial decisions — depress the metric: delaying a product launch, merging the sales force, moving a big customer onto a group contract, loading the entity with group costs. Sellers negotiate conduct covenants ("operate the business consistent with past practice; don't divert customers or opportunities"), but these sit awkwardly against the buyer's need to actually integrate and run the company. This tension is structural, not drafting error — which is why the best earnouts are short, simple, and sized so that neither side is tempted to burn the relationship over them. A deal where the earnout is 40% of total consideration and the seller-CEO reports to an integration director is a dispute with a completion date.

For the fund there is a quieter problem: an earnout is effectively debt-like consideration ranking ahead of the equity's future value creation, and lenders treat expected earnout payments as calls on cash flow when sizing debt (Lesson 6). Model it in the waterfall like any other claim.

§8.5.5Vendor loan notes and deferred consideration

A vendor loan note (VLN) turns part of the price into a loan from the seller: e.g. £70m deal, £58m cash at close, £12m VLN paying 8% (often PIK), repayable at exit or on a fixed maturity, usually subordinated to the bank debt and often to the institutional loan notes too. Why each side agrees:

  • Buyer: fills a funding gap without more bank debt or equity; cheap relative to mezzanine; signals seller confidence to the credit committee.
  • Seller: achieves the headline price, earns a coupon while waiting, ranks ahead of the ordinary equity (unlike rollover), and — unlike an earnout — the amount is fixed.

The seller's real risks are subordination and credit: a VLN behind 4x of senior debt in a deal that goes sideways is worth pennies. When you see a large VLN, ask why the institutional money didn't fill the gap — sometimes the answer is benign (fund at its concentration limit), sometimes it is the fund quietly capping its exposure to a deal it half-believes.

Plain deferred consideration — fixed sums on fixed dates, usually undocumented beyond the SPA and non-interest-bearing — is common in smaller deals and for founder-sellers staying through transition. Two disciplines: treat it as debt in the structure table (it is), and check what security or set-off rights attach — buyers love setting warranty claims off against deferred payments, which converts the seller's "guaranteed" £10m into a contingent one.

§8.5.6Contingent structures in carve-outs

Carve-outs — buying a division out of a corporate parent — are where contingent consideration earns its keep. The core problem: nobody, including the parent, knows the division's true standalone cost base. The P&L you diligence is an allocation exercise: group IT, HR, insurance and property costs are spread by formulas that will not survive separation, and transitional service agreements (TSAs) price the interim period, not steady state.

So carve-out structures push price into contingent forms: earnouts on the first one or two standalone years (pricing the actual, not allocated, cost base); deferred amounts conditional on TSA exit milestones or key contract novations; price adjustments for stranded costs above an agreed cap; and occasionally anti-embarrassment clauses protecting the parent if the buyer flips the asset quickly at a markup. The theme is consistent with the whole module: when a number can't be agreed, structure converts it from an argument into a formula — and the quality of the deal depends on how cleanly the formula is drafted.

§8.5.7What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

What looks good: earnouts of modest size (10-25% of total consideration) over 1-2 years, on a metric defined by worked example, with expert determination and conduct covenants both sides can live with; VLNs with sensible coupons and explicit subordination; deferred consideration counted as debt in every returns model.

What looks bad: an earnout that is the seller's main upside while the buyer controls the metric; EBITDA definitions that fit on one line; earnouts stretching past three years; deferred consideration ignored in the sources-and-uses; a seller-CEO whose earnout maximises FY2 EBITDA while the fund's plan front-loads investment that depresses it — perfectly opposed incentives, installed on purpose by accident.

What deal teams actually ask: "Who controls the metric, and what does each side rationally do in the final quarter of the earnout period?" If the honest answer is "the buyer defers revenue and accelerates costs, the seller does the opposite", size the provision for dispute now. And always: "What's the expected total consideration, scenario-weighted?" — because that is the real price of the deal, whatever the press release says.

Next, the other side of the balance sheet: how much debt to take, the covenants that come with it, and the mid-hold moves — cures, toggles, recaps and refinancings — that reshape a deal after completion.

Lesson 8.6/Deal Structuring

Debt-Side Structuring and Covenants

26 min read
In brief

Choosing how much leverage to take and why not the maximum, maintenance covenants with a worked headroom example, equity cures and PIK toggles, dividend recaps with a worked IRR effect and the sensible-versus-abusive test, and refinancing through the hold.

  1. 8.6.1How much leverage — and why not the maximum
  2. 8.6.2Maintenance covenants and headroom: a worked example
  3. 8.6.3Equity cures and PIK toggles
  4. 8.6.4Dividend recaps: mechanics, a worked IRR effect, and the smell test
  5. 8.6.5Refinancing through the hold
  6. 8.6.6What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

§8.6.1How much leverage — and why not the maximum

Lenders will quote a maximum: say 4.5x EBITDA of senior debt for a solid mid-market business, more in hot credit markets. The naive model says take it all — every pound of debt is a pound less equity, and leverage amplifies equity returns (Module 7). Deal teams routinely take less than the maximum, and the reasons are the substance of this lesson:

  1. Volatility. Leverage is sized against expected EBITDA; covenants are breached by actual EBITDA. A contract-based services business with 30% customer concentration should not be levered like a subscription software company, whatever the lender offers this quarter.
  2. Cash flexibility. Debt service (cash interest plus amortisation) is a first claim on cash flow. Every pound of it is a pound not available for the capex, bolt-ons and hires in the value-creation plan. Buying a company to grow it, then starving the growth plan to pay interest, is self-defeating — and common.
  3. Optionality. Headroom against covenants and against the debt capacity ceiling is what lets the company survive a bad year, fund an opportunistic acquisition, or refinance on its own timetable rather than the market's.
  4. The lender's price for the last turn. The marginal turn of leverage carries the highest margin and the tightest terms. The blended cost of going from 3.5x to 4.5x is often poor value against the equity it saves.

The working answer most teams converge on: lever to the point where the business comfortably services debt in the downside case, not the base case, and let the equity cheque flex instead.

§8.6.2Maintenance covenants and headroom: a worked example

Mid-market loan agreements typically carry maintenance covenants — ratios tested every quarter, breach of which is an event of default even if every payment has been made on time. (Large-cap "cov-lite" deals replace these with incurrence covenants, tested only when the borrower acts — pays a dividend, raises more debt. Know the difference; it decides how early lenders get a seat at the table.) The two workhorses:

  • Leverage covenant: net debt / EBITDA must not exceed a scheduled level.
  • Interest cover covenant: EBITDA / net cash interest must not fall below a level.

Covenants are set off the lender's base case with headroom — typically 25-35% cushion on EBITDA — and usually tighten (step down) over time as the plan assumes deleveraging.

Worked example. At the year-2 test date, Halton Group plc has net debt of £70m, forecast EBITDA of £20m, and net cash interest of £7m. Covenants: leverage ≤ 4.5x, interest cover ≥ 2.0x.

  • Leverage: breach when EBITDA < 70 / 4.5 = £15.6m. Cushion = (20 − 15.6) / 20 = 22% EBITDA headroom.
  • Interest cover: breach when EBITDA < 2.0 × 7 = £14.0m. Cushion = (20 − 14) / 20 = 30% headroom.

The leverage covenant is the binding one — it trips first, at a 22% EBITDA decline. That is the single number the CFO and the sponsor watch. Notice also that leverage covenants bite twice: EBITDA falling and net debt failing to amortise (weak cash conversion, a working-capital blowout) both push the ratio up. A business can hit its EBITDA budget and still breach on debt that didn't come down.

Breach consequences are rarely instant catastrophe: the realistic sequence is default → negotiation → waiver fee, margin bump, tighter terms, maybe an equity injection. But the lender now has leverage over the deal — which is exactly what covenants are for. From the sponsor's side the whole game is buying enough headroom at signing that a normal bad year is a board conversation, not a lender conversation.

§8.6.3Equity cures and PIK toggles

Two structural pressure valves appear constantly:

Equity cure: a contractual right for the sponsor to inject equity after a covenant test and have it counted — usually as a reduction in net debt, occasionally (and much more generously) as deemed EBITDA — recomputing the ratio to cure the breach. In the Halton example, suppose EBITDA comes in at £15.0m: leverage = 70 / 15 = 4.67x, a breach. A £2.5m equity cure applied to net debt gives 67.5 / 15 = 4.5x — cured exactly. Loan agreements ration cures (say, no more than two consecutive quarters, four over the life, sometimes a cap per cure) because a sponsor who cures every quarter is paying the lender's risk away instead of fixing the business.

PIK toggle: a feature of some junior debt letting the borrower elect, period by period, to pay interest in kind (rolling it into principal, usually at a 75-100bp premium) instead of cash. It converts a liquidity problem into a bigger future claim — valuable flexibility in a genuinely temporary squeeze, corrosive if toggled routinely, because the compounding balance eats the equity from above just like the institutional loan notes eat the sweet from within.

§8.6.4Dividend recaps: mechanics, a worked IRR effect, and the smell test

A dividend recapitalisation re-levers the business mid-hold to pay the proceeds out to shareholders: the company borrows more (the business has deleveraged and grown into spare debt capacity), and the new debt funds a distribution — typically repaying part of the institutional loan notes first, then dividends up the waterfall.

Worked IRR effect. A fund invests £40m of equity at completion. Base plan: exit at the end of year 5 for equity proceeds of £100m.

  • No recap: cash flows (−40, 0, 0, 0, 0, +100). MOIC = 2.50x; IRR = (100/40)1/5−1(100/40)^{1/5}-1(100/40)1/5−1 = 20.1%.
  • With recap: at the end of year 3 the company raises £20m of new debt at 10% cash interest and distributes it to the fund. The extra debt is still outstanding at exit, and the two years of interest (2 × £2m = £4m) consume cash that would otherwise have built up in the business — so year-5 equity proceeds fall to 100 − 20 − 4 = £76m. Cash flows: (−40, 0, 0, +20, 0, +76). MOIC = 96 / 40 = 2.40x; IRR ≈ 21.4%.

The recap traded 0.10x of money multiple for 1.3 points of IRR, because £20m came home two years earlier. That is the general shape: recaps raise IRR, lower MOIC, and raise risk — the business carries more debt for the rest of the hold, with covenant headroom reset tighter. They also de-risk the fund: after the recap the fund has only £20m of net capital at risk, and its downside scenarios improve even as the company's worsen.

When sensible: the business has structurally outperformed — EBITDA up materially, leverage well below entry levels — and the recap merely restores a prudent capital structure while returning early capital to LPs; debt markets are cheap; the operating plan is fully funded after the distribution. In that world a recap is just disciplined capital management.

When abusive: the recap takes leverage above entry levels on flat performance; it strips the cash buffer a cyclical business will need; it front-runs a known deterioration; or it converts a struggling deal into a "return the fund's money, let the lenders own the tail risk" trade. The tell is simple — ask whether the pro-forma capital structure would have been a responsible way to buy the business today, at today's performance. If no, the recap is extracting, not managing.

§8.6.5Refinancing through the hold

Debt is not set-and-forget. Over a five-to-seven-year hold, expect the capital structure to be revisited at least once:

  • Repricing/amend-and-extend: when credit markets tighten spreads or the maturity wall approaches, borrowers reprice margins down or push maturities out. Cheap if done from strength; expensive if done at the market's convenience.
  • Refinancing into looser docs: a deleveraged business can often replace its amortising, covenanted club loan with a cov-lite unitranche or institutional term loan — releasing amortisation cash flow and covenant risk in exchange for margin.
  • Add-on facilities: committed acquisition/capex lines, or incremental ("accordion") facilities, pre-negotiated at signing so the buy-and-build plan doesn't require a lender process per bolt-on. Structuring these at entry is far cheaper than asking mid-hold.
  • Repaying the institutional loan notes: refinancing proceeds often first redeem part of the fund's loan notes (a "soft recap") — same IRR logic as above, and it also de-risks the sweet equity's position by stopping some of the PIK compounding, which is why management teams are often quietly enthusiastic.

The through-line: a deal's debt structure at exit rarely resembles its debt structure at entry, and the flexibility to make these moves — baskets, accordions, portability, cure rights — is negotiated on day one, when the sponsor has competitive tension to spend.

§8.6.6What looks good, what looks bad, what deal teams ask

What looks good: leverage sized to the downside case with 25-35% covenant headroom; a covenant schedule that tracks a credible deleveraging profile rather than a hockey stick; equity cures available but unused; recaps done from outperformance that keep pro-forma leverage below entry; refinancing optionality (accordion, baskets) bought at signing.

What looks bad: debt at the top of what was offered "because it was available"; covenant headroom under 15% at signing (the plan has no permission to wobble); serial equity cures or a PIK toggle flipped for three straight periods (the structure is eating itself); a recap that returns the whole fund cheque on flat EBITDA; a maturity wall inside the intended exit window with no refinancing plan.

What deal teams actually ask: "How far can EBITDA fall before we're talking to the banks — and in which quarter?" (the binding covenant and its tightest test date), and "What has to be true for the recap?" — insisting the answer is stated in performance terms, not market terms. Debt that was structured with those two questions in mind is debt the deal can live with for five years. That judgement — matching the claims to the business, not the business to the claims — is where this module started, and it is the whole craft of structuring.

Lesson 9.1/Due Diligence

The Diligence Machine

25 min read
In brief

How a diligence exercise is actually organised: the seven workstreams and who runs them, how scope is phased against cost and exclusivity, and how findings translate into price chips, structural fixes, SPA protections, or a decision to walk.

  1. 9.1.1Why diligence exists
  2. 9.1.2The seven workstreams
  3. 9.1.3Phasing: scope against cost and exclusivity
  4. 9.1.4From finding to consequence: the four outcomes
  5. 9.1.5The deal team's job: synthesis
  6. 9.1.6What looks good and what looks bad in the process itself

§9.1.1Why diligence exists

By the time a fund enters exclusivity it has typically seen a CIM, a management presentation, and a data room curated by advisers whose fee depends on the deal completing. Everything the buyer "knows" has been arranged by the seller. Due diligence is the buyer's organised attempt to replace that curated picture with an independently verified one — before the money moves and while there is still negotiating leverage.

The economics are brutal and simple. A deal priced at 9.0× EBITDA means every £1m of EBITDA that turns out not to exist cost £9m of enterprise value — and because debt was sized off the same number, the overpaid deal is simultaneously over-levered. Diligence spend of £2–4m on a £200m deal is cheap insurance against a £15–20m mispricing. The converse also matters: diligence that confirms quality lets a fund bid with conviction and win auctions it would otherwise have lost to braver bidders.

One mental model to carry through this whole module: diligence does not exist to produce reports. It exists to answer four questions — is the EBITDA real, will it persist, what could kill it, and what do we do about each finding? Every workstream below is a different lens on those questions.

§9.1.2The seven workstreams

A full buyout diligence exercise typically runs seven parallel workstreams. Each has a natural owner, a natural output, and a natural failure mode.

Workstream Typical owner Core question Headline output
Financial (FDD) Big 4 / large accounting firm Is the EBITDA and cash flow real? Quality of earnings report; NWC and net debt analysis
Commercial (CDD) Strategy house (Bain, EY-Parthenon, OC&C, LEK) or specialist Will revenue and margin persist and grow? Market model, customer references, forecast view
Legal Law firm What obligations, disputes, and change-of-control traps exist? Legal DD report; feeds directly into SPA drafting
Tax Big 4 tax practice What are the historic exposures and the efficient structure? Tax DD report; structuring memo
Operational Ops consultants, sometimes the fund's own operating partners Can the business actually deliver the plan? Capacity, supply chain, systems assessment
Management Specialist assessors (e.g. psychometric + referencing firms) Is this the team to back? Individual assessments, referencing
Insurance / ESG / IT Brokers, specialists Anything uninsurable, unfundable, or unfixable? Gap analyses, W&I feasibility

Three practical notes on who does what. First, FDD is almost always a Big 4 firm (or a large challenger), because the work is forensic accounting: rebuilding EBITDA from the ledger, testing revenue recognition, tracing cash. Second, CDD is a different skill — market sizing, competitor interviews, customer referencing — and is bought from strategy consultancies. A common junior mistake is treating FDD and CDD as substitutes; FDD tells you what the earnings were, CDD tells you whether they will continue. Third, the fund's deal team owns none of the workstreams and all of the synthesis — more on that below.

§9.1.3Phasing: scope against cost and exclusivity

Diligence is expensive — often £2–5m all-in on a mid-market deal — and much of it is wasted if the deal dies. So scope is phased against deal probability:

Phase Deal stage Spend profile What actually happens
Desktop / red-flag Pre-IOI Minimal; mostly deal-team time Public information, CIM interrogation, sector experts, a "red flag" review from advisers
Confirmatory scoping Post-IOI, pre-exclusivity Moderate Advisers engaged on limited scope; focus on the 3–4 issues that would change the price
Full / confirmatory Exclusivity Full fees committed Complete FDD/CDD/legal/tax reports, management sessions, site visits

Two judgement points. The fund that spends £3m in a five-party auction it has a 20% chance of winning is burning £2.4m of expected dead-deal costs; the fund that spends nothing until exclusivity may win exclusivity on a price it then can't support. Sophisticated funds solve this by doing the price-critical work early and cheaply — a red-flag FDD focused only on the adjusted EBITDA bridge, sector expert calls instead of a full CDD — and saving confirmatory breadth for exclusivity. Second, in a vendor-DD process the seller commissions its own FDD/CDD reports and shares them with all bidders. Read them carefully but remember who paid for them: vendor DD is reliable on facts (advisers won't put their name to false numbers) and systematically generous on judgement calls (which add-backs are "one-off", how big the market is). The buyer's own "top-up" diligence should target exactly those judgement calls.

§9.1.4From finding to consequence: the four outcomes

This is the most important section in this lesson. A diligence finding is worthless until it is converted into one of four outcomes:

1. Price chip. If the finding permanently reduces sustainable EBITDA, the price moves. Worked example: FDD concludes that £0.8m of a claimed £12.0m adjusted EBITDA is a recurring cost dressed up as one-off. At the 9.0× deal multiple, the buyer's offer falls from £108.0m to £100.8m — a £7.2m chip from a £0.8m finding. Price chips are for findings that are certain and quantifiable.

2. Structure fix. If the finding is a risk rather than a certainty, you don't chip the price — you restructure so the seller bears the risk. Classic tools: an earnout (part of the price contingent on the disputed forecast being achieved), deferred consideration, a specific escrow or retention against a known dispute, or making completion conditional on renewing the customer contract in question. Example: management forecasts £3m EBITDA uplift from a signed-but-not-live contract. Rather than pay 9.0× on £3m of hope (£27m) or pay nothing and lose the deal, the buyer offers £13.5m of earnout payable when the contract delivers its first full year.

3. SPA protection. Findings about historic exposures — a tax position that might be challenged, an unresolved dispute — are handled in the sale and purchase agreement: warranties (seller's statements of fact; breach gives a damages claim), indemnities (pound-for-pound covenants against a specific identified risk), and increasingly W&I insurance, which transfers warranty risk to an insurer for a premium of roughly 1–2% of the policy limit. Judgement rule: a known, identified risk gets an indemnity or price adjustment, not a warranty — warranties protect against the unknown, and W&I insurers exclude anything the diligence reports flagged. Diligence findings therefore directly shape what protection is even available.

4. Walk away. Some findings are not priceable: fraud, a broken relationship with a customer representing 40% of gross profit, a market in structural decline that the whole thesis denied. The discipline here is cultural. Deal teams suffer from deal momentum — months of work, adviser fees spent, career capital invested — and the IC's job is to make walking away respectable. A useful test: if we saw this finding on day one, would we have started work? If no, the sunk costs don't change the answer.

§9.1.5The deal team's job: synthesis

Advisers produce hundreds of pages. Nobody pays a fund's fees for forwarding PDFs. The deal team's distinctive job is synthesis: forcing every workstream's findings into a single view of price, structure, and risk that an IC can act on.

In practice this means three things. First, cross-referencing: the most dangerous findings are the ones no single adviser sees. FDD notes revenue was pulled forward in Q4; CDD notes the top distributor complained about being "encouraged" to take stock; neither report says "channel stuffing" — the deal team must connect them. Second, maintaining the issues list: a live table of every finding, its EBITDA/value impact, its proposed treatment (chip / structure / SPA / accept), and its owner. This document is the negotiation. Third, updating the model: every accepted finding flows into the LBO model as a revised EBITDA, a revised NWC peg, a debt-like item, or a downside case — so the IC sees returns on diligenced numbers, not CIM numbers.

§9.1.6What looks good and what looks bad in the process itself

The conduct of diligence is itself evidence about the target:

Signal What it suggests
Data room complete, questions answered in days, monthly management accounts reconcile to audit Well-run business with nothing to hide — quality assets diligence easily
Key data "not tracked" (churn, margin by customer), answers routed through advisers only, management access rationed Either weak systems or something to hide — both are findings
Vendor pushes to compress exclusivity and resists FDD scope Ask why the seller fears daylight
Management privately more conservative than the CIM Normal and mildly reassuring — the CIM is the bankers' document
A finding you raise gets a fast, evidenced rebuttal Healthy; management knows its business
A finding gets a new story each time you ask Escalate — inconsistent explanations are a flag in themselves

A closing rule of thumb for the whole module: diligence rarely uncovers a single fatal document. Deals die — or get repriced — through the accumulation of a dozen medium-sized findings that each shave conviction. Your job in the coming lessons is to learn what those findings look like in the numbers, and what each one is worth.

Lesson 9.2/Due Diligence

Financial DD & Quality of Earnings

30 min read
In brief

The anatomy of a QoE report: a full worked adjusted EBITDA bridge with eight adjustments of varying legitimacy, run-rate and pro-forma treatments, why the normalised working capital peg matters with a worked example, and the hunt for net debt and debt-like items.

  1. 9.2.1What a QoE report actually is
  2. 9.2.2The adjusted EBITDA bridge: a worked example
  3. 9.2.3Run-rate and pro-forma adjustments done properly
  4. 9.2.4Normalised working capital: why the peg matters
  5. 9.2.5The net debt hunt: debt-like items
  6. 9.2.6What deal teams actually ask of FDD

§9.2.1What a QoE report actually is

Financial due diligence produces one central artefact: the quality of earnings (QoE) report. Its job is to answer, line by line, whether reported EBITDA represents the sustainable, cash-backed earning power of the business — because that number drives both the price (multiple × EBITDA) and the debt package (leverage × EBITDA).

A QoE report has a standard anatomy: an adjusted EBITDA bridge (reported → adjusted, with every adjustment evidenced and opined on), revenue and margin analysis (by customer, product, geography — looking for concentration, one-offs, and recognition issues), normalised working capital (setting the peg), net debt and debt-like items, and cash conversion (does EBITDA turn into cash?). This lesson walks the three that most often move price: the bridge, the peg, and net debt.

The stance to take throughout: the seller's adviser prepared the adjusted EBITDA number to be as high as defensibly possible. Your job is not to assume fraud — it is to re-underwrite each adjustment against a simple test: would this cost (or revenue) genuinely not recur under our ownership?

§9.2.2The adjusted EBITDA bridge: a worked example

Target: a distribution business, FY reported EBITDA £10.0m. The vendor's FDD pack presents adjusted EBITDA of £13.5m via eight adjustments:

# Adjustment £m Vendor's rationale
Reported EBITDA 10.0
1 Excess founder remuneration +0.4 Two founder-directors paid £0.9m; market cost of replacements £0.5m
2 Legal settlement +0.6 One-off dispute with former supplier, settled this year
3 Aborted transaction costs +0.3 Fees from a sale process that collapsed last year
4 "One-off" recruitment fees +0.2 Exceptional hiring campaign
5 Run-rate of January price increase +0.9 4% price rise effective month 10; full-year effect added
6 Bolt-on synergies +0.5 Acquired competitor in month 7; identified cost synergies
7 FX gains −0.2 Non-recurring translation gains removed
8 Signed contract not yet live +0.8 Three-year contract signed, service starts next quarter
Adjusted EBITDA 13.5

Now re-underwrite each one:

1. Excess founder remuneration (+0.4): legitimate, verify the number. Under new ownership the founders leave or take market salaries, so the excess genuinely doesn't recur. But test the replacement-cost assumption — if you actually need a £0.7m CEO/CFO pair, the add-back is £0.2m, not £0.4m. This is the most commonly accepted add-back and the most commonly overstated one.

2. Legal settlement (+0.6): legitimate only if genuinely isolated. Pull three to five years of history. If legal/settlement costs appear in most years (£0.3m, £0.1m, £0.6m…), the business has a recurring level of dispute cost — the add-back should be the excess over that run-rate, not the whole amount. One-offs that happen every year are called opex.

3. Aborted transaction costs (+0.3): legitimate. Costs of the sale process itself don't recur under your ownership. Usually accepted with minimal argument — which is why sellers like to classify as much as possible under this heading. Check the invoices actually relate to the process.

4. Recruitment fees (+0.2): aggressive. A business that has grown headcount every year for five years will keep hiring. Recruitment is a cost of growth, not a one-off. Reject, unless a specific abnormal event (e.g. replacing an entire finance team once) is evidenced — and even then, only the abnormal portion.

5. Price increase run-rate (+0.9): aggressive — half a story. Annualising a price rise implemented late in the year is a legitimate category of adjustment (run-rate adjustments capture the full-year effect of changes already in place), but this one assumes zero volume loss. Diligence question: what churn followed the rise? If 2% of customers left, the net effect might be +0.5m. Also check the rise wasn't a pre-sale manoeuvre that will unwind. Partial credit at best.

6. Bolt-on synergies (+0.5): aggressive. "Identified" synergies are a plan, not a result. The standard is delivered and in the ledger. What is legitimate is the pro-forma adjustment for the bolt-on itself — see the next section. Buyers may pay for synergy potential in competitive processes, but knowingly, in the multiple — not hidden inside the EBITDA the multiple is applied to.

7. FX gains (−0.2): legitimate — and note the direction. A downward adjustment is a small credibility signal: an honest bridge removes non-recurring gains too. A bridge where all eight adjustments point upward deserves extra suspicion.

8. Signed contract not yet live (+0.8): aggressive as an add-back. No revenue has been delivered; margin assumptions are untested; mobilisation costs are real. This belongs in the forecast (where CDD can test it) or in an earnout, not in historical adjusted EBITDA. Reject from the bridge; consider paying for it via structure.

A defensible buyer's view: accept 1 (say +0.3 after replacement-cost challenge), 2 in part (+0.3 over the recurring level), 3 (+0.3), 7 (−0.2), partial 5 (+0.5), reject 4, 6, 8. Buyer's adjusted EBITDA ≈ £11.2m against the vendor's £13.5m. At 9.0×, that gap is £20.7m of enterprise value — which is why the bridge, not the model, is where mid-market deals are really negotiated.

§9.2.3Run-rate and pro-forma adjustments done properly

Two adjustment families deserve their own discipline because they are legitimate in principle and abused in practice.

Run-rate adjustments restate the year as if changes already implemented had been in force throughout: a price rise, a signed lease exit, a completed redundancy programme. The test is implemented and evidenced — the cheque has been signed, the people have left, the new price is being invoiced. "Planned", "identified", and "targeted" savings fail the test.

Pro-forma acquisition adjustments arise when the target bought a business mid-year. If a bolt-on contributing £1.2m of annual EBITDA was acquired in month 7, the reported year includes only ~£0.5m of it (5/12 × 1.2 ≈ 0.5). Adding the missing £0.7m is legitimate — you are buying the combined group, and the debt will be sized on the combined group. But diligence the bolt-on's own numbers to the same standard (its EBITDA may itself be "adjusted"), check for revenue dis-synergies (shared customers who will consolidate suppliers), and confirm integration costs to come are reflected. A vendor bridge that pro-formas the EBITDA but not the integration spend is telling half the story.

§9.2.4Normalised working capital: why the peg matters

Deals are done on a cash-free, debt-free basis with a normal level of working capital. The "normal level" — the NWC peg — matters because working capital is the easiest number in the business to manipulate in the short term, and because without a peg the seller is paid twice.

The mechanics: buyer and seller agree a peg (typically the average NWC the business needs, often the last twelve months' monthly average, adjusted for seasonality and distortions). At completion, actual NWC is measured. If actual is below the peg, the price falls pound-for-pound; if above, it rises.

Worked example. The target's NWC over the last twelve month-ends averages £8.0m. In the three months before completion, the seller quietly stretches creditors and runs a debtor-collection blitz; NWC at close is £6.5m. Without a peg, the buyer pays full price and must then inject £1.5m of cash in the first quarter as creditors are paid down and debtor terms normalise — the seller has effectively extracted £1.5m of extra proceeds. With a peg at £8.0m, the completion accounts show a £1.5m shortfall and the price drops by exactly £1.5m. The peg converts a manipulation into a nullity.

FDD's job on the peg: build the monthly NWC profile (never rely on year-ends — they are the most managed balance dates of the year), strip distortions (a one-off customer prepayment, an unusually large stock build), and evidence seasonality (a retailer's "normal" NWC in November is not its normal in February — the peg may need to be set by reference to the expected completion month). Deal teams fight hard over pegs for a reason: on a seasonal business, peg positioning can be worth several million pounds, entirely divorced from any view of the business's value.

§9.2.5The net debt hunt: debt-like items

"Cash-free, debt-free" sounds clean until you ask what counts as debt. Bank borrowings are obvious. The value in FDD is the hunt for debt-like items: obligations that will consume the buyer's cash post-completion just as surely as a loan repayment, without being labelled debt.

Worked example. Headline: bank debt £20.0m, cash £3.0m → net debt £17.0m. FDD finds:

Item £m Why it's debt-like
Finance lease obligations 0.8 Contractual future payments; economically borrowing
Accrued bonuses (pre-completion year) 0.5 Earned under seller's ownership, paid under buyer's
Overdue corporation tax 0.4 Deferred payments the buyer must fund
Dilapidations provision 0.3 Committed property reinstatement cost
Declared unpaid dividend 0.5 Cash leaving the business at completion
Adjusted net debt 19.5

Adjusted net debt of £19.5m versus the headline £17.0m moves equity value by £2.5m — often more than the entire FDD fee, found in the footnotes. Other regulars on the hunt list: customer deposits and deferred income (contentious — cash received for work not yet done; sellers argue it's working capital, buyers argue it's an obligation), pension deficits, deferred consideration on the target's own past acquisitions, untaken holiday pay accruals, and "trapped" cash that isn't freely available (regulatory capital, cash in minority-owned subsidiaries, tills in stores). The classification arguments — is deferred income debt-like or working capital? — are genuinely negotiable, which is why they appear on every issues list. The buyer's rule: anything that consumes post-completion cash without generating post-completion EBITDA should reduce the price somewhere — in net debt or in the peg — but exactly once, not twice, and not zero times.

§9.2.6What deal teams actually ask of FDD

Reading a QoE report, the deal team's checklist is short: Which adjustments does the FDD firm positively support, merely note, or challenge? (FDD firms grade their language carefully — "we note management's adjustment" is not endorsement.) Does EBITDA convert to cash at ≥ 85–90%, and if not, where is it leaking — working capital build, capitalised costs, or provisions? Is the monthly NWC profile consistent with the peg being proposed? And what is on the debt-like items list that the SPA's definitions must capture? A QoE report you cannot turn into a price, a peg, and a debt definition has not finished its job.

Lesson 9.3/Due Diligence

Commercial Due Diligence

30 min read
In brief

How CDD tests whether revenue will persist and grow: TAM discipline, the evidence hierarchy for competitive position, what customer references actually reveal, churn and retention analysis, pricing power tests, and a worked bridge from management's hockey-stick forecast to the CDD view.

  1. 9.3.1What CDD is for
  2. 9.3.2Market sizing sanity: TAM discipline
  3. 9.3.3Competitive position: the evidence hierarchy
  4. 9.3.4Customer references: what they actually reveal
  5. 9.3.5Churn and retention: reading the revenue engine
  6. 9.3.6Pricing power: the cleanest quality test
  7. 9.3.7Forecast credibility: bridging the hockey stick
  8. 9.3.8What looks good and what looks bad

§9.3.1What CDD is for

Financial DD looks backwards: was the EBITDA real? Commercial DD looks forwards: will the revenue and margin persist and grow? The two are complements, not substitutes — a business can have immaculate historic earnings and a market that is about to fall off a cliff, and the QoE report will never tell you.

CDD is bought from strategy houses because the raw material is different: market models, expert interviews, competitor analysis, and — most valuable of all — direct conversations with the target's customers. The output is a view on three questions: how big and healthy is the market, how strong is the target's position in it, and how credible is the forecast? Every deal thesis rests on those three legs, and the CDD report is where each leg gets load-tested.

One framing to carry through this lesson: management's plan is a claim. CDD's job is to rebuild that claim bottom-up from evidence and report the gap. The gap is normal — almost every plan is optimistic — but its size and structure tell you whether you are looking at ambition or fiction.

§9.3.2Market sizing sanity: TAM discipline

Every CIM contains a market chart, and most of them are propaganda. The classic move is to quote an enormous TAM (total addressable market) so the target's share looks tiny and the runway infinite: "a £6bn market growing at 8%, in which the company holds under 1%".

The discipline is to force the funnel:

Level Question Worked example
TAM Everyone who could conceivably buy this category UK facilities services: £6.0bn
SAM The segment the target actually serves (geography, size band, spec) Specialist compliance maintenance for regulated sites: £450m
SOM What the target can realistically win given channels and capacity Sites within its three-region footprint: £180m

A target with £45m revenue holds 0.75% of the TAM — or 25% of its SOM. Those imply opposite theses: the first says endless headroom, the second says the easy growth is done and further share is taken from entrenched competitors' hands. Deal teams have overpaid for "1% of a huge market" stories many times; the growth ceiling was three postcodes away all along.

Two tests make sizing honest. First, triangulate top-down against bottom-up: if the top-down model says £450m and multiplying the number of regulated sites by average spend per site gives £210m, the market model is broken — find out which assumption is doing the lying. Second, reconcile market growth to the target's history: if the market "grows at 8%" but the target grew at 3% for three years, then either the market number is wrong or the target is losing share — and a share-loser priced as a share-gainer is one of the most expensive mistakes in PE.

§9.3.3Competitive position: the evidence hierarchy

Everyone claims differentiation. CDD's job is to rank the evidence, from strong to weak:

  1. Revealed behaviour: win/loss records against named competitors, retention rates through a price rise, customers who tried to leave and came back. Behaviour is the gold standard — it cannot be talked into existence.
  2. Third-party testimony: customers and channel partners describing why they chose the target and what would make them switch. Good, but filter for selection bias (see below).
  3. Structural analysis: switching costs, accreditation barriers, network effects, proprietary data — arguments about why advantage should exist.
  4. Management assertion: "we are the quality player." Worth precisely nothing until backed by 1–3.

What looks good: a documented win rate of 60%+ in competitive tenders, stable or rising share of wallet within existing customers, and competitors who — in expert interviews — describe the target with grudging respect and can name what it does better. What looks bad: "no direct competitors" (nobody has no competitors; it usually means the market is too small to attract any), wins explained mostly by price, and a market where a credible player is currently buying share with venture money.

§9.3.4Customer references: what they actually reveal

The customer referencing programme — typically 15–30 structured interviews — is the single highest-value component of CDD, because customers have no incentive to flatter. But the sample is poisoned at source: management supplies the list, and no management team nominates its angriest customer. Good CDD firms push for the full customer list and select their own sample, including lapsed and declining accounts.

What the interviews reveal, beyond the satisfaction scores nobody should take at face value:

  • Switching reality: "If they raised prices 10%, what would you do?" A customer who laughs and says "pay it — requalifying a supplier takes us nine months" is telling you the moat is real. A customer who says "I'd get two quotes by Friday" is telling you the target is a commodity with good account managers.
  • Share of wallet and dual-sourcing: a customer spending £2m of a £10m category with the target, deliberately splitting across three suppliers, will behave very differently from a sole-source customer.
  • Relationship location: if three interviews name the same salesperson as "the reason we stay", key-person risk just moved from the org chart into the revenue line.
  • Early warnings: customers mention the competitor's new product, the service slip since the last reorganisation, or their own plans to insource — quarters before any of it reaches the numbers.

Judgement rule: one grumpy customer is noise; the same specific complaint appearing unprompted in five interviews is a finding, and it goes on the issues list.

§9.3.5Churn and retention: reading the revenue engine

For any business with repeat customers, retention analysis is where CDD gets quantitative. Two measures do most of the work:

Gross revenue retention (GRR): of last year's revenue base, how much survived — counting only losses and downgrades, ignoring growth. Net revenue retention (NRR): the same, but including upsell and price increases on retained customers.

Worked example. FY23 revenue from existing customers: £40.0m. During FY24, customers representing £4.0m left entirely and continuing customers reduced spend by £1.0m; but other continuing customers expanded by £3.0m. GRR = (40.0 − 4.0 − 1.0) / 40.0 = 87.5%. NRR = (40.0 − 5.0 + 3.0) / 40.0 = 95%. Headline revenue still grew — new logos added £7.0m — so the CIM shows +5% growth and never mentions that the engine leaks 12.5% a year.

Why this matters: a business with 87.5% GRR must replace an eighth of its revenue every year before growing at all. Growth is being bought with sales and marketing spend, and the moment that spend pauses, revenue shrinks. Compare a business with 97% GRR and 108% NRR: it grows 8% by standing still. These two businesses can show identical historic revenue lines and deserve wildly different multiples.

What deal teams ask for: churn by cohort (do customers acquired recently churn faster? — a sign quality of new business is falling), churn by value not just count (losing 10 tiny customers ≠ losing one anchor), and reasons coded from exit data, not management's memory. What looks bad: churn defined generously (only counting customers lost at contract end, not downgrades; annualising a lucky quarter), or — worse — "we don't track churn". A repeat-revenue business that cannot produce a retention analysis has either weak systems or an answer it dislikes.

§9.3.6Pricing power: the cleanest quality test

Pricing power is the fastest single read on competitive position, and it leaves fingerprints in the data:

  • Realised price vs list price: pull the last three years of like-for-like price changes and what was actually achieved. A business that put through 5%, 6%, and 5% rises with churn never exceeding 2% has demonstrated pricing power. A business whose "5% rise" eroded to 1.5% net through discounts and "commercial gestures" has demonstrated the opposite.
  • Discount dispersion: if realised prices for the same product vary 40% across similar customers, pricing is a negotiation the customer usually wins.
  • Margin through input-cost shocks: did gross margin hold when input costs spiked (pass-through worked) or compress for six quarters (it didn't)?

The pricing question matters doubly in PE because "pricing" is the most commonly claimed value-creation lever in models. If the CDD evidence says the last three price rises were fought to a standstill, the model's assumed "2% annual price above inflation" is not a lever, it is a hope.

§9.3.7Forecast credibility: bridging the hockey stick

Management plans hockey-stick for structural reasons — the plan is a sales document, and the MIP is usually struck off it. CDD's most useful output is a forecast bridge that decomposes the plan into named drivers and re-underwrites each with evidence.

Worked example. Management's plan takes revenue from £50.0m (FY24) to £68.0m (FY27), an £18.0m uplift. The CDD bridge:

Driver Management (£m) CDD view (£m) Evidence
Market growth on existing base +6.0 (4%/yr) +6.0 Market model supports 4%; base assumed retained
Churn on existing base 0.0 −4.5 GRR of 97% claimed; cohort data shows 94% → 3%/yr attrition
Share gains / new logos +5.0 +2.5 Requires win rate of 55%; last 2 yrs actual = 40%
Price +3.0 (2%/yr) +1.5 Last 3 rises realised at ~1% net of discounts
New product launch +4.0 +1.0 Product 6 months late; pipeline covers £1m; no reference customers yet
Total uplift +18.0 +6.5
FY27 revenue 68.0 56.5

The plan says 10.8% revenue CAGR; the evidence supports about 4.2%. Note what the bridge achieves that "we haircut the plan by 20%" never can: each driver has a named piece of evidence attached, so the negotiation and the model can engage with specific disagreements. Management can rebut the churn line with better cohort data; nobody can rebut a blanket haircut.

The deal team then decides which case to underwrite. Common practice: base the price and debt sizing on the CDD case, treat the gap to management's plan as upside owned by the buyer, and — if the seller insists on being paid for the plan — move the difference into an earnout so the seller is paid for the hockey stick if and only if it happens.

§9.3.8What looks good and what looks bad

Signal Read
Bottom-up SOM reconciles to top-down market model within ~20% Sizing is honest
Target's growth ≥ market growth for 3+ years Share gainer — position claims are credible
GRR ≥ 95%, NRR ≥ 100%, stable by cohort Revenue base compounds by itself
Price rises realised in full, churn unmoved Genuine pricing power
Plan drivers each tie to named evidence; management concedes weak ones gracefully Team is honest with itself — the plan may even be beatable
TAM quoted, SAM unquantifiable; "no competitors"; churn "not tracked" The commercial story is decoration, not analysis
Growth entirely from new logos over a leaking base The engine is a treadmill — value the treadmill, not the speed
Forecast back-half loaded: years 1–2 flat, years 3–5 explosive The plan's author does not believe it either

CDD rarely kills deals outright. Its value is calibration: it converts "we believe in the growth story" into "we underwrite 4% and structure the rest" — which is the difference between a thesis and a wish.
