Lesson 9.4/Due Diligence

Operational, Management & Other Workstreams

25 min read
In brief

The workstreams beyond FDD and CDD: operational DD on capacity, supply chain and systems debt (where data teams plug in), how management is actually assessed, high-level legal and tax red flags, insurance DD, and ESG as a diligence lens rather than a compliance exercise.

  1. 9.4.1Operational DD: can the business deliver the plan?
  2. 9.4.2Systems debt: where the data team plugs in
  3. 9.4.3Management DD: assessing the team you are backing
  4. 9.4.4Legal and tax DD: the red-flag view
  5. 9.4.5Insurance DD and W&I
  6. 9.4.6ESG as a diligence lens
  7. 9.4.7Pulling the workstreams together

§9.4.1Operational DD: can the business deliver the plan?

FDD tells you what the earnings were; CDD tells you whether demand persists. Operational DD asks the question in between: can the business physically and organisationally deliver the plan the price assumes? A plan that needs 30% more volume through a plant already at 92% utilisation is not a plan — it is a capex requirement nobody has costed.

Ops DD typically covers four areas:

Capacity and capex. Map current utilisation against the plan's volumes. Worked example: a manufacturer runs at 85% of practical capacity; the plan assumes +40% volume by year 3. The missing 25%+ needs either a second shift (labour availability? premium cost?) or a £6.0m line extension with a 15-month lead time. If the model shows £1.5m/yr "maintenance capex" throughout, the plan and the capex line contradict each other — and EBITDA-based pricing quietly ignores the contradiction, because capex sits below EBITDA. This is one of the commonest ways a deal model flatters itself: growth in the revenue line, maintenance-only in the capex line.

Supply chain. Concentration (any supplier >20% of COGS gets diligenced like a top customer), single-sourced critical components, contract terms and pass-through rights, and geographic exposure. The question is resilience priced against cost: dual-sourcing everything is expensive; single-sourcing the one component with an 8-month requalification cycle is a thesis risk.

Operational maturity. Is performance managed or accidental? Evidence: does the business measure OTIF (on-time-in-full), scrap, labour productivity? Do site KPIs exist and do managers know them? A business with no measurement can be a positive finding for a value-creation thesis — the improvement is real and unpriced — but only if the management problem underneath it is fixable.

§9.4.2Systems debt: where the data team plugs in

Technology and data DD has grown from an afterthought into a workstream that changes prices, and it is where a PE data team most directly touches diligence. The questions:

  • Can the business produce its own numbers? If monthly reporting takes 15 working days and three spreadsheets that only the FC understands, the reporting the fund needs post-close (lender covenants, board packs, 100-day KPIs) does not exist yet. Budget for it.
  • Systems inventory and debt. A 20-year-old ERP that "works fine" but has no vendor support and one 61-year-old administrator is a deferred liability as real as a pension deficit. So is a business running on 40 unreconciled spreadsheets.
  • Data as an asset or a liability. Is customer/transaction data clean, owned, and usable (an asset the thesis can build on — pricing analytics, cross-sell), or fragmented, unconsented, or resident in a system the target does not control?
  • Carve-out entanglement. If the target is being carved out of a parent, every shared system (ERP, payroll, email) becomes a TSA line item and a migration project. Underestimating carve-out IT costs is a classic source of year-one pain: £2–5m and 18 months is routine for a mid-market carve-out that "just needs separating".

What the data team specifically brings during diligence: rebuilding analyses from raw transaction data rather than management's summaries (churn by cohort, price/volume bridges, margin by customer), testing whether the KPIs in the CIM can be reproduced from the ledger, and scoping the post-close data stack while there is still time to price it. A CIM KPI that cannot be reproduced from the underlying data is a finding.

§9.4.3Management DD: assessing the team you are backing

In a buyout, the fund backs a plan and the people who will deliver it — often with the same CEO for five years. Management DD is the least numeric workstream and one of the most decisive.

How it is actually done:

  • Structured assessment by specialist firms: competency-based interviews and psychometrics against the specific demands of the plan (a founder brilliant at £20m revenue may be wrong for a buy-and-build to £100m).
  • Referencing — the part that moves ICs. Not the referees the CEO nominates: off-list references from former colleagues, ex-employees, customers, and other investors. Patterns matter more than anecdotes: three independent references saying "brilliant commercially, burns through CFOs" is a finding with a structural answer (hire a strong CFO pre-close, adjust the MIP).
  • Depth and dependence. What breaks if the CEO is hit by a bus? Is there a layer below the founders that actually runs the business, or a hub-and-spoke where every decision routes through one person? Watch for it in meetings: a CEO who answers every question personally while the FD stares at the table is showing you the org chart's real shape.
  • Alignment and intent. Who is rolling equity, how much, and who is quietly retiring? A CFO rolling 60% of proceeds is making a statement; a CEO seeking to roll 5% while negotiating a big cash-out is making a different one. Diligence the shape of the MIP conversation, not just its size.

What looks bad: reference-dodging ("we'd rather you didn't speak to X"), a plan the second line has never seen, CVs that gloss a two-year gap, and — subtle but reliable — management teams that cannot disagree with each other in the room. What looks good: a second line that answers questions unprompted, a CEO who volunteers what they are bad at, and prior evidence of delivering under PE ownership, which is a different sport from founder-ownership.

§9.4.4Legal and tax DD: the red-flag view

Deal teams do not do legal DD, but they must know which findings matter. The legal headlines:

  • Change-of-control clauses: contracts (customer, supplier, lease, licence, debt) that terminate or become renegotiable on a sale. A top customer holding a CoC right is a pre-completion consent — and a negotiating window for them.
  • Litigation and disputes: quantify exposure; handled via indemnity or escrow rather than price if genuinely one-off.
  • IP ownership: does the company actually own its core IP, or does it sit with the founder personally, a contractor who never assigned it, or an academic collaboration? Fixing IP chain-of-title pre-close is routine; discovering the gap post-close is not.
  • Employment: contractor misclassification (an "outsourced" workforce that is legally employed), missing restrictive covenants on key staff, undocumented bonus promises.
  • Related-party arrangements: property leased from the founder's pension fund at above-market rent, services from family businesses. Not necessarily sinister, but every one must be identified, re-priced to market in the EBITDA, and either terminated or moved to arm's-length terms at completion.

Tax DD hunts historic exposures (aggressive schemes, VAT treatment, employment status, transfer pricing) and quantifies them. The standard treatment is an indemnity or, increasingly, W&I insurance with a specific tax policy — remembering the rule from Lesson 1: identified risks are excluded from standard W&I cover, so a known tax hole needs its own solution (specific indemnity, escrow, or price).

§9.4.5Insurance DD and W&I

Insurance DD does two jobs. First, a gap analysis of the target's existing cover: underinsured property, missing cyber cover, professional indemnity limits that haven't kept pace with contract sizes. Findings become post-close fixes and occasionally price items (premium step-ups on renewal).

Second, it supports W&I insurance placement. Recall the mechanics: the policy stands behind the seller's warranties so the buyer claims against an insurer, not the seller — essential when the seller is a fund that wants a clean exit and will not leave money in escrow. The diligence angle: W&I underwriters read the DD reports and exclude anything inadequately diligenced or specifically flagged. Thin diligence therefore produces a Swiss-cheese policy. This creates a virtuous discipline: doing the work properly is what makes the risk transferable.

§9.4.6ESG as a diligence lens

Treat ESG in diligence as a lens for finding real risks and value items, not a compliance checkbox:

  • Environmental: contamination on owned sites (a genuinely priceable liability — remediation estimates go straight into the funds-flow), energy intensity against rising carbon costs, products facing regulatory phase-out.
  • Social: labour practices in the supply chain (a reputational bomb with a fuse of unknown length), safety records (a rising accident rate is also an operational quality signal), staff turnover versus sector norms.
  • Governance: the quiet workhorse. Related-party transactions, override-prone controls, an owner-manager who treats the company account as personal — governance findings correlate strongly with QoE findings, because the same instincts produce both.

Two practical reasons ESG earns its place. Financing: sustainability-linked loan margins and some lenders' appetite now move on ESG credentials. Exit: the buyer universe in five years — trade acquirers with net-zero commitments, larger funds with LP-driven exclusions — may simply not include buyers for an asset with an unresolved ESG problem. An ESG finding that narrows the future buyer pool is an exit-multiple finding wearing different clothes.

§9.4.7Pulling the workstreams together

A useful closing exercise: notice how often the same underlying issue surfaces in multiple workstreams wearing different labels. Founder dependence appears in management DD (no second line), legal DD (IP in the founder's name), ops DD (pricing decisions all routed through one desk), and FDD (excess remuneration add-back). Weak systems appear in FDD (slow, unreconciled reporting), ops DD (no KPIs), and tech DD (spreadsheet sprawl). When three workstreams independently brush against the same issue, that issue is structural — and it belongs at the top of the issues list, priced or fixed, not scattered across three appendices as minor observations. Synthesis, as Lesson 1 said, is the deal team's actual job.

↑ Module 9

Lesson 9.5/Due Diligence

The Red-Flags Catalogue

30 min read
In brief

A structured catalogue of twenty classic diligence red flags across earnings quality, customers, market, management, and legal — what each looks like in the data, why it matters, and whether the right response is a price chip, a structural fix, or walking away.

  1. 9.5.1How to use this catalogue
  2. 9.5.2Family 1: Earnings quality
  3. 9.5.3Family 2: Customers and revenue base
  4. 9.5.4Family 3: Market and competitive position
  5. 9.5.5Family 4: Management and governance
  6. 9.5.6Family 5: Legal, tax, and compliance
  7. 9.5.7Reading flags in combination
  8. 9.5.8The discipline of the issues list

§9.5.1How to use this catalogue

This lesson is the module's reference core: twenty flags you will actually meet, grouped into five families. For each one: what it looks like in the data (so you can find it), why it matters (so you can argue it), and the default treatment — price chip, structure fix, or walk away — using the framework from Lesson 1.

Three rules before the tables. First, the treatment column is a default, not a law: a flag that is certain and quantifiable chips the price; a flag that is a contingent risk gets structured; a flag that poisons trust or the thesis itself means walking. The same flag can move category depending on severity — 25% customer concentration is a price conversation, 60% is a walk-away conversation. Second, flags compound non-linearly: two medium flags that share a root cause (say, channel stuffing and a founder who blocks customer references) are worse than four unrelated ones. Third, the most dangerous flag is the one you rationalise: if you catch yourself building the seller's defence for them, hand the finding to the most sceptical person on the team.

§9.5.2Family 1: Earnings quality

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
1 Revenue recognised ahead of substance Revenue spikes in Q4/period-end; debtor days climbing (58→74); bill-and-hold or ship-to-distributor terms; deferred income falling while revenue grows Earnings are borrowed from next year — the year you own Price chip on restated EBITDA; walk if deliberate and pervasive
2 Channel stuffing Distributor/wholesale sales outgrowing end-market sell-through; extended payment terms or return rights on late-period orders; distributor inventory building Post-close revenue air-pocket as the channel destocks; often shades into misstatement Price chip on normalised run-rate; walk if concealed
3 Serial "one-offs" The same category of add-back (legal, restructuring, "exceptional" hiring) appears 3+ years running One-offs that recur are opex; adjusted EBITDA is overstated by the recurring level Price chip — add back only the excess over run-rate
4 Provision releases flattering EBITDA Warranty/bad-debt/stock provisions falling while the activity that drives them grows; releases credited to P&L Non-cash, non-recurring profit inside "clean" EBITDA; may signal under-provision building future cost Price chip — strip releases, restate provision to adequate level
5 Rising capitalisation of costs Capitalised development/commissions jump (e.g. £0.4m→£1.6m) with no policy note; amortisation lags Costs moved from P&L to balance sheet inflate EBITDA ~pound-for-pound; conversion to cash worsens Price chip — normalise to historic capitalisation rate; check cash conversion
6 Weak cash conversion EBITDA-to-operating-cash conversion <80% with no growth-capex story; working capital absorbing cash every year EBITDA is an opinion, cash is a fact; leverage is serviced with cash Price chip (value on cash-adjusted earnings); investigate before assuming benign
7 Peg games / window-dressed balance sheet Completion NWC well below 12-month monthly average; creditor stretch and debtor blitz in final quarter Seller extracts value through working capital rather than price Structure fix — set the peg on the monthly average; pound-for-pound true-up

§9.5.3Family 2: Customers and revenue base

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
8 Customer concentration Top customer >20–25% of revenue (or, worse, of gross profit); top 5 >60% One renegotiation resets margins; one loss impairs the thesis; lenders cut leverage for it Price chip via lower multiple; structure (earnout/retention tied to renewal); walk above ~40% with a near-term renewal
9 Hidden churn under headline growth GRR <90% with growth driven by new logos; recent cohorts churning faster than old ones The engine leaks — growth stops the moment acquisition spend does; declining new-cohort quality says the leak is worsening Price chip — underwrite the CDD case, not the plan
10 Contract cliff Large contracts or framework agreements expiring within 12–18 months of close; renewal history thin The revenue you are pricing may not survive year one Structure fix — condition or earnout on renewal; chip if renewal terms already known to be worse
11 Loss-making "strategic" revenue Named contracts at negative or near-zero gross margin, justified as market entry or "land and expand" Revenue quality overstated; exiting the contract shrinks the top line the price was set on Price chip — value the business excluding it; make management's expansion story an earnout
12 Pricing erosion beneath list prices Realised price/mix falling while list prices rise; discount dispersion widening; rebates growing The pricing "lever" in the model runs backwards; competitive position weaker than claimed Price chip on forecast; revisit thesis if pricing is the value-creation plan

§9.5.4Family 3: Market and competitive position

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
13 Share loss dressed as market growth Target CAGR 3% in a market growing 7%; win rates falling; expert calls name a rising competitor You are paying a growth multiple for a share-loser; the gap compounds Price chip at best; walk if the thesis was "market leader"
14 Structural demand risk Core product exposed to regulation, technology substitution, or a single channel shifting (e.g. retail to D2C); customers' own industries declining Terminal value is the majority of any price; a melting terminal value cannot be chipped accurately Walk in most cases — or price as a run-off with structure carrying the tail risk
15 Cyclical peak presented as trend Record year driven by a commodity spike, post-crisis catch-up, or one-off regulation change; "normalised" year never defined Buying peak earnings at a full multiple is double-counting the cycle Price chip — underwrite through-cycle EBITDA; structure with earnout if seller disputes the cycle

§9.5.5Family 4: Management and governance

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
16 Founder dependence All key relationships, pricing decisions, and technical knowledge route through one person; no second line in meetings; IP or customer contracts in the founder's personal orbit The asset walks out of the door at completion — or holds you hostage after it Structure fix — rollover, earnout, retention, pre-close hires; walk if the founder is also exiting fully
17 Inconsistent answers / data access friction The same question gets different answers over time; basic data "not tracked"; management access rationed through advisers Either systems cannot produce truth or someone prefers you not to have it — both are findings, and the second is disqualifying Escalate and test; walk if the pattern persists — trust is not warrantable
18 Related-party transactions Sales to, purchases from, or leases with entities owned by directors/family; terms not benchmarked; e.g. founder's brother as top supplier Margins may be artificial in either direction; post-close continuity at those terms is not assured; governance signal Price chip — restate to arm's-length terms; structure the transition; walk if concealed rather than disclosed

§9.5.6Family 5: Legal, tax, and compliance

# Flag What it looks like in the data Why it matters Default treatment
19 Change-of-control traps CoC clauses in top customer contracts, key licences, or property leases; consents required to complete Key counterparties gain a renegotiation window your completion timetable pays for Structure fix — consents as conditions precedent; chip for known re-pricing
20 Historic tax/compliance exposure Aggressive schemes in the ledger; contractor workforce with employee characteristics; VAT treatment inconsistent with rulings; data-protection posture incompatible with the customer base Crystallisation costs cash and reputation post-close; standard W&I excludes identified issues Structure fix — specific indemnity or escrow, quantified; walk if exposure threatens licence to operate

§9.5.7Reading flags in combination

Single flags have prices. Patterns have verdicts. Three patterns to memorise:

The manufactured year. Flags 1, 4, 5, and 7 together — revenue pulled forward, provisions released, costs capitalised, working capital squeezed — describe a business groomed for sale. Each item might individually be worth £0.3–0.8m of EBITDA; together they mean the whole current year is unreliable, and your baseline should be built from prior years plus verified run-rate changes. Expect the true EBITDA to be 15–25% below the headline, and expect the seller to know it.

The dependent business. Flags 8, 16, and 18 together — concentrated customers, founder dependence, related-party supply — describe a business that is really a web of personal relationships wearing a company's clothes. No price chip fixes this; only structure (rollover, earnouts, long transitions) keeps the relationships attached to the asset, and only partially.

The treadmill. Flags 9, 11, and 12 together — leaky retention, bought revenue, eroding price — describe growth that costs more than it returns. This is the classic value trap covered in the next lesson: optically cheap, cheap for a reason.

§9.5.8The discipline of the issues list

Every flag you find goes onto the issues list from Lesson 1 with four entries: the evidence, the quantum, the proposed treatment, and the owner. Two closing disciplines. First, quantify even the awkward ones — "customer concentration: bad" is not actionable; "a 25% probability of losing the top customer at renewal is £2.1m of gross-profit-at-risk, which at the deal multiple justifies a £6–8m chip or an earnout of similar size" is a negotiating position. Second, track the aggregate. Deals rarely die of one flag; they should sometimes die of twelve. If the issues list's combined EBITDA impact exceeds ~20% of the headline number, the question is no longer "what's the right chip?" but "is this the business we thought we were buying?" — and that question belongs in front of the IC, not buried in a schedule.

Lesson 9.6/Due Diligence

What Good Looks Like

25 min read
In brief

The anatomy of a high-quality asset — revenue visibility, diversified customers, cash conversion, management depth, clean data — why quality compounds through better exits and easier financing, when paying up beats buying value traps, and how diligence findings are assembled into genuine IC conviction.

  1. 9.6.1Why "good" needs its own lesson
  2. 9.6.2The anatomy of a high-quality asset
  3. 9.6.3Why quality compounds
  4. 9.6.4Paying up versus value traps
  5. 9.6.5How conviction is actually built: the IC memo
  6. 9.6.6The closing test

§9.6.1Why "good" needs its own lesson

Five lessons of scepticism can leave the impression that diligence is a fault-finding exercise. It is not — it is a calibration exercise, and it fails in both directions. Missing a red flag costs money; failing to recognise quality costs deals, because quality assets go to the bidder who diligences fast enough to underwrite boldly. The funds that consistently win good auctions are not the most optimistic; they are the ones whose diligence lets them tell the difference between expensive-and-worth-it and expensive.

So this lesson inverts the catalogue: what does a genuinely high-quality asset look like in the data, why does quality compound rather than merely add, and how does a deal team convert diligence output into the thing an IC actually buys — conviction.

§9.6.2The anatomy of a high-quality asset

Five traits recur in the assets that make funds' track records, each observable in diligence:

1. Revenue visibility. At the start of the year, how much of the year's revenue is already secured? Rank the spectrum: contracted recurring revenue (multi-year contracts, auto-renewing subscriptions) > re-occurring revenue (repeat purchases with no contract — high empirical retention, no legal commitment) > backlog/order book > pipeline > walk-in. Worked test: a business with £50m revenue where £38m renews contractually and historic GRR is 96% enters the year needing to find £12m; a same- size business with £8m contracted needs to find £42m. Same P&L, utterly different risk. What good looks like: opening-year visibility ≥70%, renewal rates stable across cohorts, and — the detail that separates real visibility from decoration — contracts that customers actually honour (check the enforcement history, not just the terms).

2. Diversified, sticky customers. Top customer <10% of revenue, top ten <40%, churn low and boring — losses concentrated in small accounts, none through dissatisfaction of a reference customer. Plus stickiness with a mechanism you can name: switching costs, integration, accreditation, data lock-in — not just habit.

3. Cash conversion. EBITDA-to-operating-cash conversion ≥90% sustained across years, working capital scaling sub-linearly with revenue, maintenance capex modest and honestly separated from growth capex. Cash conversion is the trait lenders price most directly, and the hardest to fake for long: over five years, cumulative free cash flow either showed up or it didn't.

4. Management depth. A second line that runs the business day-to-day, decisions that survive the CEO's holiday, succession candidates visible for every key role, and a team that has already operated with proper governance (board packs, budgets it holds itself to). Depth converts key-person risk from a structural flaw into a personnel question.

5. Clean data and self-knowledge. The trait that predicts the others: monthly accounts closed in five days that reconcile to audit; KPIs the CIM quotes reproducible from raw data; management that knows its churn, its price realisation, its margin by customer — including the unflattering ones. A business that measures itself honestly almost always diligences cleanly, because the habits are the same habits.

Notice what is not on the list: growth rate. Growth is an amplifier, not a quality. Fast growth over a leaky base is the treadmill from Lesson 5; even fast profitable growth built on one customer is fragile. Quality is about the durability of the economics; growth then multiplies whatever durability is there.

§9.6.3Why quality compounds

Quality traits do not add — they multiply, through three loops that all pay out at exit:

The financing loop. Lenders lend more, cheaper, and on looser terms against visible revenue and strong cash conversion. Worked example: two businesses each with £10m EBITDA. The quality asset supports 5.0× leverage at SONIA+375; the mixed asset supports 3.5× at SONIA+500. On identical entry multiples the quality buyer puts in £15m less equity, and over a five-year hold pays roughly £2m less cash interest — higher MOIC before either business does anything differently. Debt capacity is the market's real-time quality score.

The exit loop. The next buyer's diligence will find what yours found. A business that diligences cleanly — data room ready, KPIs reproducible, no skeletons — commands a broader buyer universe (trade, larger funds, IPO all available), a faster process, and a fuller multiple. Multiple expansion is often described as luck; buying assets whose quality the next diligence process will confirm is the version of it you can underwrite. The converse: every unresolved flag you accept at entry is a chip the next buyer takes at exit — you rent red flags, you don't buy them once.

The optionality loop. Quality assets survive their own bad years. Strong cash conversion and headroom mean a downturn is a slow year, not a covenant breach; a crisis becomes a chance to buy a weakened competitor rather than a forced sale. Over a five-year hold, something always goes wrong; quality determines whether "wrong" is a chapter or the ending.

§9.6.4Paying up versus value traps

The perennial IC argument: 11× for the clean asset or 7× for the flawed one? The honest maths is less forgiving of "cheap" than intuition suggests.

Worked example. Asset A: £10m EBITDA at 11.0× (EV £110m), 5.0× debt, quality traits throughout; underwrite 6% EBITDA growth and exit at 10.5× (modest compression). Year-5 EBITDA £13.4m; exit EV £140.7m; debt paid down to say £30m; equity £110.7m on £60m in ≈ 1.85× MOIC — with a narrow distribution of outcomes. Asset B: £10m EBITDA at 7.0× (EV £70m), but a leaky base: underwrite 0% net growth (churn offsets wins), 3.5× debt, and exit to a buyer who diligences the same flaws you found — 6.0× exit. Year-5 EBITDA £10m; exit EV £60m; debt down to £20m; equity £40m on £35m in ≈ 1.14× MOIC — with a wide distribution including zeros. The trap is that Asset B's entry price looks like the bargain; but you exit through the same door you entered, and the discount travels with the flaws.

This is not an argument that quality always wins — it is an argument about which question to ask. For the premium asset: "what has to be true for 11× to work, and does diligence support it?" For the cheap asset: "is the flaw fixable by us, priced in, and re-rateable at exit — or is it the permanent reason for the price?" A fixable flaw (weak reporting, absent pricing discipline, an underinvested salesforce) is a value-creation thesis wearing a discount. A permanent flaw (structural decline, an unmovable customer concentration) is just a smaller multiple forever. Turnarounds and deep-value deals can make spectacular returns — but only for funds that resource them deliberately, and never by accident to a buyer who mistook cheap for safe.

§9.6.5How conviction is actually built: the IC memo

Diligence ends as an IC memo, and the diligence section of a good memo has a specific architecture — not a summary of reports, but a chain of underwriting logic:

  1. The thesis, stated falsifiably. "We are buying the #2 player in a consolidating £450m niche, underwriting 4% organic growth and two bolt-ons." A thesis that cannot be wrong cannot be diligenced.
  2. What we tested and what we found. Each thesis leg mapped to the workstream that load-tested it and the evidence that came back — including the tests that failed and moved the plan. "CDD supports 4% not management's 7%; we underwrite 4%."
  3. The issues list, disposed of. Every material finding with its treatment: chipped (the price moved from £108m to £101m for the QoE findings), structured (£8m earnout against the disputed contract), protected (specific tax indemnity, £3m escrow), or accepted with eyes open (25% top-customer concentration; renewal history strong; downside case run). Nothing merely "noted".
  4. The downside case that still works. Not the base case minus 10% — a named scenario built from the actual flags: "top customer halves at renewal, price rises realise at 1%: EBITDA £8.2m, covenants hold with £1.4m headroom, equity returns 1.2×." Conviction is not believing the base case; it is knowing the specific downside is survivable.
  5. Why we win. In an auction, the honest question: what do we see that the underbidder doesn't — a genuine angle (synergy with a portfolio company, sector insight, operational capability), or just a higher number? "We are paying more because we know more" is a thesis. "We are paying more" is the winner's curse.

The tell of a weak memo is adjectives where numbers should be — "strong management", "attractive market", "robust margins". The tell of a strong one is that a sceptical reader can find the load-bearing assumptions in five minutes, because they are labelled as such. Diligence, done properly, does not manufacture certainty. It buys down the cost of being wrong — and tells you, precisely, what you are still betting on.

§9.6.6The closing test

Before the IC votes, the best deal teams can answer five questions in one sentence each: What exactly are we buying (the diligenced EBITDA, not the CIM's)? What are we paying for it, and what did diligence move? What do we believe that the market doesn't, and what evidence carries that belief? What kills this deal, and why does the structure survive it? And who buys this from us in five years, and what will their diligence find? If the fifth answer is "the same flags we're rationalising today", the deal has failed the module's whole test — because in the end, the exit is just someone else's due diligence.

Lesson 10.1/Value Creation

The Value Creation Plan

24 min read
In brief

What a value creation plan (VCP) is, the full lever taxonomy (revenue, margin, cash/capital efficiency, multiple, leverage), how much each lever typically contributes to returns, why the plan is written before the deal closes, and what actually goes into a 100-day plan — with a worked returns-attribution example.

  1. 10.1.1From deal thesis to value creation plan
  2. 10.1.2The five levers
  3. 10.1.3How much each lever contributes
  4. 10.1.4Why the plan is written pre-close
  5. 10.1.5The 100-day plan
  6. 10.1.6What deal teams actually ask

§10.1.1From deal thesis to value creation plan

Every deal is bought on a thesis — a two-or-three sentence claim about why this business, at this price, will make money. "Fragmented market, we consolidate it." "Under-priced product, we fix pricing." "Great product, amateur cost base." The value creation plan (VCP) is what that thesis becomes when someone forces it to be specific: a lever-by-lever programme, with named initiatives, owners, timelines, and — critically — numbers that reconcile to the returns model the investment committee approved.

The distinction matters. A thesis is a belief; a VCP is a budget. If the IC model assumes EBITDA grows from £10m to £15m over five years, the VCP has to say which £5m: £2m from pricing, £1.5m from procurement, £1m from new site openings, £0.5m from mix. Each of those lines then gets an initiative, an owner, a cost to achieve, and a milestone plan. When the deal team presents at IC, a good committee asks exactly this question: "Show me the bridge from today's EBITDA to your exit EBITDA, line by line, and tell me who delivers each line." A deal where the answer is "growth" is a deal where nobody has done the work.

For someone in a PE data team this document is your map of the next five years. Every initiative in the VCP eventually becomes a KPI someone has to track, a dashboard someone has to build, and a monthly variance someone has to explain. Read the VCP on day one and you know what the fund actually cares about.

§10.1.2The five levers

All PE value creation decomposes into five levers. Everything a portfolio company does fits somewhere in this taxonomy, and every returns attribution you will ever build uses it:

Lever What it means Typical initiatives
Revenue growth Grow EBITDA by growing the top line Pricing, salesforce effectiveness, new products/markets, cross-sell, bolt-on acquisitions
Margin expansion Grow EBITDA at constant revenue Procurement, spans & layers, footprint consolidation, shared services, automation, zero-based budgeting
Cash & capital efficiency Convert more EBITDA into cash; use less capital Working-capital reduction (stock, debtors), capex discipline, sale-and-leaseback
Multiple expansion Sell the same EBITDA for a higher multiple Reposition the business (recurring revenue, sector re-rating), improve growth profile, professionalise reporting, buy-and-build arbitrage
Leverage / deleveraging Debt paydown transfers enterprise value to equity Amortisation from free cash flow — the mechanical partner of the cash lever

Two of these deserve a flag. Multiple expansion is the lever the deal team controls least: most of it is market beta (what sector multiples do over the hold) and only some of it is earned (making the business genuinely higher-quality). Underwriting a deal on assumed multiple expansion is how funds overpay at the top of cycles, and most ICs force the base case to assume exit multiple = entry multiple. Leverage is not really a value creation lever at all — it is an amplifier. Debt paydown moves value from the debt column to the equity column, but the cash that pays the debt down was generated by the operating levers.

§10.1.3How much each lever contributes

The industry's own attribution studies (the kind consultancies publish annually) tell a consistent story about how the mix has shifted. In the 1980s, the majority of buyout returns came from leverage and multiple expansion — buy cheap, gear up, ride the market. Entry multiples were low and debt was the product. Today, with entry multiples in the 9–12× range for quality assets and every auction fully competitive, roughly half or more of value created in a typical modern buyout comes from EBITDA growth — split between revenue growth (the largest single contributor, often 30–50% of value created) and margin expansion (typically 15–25%) — with multiple expansion and deleveraging sharing the rest. Treat these as framing, not physics: attribution varies hugely by vintage, sector, and strategy, and a buy-and-build deal will show a very different mix from a single-asset carve-out. The direction of travel, though, is unambiguous: you can no longer buy your returns; you have to build them.

Here is the standard attribution arithmetic on a worked example. A fund buys a business at 10.0× EBITDA of £10.0m = £100m EV, funded with £60m debt and £40m equity. Five years later it exits at 11.0× EBITDA of £15.0m = £165m EV, with debt paid down to £30m.

Entry Exit
EBITDA £10.0m £15.0m
Multiple 10.0× 11.0×
Enterprise value £100.0m £165.0m
Net debt £60.0m £30.0m
Equity value £40.0m £135.0m

Equity gain = £95.0m (a 3.4× gross MOIC). Attribution:

Lever Calculation Value created Share
EBITDA growth £5.0m × 10.0× entry multiple £50.0m 53%
Multiple expansion 1.0× × £15.0m exit EBITDA £15.0m 16%
Deleveraging £60.0m − £30.0m £30.0m 32%
Total £95.0m 100%

(Convention note: multiple expansion is measured on exit EBITDA and EBITDA growth at the entry multiple; the cross-term has to sit somewhere, and this is the standard allocation. Shares are rounded.) What looks good in an attribution: EBITDA growth dominating. What looks bad: a deal where most of the gain is multiple expansion — the deal team will hear "you got lucky" at the next fundraise.

§10.1.4Why the plan is written pre-close

The VCP is drafted before the deal closes, usually in parallel with confirmatory due diligence, and there are hard commercial reasons why:

  1. It disciplines the price. The maximum price you can pay is a function of the value you can create. If the VCP can only find £3m of EBITDA improvement, you cannot pay a price that needs £5m. Writing the plan pre-close forces the deal team to underwrite initiatives, not hopes, and the IC will mark the model to the plan.
  2. DD is the evidence base. Commercial and operational due diligence is the one window when consultants are crawling over the business at the fund's expense. Their findings — pricing dispersion, procurement benchmarks, span-of-control data — are the raw material of the VCP. If you wait until after close to plan, you pay twice for the analysis.
  3. The first 100 days are the window. Organisations accept change at a moment of ownership transition in a way they never do in steady state. A new owner asking for a price rise, a new reporting pack, or an organisational redesign in month two is "the new owners' way of doing things"; the same request in month eighteen is a fight. You cannot exploit that window if you spend it deciding what to do.
  4. Management alignment is negotiated at close. The management incentive plan is struck at completion, and management need to know what they are signing up to deliver. Agreeing the VCP (or at least its headlines) with the CEO pre-close is how you find out whether the incumbent team believes in the plan — and whether you believe in them.

The practical corollary: by the time the wire transfer clears, the fund should already know its top five initiatives, who owns each, and what the first board meeting will demand.

§10.1.5The 100-day plan

The 100-day plan is the execution front-end of the VCP: not a strategy document but a mobilisation schedule for the first three months of ownership. Its jobs are (a) take control, (b) build the baseline, (c) bank the quick wins, and (d) launch the big initiatives properly. A real one looks like a workstream grid, not an essay:

Workstream Owner By day 30 By day 60 By day 100
Cash & controls CFO Daily cash reporting live; banking mandates changed; capex approvals >£50k to board 13-week cash-flow forecast embedded Working-capital reduction targets set per site
Management reporting CFO + data team Define monthly KPI pack; baseline data pulled First monthly pack delivered ≤10 working days after month end Dashboard automated; budget reforecast complete
Pricing Commercial director Price/discount data extracted; dispersion analysis done Discount authority matrix imposed; list-price rise announced Price increase in market; realisation tracked weekly
Procurement Ops director Spend cube built; top-20 suppliers identified RFQs out on top categories First renegotiated contracts signed; savings run-rate tracked
Organisation CEO Top-team assessment complete Key hires launched (typically CFO/CRO); spans & layers review scoped Any structural changes announced
VCP mobilisation Deal team Initiative owners confirmed; targets cascaded Initiative charters signed off at board Full VCP tracking in monthly board pack

Note what is — and is not — in there. In: diagnostics, baselines, control systems, quick wins (pricing and procurement almost always), and the launch of long-cycle work. Not in: completing a warehouse consolidation, an ERP migration, or a culture change. Those take years; the 100-day plan's job is to start them from a position of knowledge, not finish them. A 100-day plan that promises structural transformation by day 100 is a red flag in itself — it means nobody has scoped the work.

§10.1.6What deal teams actually ask

When you see a VCP — yours or a competitor's asset coming to market with one attached — here is the judgement checklist:

  • Does the bridge tie to the model? Sum the initiatives; if they add to £4m and the model needs £6m, the gap is being filled by hope. Conversely, a plan showing £8m against a £5m need has sandbagging or double counting in it.
  • Are the top three initiatives evidenced from DD? "Pricing opportunity of £2m" should trace to a specific finding — dispersion data, unpassed cost inflation — not a benchmark percentage applied to revenue.
  • Who delivers it? Every initiative needs a named owner inside the business. A plan whose owners are all "consultants TBC" will cost twice as much and land half.
  • What does it cost? Every cost-out programme has one-off costs to achieve (redundancy, site exits, systems). A plan with savings but no costs is unfinished.
  • What breaks if it slips? The debt package was sized on the plan. Ask which initiatives the covenant headroom depends on — those get board-level tracking from month one.

The rest of this module walks the levers one at a time: revenue (lesson 2), margin and cost (lesson 3), buy-and-build — the lever that spans revenue and multiple at once (lesson 4) — and the governance machine that makes any of it actually happen (lesson 5).

Lesson 10.2/Value Creation

Revenue Levers

24 min read
In brief

The revenue side of the value creation plan: pricing as the most underused lever (with a worked example of a 3% price rise flowing to EBITDA), salesforce effectiveness, new products and markets, cross-sell, commercial excellence programmes, and why growth investments that hurt short-term EBITDA are often exactly the right call.

  1. 10.2.1Why pricing is the most underused lever
  2. 10.2.2Worked example: 3% through to EBITDA
  3. 10.2.3Salesforce effectiveness
  4. 10.2.4New products, new markets, cross-sell
  5. 10.2.5Commercial excellence programmes
  6. 10.2.6When growth investment hurts EBITDA — and why that's fine
  7. 10.2.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.2.1Why pricing is the most underused lever

Ask an operating partner which lever delivers the most EBITDA per unit of effort and the answer is almost always pricing. The reason is pure arithmetic: a price increase, net of any volume loss, flows straight through to EBITDA. There is no cost of goods against it, no headcount to hire, no capex. Compare the three classic 1% moves on a business with £100m revenue, £60m variable costs, £30m fixed costs, £10m EBITDA:

Move EBITDA impact Why
+1% price (volume held) +£1.0m (+10%) 100% flow-through
+1% volume +£0.4m (+4%) Only the 40% contribution margin flows through
−1% variable cost +£0.6m (+6%) 1% × £60m

Price is worth two and a half times volume. Yet mid-market companies systematically under-price, for reasons that are organisational, not economic: founders price on cost-plus and never revisit; sales reps have unlimited discount authority and are paid on revenue, not margin; list prices haven't moved since the last crisis because "our customers won't wear it"; and nobody owns pricing — it falls between sales, finance and marketing. This is why pricing is nearly always in the 100-day plan: the opportunity is usually large, fast, and invisible to the previous owner.

§10.2.2Worked example: 3% through to EBITDA

Take a distribution business: revenue £100.0m, gross margin 25% (£25.0m), overheads £17.0m, EBITDA £8.0m (8.0% margin). The new owner puts through a 3% price increase across the book.

Case 1 — no volume loss. Revenue becomes £103.0m. COGS is unchanged at £75.0m (same units shipped), overheads unchanged. Every pound of the increase lands in profit:

£m Before After
Revenue 100.0 103.0
COGS (75.0) (75.0)
Gross profit 25.0 28.0
Overheads (17.0) (17.0)
EBITDA 8.0 11.0

A 3% price move produces a 37.5% EBITDA increase. At an 8× multiple, that £3.0m is £24m of enterprise value — on a £60–80m business, potentially a third of the equity cheque, from one initiative. This leverage is why low-margin businesses (distributors, logistics, services) are the most price-sensitive value creation stories, not the least: the thinner the margin, the more violent the flow-through.

Case 2 — with some churn. Suppose 2% of volume walks. Retained volume is 98%, priced 3% higher: revenue = £100.0m × 0.98 × 1.03 = £100.9m. COGS falls with volume to £75.0m × 0.98 = £73.5m. Gross profit = £27.4m; EBITDA = £10.4m. Still up 30%. Run the break-even: with a 25% gross margin, the price rise only destroys value if volume falls by more than roughly 3/(25+3) ≈ 11% — and in practice, well-executed B2B price increases on non-contracted business lose low-single-digit volume at worst. The asymmetry is the whole point: the downside case still makes money.

What deal teams actually look for as pricing evidence in DD: price dispersion (the same SKU sold to similar customers at prices 10–20% apart — the low end is pure leakage), unpassed input inflation (supplier costs up 8%, prices up 2% — visible as gross margin erosion), discounting without governance (no approval matrix, discounts clustering just below whatever threshold triggers sign-off), and no price rise in 2+ years. Each of these converts to a sized opportunity, which is exactly the exercise in this module's case study.

§10.2.3Salesforce effectiveness

The second commercial lever is making the existing salesforce sell more. Typical mid-market findings and fixes:

  • Coverage and territory design. The best rep produces 4–5× the worst, and territories reflect history, not opportunity. Rebalancing accounts and putting the best people on the biggest whitespace is free capacity.
  • Activity and pipeline discipline. No CRM hygiene, no stage definitions, forecasts that are guesses. Instrumenting the funnel (this is data-team work) converts sales management from anecdote to arithmetic: if win rates are 20% and the plan needs £10m of new revenue at a £100k average deal, the pipeline must hold £50m — is it there?
  • Incentives. Reps paid on revenue will discount to close; move comp toward gross margin and mix, and behaviour follows within a quarter.
  • Pricing the funnel, not just the book. Discount approval at quote stage, floor prices by segment, win/loss tracking on price.

None of this is glamorous, and that is the point: salesforce effectiveness is a 5–15% revenue uplift hiding in process, measurable within two quarters.

§10.2.4New products, new markets, cross-sell

The longer-cycle revenue levers, in rough order of risk:

  1. Cross-sell — selling existing products to existing customers who buy only one line. Lowest risk, because both the product and the relationship already exist. The diagnostic is a simple matrix: customers × product lines, filled with revenue. In most multi-line businesses the matrix is startlingly empty. If the average customer buys 1.4 of 5 lines and the best accounts buy 4, the gap is the opportunity — though be honest about why it's empty (sometimes the products genuinely don't co-purchase).
  2. New segments and geographies for existing products — medium risk. The product is proven; the go-to-market is not. Bolt-on acquisitions (lesson 4) are often a faster route into a new region than organic entry.
  3. New products — highest risk and slowest payback; genuinely new product development rarely pays back inside a 4–5 year hold. PE funds mostly buy new products (bolt-ons) rather than build them, unless the pipeline was already late-stage at entry.

What looks good: a growth plan weighted to cross-sell and share-of-wallet, evidenced from the customer matrix. What looks bad: a hockey stick driven by products that don't exist yet, in markets the company has never sold to.

§10.2.5Commercial excellence programmes

"Commercial excellence" is the umbrella term for doing all of the above as one programme rather than piecemeal: pricing governance, salesforce effectiveness, funnel instrumentation, key-account plans, and churn management under a single owner (often a newly hired Chief Revenue Officer) with a single dashboard. Structurally it mirrors a cost-out programme — baseline, initiative charters, weekly cadence, tracked benefits — and that structure is what separates it from "we told sales to try harder."

The data team is load-bearing here. Every commercial excellence programme runs on three datasets that typically don't exist at entry: a transaction-level price file (every invoice line: customer, SKU, list price, realised price, cost — this powers the dispersion analysis), a clean pipeline with staged probabilities, and cohorted customer revenue (retention, churn, and share-of-wallet by vintage). Building these is often literally the first quarter of the programme, and it is why commercial DD providers and operating teams now bring data engineers, not just strategists.

Typical programme economics, for calibration: 2–5% revenue uplift from pricing and leakage alone within 12–18 months, a further 3–10% from salesforce effectiveness and cross-sell over the hold — with the pricing tranche flowing through at close to 100% margin and the volume tranche at contribution margin.

§10.2.6When growth investment hurts EBITDA — and why that's fine

Here is the tension every owner faces: most revenue levers beyond pricing cost money before they pay. New sales hires carry a 6–12 month ramp; a new site loses money for 18 months; entering a new geography means a year of overhead before revenue. All of it depresses EBITDA now to build EBITDA later — and since the business is valued as a multiple of EBITDA, undisciplined thinking says "protect this year's number."

Run the arithmetic instead. EBITDA today is £10.0m; assume an 8× exit either way. Option A: cut £2.0m of growth spend. EBITDA is £12.0m immediately, but growth stalls and exit EBITDA is £12.0m → EV £96m. Option B: keep investing. EBITDA stays £10.0m this year but compounds to £15.0m by exit → EV £120m. Option B is worth £24m more — and in reality the gap is wider, because a business exiting with visible growth sells at a higher multiple than one that has been harvested. Buyers at exit will run the same QofE analysis your fund ran at entry, and "EBITDA propped up by cutting sales capacity" is one of the first adjustments they'll make.

So the judgement rule deal teams apply: short-term EBITDA pain is fine when it is legible. That means (a) the investment is ring-fenced and separately reported — boards often track "EBITDA before growth investment" as a memo line so the underlying engine stays visible; (b) the payback case is explicit (cohort economics for sales hires, site-level P&Ls for new locations) and is being tracked against actuals; and (c) the capital structure can afford it — covenant headroom is measured on actual EBITDA, and a levered balance sheet can turn a sensible investment into a default. What looks bad is the mirror image: EBITDA "investment" that is really margin erosion with a story attached, never ring-fenced, never tracked, never paying back. The difference between the two is a reporting discipline — which is to say, it is the data team's job to make the difference visible.

§10.2.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me realised price by customer for your top SKUs" — the dispersion chart is the single fastest pricing diagnostic in existence.
  • "When did you last raise list prices, and what happened to volume?" — the answer is usually "2022" and "nothing", which is the opportunity in one sentence.
  • "What's the gross margin trend?" — eroding gross margin with stable volumes means input inflation is not being passed through: a pricing initiative, pre-sized.
  • "What does a rep cost, what does a ramped rep produce, and how long is the ramp?" — the unit economics that justify (or kill) a salesforce expansion.
  • "Which growth spend would you cut if you had to protect EBITDA — and why haven't you?" — the question that reveals whether management can tell investment from waste.

Lesson 10.3/Value Creation

Margin & Cost Levers

24 min read
In brief

The cost side of the value creation plan: procurement, spans & layers, footprint consolidation, shared services, automation and zero-based budgeting — with a worked margin bridge from 15% to 19% EBITDA margin over three years, and the credibility tests deal teams apply to cost-out plans, especially the scrutiny of one-off costs to achieve.

  1. 10.3.1Why margin is the "bankable" lever
  2. 10.3.2Procurement: the reliable first wave
  3. 10.3.3Organisational levers: spans, layers, and shared services
  4. 10.3.4Footprint, automation, and zero-based budgeting
  5. 10.3.5Worked example: the 15% → 19% margin bridge
  6. 10.3.6Costs to achieve: where cost-out plans go to be audited
  7. 10.3.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.3.1Why margin is the "bankable" lever

Revenue levers create the most value over a hold, but margin levers are the ones lenders and investment committees treat as bankable — you can size them from data the business already has, they don't depend on customers doing anything, and delivery is largely within management's control. That is why a debt package will often be sized giving partial credit for cost-out but none for growth: a bank will believe you can renegotiate your freight contract; it will not believe your cross-sell hockey stick.

The flip side is that cost-out is finite and margin expansion has a floor. You can take a business from 15% to 19% EBITDA margin once; you cannot do it every hold, and a buyer at exit will ask "what's left?" A VCP that leans entirely on cost with no growth story tends to exit at a lower multiple — buyers pay for engines, not squeezed lemons. The craft is sequencing: bank the cost levers early (they fund the growth investment and pay down debt), and let the growth levers carry the exit story.

The standard cost levers, roughly in order of speed:

Lever Typical timing Typical size
Procurement Months 3–18 2–5% of addressable spend
Zero-based budgeting (discretionary) Months 3–12 10–20% of discretionary opex
Spans & layers Months 6–18 5–10% of management cost
Shared services Year 1–2 15–30% of back-office cost
Automation / digital Year 1–3 Varies; longest payback
Footprint consolidation Year 1–3 Site fixed costs, net of transfer costs

§10.3.2Procurement: the reliable first wave

Procurement is nearly always the first big cost initiative because the money is real, the method is proven, and nobody gets made redundant. The playbook:

  1. Build the spend cube — every supplier invoice line coded by category, supplier, site, and unit price. This is data-team work, it takes 4–8 weeks, and it is the single prerequisite for everything else. Most mid-market companies cannot tell you their top-20 suppliers by addressable spend on day one.
  2. Segment addressable spend. Not all spend is negotiable this year — some is contracted, some is monopoly-supplied, some is spec-locked. On £50m of third-party spend, perhaps £35m is addressable in wave one.
  3. Run the levers per category: competitive tender (RFQs to 3–5 suppliers), consolidation (move 8 packaging suppliers to 2 for volume pricing), specification changes (do we need this grade?), payment terms, and simple renegotiation — a supplier who has had the account uncontested for six years has margin to give.
  4. Track savings at run-rate and lock them. A negotiated 4% price reduction that purchasing then erodes with maverick off-contract buying is worth nothing. Compliance tracking is, again, a data problem.

Calibration: 2–5% of addressable spend within 18 months is the standard underwriting range for a business that has never run professional procurement; 5%+ claims need category-level evidence. On £35m addressable, that is £0.7m–£1.75m of EBITDA — often the largest single line in the year-one bridge.

§10.3.3Organisational levers: spans, layers, and shared services

Spans & layers is the analysis of how many people each manager manages (span) and how many management levels sit between CEO and front line (layers). Benchmarks: spans of 6–10 for most functions; layers of 5–6 for a mid-market business. What DD often finds instead: spans of 2–3 ("managers managing managers managing one person") and 8 layers built by years of promoting without restructuring. Removing one thin layer of, say, 16 roles at £50k fully-loaded cost each is £0.8m — but the real benefit is speed: every layer adds approval latency and dilutes accountability.

Shared services consolidates duplicated back-office functions — finance, HR, payroll, IT support, often scattered across sites or acquired-and-never-integrated companies — into one centre. Typical saving is 15–30% of the affected cost base, from eliminating duplication and standardising processes. It is also the enabler for buy-and-build (lesson 4): a platform with a working shared-service centre can strip the back office out of every bolt-on it buys, which is where much of the synergy case lives.

The judgement point on organisational cost-out: it is the lever with the highest execution risk per pound. Redundancy programmes cost money up front (see costs to achieve, below), consume management attention for months, and done badly they take out the wrong people — the institutional knowledge walks and the politics stays.

§10.3.4Footprint, automation, and zero-based budgeting

Footprint consolidation — closing a site and serving its demand from the remaining network — trades fixed-cost savings against transfer costs. The arithmetic must be done honestly: closing a £1.5m-a-year warehouse only nets £0.7m if freight to the transferred customers rises £0.6m and you carry £0.2m of stranded costs. Site closures also have the longest tail of one-off costs (lease exits, dilapidations, redundancy, dual-running) and the most operational risk — service levels dip during the move, and in distribution businesses customers notice within a week.

Automation and digital covers everything from robotic invoice processing in finance to warehouse-management systems to replacing manual quote generation. Paybacks are longer (18 months–3 years) and business cases are routinely oversold, so ICs typically want automation in the plan but not load-bearing in the bridge. The honest framing: automation mostly buys capacity and accuracy first, headcount second.

Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) rebuilds discretionary budgets from zero each year — every line justified afresh rather than "last year plus 3%". Applied to travel, marketing, professional fees, subscriptions, and facilities, it reliably finds 10–20% of discretionary spend in the first pass, mostly legacy commitments nobody had examined. The caution: ZBB applied crudely to growth-relevant spend (marketing that drives the funnel, sales tools) is how you harvest the business by accident. Ring-fence the growth investment (lesson 2) before you zero-base anything.

§10.3.5Worked example: the 15% → 19% margin bridge

A business with revenue of £100.0m and EBITDA of £15.0m (15.0% margin) is underwritten to reach 19.0% margin over three years. Hold revenue flat for clarity (in reality revenue grows and the percentages move; the £m are what matter). The bridge the IC signed:

Bridge item Initiative detail Year landed EBITDA impact
Opening EBITDA £15.0m
Procurement waves 1–2 Tender top categories; £50m spend, 3% on addressable Yr 1–2 +£1.5m
Spans & layers Remove one management layer: 16 roles × £50k Yr 2 +£0.8m
Footprint consolidation Close site 4 of 4; £1.2m fixed cost saved, −£0.5m transfer freight Yr 2–3 +£0.7m
Shared services Consolidate 3 finance/HR teams into one centre Yr 2–3 +£0.4m
Automation Invoice processing + warehouse WMS Yr 3 +£0.6m
Zero-based budgeting Discretionary opex: travel, marketing agencies, professional fees Yr 1 +£0.5m
Inflation & reinvestment Unrecovered wage inflation; new pricing/data roles Yr 1–3 −£0.5m
Exit EBITDA £19.0m

Check the arithmetic: gross initiatives = 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.5 = £4.5m; net of the £0.5m inflation/reinvestment line, +£4.0m, landing at £19.0m on £100.0m — 19.0%. At an 8× multiple that £4.0m is £32m of enterprise value.

Three features make this bridge credible rather than decorative. First, every line is an initiative with a mechanism, not a percentage ("procurement 3% on addressable spend of £50m", not "efficiencies £1.5m"). Second, it carries a negative line: real bridges leak — wage inflation outruns price recovery, and the VCP itself needs new hires. A bridge with no negative items has not been stress-tested. Third, it is phased: nobody lands spans-and-layers in month six or automation in year one, and the phasing drives the debt model's covenant headroom.

§10.3.6Costs to achieve: where cost-out plans go to be audited

Every saving above has a one-off price tag, and "costs to achieve" is where deal teams, lenders, and — at exit — buyers apply the most scrutiny. For the bridge above:

One-off cost £m
Redundancy (spans & layers + shared services) 1.0
Site exit: lease break, dilapidations, dual-running 1.1
Systems: WMS, invoice automation, shared-service platform 0.7
Consultant support (procurement wave 1) 0.4
Total costs to achieve 3.2

That is 0.7× the £4.5m gross run-rate savings — comfortably inside the typical 0.5–1.5× range (redundancy-led programmes run ~0.5–1.0×; site- and systems-heavy programmes push toward 1.5×). A plan claiming big savings at 0.2× cost is either genuinely low-hanging fruit (possible in a never-optimised founder business) or unpriced; a plan at 2.0×+ needs a very long hold to pay back.

The credibility tests to run on any cost-out plan:

  • Run-rate vs in-year. "£4.5m of savings" landing in December contributes almost nothing to that year's EBITDA. Demand both numbers, phased by quarter.
  • Where do the one-offs sit? The classic game is booking savings in EBITDA while pushing costs to achieve below the line as "exceptional items" — inflating the adjusted EBITDA a buyer or lender sees. Fine if disclosed and genuinely one-off; a red flag when "exceptionals" recur every year of the hold.
  • Net of inflation and reinvestment? £1.5m of procurement saving in a year when input costs rose £1.0m is £0.5m of net margin. Gross-of-inflation bridges double-count.
  • Double counting across initiatives. The same back-office role cannot be saved by spans-and-layers and shared services and automation. Sum the headcount reductions by department and check them against the actual org chart.
  • Attrition vs redundancy. Plans assuming half the reduction comes free via natural attrition need the attrition rate to support it — and attrition doesn't choose which roles it removes.

§10.3.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me the bridge with dates, owners, and costs to achieve on the same page" — a savings number without its cost and calendar is a press release, not a plan.
  • "What's the addressable spend, and who said 3% was achievable?" — benchmark provenance: a category-level consultant benchmark is evidence; 'industry standard' is not.
  • "Which of these savings has the customer noticing?" — footprint and service-touching automation carry revenue risk that must appear in the bridge, not the footnotes.
  • "What did last year's exceptionals contain?" — the fastest test of whether this management team runs one-offs through EBITDA honestly.
  • "If we only did procurement and ZBB, what do we get?" — the no-regrets floor. Good plans have a bankable core plus upside; bad plans need every initiative to land.

Lesson 10.4/Value Creation

Buy-and-Build

25 min read
In brief

Platform and bolt-on economics: the multiple arbitrage worked example (platform at 9x, bolt-ons at 5-6x, the blended entry multiple maths), what makes a good platform, the integration realities of systems, culture and synergy double-counting, and the classic roll-up failure modes deal teams screen for.

  1. 10.4.1The strategy in one sentence
  2. 10.4.2The multiple arbitrage engine
  3. 10.4.3What makes a good platform
  4. 10.4.4Integration realities
  5. 10.4.5Roll-up failure modes
  6. 10.4.6What deal teams actually ask

§10.4.1The strategy in one sentence

Buy-and-build means acquiring one company as a platform and then bolting on smaller competitors or adjacent businesses, integrating them into a group that is worth more than the sum of its parts. It is the single most common strategy in mid-market PE — by some counts the majority of mid-market deals are now either platforms bought with a build thesis or bolt-ons to existing platforms — because it attacks two levers at once: revenue growth (you buy revenue you couldn't grow organically) and multiple expansion (through arbitrage and scale, below). Done well it manufactures a larger, more professional, more diversified business that a bigger buyer pays a bigger multiple for. Done badly it manufactures a pile of unintegrated acquisitions with a shared letterhead — and the market has seen enough of those to check.

§10.4.2The multiple arbitrage engine

The core arithmetic rests on a durable feature of private markets: small companies trade at lower multiples than big ones. A £2m-EBITDA business sells for 5–6× (key-person risk, customer concentration, no management depth, few buyers); a £20m-EBITDA business in the same sector sells for 9–10× (professional management, diversification, debt-financeable, and both trade buyers and larger funds can bid). Buy small, sell as part of big, and the same £1 of EBITDA re-rates.

Worked example. A fund buys a platform with £10.0m EBITDA at 9.0× = £90.0m EV, then executes four bolt-ons over three years:

Acquisition EBITDA Multiple Price
Platform £10.0m 9.0× £90.0m
Bolt-on A (regional competitor) £3.0m 6.0× £18.0m
Bolt-on B (adjacent service line) £2.0m 5.0× £10.0m
Bolt-on C (regional competitor) £2.0m 5.5× £11.0m
Bolt-on D (small tuck-in) £1.0m 5.0× £5.0m
Total £18.0m 7.4× blended £134.0m

The bolt-ons contribute £8.0m of EBITDA for £44.0m — a 5.5× average — and pull the blended entry multiple down to £134.0m ÷ £18.0m = 7.4×.

Now the arbitrage. Suppose the group simply exits at the platform's own 9.0× entry multiple, with zero organic growth and zero synergies: £18.0m × 9.0× = £162.0m against £134.0m invested — £28.0m of value from arbitrage alone, which is exactly the £8.0m of bolt-on EBITDA re-rated from 5.5× to 9.0× (£8.0m × 3.5× = £28.0m). Layer on what a real deal underwrites — say £1.5m of synergies and organic growth taking group EBITDA to £21.0m, plus a scale re-rating to 9.5× because a £21m-EBITDA group clears the size threshold for larger buyers — and exit EV is £199.5m. The strategy compounds three levers: bought EBITDA, built EBITDA, and the re-rating of both.

Two honesty checks on this maths. First, transaction and integration costs are real: each bolt-on carries 3–5% of deal value in fees plus integration costs (systems migration, rebranding, redundancy), so the true blended cost is higher than the headline — on the example above, perhaps £4–6m across the programme. Second, the arbitrage only monetises if the integration is real. Buyers at exit run a simple test: is this one company or five? Five P&Ls consolidated in Excel, five ERPs, five brands and five MDs who never meet gets valued as five small companies — at small-company multiples — and the arbitrage evaporates precisely when you try to bank it.

§10.4.3What makes a good platform

The platform choice matters more than any individual bolt-on, because everything bolts onto it. Deal teams screen for:

  • A fragmented market with willing sellers. You need a pipeline: dozens of £1–5m-EBITDA targets, typically founder-owned with succession problems. A "roll-up" of a market with three targets is just three deals.
  • Scalable infrastructure. The platform's systems, finance function and management must be able to absorb acquisitions. This is why funds often over-invest in the platform's ERP, shared services and CFO before the first bolt-on — the integration factory is built once and reused.
  • Management that can integrate, not just operate. Running one company and absorbing four are different jobs. The best platforms have (or hire) an M&A/integration lead and treat integration as a repeatable process with a playbook — day-1 checklist, 100-day integration plan per target, standard systems migration.
  • A genuine sharing logic. The group must be worth more together: shared purchasing scale, cross-sold products, national coverage that wins contracts no regional player could, one brand. If the only logic is "same sector", you are assembling a conglomerate, not building a company.
  • Multiple headroom. The arbitrage needs a real gap between bolt-on prices and the platform's exit multiple. In sectors where roll-ups are crowded (vets, dental, MSPs at various points in the cycle), bolt-on prices get bid up from 5× toward 8× and the engine stalls.

§10.4.4Integration realities

The gap between the model and reality is integration, and three issues dominate.

Systems. Every bolt-on arrives with its own accounting system, customer file, product codes and payroll. Until they are migrated, "group reporting" means a spreadsheet consolidation with mismatched charts of accounts — month-end takes longer with each deal, and nobody can answer "what do we sell to customer X across the group?" The data team angle is blunt: integration is mostly a data migration programme with a company attached. The playbook answer is a standard target operating model — one chart of accounts, one ERP instance, one CRM — that every acquisition is migrated onto within a defined window (usually 6–12 months), plus a group-wide KPI layer that works even before full migration.

Culture and people. Bolt-ons are usually founder businesses; the founder often leaves after an earnout, and the staff's loyalty was to the founder. Heavy-handed integration (rebrand on day one, strip the local office, impose group process everywhere) can trigger the departure of exactly the client relationships you paid for. The craft is deciding what must be standardised (finance, systems, pricing governance, safety) versus what stays local (client relationships, service delivery style) — and saying so explicitly on day one.

Synergy double-counting. Synergies are underwritten deal by deal, and the same saving gets counted repeatedly: bolt-on A's case includes "consolidate purchasing", B's includes "consolidate purchasing"… but there is only one purchasing consolidation. The same happens with back-office headcount and with cross-sell (A's case sells to B's customers; B's case sells to A's). The discipline is a single group-level synergy tracker, with each initiative counted once, netted against dis-synergies (group insurance, an integration team's salaries, systems costs), and reconciled to the actual P&L — not to a stack of deal models.

§10.4.5Roll-up failure modes

The strategy has a well-documented graveyard, and the failure modes rhyme:

  1. Buying velocity over quality. The model rewards deal count, so the pipeline gets less picky: weaker businesses, higher prices, stretched geographies. EBITDA "grows" while quality falls — and diligence-per-deal shrinks as the team saturates.
  2. Integration debt. Each unintegrated deal adds systems, entities and complexity. Like technical debt, it compounds quietly, then surfaces all at once — usually in month-end chaos, a failed audit, or the buyer's DD at exit.
  3. Leverage on un-landed synergies. Debt is raised against pro-forma EBITDA including synergies "to come". If integration slips, actual EBITDA misses pro-forma, leverage ratios spike, and the acquisition line gets pulled exactly when the pipeline was the point. Many famous roll-up collapses are this mechanism.
  4. The acquisition treadmill masking organic decline. Group revenue grows every year because deals close every year — while like-for-like revenue of already-owned businesses shrinks. Exit buyers now routinely demand organic vs acquired growth splits; a platform that cannot produce them is assumed to be hiding the answer.
  5. Founder-dependence transferred, not solved. Ten founder businesses whose founders all left is ten sets of orphaned relationships.

What looks good, for calibration: a platform doing 2–4 well-integrated bolt-ons a year, flat or falling month-end close times, one systems stack, positive like-for-like growth, and a synergy tracker reconciled to the P&L. What looks bad: deal count as the KPI, "integration to follow", and pro-forma adjustments growing as a share of EBITDA.

§10.4.6What deal teams actually ask

  • "Show me organic vs acquired growth, like-for-like" — the first question every exit buyer asks, so ask it of yourself from year one.
  • "What's the blended multiple including fees and integration costs?" — the honest denominator, not the headline one.
  • "Walk me through the last integration: timeline, what slipped, what it cost" — one real post-mortem beats any playbook document.
  • "Which synergies are in the bank vs in the model?" — banked means visible in the P&L and reconciled; everything else is a plan.
  • "If you stopped acquiring today, what does next year look like?" — the treadmill test. A good platform is a good business standing still; a bad one is a growth story that dies the moment the music stops.
