↑ Module 10

Lesson 10.5/Value Creation

Governance & the Operating Cadence

24 min read
In brief

How PE actually makes the plan happen: the post-deal board, operating partners, KPI dashboards and the monthly reporting rhythm (where data teams become critical), when and why funds change management, building exit readiness from year one, and the margin versus growth trade-off an owner debates every single year.

  1. 10.5.1Governance is the delivery mechanism
  2. 10.5.2The post-deal board
  3. 10.5.3The KPI dashboard and the monthly rhythm
  4. 10.5.4Changing management
  5. 10.5.5Exit readiness from year one
  6. 10.5.6The annual debate: margin now or growth later
  7. 10.5.7What deal teams actually ask

§10.5.1Governance is the delivery mechanism

Everything in lessons 1–4 is a plan; governance is why it happens. The uncomfortable truth of value creation is that most initiatives fail not because they were wrong but because they were never really run: no owner, no baseline, no cadence, no consequence for slippage. PE's genuine edge over public-company ownership is not cleverer strategy — it is concentrated ownership plus relentless cadence: a small board that owns the company, meets monthly, tracks a dozen numbers, and acts within weeks when they move the wrong way. A public company reviews strategy annually for the market; a PE portfolio company reviews delivery monthly for its owner. Over a five-year hold, that difference in clock speed is the value creation.

§10.5.2The post-deal board

At completion the board is rebuilt around the deal. A typical mid-market configuration is five to seven seats:

Seat Who Role on the board
Chair External, fund-appointed Runs the board; coaches the CEO; often ex-CEO of a larger business in the sector
CEO Management Delivers the plan
CFO Management Owns the numbers and the board pack
Investor directors (1–2) Deal partner + principal The fund's voice; own the returns model
Operating partner / NED Fund operating team or external Functional depth — pricing, ops, digital — matched to the VCP's biggest lever

Three design points. First, the chair is usually the single most important hire of the hold: an experienced chair converts fund pressure into management action without the deal partner having to manage the CEO directly. Second, the board is deliberately small — this is a delivery committee, not a governance showpiece; there are no independence quotas, and everyone in the room is economically aligned through the fund or the management incentive plan. Third, real power also runs through what sits around the board: shareholder consent rights in the investment agreement (budget approval, M&A, senior hires, capex over a threshold) mean the fund's control does not depend on board votes.

Operating partners deserve their own note because they are the growth industry within PE. Models vary by fund: a generalist "portfolio talent" bench, functional specialists (pricing, procurement, digital, pricing data) parachuted into initiatives, or full-time executives seconded as interim CFO/CRO. The tension to manage is accountability — an operating partner who quietly becomes shadow CEO destroys the management team's ownership of the plan. The best practice is explicit: operating partners accelerate initiatives; management owns the P&L.

§10.5.3The KPI dashboard and the monthly rhythm

The operating cadence runs on a monthly board pack, and building it is usually the first serious piece of data work in the hold (it appears in every 100-day plan, lesson 1). The standard shape:

  • Trading summary: revenue, gross margin, EBITDA vs budget and prior year, with a bridge explaining variances — not just the numbers, the why.
  • Cash: closing cash, 13-week rolling forecast, covenant headroom. In the first year, and always in leveraged deals, cash gets more board time than profit.
  • KPI dashboard: 10–15 leading indicators chosen to track the VCP — realised price vs list, pipeline coverage, order intake, churn, on-time-in-full delivery, procurement savings at run-rate, headcount vs plan. The design rule: every big VCP initiative gets a KPI that moves before the P&L does. If pricing is the thesis, realised-price tracking is on page one.
  • Initiative tracker: each VCP workstream — owner, milestone status, benefits banked vs plan, RAG status. Red items get their own page and a named recovery plan.

The cadence around the pack: monthly board meeting within ~10 working days of month end; a short weekly trading call (sales, cash, operations) during the first year or whenever performance wobbles; quarterly deep-dives on one topic (pricing, a bolt-on, the tech stack); annual budget negotiated hard in Q4.

This is where a fund's or portfolio company's data team becomes critical infrastructure. At entry, most mid-market companies cannot produce this pack: the ERP can't report realised price by customer, "pipeline" lives in a rep's notebook, and month-end takes 20+ working days. The first-year data agenda is therefore load-bearing for the entire VCP: automate the monthly pack (10 working days is a discipline, and it is won by pipeline automation, not heroics), build the transaction-level price file, instrument the sales funnel, and create one version of the truth so board meetings argue about actions, not about whose spreadsheet is right. A useful test of any portfolio company's maturity: how many days after month end can the board see reliable numbers, and how many manual steps does it take?

§10.5.4Changing management

The evidence across the industry is consistent and blunt: in roughly half or more of buyouts, the CEO is replaced during the hold, and the CFO is changed even more often — frequently in year one, because the reporting and cash disciplines above demand a CFO who has done this before. Almost every post-deal review says the same thing: we moved too slowly on people.

The judgement framework deal teams use:

  • Upgrade for the next phase, not punishment for the last. The founder-CFO who got the business to £8m EBITDA may simply never have run a leveraged, board-governed, monthly cadence. That is a mismatch, not a failing — but it is still a change.
  • Decide on evidence, fast. The first two board cycles tell you most of what you need: does the CEO own the plan or relitigate it? Do numbers arrive on time and survive scrutiny? Are bad news volunteered early? Six months of doubt is a decision.
  • Sequence deliberately. CFO first (the numbers must be trustworthy before anything else is decidable), commercial leadership where the thesis is commercial, CEO only with a succession plan — an empty CEO chair mid-hold costs a year of momentum.
  • Cost it honestly. A CEO change costs 6–12 months of drift plus search and severance; keeping the wrong CEO costs the plan. Both numbers belong in the discussion.

The management incentive plan is the other half of this lever: leavers' equity terms (good leaver/bad leaver), top-up pools for new hires, and re-vesting all get negotiated at the moment of change — structuring covered in the deal structuring module.

§10.5.5Exit readiness from year one

Funds increasingly run the hold as a five-year preparation for sale, because the difference between a prepared and an unprepared exit is measured in turns of multiple. Exit readiness built from year one means:

  • Numbers that survive diligence. Monthly packs reconciled to audited accounts, a clean revenue recognition policy, organic vs acquired growth split maintained continuously (lesson 4), and no "we'll explain that at exit" items accumulating in adjusted EBITDA. The buyer's QofE team will find in week two whatever you hoped to explain away in year four.
  • A forecasting track record. A company that has hit or beaten budget for three straight years sells its forecast; one that misses annually sells only its history. Boards manage this deliberately — budgets are set to be beaten from about year three.
  • Documented value creation. The margin bridge, the pricing programme, the integration playbook — written up as evidence of how EBITDA grew, which is what persuades the next buyer the growth is repeatable (and what supports their own VCP).
  • An always-warm data room. Contracts, statutory accounts, board minutes, KPI history maintained continuously rather than assembled in a six-week panic that distracts management exactly when trading must not dip.

Exit routes and vendor due diligence get a full treatment in the exits module; the point here is that exit-readiness is an operating habit, not a project that starts when the bankers arrive.

§10.5.6The annual debate: margin now or growth later

Every budget season, the board has the same argument, and it is worth staging explicitly because it is the whole ownership problem in miniature. The company can spend the marginal £1.0m on growth (sales hires, a new site, product) or drop it to EBITDA. Take a business at £10.0m EBITDA in year 3 of a five-year hold, 8× assumed exit:

  • Harvest: EBITDA £11.0m by exit → EV £88m. Covenants comfortable, but the buyer sees decelerating revenue and prices the growth risk: perhaps 7× — EV £77m.
  • Invest: EBITDA £10.0m now, £12.5m by exit as the investment pays back → EV £100m at 8× — and a demonstrated growth engine can re-rate the multiple higher still.

The honest answer is that it depends on three things the board must weigh every year: time to exit (growth spend in the final year rarely pays back before the sale — but a visible growth story still sells), covenant headroom (a levered balance sheet can make harvesting temporarily rational — leverage disciplines and distorts), and legibility (ring-fenced, tracked, cohort-evidenced growth spend gets credited by buyers; vague investment reads as margin erosion — lesson 2's rule). What looks bad is not either answer; it is drift — a board that never decides, under-invests and misses margin, and arrives at exit with neither story. The operating cadence exists precisely so that this trade-off is made once a year, on evidence, out loud.

§10.5.7What deal teams actually ask

  • "How many days to close the month, and how many manual steps in the pack?" — the one-question maturity test of the finance and data stack.
  • "Which KPI tells us the pricing programme is working before the P&L does?" — every initiative needs a leading indicator, or slippage surfaces two quarters late.
  • "If we could only keep five numbers on page one, which five?" — forces the board pack to mirror the thesis rather than the ERP's default reports.
  • "Would you rehire the CFO today?" — asked at every portfolio review; a hesitant answer is the answer.
  • "What would a buyer's QofE team flag if they arrived Monday?" — the exit-readiness audit, run years before exit.

Lesson 11.1/Exits

Exit Routes Compared

24 min read
In brief

The menu of exit routes — trade sale, secondary buyout, IPO, continuation vehicle, dividend recap, and minority sale — compared on process, valuation dynamics, certainty, and speed; who the natural buyers are, and why strategics can pay more but often don't.

  1. 11.1.1The exit is the investment case
  2. 11.1.2Trade sale: selling to a strategic
  3. 11.1.3Secondary buyout: selling to another sponsor
  4. 11.1.4IPO: selling to the public markets
  5. 11.1.5Continuation vehicles: selling to yourself, properly
  6. 11.1.6Partial exits: dividend recaps and minority sales
  7. 11.1.7The comparison table
  8. 11.1.8Why strategics can pay more — and often don't

§11.1.1The exit is the investment case

A PE fund does not make money when it buys a company; it makes money when it sells one. Every investment committee paper has a slide titled "exit routes", written before the fund has owned the business for a single day, because the underwriting question is always the same: who buys this from us in five years, and why will they pay more than we did? If the deal team cannot name two or three credible future buyers at entry, the deal usually dies.

The menu is short. Full exits: sell to a strategic acquirer (trade sale), sell to another sponsor (secondary buyout, "SBO"), or sell to public market investors (IPO). A fourth route — the continuation vehicle (CV) — sells the asset to a new fund managed by the same GP, funded largely by secondaries investors. Partial exits: a dividend recapitalisation returns cash by re-levering the business, and a minority sale brings in a new investor for part of the equity while the fund stays in control.

Each route trades off four things: price, certainty (probability the deal actually closes at the agreed number), speed (time to cash), and cleanliness (how much of the position is actually realised, and what liabilities the seller retains). No route wins on all four. Choosing between them is the judgement this module teaches.

§11.1.2Trade sale: selling to a strategic

A trade sale means selling 100% of the business to a corporate acquirer — a competitor, a customer, a supplier, or a company entering the market. It is the classic "best price" route, because a strategic can pay for synergies that no financial buyer has access to (more on the maths below).

Process. Usually an auction run by a sell-side bank (Module 6 covered the buyer's view; lesson 3 of this module covers the seller's). Strategics move more slowly than sponsors: they need board approval, sometimes shareholder approval, and their internal M&A teams run diligence alongside day jobs. Expect six to nine months from launch to completion, longer if antitrust review bites — a strategic buying a direct competitor is exactly the transaction competition authorities exist to examine. A CMA or European Commission Phase 1 review adds months; a Phase 2 adds six months or more and carries real risk of a block or forced remedies.

Valuation dynamics. Highest potential price, widest variance. A motivated strategic with real synergies can pay one to three turns of EBITDA above the financial-buyer clearing price. An unmotivated one bids below sponsors, because its board sees no urgency.

Certainty and speed. Medium certainty (board changes of heart, antitrust), medium-to-slow speed. But it is a clean, full exit: 100% sold, cash on completion, and strategics often accept lighter warranty packages than sponsors demand because they know the industry.

When it's the right answer. When a strategic genuinely needs the asset — consolidation plays, technology or capability gaps, geographic entry — and antitrust risk is manageable.

§11.1.3Secondary buyout: selling to another sponsor

An SBO sells the company to another PE fund. To outsiders this looks circular — "PE selling to PE" — but it is the single most common exit route in the European mid-market, routinely 40–50% of sponsor exits by count. The logic is straightforward: the buying fund has a different angle (bigger fund, buy-and-build thesis, sector platform), the business has another leg of growth the selling fund cannot stay for, and sponsors are fast, reliable buyers who do this for a living.

Process. Auction or bilateral. Sponsors run diligence in weeks, not months, use debt markets they know intimately, and need no board or antitrust drama (competition issues are rare because funds seldom own direct competitors at scale). Three to five months, end to end.

Valuation dynamics. The price is capped by LBO maths: the buyer must underwrite their own 20%+ IRR, so they pay what leverage and their value-creation plan support — typically at or slightly below the strategic ceiling. In hot debt markets SBO prices rival trade prices; when credit tightens, the SBO bid falls first.

Certainty and speed. The highest-certainty, fastest full-exit route, especially with committed financing. Sponsors rarely retrade without cause — their reputation with advisors is an asset they protect.

When it's the right answer. Good business, more to go, no natural strategic at a full price, and a seller who values speed and certainty — very common when the selling fund is late in its life and needs DPI (distributions to paid-in capital).

§11.1.4IPO: selling to the public markets

An IPO lists the company's shares on a public exchange. Two things make it unlike every other route. First, it is not an exit on day one — it is the start of one. The fund typically sells only 20–40% of its stake in the offering, is locked up for 180 days, and sells the rest in blocks over 18–36 months at whatever the market price then is. Second, the price is set by fund managers building a book, not by one buyer in a negotiation, and IPOs price at a discount (often 10–15% to fair value) to ensure the shares trade up.

Worked example. Fund owns 100% of a company worth £600m of equity. At IPO it sells 30% for £180m, priced at a 10% discount. If the shares then drift down 20% during the lock-up and the fund exits the remaining 70% at the lower price, it collects £336m more — £516m total, versus £600m from a clean £600m trade sale. The IPO route delivered 86p in the pound and took two extra years. That is why deal teams call an IPO "a route to liquidity, not liquidity".

When it's the right answer. Very large businesses (too big for most sponsors, few strategics), strong growth stories the public market pays up for, and open equity windows. IPO markets shut abruptly and stay shut for quarters at a time; nobody sensible runs an IPO as the only track.

§11.1.5Continuation vehicles: selling to yourself, properly

A CV moves the asset from the current fund into a new vehicle managed by the same GP, funded by secondaries investors plus whatever existing LPs choose to roll. The old fund's LPs get a genuine choice: cash out at the deal price, or roll into the CV. The GP keeps managing the asset — typically with reset economics and fresh capital for the next phase.

Why it exists: sometimes the best asset in the fund still has years of compounding left, but the fund is out of time and follow-on capital. Selling a great business at year 9 of a 10-year fund because the fund has expired, not because the asset is done, destroys value. The CV lets the GP keep the winner and still hand cash to LPs who want it.

The obvious problem — the GP sits on both sides of the price — and the machinery that manages it (LPAC approval, fairness opinions, market checks, election mechanics) gets a full lesson later in this module. For route-comparison purposes: price is usually at or near the third-party market level but rarely above it; certainty is high; speed is moderate (four to six months including the LP election); and the fund's realisation is partial by construction — typically 30–50% cash, the rest rolled.

§11.1.6Partial exits: dividend recaps and minority sales

A dividend recap is not a sale at all: the company borrows more and pays the proceeds to shareholders. Worked example: portfolio company with £20m EBITDA, current net debt £30m (1.5x). Lenders will support 4.0x, so the company raises new facilities of £80m, repays the £30m, pays £2m of fees, and distributes £48m to the fund. If the fund's equity cost £60m, it has now returned 0.8x its money while still owning 100% of the business. What looks good: de-risking a winner mid-hold, resetting the IRR clock on capital that was just sitting in the asset. What looks bad: recapping a fragile business — the extra leverage is still there when trading turns, and lenders, management, and the next buyer all remember who took the money out.

A minority sale sells (say) 20–30% of the equity to a new investor — a minority/growth fund, a sovereign fund, occasionally a strategic — at a negotiated valuation. It delivers some cash, an external valuation mark that validates the carrying value, and sometimes a useful partner. The costs: governance complexity (consent rights, exit provisions) and a signal buyers read carefully — why sell a slice rather than the whole? Partial exits are tools for managing the hold, not substitutes for the real exit.

§11.1.7The comparison table

Route Typical price vs field Certainty Speed to cash % realised Right answer when…
Trade sale Highest potential (synergies) Medium (boards, antitrust) 6–9 months 100% A strategic truly needs it; antitrust manageable
Secondary buyout At/near market, capped by LBO maths High (committed financing) 3–5 months 100% Asset has another PE-shaped leg; seller wants certainty/DPI
IPO Discounted at pricing; market sets the rest Low (windows close) 2–4 years for full exit 20–40% at IPO Very large, strong growth story, open window
Continuation vehicle At/near market, rarely above High once priced 4–6 months 30–50% cash, rest rolled Fund expiring, asset isn't; LPs get real choice
Dividend recap n/a (no sale) High if debt available 2–3 months Partial cash, 0% of equity De-risk a stable winner mid-hold
Minority sale Negotiated, often with structure Medium 3–6 months 20–30% Need validation, partner, or partial liquidity

Deal teams run dual-track (or triple-track) processes precisely because these profiles differ: prepare an IPO and an M&A sale in parallel, let each discipline the other's price, and choose late.

§11.1.8Why strategics can pay more — and often don't

The synergy maths first. Target: £15m EBITDA, standalone value 9.0x = £135m. A strategic acquirer expects £4m of annual synergies — procurement savings, merged head office, cross-sold products. Capitalise those at the same 9.0x and the business is worth £135m + £36m = £171m to that buyer: 11.4x the standalone EBITDA. Any price below £171m creates value for the strategic; a sponsor with no synergies is stuck near 9.0x plus whatever its leverage and operating plan justify.

So why do sponsors win so many auctions? Because the synergy ceiling is not the synergy bid:

  • Discipline. Corporate boards refuse to "pay away the synergies" — a common internal rule is to concede at most a third to half of synergy value to the seller. The bid becomes £147–153m, not £171m.
  • Integration risk. Synergy cases fail often enough that experienced acquirers haircut them before bidding. £4m on paper is £2.5m in the board pack.
  • No clock. A fund in year 8 must transact; a strategic can wait for the next asset, the next cycle, the next CEO.
  • Process friction. Slower diligence, board calendars, antitrust conditions and the remedies/break-fee negotiation that comes with them. Sellers discount uncertain bids: a £300m offer with a six-month regulatory tail is not worth £300m.
  • Cycles. Corporate M&A appetite is procyclical and confidence-driven; sponsors with committed funds are structurally always in the market.

What deal teams actually ask when comparing routes: Who are the three most likely buyers and what does each one's maths support? What does each route's certainty-adjusted, time-adjusted price look like — not just the headline? A disciplined seller writes down, for every serious option: headline EV, expected proceeds after conditions and retained risks, and expected months to cash. The best exit is the best risk-adjusted, time-adjusted number — which, as the rest of this module shows, is frequently not the biggest headline.

Lesson 11.2/Exits

Exit Timing and Preparation

22 min read
In brief

How deal teams decide when to sell — the incremental-IRR framework, market windows, and fund-level pressures — and how they prepare: the exit readiness checklist, grooming the equity story, and why selling "too early" is often right.

  1. 11.2.1Two clocks, one decision
  2. 11.2.2The incremental-IRR framework
  3. 11.2.3Market windows: the multiple you don't control
  4. 11.2.4The exit readiness checklist
  5. 11.2.5Grooming the equity story
  6. 11.2.6When selling "too early" is right
  7. 11.2.7What the IC actually debates

§11.2.1Two clocks, one decision

Every hold/sell decision is a fight between two clocks. The IRR clock started ticking the day the equity was wired: every extra month of holding divides the same gain by a longer period, so IRR decays even when value keeps rising. The value clock runs the other way: the plan still has levers unpulled, EBITDA is compounding, and selling now means handing that growth to the next owner.

The mistake juniors make is arguing about which clock "matters more". Deal teams resolve it with one number: the incremental IRR of the extension — the annualised return on the money you could take off the table today but choose to leave in. Frame every hold/sell debate as: if we sold today, would we reinvest the proceeds in this same asset at today's price? Because economically, that is exactly what holding is.

§11.2.2The incremental-IRR framework

Worked example. A fund invested £100m of equity three years ago. The position is worth £250m today (2.5x, IRR of 2.51/3−1=35.7%2.5^{1/3}-1 = 35.7\%2.51/3−1=35.7%). The value creation plan says two more years of trading and one more bolt-on gets the exit to £320m (3.2x).

Holding looks obviously right — 3.2x beats 2.5x. But run the marginal maths:

Incremental IRR=(320250)1/2−1=13.1%\text{Incremental IRR} = \left(\frac{320}{250}\right)^{1/2} - 1 = 13.1\%Incremental IRR=(250320​)1/2−1=13.1%

The last two years of this deal earn 13.1% a year on £250m of LP capital. The fund underwrites new deals at 20–25%. If the team believes its own pipeline, the £250m works harder in the next deal than in this one. Meanwhile the blended IRR degrades:

Sell now (yr 3) Hold (yr 5)
MOIC 2.5x 3.2x
IRR 35.7% 26.2%
Incremental IRR of the extension — 13.1%

Neither answer is automatically correct — 13.1% of low-risk compounding in an asset you know intimately can beat 22% of underwritten hope in an asset you haven't met. But the question must be asked in this form. What looks bad in an IC memo: "we're holding because the business is performing" — performance is in the price. What looks good: "the extension earns 13% against our 22% redeployment rate, but execution risk on the remaining plan is minimal and the exit multiple is more defensible with the bolt-on integrated — we hold 12 more months, not 24."

One refinement deal teams apply: the future £320m is not certain. Haircut it for plan risk — at 80% weight on £320m and 20% on a stumble to £260m, expected exit is £308m and the incremental IRR drops to (308/250)1/2−1=11.0%\left(308/250\right)^{1/2}-1 = 11.0\%(308/250)1/2−1=11.0%. Certainty-adjust both sides before comparing.

§11.2.3Market windows: the multiple you don't control

Roughly half of a typical exit outcome is the multiple, and the multiple is rented from the market, not earned. Sector sentiment, debt availability, and public comps move exit multiples by two to four turns across a cycle — far more than a year of good trading is worth.

The treadmill maths makes the point. Entry at 12.0x on £20m EBITDA = £240m EV. Two years later EBITDA is £26m (+30%), but the sector has de-rated to 9.0x: EV is £234m — lower than entry despite 30% EBITDA growth. With £90m of constant net debt, equity has gone from £150m to £144m. You can grow into a falling multiple and stand still.

Practical implications:

  • Sell into strength, not at the top. Nobody rings a bell at the peak. A team that waits for the perfect multiple usually sells one year past it. The discipline is: when the market pays a multiple your underwriting never dared assume, that is the signal.
  • Debt windows matter as much as equity windows. SBO and recap prices are set by what lenders will fund. When leveraged loan markets are wide open, financial buyers can pay strategic-level prices; when credit tightens, the sponsor bid drops a turn within months.
  • IPO windows are binary. M&A markets soften; IPO markets close. A dual-track that loses its IPO leg mid-process is normal, which is why the M&A leg is never optional.
  • Windows are sector-specific. A market that is shut for consumer assets can be wide open for infrastructure-adjacent software in the same quarter.

What deal teams actually ask each portfolio review: if we launched this asset in four months, what would it clear at today? Keeping a live, honest answer to that question — updated comps, sounding conversations with bankers, inbound interest logged — is what separates funds that catch windows from funds that read about them.

§11.2.4The exit readiness checklist

Buyers pay for what they can verify and discount what they can't. Exit preparation is mostly about converting true things into provable things before the process starts. The core checklist:

Item Why buyers care Typical time to fix
Clean financials — audited accounts, fast monthly close, revenue recognition defensible, data room-ready MI Every unresolved question becomes a price chip or an escrow 6–12 months
Locked-in management — CEO/CFO committed through exit and beyond, MIP rollover agreed in principle, no key-person gaps Buyers underwrite the team; a wobbly CFO in management presentations costs a turn 6–12 months
Resolved legal issues — litigation settled or provisioned, tax structure defensible, change-of-control consents mapped, IP assignments complete Open legal items become indemnities, escrows, or Phase 2 questions 3–18 months
Demonstrated run-rate — pricing and cost initiatives visible in delivered monthly P&L, not in an "adjusted" bridge Buyers pay ~1.0x credit for delivered EBITDA vs heavily-discounted credit for pro-forma claims 6+ months of trading

The last row is the one data teams touch most. A £3m pricing initiative that went live in January is worth full value in a September process — nine months of actuals prove it. The same initiative launched in July is an "adjustment" that buyers will haircut by half and QoE advisers will attack. This is why exit preparation starts 12–24 months before launch: the run-rate needs time to become history.

The meta-rule: fix it or disclose it, never hope it. Any issue the seller finds first can be framed, priced, and papered. Any issue the buyer finds first costs double — the issue itself, plus the credibility of everything else in the data room.

§11.2.5Grooming the equity story

The equity story is the two-line answer to "why does the next owner make money?" — and it gets engineered, legitimately, in the final 12–24 months:

  • Positioning. Reclassify and report the revenue base the way the target buyer universe values it: recurring vs non-recurring split, net revenue retention, cohort behaviour. A business that is 70% recurring but has never reported it that way is leaving a turn of multiple on the table. (This is real work for the data team — KPI definitions must survive diligence, not just decorate the CIM.)
  • Pruning. Sell or close the loss-making side business now. A £1m-loss division inside a £20m-EBITDA company doesn't reduce the price by £1m — at 10x it reduces it by £10m, and it muddies the story. Clean perimeter, cleaner multiple.
  • Proving the next leg. Buyers pay for a value-creation plan they can believe. Sign (or credibly pipeline) one bolt-on to prove the M&A thesis; land one flagship customer in the new segment to prove the expansion thesis. One delivered proof point beats ten slides of TAM.
  • Leaving something in the tank. Counterintuitive but essential: the next owner needs their own upside. A business squeezed to perfection — pricing maxed, costs cut to bone, capex deferred — offers the buyer nothing to underwrite, and sophisticated buyers price deferred capex and channel-stuffing negatively once they spot them.

What looks bad — and gets found: cost cuts that degrade the product (support headcount slashed two quarters before launch), pulling forward revenue, capitalising costs that were always expensed, and "run-rate" adjustments for initiatives with no run history. Every one of these is a standard QoE test. Window dressing doesn't just fail; it contaminates the genuine adjustments sitting next to it.

§11.2.6When selling "too early" is right

"We left money on the table" is the most survivable mistake in private equity. The opposite mistake — riding a winner into a closed window — is the one that ends up in the fund's track-record footnotes. Selling early is systematically right more often than it feels, for reasons that are structural, not psychological:

  • You are paid for certainty, not perfection. A 2.8x banked today beats a 60% probability of 3.5x in two years for almost any risk-adjusted weighting — and the incremental IRR of that gamble is usually below the fund's bar anyway.
  • The buyer needs the next leg. The best exits happen while the story still has an obvious chapter left, because that chapter is what the buyer underwrites. Sell the future to the buyer; don't consume it yourself.
  • Fund-level maths outranks deal-level maths. A fund in year 7–8 raising its successor needs DPI — cash distributed, not paper marks. LPs re-up on DPI. One realised 2.8x does more for the next fundraise than two unrealised 3.5x marks. The deal team's "hold for more" instinct is routinely, and correctly, overridden by the managing partners for exactly this reason.
  • Concentration risk compounds. A winner that has grown to 25–30% of remaining fund NAV is no longer a deal decision; it's a portfolio decision. De-risking the fund can justify accepting a below-bar incremental IRR on the asset.

The honest test for "too early": would you buy this business at this price today, with fresh capital and a fresh five-year clock? If yes — genuinely yes, at this price — then holding may be right (or a continuation vehicle may be the honest structure, as lesson 4 covers). If you hesitate, you are holding out of attachment, not analysis.

§11.2.7What the IC actually debates

Pulling it together — the exit-timing section of a portfolio review answers five questions, in order:

  1. What is it worth today? Live comps, banker soundings, inbound interest — a real number, not the holding-value mark.
  2. What is the incremental IRR of holding? Against the fund's redeployment rate, certainty-adjusted on both sides.
  3. Is the window open? For this asset, in this sector, in today's debt market — and what is the cost of missing it (the treadmill maths above)?
  4. Are we ready? The checklist: financials, management, legal, run-rate. If not, what is the fastest credible path to ready, and does the window survive it?
  5. What does the fund need? DPI, concentration, fundraise timing. The best answer for the asset and the best answer for the fund differ more often than IC memos admit — and when they do, the fund wins.

A team that can answer all five with numbers is prepared. A team that answers with adjectives is holding by default — and holding by default is a decision too, just an unexamined one.

Lesson 11.3/Exits

Running the Sell-Side

24 min read
In brief

The seller's playbook: hiring and paying the bank, vendor due diligence and how buyers read it, authoring the CIM, engineering auction tension, handling pre-emptive bids, stapled financing, and managing management's conflicts of interest during a sale.

  1. 11.3.1The seller's job is manufacturing competition
  2. 11.3.2Hiring the bank
  3. 11.3.3Vendor due diligence: paying for the buyer's homework
  4. 11.3.4The CIM, written from this side of the table
  5. 11.3.5Engineering auction tension
  6. 11.3.6Pre-emptive bids
  7. 11.3.7Stapled financing
  8. 11.3.8Managing management's conflicts

§11.3.1The seller's job is manufacturing competition

Module 6 walked through an auction from the buyer's side — the CIM lands, the IOI goes in, the process grinds on. This lesson flips the table. From the seller's chair, an exit process has one objective: make several credible buyers believe, simultaneously, that they might lose. Everything in the sell-side playbook — the bank, the VDD, the CIM, the process design — exists to create and sustain that fear of loss, because fear of loss, not spreadsheet outputs, is what moves a bid from 9.5x to 11x.

The seller's second objective is nearly as important: certainty of close. A process that collapses is expensive — management is exhausted, competitors have read the CIM, staff have heard rumours, and the asset is "shopped". Buyers price shopped assets lower the second time. So every design choice below trades a little price for a lot of certainty, or vice versa, and the good sell-side adviser is explicit about which.

§11.3.2Hiring the bank

The process starts with a beauty parade (pitch process): three to five banks present their view of value, buyer list, positioning, and process design. Reading the pitches is an art:

  • The bank pitching the highest valuation is often buying the mandate — they will walk the number down after signing. Ask how they get to the number: which buyers, at which multiples, anchored to which precedents. A £450m headline supported by two named strategics with board-level logic beats a £500m headline supported by "sector momentum".
  • The buyer list is the real product. The right bank knows which corporate development head answers their calls, which sponsor just raised and needs deployment, and which "obvious" buyer is quietly broken inside. Sector coverage beats brand.
  • Conflicts must be surfaced: is the bank also lending to likely bidders, running a competing sell-side, or angling to offer staple financing (see below)?

Fees are almost entirely success-based: typically 0.75–1.5% of enterprise value in the mid-market (higher percentages on smaller deals), with a modest monthly retainer that is usually credited against the success fee. The structural problem: a flat percentage pays the bank for any close, not a good close — on a £400m deal, the difference between a great and mediocre outcome might be £40m to the seller but only £0.4m to the bank, while a collapsed process pays the bank nearly nothing. Banks are therefore biased towards getting a deal done. The fix is a ratchet (incentive fee): say 1.0% up to £380m, plus 3–5% of proceeds above £380m. Now the bank's marginal economics point the same way as the seller's. What deal teams actually ask when reviewing an engagement letter: where does the ratchet kick in, and who chose that number — because a ratchet that starts below the expected clearing price is just a disguised fee increase.

§11.3.3Vendor due diligence: paying for the buyer's homework

Vendor due diligence (VDD) inverts the normal arrangement: the seller commissions Big-4-style financial (and often commercial, tax, and legal) due diligence on its own company, and shares the reports with all bidders. Sellers pay £300k–£1m+ for this, willingly, because:

  • It controls the narrative. The first quantified view of quality of earnings that any bidder sees is the seller's — professionally prepared, but framing every judgement call (revenue recognition, add-backs, run-rates) the seller's way. Anchoring works.
  • It keeps the auction wide. Six bidders can each stay in the process without each spending £500k on their own advisers at the IOI stage. More bidders, longer, for less of their money — which is precisely the tension the seller wants.
  • It compresses the timetable. Bidders' confirmatory work shrinks from months to weeks, and speed is certainty: fewer weeks in exclusivity means fewer chances for markets, trading, or nerves to break the deal.
  • It flushes issues early, on the seller's terms. The £2m revenue-recognition issue found by your own VDD in month one gets framed and priced; the same issue found by the buyer's QoE in exclusivity costs a price chip plus credibility.

The winning bidder typically gets reliance on the VDD report — the adviser owes them a duty of care (capped), which is what makes the report more than marketing.

How buyers read VDD — and your team will sit on both sides over a career: start from the scope section, not the numbers. What was excluded, sampled rather than tested, or "management-confirmed" rather than verified is where the bodies are. Read the databook before the prose; the prose is negotiated, the databook less so. Treat every judgement call as opening position, not finding: VDD saying adjusted EBITDA is £22m means the seller's paid adviser could defend £22m — buyers' QoE teams routinely land £1–2m lower on the same facts. And note what the VDD is conspicuously quiet about; silence in a seller-commissioned report is a hint, never an accident.

§11.3.4The CIM, written from this side of the table

The Confidential Information Memorandum is the seller's brief: 60–100 pages of company, market, financials, and projections. Authoring rules that experienced sellers enforce:

  • Everything in the CIM will be diligenced. The CIM is advocacy, but every number in it becomes a checklist item for the buyer's advisers. A claim that dies in diligence costs more than it earned — retrades anchor on broken claims. Ambitious framing, yes; unsupportable numbers, never.
  • The adjusted EBITDA bridge is the most-read page. Each add-back should be individually defensible with evidence sitting ready in the data room. One indefensible add-back (pro-forma synergies from an unsigned bolt-on, say) taints the four legitimate ones next to it.
  • Projections: ambitious but anchored. The forecast should extend delivered momentum, not hockey-stick from it. Buyers underwrite their own numbers anyway; the CIM forecast mostly signals management's credibility. A plan showing 12% growth after three years of delivered 11% is believed; 25% after 11% is discounted and remembered.
  • Write for the second reader. The first reader is the deal partner; the second is their investment committee. Give the deal team the slides they need to sell the asset internally — that is what the CIM is actually for.

§11.3.5Engineering auction tension

A standard two-round process: teaser and NDA to 30–80 parties → CIM to those who sign → indicative offers (IOIs) in ~4–6 weeks → shortlist of 4–6 into round two with management presentations, data room, and VDD access → binding offers with marked-up SPA in ~6–8 weeks → select, negotiate, sign. The seller's levers for maximum tension:

  • Keep at least three credible bidders to the final round. Two is a negotiation; one is a hostage situation. Bidders can smell an empty room — banks work the phones to keep the third and fourth warm, and sensible sellers give losing bidders honest feedback fast (the same funds will bid in the seller's next process).
  • Ration information and calendar. Simultaneous deadlines, controlled Q&A, and management access granted in equal, scheduled doses. Asymmetric access leaks; leaks kill tension.
  • Never lie about competition, but never volunteer clarity either. "The process is competitive" must always be technically true — banks that invent phantom bidders get caught, and their next ten processes suffer for it.
  • Use the SPA as a bid dimension. Final bids are ranked on price and markup: conditions, warranty caps, escrow demands, financing outs. A £405m bid with a clean SPA beats £415m with a financing condition and a six-month regulatory tail. Force bidders to compete on certainty by scoring it openly.

Worked example of what tension is worth: a process with one bidder settles at the bidder's walk-away discipline — say 9.5x on £30m EBITDA, £285m. The same asset with three bidders in the final round, each fearing loss, clears at 11.0x — £330m. The £45m difference is pure process design, on the same asset, and is why sellers accept the cost, leak risk, and management distraction of a full auction.

§11.3.6Pre-emptive bids

A pre-emptive bid is a buyer's attempt to shoot the auction before it starts: a strong price with heavy conditions attached to speed — "£210m, proof of funds attached, four weeks of exclusivity starting Friday, withdrawn if the process launches." The buyer is explicitly paying a premium to avoid competing.

When should a seller take it? Do the expected-value maths rather than react to the headline. Suppose the bank believes a full auction clears at £220m with 75% probability of closing there; a failed process means re-running a shopped asset a year later at ~£190m. Expected headline from the auction:

0.75×£220m+0.25×£190m=£212.5m0.75 \times £220m + 0.25 \times £190m = £212.5m0.75×£220m+0.25×£190m=£212.5m

— before counting five extra months of time, management distraction, and leak risk. A credible pre-empt at £210m with 95% certainty and cash in eight weeks is better than that on any risk- and time-adjusted view. What makes a pre-empt credible enough to accept: completed diligence (they've clearly done the work already), committed financing, a short exclusivity with automatic expiry, and a reputation for closing at the number. What looks bad: a fat headline from a bidder with a retrade history — that is not a pre-empt, it is a free option on your asset, paid for with your process momentum.

§11.3.7Stapled financing

Stapled financing (a "staple") is a pre-arranged debt package that the sell-side bank's leveraged-finance desk offers to any winning bidder — terms "stapled" to the back of the CIM: say, 4.5x total leverage at agreed pricing, available to whoever wins.

Why sellers like it: it sets a floor under every sponsor's bid (no bidder can plead "we couldn't raise the debt"), levels the field between large sponsors with captive lender relationships and smaller ones without, speeds the process (financing diligence is pre-done), and signals the bank's own conviction — a bank refusing to lend against its own sell-side story is telling you something.

The conflict is obvious: the same bank earns an advisory fee from the seller and financing fees from the buyer, and a bank keen to see any deal close on its staple is not neutral when advising which bid to take. Standard mitigants: bidders are free to bring their own financing (the staple is a floor, not a requirement — and it is usually beaten), the advisory and financing teams sit behind information barriers, and the seller's board sees the bid comparison built by the deal team, not the financing desk. In practice staples are used most when debt markets are shaky — exactly when the floor is worth the most and the conflict is worth tolerating.

§11.3.8Managing management's conflicts

The most under-managed risk in any sell-side is that the people presenting the asset have interests that diverge from the seller's. Management will work for the winner. Sponsors know this and court them: a generous management incentive plan in NewCo, hints about rollover terms, flattery about the next chapter. A trade buyer, by contrast, may be buying synergies — and management's head office is the synergy. So a CEO facing Sponsor A (sweet equity, bigger platform, keeps their job) versus Strategic B (higher price for the fund, integration committee, probable exit for the CEO) has every human reason to shine in one management presentation and go through the motions in the other. A flat CEO performance can move a bid by a turn — £30m on a £30m-EBITDA asset — without anyone doing anything visibly wrong.

The standard guardrails:

  • Pay management for the price, not the buyer. An exit bonus scaled to proceeds (and the existing MIP itself, which pays on the same waterfall) points their economics at the seller's outcome regardless of who wins.
  • Sequence the package talk. No discussion of go-forward packages, rollover, or NewCo equity between management and bidders until the seller permits it — typically only with the final one or two bidders, with the seller's adviser in the room. Sponsors will push earlier; the process letter says no, and breaches get bidders ejected (and it must be enforced at least once to be believed).
  • Control the channel. All buyer–management contact scheduled and chaperoned by the bank; no private dinners, no side calls. Not paranoia — hygiene.
  • Diligence your own management first. The seller should know about the CEO's view of each bidder, their retirement plans, and their MIP maths before buyers do.

What deal teams actually ask when a process wobbles: has management picked a winner? It is the first hypothesis for unexplained asymmetries — one bidder's questions getting answered faster, one management presentation mysteriously sharper. The fix is rarely punishment; it is realignment — because by the final round, a motivated management team selling hard to every remaining bidder is the single cheapest source of price tension the seller has.

Lesson 11.4/Exits

Continuation Vehicles and the Secondaries Market

25 min read
In brief

GP-led secondaries mechanics and the conflict-of-interest machinery (LPAC, fairness opinions, market checks), LP-led secondaries and NAV lending, single- vs multi-asset CVs, how an LP should judge a CV election, and what each exit choice signals about the asset.

  1. 11.4.1The secondaries market in one page
  2. 11.4.2Why GP-leds exist
  3. 11.4.3Mechanics of a GP-led CV
  4. 11.4.4The conflict, and the machinery that manages it
  5. 11.4.5LP-led secondaries and NAV lending
  6. 11.4.6Single-asset vs multi-asset CVs
  7. 11.4.7Judging a CV as an LP: sell or roll?
  8. 11.4.8What the exit choice signals

§11.4.1The secondaries market in one page

Private equity's original design flaw is a timing mismatch: funds have ten-year lives, but LP liquidity needs and asset maturities follow their own calendars. The secondaries market exists to trade around that mismatch, and it has two halves that share a name but little else:

  • LP-led secondaries: an LP sells its fund interests — its stakes in one or many funds — to a secondaries buyer. The GP's job is limited to consenting to the transfer. This is portfolio trading; the underlying companies never notice.
  • GP-led secondaries: the GP initiates a transaction on an asset (or several) in its own fund — overwhelmingly via a continuation vehicle (CV). This is an exit route, which is why it gets most of this lesson.

The market has grown from a distressed backwater into core infrastructure — well over $150bn of annual volume in recent years, roughly half of it GP-led. Dedicated secondaries funds (and the secondaries arms of the mega-managers) are the buyers; for a deal team, they are now a standing part of the buyer universe alongside strategics and sponsors.

§11.4.2Why GP-leds exist

Lesson 1 gave the short version: sometimes the fund is out of time but the asset isn't. The fuller list of legitimate motives:

  • Keep the winner. The best business in a 2016-vintage fund may have five more years of compounding at 20%+. Selling it at year 9 because a document signed in 2016 says so destroys value for everyone. The CV moves it to a vehicle with a fresh clock.
  • Fresh capital. The old fund's follow-on reserves are spent. The CV raises new money for the next acquisition programme alongside the rolled stake.
  • DPI without goodbye. LPs in year 8–9 want distributions (lesson 2's fund-level maths); the GP wants the asset. A CV pays cash to LPs who elect out while the GP keeps managing what it knows best.
  • Crystallise and re-strike economics. Carry on the old fund's gain is realised; the GP typically rolls it and earns new (often tiered) carry on future performance.

Note what is not on the list: "we couldn't sell it". A CV for an asset that failed an auction is a warehouse for a problem, and secondaries buyers — who see hundreds of these — price accordingly or walk.

§11.4.3Mechanics of a GP-led CV

The standard sequence, four to six months end to end:

  1. Asset selection and advisor hire. The GP mandates a secondaries advisor to structure the deal and run price discovery.
  2. Price discovery. The advisor runs a competitive process among secondaries buyers — effectively a mini-auction — to find a lead investor who sets the price and anchors the new vehicle. This market check is the single most important protection in the whole structure: a price set by competing third parties writing nine-figure cheques is evidence; a price set by the GP's own holding-value mark is not.
  3. LPAC engagement. The fund's LP Advisory Committee reviews the conflict, the process, and the terms, and (per the LPA) waives or approves the conflicted transaction. A fairness opinion from an independent adviser is commonly obtained.
  4. The LP election. Every LP in the old fund chooses: sell (take cash at the deal price) or roll (convert into the CV, often on materially similar economics — the option regulators and ILPA guidance push for as a "status quo" choice). Election windows of 20+ business days, with full disclosure packs, are the standard.
  5. Close. The CV — new fund, same GP — buys the asset from the old fund. Selling LPs get cash; rolling LPs get CV interests; the lead secondaries investor funds the balance plus fresh follow-on capital; the GP typically rolls 100% of its crystallised carry into the CV and adds new GP commitment.

CV terms differ from a classic fund: management fees nearer 1% on invested capital, and tiered carry — e.g. 10% up to 1.5x, 15% to 2.0x, 20% above — so the GP is paid mostly for future performance, not for re-marking the past.

§11.4.4The conflict, and the machinery that manages it

Strip the structure away and the problem is stark: the GP sets the price at which it sells an asset from investors it owes duties to, to investors it owes duties to — and its own economics sit on both sides. A low price cheats the old fund's LPs; a high price cheats the CV's investors (including every LP who rolls). Nobody involved is neutral, least of all the GP, whose carry crystallises at whatever number emerges.

The market's answer is process, layered:

Safeguard What it actually does
Competitive market check Real third-party capital sets the price; the more genuine bidders for the lead role, the better the evidence
LPAC approval The conflict is disclosed and formally waived by LP representatives before the deal proceeds
Fairness opinion Independent adviser opines the price is within a fair range — a floor of protection, not a substitute for competition
Status quo election LPs who do nothing (or roll) keep economics no worse than they had; nobody is forced to sell
GP rolls its carry The GP's crystallised gain goes back in alongside rolling LPs — it eats the price it set
Adequate time and disclosure 20+ business day elections with full information packs; rushed elections are the classic red flag

What looks bad, and LPs increasingly say so: an election window of ten days over a holiday period; a price supported only by a fairness opinion with no market check; a GP taking part of its carry in cash rather than rolling it; and any hint that participation in the CV is linked to access to the GP's next flagship fund (a soft staple — buyers and regulators both watch for it).

§11.4.5LP-led secondaries and NAV lending

Two adjacent tools complete the liquidity toolkit.

LP-led secondaries. An LP sells fund stakes at a negotiated percentage of NAV — buyout fund interests commonly trade in the 85–100% range, venture and tail-end funds lower. Sellers are rarely distressed: they are rebalancing (the "denominator effect" after public markets fall), exiting a strategy, or freeing capital to re-up. Worked example of why buyers like it: pay 85% of a £100m NAV (£85m) for a mature fund that then distributes £120m over three years — that is 120/85=1.41x120/85 = 1.41x120/85=1.41x on a short, already-diversified, already-de-risked portfolio. The discount plus the shortened duration is the whole trade. For the deal team's purposes, LP-led activity matters as a signal: heavy LP selling at deep discounts means LPs need cash — which feeds straight back into how much DPI pressure your own fund is under.

NAV lending. A NAV facility is a loan to the fund itself, secured against the whole portfolio's NAV — typically at conservative loan-to-value (5–20%). Legitimate uses: funding follow-ons when the fund is fully drawn, bridging to a signed exit. The controversial use: borrowing to pay LPs a distribution — "levered DPI". The cash is real but the exposure isn't reduced: LPs still own the same assets, now with fund-level leverage on top and interest running at meaningful spreads. Worked example: a fund with £500m NAV borrows £50m (10% LTV) and distributes it. DPI ticks up; but if the portfolio takes three more years to exit, the facility costs perhaps £15m in interest — paid out of LP proceeds — to move a distribution forward, not to create one. ILPA guidance now pushes for disclosure and LPAC consultation precisely because a DPI figure needs a footnote: was this earned by exits or borrowed against them?

§11.4.6Single-asset vs multi-asset CVs

  • Single-asset CVs are the trophy format: the fund's best company, moved on its own. Secondaries buyers can diligence it like a direct deal, price it sharply, and the "keep the winner" logic is at its cleanest. The cost is concentration — the CV is a one-company fund, and its investors underwrite it as such. This is where the conflict machinery matters most: one asset, one price, nowhere to hide.
  • Multi-asset CVs move several companies (sometimes an entire tail of a fund) into one vehicle. Diversification makes them easier for some buyers to hold, and they can be an honest way to give an old fund's stragglers more time. But blending assets blends prices — strong assets can subsidise weak ones inside a single headline number — and the format has historically been used to sweep problems into a vehicle where fees keep running. Buyers apply portfolio-level discounts and LPs should read the asset-by-asset pricing, not just the total.

Rule of thumb the market itself uses: single-asset CVs are done from strength, multi-asset CVs need to prove they aren't done from weakness.

§11.4.7Judging a CV as an LP: sell or roll?

The election lands on an LP's desk with a few weeks to answer. A disciplined checklist:

  1. How was the price set? Competitive market check with named lead investors → credible. Fairness opinion only → weak. Price versus the fund's most recent mark matters too: a CV at or above carrying value is ordinary; one below recent marks asks why the mark was where it was.
  2. Is the GP rolling everything? 100% of crystallised carry rolled, plus new GP money → the GP eats its own price. Carry partly cashed out → the GP is telling you its own risk appetite; listen.
  3. What are the new economics? Tiered carry rewarding only future performance and ~1% fees on invested → market standard. Full 20% from the re-struck base → the GP is being paid twice for the same gain.
  4. Do I have the capacity to underwrite the asset? Rolling is a new investment decision in a concentrated position. An LP without the resources to diligence a single company is structurally a seller — which is fine, and is most LPs.
  5. What does my portfolio need? The same DPI/redeployment logic funds apply (lesson 2) applies to the LP: cash today at a market-checked price versus a concentrated continuation of a known winner.

Empirically, most LPs elect to sell — commonly 70–90% of them — driven as much by liquidity preference and bandwidth as by any view on the asset. That is not a verdict on CVs; it is what the option existing is for.

§11.4.8What the exit choice signals

Finish where lesson 1 started: the route chosen is itself information, and buyers, LPs, and the next fund's diligence teams all read it.

  • Trade sale: the strongest external validation — an informed industry player paid a synergy premium. Says the asset matters strategically.
  • Secondary buyout: a sophisticated financial buyer underwrote the next five years at a full price. Healthy, ordinary, and says the value-creation story has another chapter someone else believes in.
  • IPO: public markets validated scale and growth — but the fund still owns most of its position, so conviction is being expressed with retained risk.
  • Continuation vehicle: read it with the checklist above. Done well — competitive price, GP rolling everything, LPs choosing freely — it signals the GP's highest conviction: they had a market price and chose to stay invested. Done badly, it signals the opposite: an asset that couldn't clear a real process, warehoused at a negotiated mark.
  • Dividend recap without a sale, repeated: cash is being manufactured from leverage rather than realised from buyers — fine once in a strong business, a pattern worth questioning twice.

What deal teams actually ask when they see any exit announcement in their sector: who bought, who priced it, and what did the seller keep? Those three answers, more than the headline multiple, tell you what the people with the most information really believed. That habit of reading exits as evidence — not just outcomes — is the skill this module has been building, and it is exactly the judgement the case study now asks you to exercise.

Lesson 12.1/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

What Deal Teams Watch and Why: The Monthly KPI Stack

25 min read
In brief

The monthly KPI stack deal teams actually track — trading versus budget, liquidity and covenant headroom, and leading indicators — why variance-to-thesis matters more than variance-to-budget, and the escalation ladder that kicks in when numbers slip.

  1. 12.1.1The thesis is a forecast — monitoring is how you test it
  2. 12.1.2The trading block: revenue and EBITDA versus budget
  3. 12.1.3The cash block: liquidity headroom and covenant headroom
  4. 12.1.4Leading indicators: the numbers that move before the P&L
  5. 12.1.5Variance-to-budget versus variance-to-thesis
  6. 12.1.6The escalation ladder: what happens when numbers slip
  7. 12.1.7Why this is your job

§12.1.1The thesis is a forecast — monitoring is how you test it

Every deal in the portfolio was bought on a thesis: a specific, numeric story about how £X of equity becomes £2.5X in five years. "Grow revenue 12% a year, expand EBITDA margin from 18% to 22%, delever from 4.5× to 2.0×, exit at the entry multiple." The investment committee approved that story, the fund wired the money, and from completion day onwards the thesis stops being a plan and becomes a hypothesis under continuous test.

Portfolio monitoring is that test. Every month, each portfolio company sends numbers up to the fund, and the deal team's job is to answer one question: is the thesis still on track, and if not, how early can we know and how fast can we act? The five-year hold is short. A company that drifts for 18 months before anyone reacts has burned a third of the hold period — and because IRR is time-weighted, delay is expensive even when the problem is eventually fixed.

If you work in a PE data team, the monthly monitoring cycle is probably where you spend most of your time. This lesson is about what the deal teams consuming your output are actually looking for, so that you can build reports that answer their questions rather than merely display data.

§12.1.2The trading block: revenue and EBITDA versus budget

The top of every monthly pack is the trading summary: actuals versus budget versus prior year, for the month and year-to-date. A typical extract:

£m, YTD June Actual Budget Var Prior year Var
Revenue 24.0 22.5 +1.5 20.9 +3.1
Gross profit 14.4 14.4 0.0 13.6 +0.8
Gross margin 60.0% 64.0% −4.0pts 65.1% −5.1pts
EBITDA 4.8 4.9 −0.1 4.7 +0.1
EBITDA margin 20.0% 21.8% −1.8pts 22.5% −2.5pts

Read that table the way a deal team does. Revenue is 6.7% ahead of budget — good headline. But gross profit is exactly on budget despite £1.5m more revenue, which means every incremental pound of sales came in at roughly zero gross margin, or (more likely) the whole book is being discounted. EBITDA is flat against a budget that assumed growth. The company is running harder to stand still.

What looks good: revenue and EBITDA both ahead, margins stable or expanding, and the beat explained by volume or price in the segments the thesis said would grow. What looks bad: a revenue beat with a margin miss (growth is being bought), or an EBITDA "beat" driven by cost deferral — marketing cut, hiring frozen, maintenance pushed — which borrows from next year's P&L. What deal teams ask: "What's driving the gross margin fade — mix, price, or cost inflation we haven't passed through? Show me the price/volume/mix split."

§12.1.3The cash block: liquidity headroom and covenant headroom

EBITDA is an opinion; cash is a fact — a line you met in quality of earnings and it runs the whole way through monitoring. Two numbers matter monthly.

Liquidity headroom is cash plus undrawn committed facilities (usually the revolving credit facility), less any minimum operating cash the business needs. A company with £3.4m of cash and a £2.5m undrawn RCF has £5.9m of liquidity. Whether that is comfortable depends on the monthly cash profile: a business with a £2m intra-month working capital swing and a quarterly interest payment of £1.2m has far less real headroom than the headline suggests. Deal teams want a 13-week rolling cash forecast whenever headroom gets thin, because insolvency is a cash event, not a P&L event.

Covenant headroom measures distance to the tests in the credit agreement (Module 8 covered how covenants are set; here you live with them). The workhorse is the net leverage covenant, tested quarterly on last-twelve-months (LTM) EBITDA:

Net leverage=Gross debt−CashLTM EBITDA\text{Net leverage} = \frac{\text{Gross debt} - \text{Cash}}{\text{LTM EBITDA}}Net leverage=LTM EBITDAGross debt−Cash​

Worked example: gross debt £42.0m, cash £3.4m, LTM EBITDA £9.7m, covenant ≤ 4.25×.

  • Current leverage: (42.0−3.4)/9.7=38.6/9.7=3.98×(42.0 - 3.4) / 9.7 = 38.6 / 9.7 = 3.98×(42.0−3.4)/9.7=38.6/9.7=3.98×
  • Minimum EBITDA before breach (debt constant): 38.6/4.25=£9.1m38.6 / 4.25 = £9.1m38.6/4.25=£9.1m
  • EBITDA headroom: 9.7−9.1=£0.6m9.7 - 9.1 = £0.6m9.7−9.1=£0.6m, i.e. about 6%

Six per cent EBITDA headroom is thin. One lost customer, one bad quarter rolling into the LTM figure, and the company is negotiating a waiver. Notice the double jeopardy in the formula: if the company burns cash, net debt rises at the same time as EBITDA weakness cuts the denominator — the ratio deteriorates from both ends. This is why deal teams track covenant headroom as a monthly line even though the test is only quarterly: they want to see the breach coming two quarters out, while there is still time to fix it cheaply.

What deal teams ask: "What does the covenant look like at the next two test dates on current run-rate, and what has to go wrong for us to breach?"

§12.1.4Leading indicators: the numbers that move before the P&L

Revenue and EBITDA are lagging indicators — by the time they slip, the damage happened months ago. The best monthly packs give equal weight to the numbers that predict the P&L:

  • Pipeline and pipeline coverage. Qualified pipeline divided by the next period's new-business target. Coverage of 3–4× is a common rule of thumb for B2B sales; coverage falling from 3.5× to 2.1× tells you Q4 revenue is at risk in Q2, when you can still act.
  • Order intake and book-to-bill. For industrials: orders ÷ revenue in the period. Below 1.0× for two consecutive quarters means the backlog is being eaten.
  • Churn and retention. For subscription businesses: gross revenue churn, logo churn, and net revenue retention (NRR). Gross churn moving from 8% to 14% annualised is a flashing red light even while reported revenue still grows, because new bookings are temporarily masking the leak.
  • Working capital canaries. Days sales outstanding (DSO) creeping from 52 to 68 days can mean collections discipline slipping — or that sales are being "bought" with extended payment terms, or worse, that disputed invoices are piling up because delivery quality has fallen.
  • People. Regretted attrition, open-role ageing, sales headcount versus plan. A growth thesis with an understaffed sales team is a fantasy with a spreadsheet.

The specific set varies by sector — same logic as the unit-economics lens from Module 3. The design principle does not: every thesis driver needs at least one indicator that moves a quarter or more before the P&L does.

§12.1.5Variance-to-budget versus variance-to-thesis

Here is the subtlety that separates good monitoring from box-ticking. Budgets are set annually by management, and management has learned to sandbag: a budget you beat by 5% every year is a negotiation artefact, not a forecast. The deal model — the underwriting case the IC approved — is the benchmark that actually matters, because the fund's returns are keyed to it.

Worked example. The deal model said Year 2 revenue £52m and EBITDA £12.5m (24% margin). Management's Year 2 budget, set after a soft Year 1, says £46m and £9.7m. Actuals come in at £47.5m revenue and £10.0m EBITDA:

£m Actual vs budget vs deal model
Revenue 47.5 +1.5 (+3.3%) −4.5 (−8.7%)
EBITDA 10.0 +0.3 (+3.1%) −2.5 (−20.0%)

The board pack narrative writes itself as a success: ahead of budget on both lines. But against the thesis, EBITDA is 20% adrift, and if that gap persists to exit at the model's 10× multiple, that is £25m of enterprise value gone — likely most of the planned equity upside once leverage magnifies it (Module 7 maths). A monitoring system that only shows variance-to-budget will report green for two years while the deal quietly dies. Good deal teams — and good data teams — carry the underwriting case in the reporting stack permanently and show both variances side by side. The budget tells you how management is performing against their own promises; the deal model tells you whether the fund is going to make its returns.

What deal teams ask: "Are we behind plan, or behind the plan we paid for?"

§12.1.6The escalation ladder: what happens when numbers slip

Monitoring only matters if it triggers action. Most firms run an explicit or implicit escalation ladder, and it is worth knowing where a company sits on it because the information demands on the portfolio company — and on the data team — escalate with it.

  1. Green — routine. Monthly pack, quarterly board meeting, thesis on track. Deal team attention: a few hours a month.
  2. Amber — watch list. A thesis driver has slipped (two soft quarters, leading indicators deteriorating, covenant headroom below ~15%). Reporting steps up: weekly flash numbers on the problem KPI, a named remediation plan with milestones, the deal partner talking to the CEO between boards. The fund's own valuation of the asset may be nudged down.
  3. Red — intervention. The thesis is broken or cash is at risk. Now the toolkit gets heavy: 13-week cash forecasting, management change (CFO first, statistically), operating partners or advisers deployed, board meetings monthly, lender dialogue opened before the covenant test is failed — waivers are cheapest when asked for early, and most expensive when the lender finds out from the compliance certificate.
  4. Workout. Restructuring territory — covenant reset or equity cure, new money, possibly a debt-for-equity handover. The goal shifts from maximising return to protecting whatever equity value is left.

The whole point of the KPI stack is to catch problems at amber, where the fixes are operational, rather than at red, where they are financial and dilutive. An equity cure — the sponsor injecting cash to mathematically cure a covenant breach — costs real money from the fund; noticing DSO creep six months earlier costs a phone call.

§12.1.7Why this is your job

Everything above lands on a data team's desk as a build request eventually: the variance pack, the covenant bridge, the leading-indicator dashboard, the underwriting-case overlay. The teams that add most value do not wait for the request. They know that a revenue beat with flat gross profit is a discounting story, that DSO and churn are the canaries, that covenant headroom needs a forward view not a rear-view snapshot — and they surface the question before the deal team asks it. The rest of this module builds that capability layer by layer: the infrastructure that gets the data in (Lesson 2), the valuation and LP reporting it feeds (Lesson 3), the performance analytics on top (Lesson 4), and where data work genuinely changes deal outcomes (Lesson 5).
