Lesson 12.2/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

Portfolio Monitoring Infrastructure: How the Numbers Actually Flow

25 min read
In brief

The pipeline that moves numbers from portfolio-company finance teams to partners' screens, the data quality problems endemic to portcos, KPI definition drift, and why standardisation is hard, valuable, and exactly where a data team earns its keep.

  1. 12.2.1The pipeline: five hops from ledger to partner
  2. 12.2.2Why portco data is messy: the endemic problems
  3. 12.2.3KPI definition drift: same word, different formula
  4. 12.2.4Why standardisation is hard — and valuable
  5. 12.2.5Where the data team adds leverage
  6. 12.2.6Worked example: one number, end to end

§12.2.1The pipeline: five hops from ledger to partner

Lesson 1 covered what deal teams want to see. This lesson is about how those numbers get to them — because the gap between "the portco knows its revenue" and "the partner can see it" is where most monitoring effort, and most monitoring failure, lives.

The standard pipeline has five hops:

  1. Portfolio company finance closes its books — usually to a working-day timetable ("WD5 close") — and produces management accounts in whatever system it runs.
  2. A reporting template — typically an Excel workbook or a web form the fund issued at completion — is filled in by the portco's finance team: P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, KPIs, covenant calculations, and a management commentary section.
  3. Fund operations / the data team receives templates from every portco, checks them, chases what is late or broken, and loads them into whatever the firm uses as a central store — anything from a consolidation spreadsheet to a proper warehouse.
  4. Dashboards and packs are built from the central store: a per-company monthly pack for the deal team, a portfolio-wide summary for the partnership, covenant and liquidity flags, and the quarterly inputs to valuation and LP reporting (Lesson 3).
  5. Partners and deal teams consume the output — and fire questions back down the pipe, which is how you know it is being read.

A ten-company portfolio reporting monthly means 120 template submissions a year, each with hundreds of line items. At a firm with thirty portfolio companies, the monitoring pipeline is an industrial process, and it is usually run by a team of two to four people. That ratio — thousands of data points per person per month — is why automation and validation are not luxuries.

The timetable matters too. A typical cycle: portcos close by WD5, templates due WD8–10, data team validates and chases by WD12, packs out by WD15, deal-team review in week three, board meetings in week four. Anything that slips at the top slips everything below it. One of the most useful metrics a data team can publish is simply on-time, first-time-right submission rates by company — late, error-ridden reporting is itself a leading indicator of a finance function in trouble.

§12.2.2Why portco data is messy: the endemic problems

Portfolio companies are not FTSE 100 finance functions. A £60m-revenue business typically has a finance team of four to eight people, one mid-market ERP (or three, after acquisitions), and a finance director who inherited the chart of accounts from a predecessor. Data quality problems are not occasional — they are structural:

  • Restatements without flags. March's pack shows YTD February revenue of £8.4m; the February pack said £8.6m. Someone reclassified a rebate. Nobody mentioned it. Your stored history is now silently wrong unless you detect it.
  • Late and partial submissions. The commentary tab is filled in, the cash flow is not. The KPI tab says "TBC" for churn — for the third month running.
  • Spreadsheet fragility. Templates come back with inserted rows, broken formulas, hard-coded overrides where links used to be, or last month's file resubmitted with a new filename. If your loader assumes cell B14 is EBITDA, one inserted row corrupts the load.
  • Chart-of-accounts churn. A new CFO re-maps cost lines; "distribution costs" moves from cost of sales to overheads and gross margin jumps 3 points with no trading change.
  • Perimeter changes. A bolt-on acquisition (Module 10) joins mid-year. Is it in the budget? In the prior-year comparative? Organic and reported growth now differ, and if the pack does not split them, every variance is ambiguous.
  • Non-financial KPIs of unknown provenance. Finance owns the P&L, but churn comes from the CRM, pipeline from the sales director's own tracker, and headcount from HR. Each has an owner, a refresh lag, and a different idea of "as at" dates.

None of this is malice, and only occasionally is it manipulation — mostly it is small teams doing their best under time pressure. But the consequence is the same: numbers that reach the fund unvalidated are numbers the fund will eventually be embarrassed by, in an IC paper, an LP report, or a covenant certificate.

What looks good: a portco that submits on time, flags restatements proactively, and reconciles its KPI tab to source systems. What looks bad: persistent lateness, "TBC" KPIs, or management accounts that do not tie to the audited statutory accounts at year end. Deal teams treat reporting quality as a proxy for management quality — with reason.

§12.2.3KPI definition drift: same word, different formula

The deepest data quality problem is not errors — it is definitions. Across a portfolio, the same KPI name routinely hides different formulas. Concrete example: three portcos all report "gross churn of 2% for the quarter".

Portco A Portco B Portco C
Basis Logo count Revenue (MRR) Revenue (ARR)
Numerator Customers lost Churned MRR only Churned + downgraded ARR
Denominator Opening customers Opening MRR Average ARR in quarter
Timing Cancellation notice date Service end date Renewal date

All three cells say "2%". They are not comparable. Portco A lost 4 of 200 customers — but if those 4 were worth £1.6m of £16m ARR, its revenue churn is 10%, five times what the pack implies. Portco C's inclusion of downgrades makes it look worse than B on identical trading. Rank these companies on a dashboard and you are ranking their formulas, not their retention.

The same drift infects financial lines. "EBITDA" is the worst offender: one company reports pre-IFRS 16 (rent as a cost), another post-IFRS 16 (rent as depreciation and interest, EBITDA higher by the whole rent bill); one includes the management fee to the sponsor as a cost, another adds it back; exceptional items are self-declared. Two portcos with identical economics can report EBITDA margins 4 points apart. "Net debt" drifts on whether lease liabilities, earn-out obligations, and shareholder loans count. "Organic growth" drifts on how many months an acquisition must be owned before it counts as organic. Even "revenue" drifts in businesses with gross-versus-net agency questions (Module 1).

Why does drift happen? Because each definition was locally rational: it matched the company's old board pack, its credit agreement, or its previous owner's habits. Nobody chose inconsistency; it accreted deal by deal — each template negotiated at close, under time pressure, by a deal team focused on getting the deal done, not on portfolio-wide comparability.

§12.2.4Why standardisation is hard — and valuable

Standardisation sounds like a memo: "everyone reports churn on the ARR basis from next quarter." In practice it is a negotiation, and it is worth understanding the resistance:

  • Real heterogeneity. A software portco and a distribution portco should not report identical KPIs. Standardisation means a common core (P&L, cash, net debt, headcount, a defined EBITDA) plus sector-specific KPI sets — not one template to rule them all.
  • Credit agreements pin definitions. Covenant EBITDA is defined in the loan docs and cannot be "standardised" away; the fix is to report both covenant EBITDA and fund-basis EBITDA, explicitly bridged.
  • Management time is finite. Every extra reporting field competes with running the business, and CFOs push back — often rightly. The template that gets filled in accurately is the one that is no longer than it needs to be.
  • History has to be restated. Changing a definition breaks trend lines unless someone rebuilds the back-series on the new basis — real work the data team owns.

Against that cost, the value: comparability (which portco's churn problem is real), aggregation (portfolio-level revenue, EBITDA, net debt, and covenant status that the CFO and IR team can trust), speed (validated data loads straight through instead of a month of manual tidying), and institutional memory (when the deal team asks "what did DSO do in the last downturn", the answer exists). Firms increasingly pitch exactly this to LPs as evidence of a professionalised platform.

What deal teams ask: "Is that churn number on our standard basis or theirs?" — and if the answer is a shrug, the dashboard has already lost the room.

§12.2.5Where the data team adds leverage

Pull the threads together and the high-leverage data team contributions are concrete:

  1. A KPI dictionary. One page per metric: name, formula, source system, owner, reporting basis, known exceptions per company. Agreed with each portco at onboarding — the first 100 days (Module 10) is the moment of maximum leverage to set reporting expectations, because everything is being renegotiated anyway.
  2. Validation at the point of load. Automated checks before a number enters the store: does the balance sheet balance; does cash movement tie to the cash flow; does YTD this month equal YTD last month plus the month; is any figure >20% off trend without commentary? A restatement then triggers a flag, not a silent overwrite.
  3. A versioned central store. Every submission kept as-submitted, every restatement tracked, so "what did we believe about June as of July?" is answerable — which matters enormously when a number that went into an LP report later changes.
  4. The underwriting-case overlay. Loading each deal's IC model into the same store so variance-to-thesis (Lesson 1) is a standing column, not a one-off analysis.
  5. Exception-first outputs. Partners do not read 30 packs; they read a one-page exception report — covenant headroom below threshold, EBITDA behind thesis by >10%, DSO trend breaching limits, late submissions. The dashboard's job is triage.

Notice what is not on the list: exotic modelling. The compounding value in monitoring infrastructure comes from boring things done relentlessly — definitions, validation, lineage, timeliness. Lesson 5 covers where genuine data science lands; it lands on top of this foundation or not at all.

§12.2.6Worked example: one number, end to end

Trace a single figure to see the whole system. Portco Kestrel's July template arrives on WD9 showing YTD revenue £14.2m. Validation flags two issues: June's stored YTD was £12.4m, implying July revenue of £1.8m against a trend of £2.1m; and the KPI tab's "invoiced revenue" says £15.0m. The chase email goes out WD10. Answer: a £0.3m credit note was issued against a disputed Q2 invoice (so June is restated to £12.1m), and the £0.8m gap to invoiced revenue is deferred income on annual licences — fine, but the credit note relates to the same customer whose receivable has been outstanding 95 days.

The data team logs the restatement, updates the store with lineage, and adds one line to the exception report: "Kestrel: £0.3m credit note against disputed Q2 invoice; same customer 95 days overdue on further £0.4m — collectability question." The deal team walks into the board meeting asking about a specific customer dispute rather than discovering it in Q4 when the receivable is written off. That is the difference between a data team that forwards spreadsheets and one that produces intelligence — and no part of it needed anything fancier than validation rules and a suspicious mind.

Lesson 12.3/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

Valuation and Fund Reporting: Marks, NAV, and What LPs See

25 min read
In brief

How sponsors mark unrealised holdings each quarter — multiples-based valuation with calibration under the IPEV guidelines — what NAV is and who consumes it, how fund-level reporting to LPs works (DPI/TVPI, capital account statements), and why marks are smoothed.

  1. 12.3.1From monitoring to marks
  2. 12.3.2The workhorse: a multiples-based mark
  3. 12.3.3NAV: one number, many consumers
  4. 12.3.4What LPs receive each quarter
  5. 12.3.5Why marks are smoothed — and how to read them
  6. 12.3.6Where the data team sits in all this

§12.3.1From monitoring to marks

Everything the monitoring pipeline collects has a second life. Once a quarter, the same EBITDA and net debt figures that fed the board pack feed a different machine: the valuation of every unrealised holding, the fund's Net Asset Value, and the quarterly report to LPs. If you work in a PE data team, quarter-end is when your numbers stop being internal management information and become the basis of what investors are told their stake is worth. The tolerance for error drops to zero, because these numbers are audited, they appear in LPs' own accounts, and they underpin the track record the firm will raise its next fund on.

Public equities are priced by the market every second. A private company owned by a fund has no price — so the sponsor must estimate fair value: the price that would be received in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. That phrase comes from accounting standards (IFRS 13 / ASC 820), and the practical playbook for applying it to private companies is the IPEV guidelines (International Private Equity and Venture Capital Valuation guidelines) — the industry's shared rulebook. IPEV does not prescribe a single method; it requires the valuer to choose appropriate techniques, use them consistently, and — crucially — calibrate them to the price actually paid at entry.

§12.3.2The workhorse: a multiples-based mark

For a cash-generative buyout asset, the standard technique is exactly the comparable multiples method from Module 4, applied quarterly:

Equity fair value=Maintainable EBITDA×Multiple−Net debt (adjusted)\text{Equity fair value} = \text{Maintainable EBITDA} \times \text{Multiple} - \text{Net debt (adjusted)}Equity fair value=Maintainable EBITDA×Multiple−Net debt (adjusted)

Worked example. Fund III bought Osprey Group in January 2024:

  • Entry: EV £90m on LTM EBITDA of £10.0m → 9.0× entry multiple; funded with £54m net debt and £36m equity.
  • At entry, the chosen basket of listed comparables traded at 10.0× — so Osprey was bought at a 10% discount to comps (size, liquidity, and the usual private-company arguments from Module 4).

Now it is Q2 2026. LTM EBITDA is £12.0m, net debt has fallen to £38m, and the comp basket trades at 9.5×.

Calibration is the discipline that turns this into a defensible mark. At entry, the model (comps at 10.0×) and the actual price (9.0×) differed by 10%; unless something has changed about Osprey's relative quality, that 10% discount should persist. So:

  • Calibrated multiple: 9.5××0.90=8.55×9.5\times \times 0.90 = 8.55\times9.5××0.90=8.55×, say 8.5×
  • Enterprise value: 12.0×8.5=£102m12.0 \times 8.5 = £102m12.0×8.5=£102m
  • Equity fair value: 102−38=£64m102 - 38 = £64m102−38=£64m
  • Mark on cost: 64/36=1.78×64 / 36 = 1.78\times64/36=1.78× — carried at 1.8× MOIC, unrealised.

Note what moved the mark: two-thirds of the gain is EBITDA growth and deleveraging — facts from the monitoring pipeline — and the multiple actually fell. A mark that went up purely because the valuer nudged the multiple up would attract very different scrutiny from auditors and LPs. Common adjustments layered on top: using maintainable rather than raw LTM EBITDA (stripping one-offs — the QofE mindset from Module 9 again), deducting transaction or exit costs, and reflecting structure — if the sponsor holds preferred instruments (Module 8), the equity value must be run through the waterfall before it becomes the fund's share.

Other IPEV-sanctioned techniques exist — DCF (usually as a cross-check), recent transaction price (the entry price itself is the best fair-value evidence for the first few quarters), industry-specific metrics, and NAV-based approaches for asset-heavy businesses. A recent funding round or credible offer for the asset trumps a model. But for mainstream buyouts, calibrated multiples do the work.

§12.3.3NAV: one number, many consumers

Sum the fair values of every holding, add fund-level cash, subtract fund-level liabilities, and you have the fund's NAV — the number a surprising range of people rely on:

  • LPs book their share of NAV in their own accounts; a pension fund's asset allocation and its own funding ratio move with your marks.
  • Auditors test the marks annually; valuation is almost always the key audit matter for a fund.
  • The secondaries market prices LP stakes as a percentage of NAV ("bid at 92% of NAV"). If marks are stale, secondary pricing is where the market says so out loud.
  • The next fundraise. Interim performance for Fund III is mostly unrealised marks (the RVPI component below). LPs diligence the marks of the current portfolio hard when deciding on Fund IV — including comparing the entry-to-mark uplift on assets against what those assets eventually exit at ("mark accuracy" analysis).
  • The GP itself. NAV drives carry accruals in the waterfall model, drives any NAV-based fund financing facility, and — increasingly — drives compensation conversations. The incentive to mark generously is obvious, which is exactly why process, calibration, and audit exist.

§12.3.4What LPs receive each quarter

The quarterly LP package is the fund's shop window, and the data team usually builds large parts of it:

  1. Capital account statement — each LP's ledger: capital committed, capital called to date, distributions received, their share of NAV, and the movement in the period. This is the document an LP's back office actually reconciles.
  2. Fund-level metrics — the Module 5 measures, updated: DPI (distributions ÷ called capital — cash actually returned), RVPI (residual NAV ÷ called capital — the unrealised marks), TVPI = DPI + RVPI, and net IRR. Worked example: a fund with £400m committed has called £280m, distributed £140m, and holds NAV of £250m. DPI = 140/280 = 0.50×; RVPI = 250/280 = 0.89×; TVPI = 390/280 = 1.39×. An LP reads that as: on paper 1.4×, but only half my capital is back — the rest is marks.
  3. Portfolio company pages — one page per holding: cost, mark, MOIC, ownership, a trading summary (revenue and EBITDA, LTM and versus prior year), leverage, and a paragraph of commentary. This is monitoring data, redacted and polished.
  4. The quarterly letter and, for larger LPs, ILPA-template reporting on fees, expenses, and carry — plus a growing stack of side-letter special requests: ESG data, exposure cuts by geography and sector, currency splits. Every bespoke request lands on the data team, which is why firms increasingly push LP reporting onto the same central store as monitoring: one source, many views.

What looks good to an LP: DPI growing steadily mid-fund, marks that exits later confirm ("exited at or above the last mark" is a track-record talking point), clean and punctual reporting. What looks bad: TVPI built entirely on RVPI deep into a fund's life ("everything is marked up, nothing is sold"), marks that fall precisely when an asset goes to market, restated capital accounts.

§12.3.5Why marks are smoothed — and how to read them

Compare a PE fund's quarterly marks to a listed small-cap index and you will see the fund's line is far smoother. In 2022, public software comps fell 30–50%; typical sponsor marks on software assets fell a fraction of that. Four mechanisms produce this smoothing:

  • Calibration and discretion. The valuer chooses the comp basket, the maintainable EBITDA, and how much of a public de-rating to pass through, and can argue the entry discount has narrowed. Each choice is individually defensible; collectively they damp volatility — overwhelmingly in the downward direction.
  • Offsetting fundamentals. If EBITDA grew 15% while comps de-rated 15%, the mark is genuinely flat. Private marks mix price and performance in one number.
  • Lag. Q1 marks are finalised weeks after quarter-end, often anchored on three-month-old LTM figures; a March market fall may not fully land until the June marks.
  • Event-driven step-ups. Many sponsors hold assets near cost until an event — a strong audited year, a refinancing, a partial sale — justifies a step-up. Value arrives in stair-steps, not a wiggle.

What this means for interpretation — the judgement layer:

  • Do not read quarterly NAV moves as market prices. A flat mark against comps down 25% is not evidence PE assets are immune; it is a modelling choice plus a lag. The informative check is the assumptions: did EBITDA actually grow? What multiple is implied, and how does it compare to comps and to entry?
  • Smoothed marks flatter risk metrics. Reported volatility and correlation of PE returns are artificially low, which flatters Sharpe ratios and allocation models. LPs know this ("volatility laundering" is the sceptic's phrase); sophisticated ones de-smooth the series before using it.
  • The truth arrives at exit. DPI is the audit of RVPI. Over a fund's life, marks and reality must converge — which is why exits versus last-mark is one of the most informative analyses a data team can maintain (Lesson 4).
  • Down-rounds of trust are expensive. A sponsor that marks aggressively and then exits below marks poisons its next fundraise. Most sponsors therefore mark conservatively-but-smoothly: the typical pattern is exits modestly above final marks.

§12.3.6Where the data team sits in all this

Quarter-end valuation is a process with hard deadlines and audit trails, and it runs on monitoring data. The data team's leverage points: making sure LTM EBITDA and net debt used by the valuation team reconcile exactly to the monitoring store (auditors will trace them); maintaining the comp sets and pulling quarter-end trading multiples reproducibly; keeping the calibration history per asset (entry multiple versus comps at entry, and every quarter since — a table auditors and LPs both love); automating the capital account and fund-metric calculations so DPI/TVPI updates are generated, not hand-built; and building the mark-accuracy backtest — for every exit, final mark versus realised proceeds. None of it is glamorous; all of it compounds, because in fund reporting the firm's product is credibility, and credibility is a data quality property.

Lesson 12.4/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

The Value Bridge and Performance Analytics

25 min read
In brief

Building a portfolio-company value bridge (worked example), fund-level attribution across deals, loss ratios and concentration analysis, what underwriting-versus-actual tracking teaches a firm, and the benchmarking datasets a data team can build.

  1. 12.4.1Why attribution is the firm's mirror
  2. 12.4.2The portfolio-company value bridge: worked example
  3. 12.4.3Fund-level attribution: which deals made the fund
  4. 12.4.4Loss ratios and concentration
  5. 12.4.5Underwriting versus actual: the institutional learning loop
  6. 12.4.6Benchmarking: the portfolio as its own dataset

§12.4.1Why attribution is the firm's mirror

Monitoring (Lesson 1) asks "is this deal on track?". Attribution asks a harder question: where did the money actually come from? A fund can make 2.5× and not know whether it was skill in operations, courage on leverage, or luck on multiples — and a firm that cannot answer that cannot honestly tell LPs what it is good at, cannot underwrite the next deal better, and cannot see its own bad habits. The tools of this lesson — value bridges, fund-level attribution, loss ratios, concentration analysis, underwriting-versus-actual — are how a firm holds up the mirror. They are also, not coincidentally, almost entirely data-team deliverables: they need clean entry data, consistent marks, and the underwriting cases preserved in queryable form.

§12.4.2The portfolio-company value bridge: worked example

You met the idea in Module 7 as returns attribution; here it becomes a standing report. The bridge decomposes the change in equity value into three drivers: EBITDA growth, multiple change, and deleveraging.

Osprey-style example, five-year hold:

Entry Exit
Revenue £50.0m £65.0m
EBITDA £10.0m £15.0m
EV multiple 10.0× 10.4×
Enterprise value £100.0m £156.0m
Net debt £60.0m £24.0m
Equity value £40.0m £132.0m

Equity gain: £92m, a 3.3× MOIC. The standard decomposition:

  • EBITDA growth at the entry multiple: (15.0−10.0)×10.0=£50m(15.0 - 10.0) \times 10.0 = £50m(15.0−10.0)×10.0=£50m
  • Multiple expansion on exit EBITDA: (10.4−10.0)×15.0=£6m(10.4 - 10.0) \times 15.0 = £6m(10.4−10.0)×15.0=£6m
  • Deleveraging (net debt paid down): 60.0−24.0=£36m60.0 - 24.0 = £36m60.0−24.0=£36m
  • Check: 50+6+36=£92m50 + 6 + 36 = £92m50+6+36=£92m ✓

One honesty note: the split of the cross-term (growth × multiple change) is a convention. Here multiple expansion is measured on exit EBITDA; some houses measure it on entry EBITDA and price growth at the exit multiple — (10.4−10.0)×10=£4m(10.4-10.0)\times 10 = £4m(10.4−10.0)×10=£4m and (15−10)×10.4=£52m(15-10)\times 10.4 = £52m(15−10)×10.4=£52m, same £56m EV gain, different labels. It rarely changes the story, but a data team must pick one convention and apply it identically to every deal, or cross-deal comparisons are quietly corrupted (Lesson 2's definition-drift problem in miniature).

The bridge gets more useful the further you push it:

  • Split EBITDA growth into revenue and margin. Revenue grew £50m→£65m at a constant 20% margin contributes 15×0.20×10=£30m15 \times 0.20 \times 10 = £30m15×0.20×10=£30m; margin expansion from 20.0% to 23.1% on exit revenue contributes (0.231−0.200)×65×10=£20m(0.231-0.200)\times 65 \times 10 = £20m(0.231−0.200)×65×10=£20m. Now ask: did the thesis say margin or growth? A deal underwritten as a growth story that delivered via cost-out did not prove its thesis — it got lucky differently.
  • Split organic from M&A. If two bolt-ons added £2.5m of the £5m EBITDA growth, organic growth was half the headline — and the bolt-ons consumed capital that belongs in the denominator.
  • Question the deleveraging line. £36m of debt paydown is cash the business threw off. If it came from genuine conversion, excellent; if £10m of it came from squeezing working capital or starving capex, some of that value was borrowed from the buyer — the exact adjustments a vendor DD process (Module 11) will probe.

What looks good: value built mainly on EBITDA growth, ideally the kind the thesis predicted. What looks bad: a bridge dominated by multiple expansion — that is market beta the firm cannot repeat and LPs discount it accordingly. What deal teams ask: "run the bridge at entry multiple — would we still have carry if the market hadn't re-rated?"

§12.4.3Fund-level attribution: which deals made the fund

Aggregate across the portfolio and patterns appear. A stylised Fund II, all figures total value (realised + marked) versus invested cost:

Deal Invested Value MOIC Gain/(loss)
Alpha £50m £150m 3.0× +£100m
Beta £60m £120m 2.0× +£60m
Gamma £40m £100m 2.5× +£60m
Delta £45m £45m 1.0× £0m
Epsilon £35m £15m 0.4× −£20m
Fund £230m £430m 1.87× +£200m

Read it like a partner would. Alpha alone is half the fund's gains; Alpha plus Beta and Gamma are all of them (the other two net to −£20m). This is typical — buyout returns are less skewed than venture but still concentrated — and it drives real decisions: which partners' deals actually made the money (carry politics live here), whether the fund's winners share a sector or a playbook (strategy), and what the next fund's pacing and sizing should look like. Cut the same table by sector, by deal size, by entry year, by sourcing channel (auction versus proprietary), by entry multiple paid — every cut is a question about what the firm is good at, and the data team is the only place the cuts can be produced consistently.

§12.4.4Loss ratios and concentration

Two risk lenses LPs apply to every track record:

Loss ratio — the share of invested capital in deals returning below cost. Fund II above: Delta returned exactly 1.0× (not a loss); Epsilon's £35m returned 0.4×. Loss ratio = 35/230 ≈ 15% of capital in losing deals; the harsher variant, capital impairment, is the capital actually destroyed: (35−15)/230 ≈ 9%. Buyout LPs typically expect loss ratios in the 10–20% range; a 5% loss ratio with a 1.6× fund suggests admirable discipline or insufficient risk appetite; a 35% loss ratio needs a very good story. The two variants get conflated constantly — a data team should publish both, defined, per fund vintage.

Concentration — how much of the fund rides on few names. In Fund II, Alpha is 150/430 = 35% of total value — a single asset's exit timing now dominates the fund's DPI. Funds manage this ex ante with position limits (commonly no deal >10–15% of commitments at cost) and ex post by watching value concentration; the fund CFO also watches it for the NAV facility covenants. Related cuts: top-3 assets as % of NAV, sector concentration, and — subtler — shared-factor concentration (five deals that are all "US consumer discretionary with floating-rate debt" are one bet wearing five names).

§12.4.5Underwriting versus actual: the institutional learning loop

The single highest-value dataset a PE data team can build is also the simplest to describe: for every deal, the IC-approved underwriting case, frozen at close, joined to actuals forever. Most firms have this in principle; few have it queryable. What it teaches:

Question Typical finding
Do we hit Year-1 EBITDA? Underwriting misses Y1 by 5–10% at many firms — the "J-curve of optimism". If your firm's Y1 miss averages 8%, ICs can haircut systematically.
Which assumptions miss most? Revenue growth is usually the optimistic line; cost synergies in buy-and-build second. Exit multiples underwritten flat-to-entry are usually the conservative line in rising markets.
Where do we win? If actual outperformance clusters in one sector or one operating lever (pricing, say), that is the firm's genuine edge — bid harder there, staff it better.
Are our marks honest? Join to Lesson 3: final mark versus exit proceeds, per deal. A firm that exits 10% above final marks can prove conservatism to LPs with a table, not an adjective.

The cultural obstacle is obvious: this dataset grades named partners' past promises. Building it anyway — neutrally, systematically, without editorialising — is one of the clearest ways a data function demonstrates it works for the firm rather than for any deal team. The output shows up directly in IC memos ("our last four industrials deals underwrote 12% growth and delivered 7% — why is this one different?"), which is precisely the seat-at-the-table currency Lesson 5 is about.

§12.4.6Benchmarking: the portfolio as its own dataset

A firm with 25 portfolio companies sits on a private benchmarking asset no consultant can sell it — if the data is standardised (Lesson 2). Useful builds, roughly in order of effort:

  1. Cross-portfolio KPI benchmarks. DSO, DPO, inventory turns, EBITDA margin by sector, revenue per head, IT spend as % of revenue. A portco CFO told "your DSO is 68 against a portfolio median of 49 for similar businesses" has been handed a target with evidence attached.
  2. Functional cost benchmarks. Finance function cost as % of revenue across the portfolio; procurement rates for the same categories (insurance, freight, software licences) — feeding portfolio-wide procurement programmes, a classic value-creation lever from Module 10.
  3. Pricing and retention benchmarks. Realised price increases versus list, churn by cohort and by tier, discount depth by sales rep — comparable across software portcos on a standard basis, and instantly actionable inside each.
  4. External data joins. Public comp multiples (feeding Lesson 3's calibration), credit market conditions, sector datasets. The join key problems are real — company identifiers, fiscal-year misalignment, currency — and solving them robustly is unglamorous, compounding work.

What looks good in a firm's analytics stack: one store, standard definitions, the underwriting overlay live, exception-driven reporting, and every number in an IC paper or LP report traceable to source. What looks bad: five spreadsheets that disagree about last quarter's EBITDA, attribution rebuilt by hand for each fundraise, and a "data team" that spends quarter-end retyping numbers. The difference between the two is rarely tooling; it is whether the firm decided the portfolio's history is an asset worth engineering. The final lesson turns to where that asset — and the person who builds it — changes actual deal outcomes.

Lesson 12.5/Portfolio Monitoring & the Data Angle

The Data-Driven PE Firm: Where Data Work Changes Deal Outcomes

25 min read
In brief

Where data science genuinely lands in PE — sourcing signals, diligence analytics, portfolio pricing and churn work, exit preparation — the realistic limits, how a data professional earns a seat at the deal table by speaking returns language, and a closing synthesis: reading any company through the deal-team lens.

  1. 12.5.1Separating the real from the deck-ware
  2. 12.5.2Sourcing: signals before the banker calls
  3. 12.5.3Diligence: the data room as a dataset
  4. 12.5.4Portfolio: pricing, churn, and the operating levers
  5. 12.5.5Realistic limits: where data science doesn't land
  6. 12.5.6Earning the seat: speak returns, translate to thesis
  7. 12.5.7Closing synthesis: reading any company through the deal lens

§12.5.1Separating the real from the deck-ware

"Data-driven private equity" appears in every fundraising deck; the reality inside firms ranges from a genuinely industrialised capability to one analyst with a Bloomberg login. This lesson maps where data work has actually changed deal outcomes, where it reliably disappoints, and — since you are the person doing it — how to convert analytical work into standing in a deal-led organisation. The honest headline: the wins are concentrated in four places, and none of them look like a Kaggle competition. They look like the deal lifecycle from Module 6 with better inputs at each stage.

§12.5.2Sourcing: signals before the banker calls

The economics of sourcing reward earliness. A proprietary conversation started a year before a process means relationship, information advantage, and sometimes a pre-empt (Module 6); data work is one of the few scalable ways to get there.

What works in practice: a universe-and-signals engine. Build the universe of companies in the firm's target sectors and size range (filings, registries, and commercial databases — in the UK, Companies House filings give you revenue, margins, and debt for private companies, on a lag); layer on signals that suggest change or quality: hiring velocity by function (a sales-hiring spike implies growth ambitions), web traffic and review trajectories, customer-review scores versus competitors, technology stack changes, founder age and tenure, lease events, grant awards, import/export records. Score and rank; feed the top of the list to sector teams as call sheets, and track conversion: signals → meetings → deals.

Two design truths. First, the model's job is triage, not prediction — reducing 40,000 companies to the 200 a human should ring this quarter. Precision at the top of the list is what matters; a plausible-looking company that takes a meeting is a success even if it never transacts. Second, the moat is mostly the plumbing: entity resolution (matching "Hartwell Systems Ltd" across five databases), deduplication against the CRM, and keeping signals fresh. Firms that treat sourcing data science as a matching-and-freshness engineering problem get compounding value; firms that treat it as a modelling problem build an impressive notebook and quietly stop using it.

§12.5.3Diligence: the data room as a dataset

Module 9 covered what diligence asks; data teams change what it can answer. Modern processes drop transaction-level data into the room — invoice lines, subscription logs, SKU-level sales — and a team that can process a few million rows in a week can test claims the CIM makes in prose:

  • Cohort and retention analysis from raw subscription or repeat-purchase data: compute NRR and churn yourself rather than accepting management's definition (Lesson 2's drift problem, adversarial edition). Classic finding: headline "95% retention" that is really 84% once downgrades and a definition quirk are unwound.
  • Pricing forensics from invoice lines: realised price versus list, discount depth by rep and segment, price change stick-rates. Classic finding: list prices rose 5% but realised prices rose 1.4% — the pricing lever the thesis relies on has never actually been pulled successfully.
  • Customer concentration and cross-sell, computed from transactions rather than the top-10 table the vendor curated — including revenue at risk from customers already shrinking year-on-year.
  • Speed as advantage. In a compressed auction (Module 6), producing the cohort analysis in three days rather than outsourcing it in three weeks changes what the deal team can know before the bid deadline — sometimes the difference between conviction to stretch and a pass.

The same skill set points the other way at exit (Module 11): sell-side analytics. Exit preparation increasingly means building the clean KPI dataset eighteen months early, so vendor DD tells a verified growth story and buyers' data teams find order instead of excuses to chip. A data team that knows its portco's numbers will be recomputed by someone exactly like them prepares accordingly.

§12.5.4Portfolio: pricing, churn, and the operating levers

Inside the portfolio, data work is value creation (Module 10) with a keyboard. The two recurring wins:

Pricing. Most mid-market companies underprice through inertia — annual increases not taken, discounts unmanaged, no segmentation. The analytical work is often mundane (dispersion analysis: who pays what for the same thing, and why) and the value is not. Worked example: a portco with £40m revenue where analysis shows bottom-quartile-priced customers are no more price-sensitive than the median; a targeted 3% realised increase on half the book adds 40×0.5×0.03=£0.6m40 \times 0.5 \times 0.03 = £0.6m40×0.5×0.03=£0.6m of revenue at ~90% flow-through — £0.54m of EBITDA, worth ~£5m of EV at a 9× exit. That is a partner-visible result from six weeks of SQL.

Churn and retention. A churn model's value is not the AUC; it is the intervention economics. Example: a portco with £30m ARR losing 12% gross; risk-scoring accounts and triggering save-plays cuts gross churn by 2 points. Retained revenue: £0.6m a year; at 70% incremental margin, £0.42m of EBITDA; at a 10× exit multiple, ~£4.2m of enterprise value — before compounding (retained customers renew again). Presenting it that way — churn points → EBITDA → exit value — rather than as model metrics is the difference between analytics and value creation.

Beyond these: demand forecasting for inventory-heavy portcos, procurement analytics across the portfolio, salesforce productivity, and the cross-portfolio benchmarks from Lesson 4. The pattern holds — the technique is rarely novel; the leverage comes from tying it to a thesis lever and quantifying it in deal currency.

§12.5.5Realistic limits: where data science doesn't land

Being clear-eyed about limits is itself a credibility asset:

  • Small n, huge stakes. A firm does 4–8 deals a year; a fund's outcome hinges on two or three of them. You cannot train "will this deal work?" on 25 observations from a vanished rate regime. Deal selection remains judgement; data narrows the funnel and arms the judgement.
  • The decisive variables are often unquantified. Management quality, a founder's real reason for selling, a competitor's next move — diligence findings that kill deals are frequently qualitative. The model sees none of it.
  • Relationships still win deals. Proprietary deal flow is mostly trust and years of coffee; a signals engine gets you the meeting sooner, not the deal.
  • Analytics can't fix a bad thesis. No dashboard rescues a structurally declining asset bought at 11× (Module 3's lens comes first).
  • Integration cost is chronically underestimated. Every model needs the Lesson 2 foundation — definitions, pipelines, validation. Firms that hire data scientists before data plumbing produce demos, then disillusionment.

What looks bad, from the deal team's chair: black-box scores with no explanation, analysis that arrives after the decision, precision theatre (four significant figures on garbage inputs), and any answer that cannot survive "so what should we do?".

§12.5.6Earning the seat: speak returns, translate to thesis

The recurring career question for PE data professionals: how do you stop being a service desk and start being in the room? The consistent pattern across firms:

  1. Denominate everything in returns. The firm's native units are EBITDA, multiple, IRR, MOIC, covenant headroom. "Churn down 2 points" is a KPI; "~£4m of exit equity value, roughly 0.1× on this deal's MOIC" is a contribution. You now have the entire course's vocabulary — use it in every deliverable.
  2. Anchor on the thesis. Before analysing anything, read the IC paper. Every piece of analysis should locate itself on a thesis driver: does this support, threaten, or quantify the case we underwrote? Analysis with no thesis coordinate is trivia.
  3. Volunteer the question, not just the answer. Lesson 1's discipline: the data team that says "revenue beat but incremental gross margin was 30% — are we buying growth?" before the board meeting becomes part of the deal conversation permanently.
  4. Be flawless on the boring cycle. The monitoring pack, quarter-end marks data, LP reporting — delivered on time, reconciled, twelve times a year. Trust in PE is built on operational reliability first; the interesting work is awarded to people who have it.
  5. Pick one deal and go deep. Knowing one portfolio company to board-pack depth — its covenant position, its DSO story, its pricing cohorts — teaches you more about what deal teams need than broad tooling work, and makes you the person the deal partner actually rings.

§12.5.7Closing synthesis: reading any company through the deal lens

This module ends the course, so zoom out. Twelve modules ago a set of accounts was a compliance document. Now, handed any company, you can run the full deal-team read:

  • What does it sell and why do customers stay? (Module 3) — the moat and unit economics before any multiple.
  • Are the earnings real? (Modules 1–2, 9) — cash conversion, working capital, one-offs, the QofE instincts.
  • What is it worth, and to whom? (Module 4) — multiples with calibration scepticism, EV versus equity always.
  • How would a deal be built? (Modules 5–8) — who funds it, the leverage it can carry, the structure and covenants, what the returns maths requires of the exit.
  • What would you do with it, and how would you leave? (Modules 10–11) — the levers, the 100-day plan, the exit route and its timing.
  • And how would you know it's working? — this module: the KPI stack, variance to thesis, the marks, the bridge.

That last question is yours professionally. Every lesson in this course ultimately described a forecast someone made with other people's money; portfolio monitoring is where the forecast meets the actuals, and the data team is where that meeting is engineered honestly. Do it well and you are not adjacent to the investing — you are the part of the machine that tells the firm the truth. There is no more valuable seat to earn.

Case C1/Case studies

Hilton: The Best Buyout That Nearly Wasn't

GoodReal deal15 min read

USD 26bn take-private at the peak, rescued by a debt restructuring, roughly USD 14bn of profit

Sponsor
Blackstone
Sector
Hotels & hospitality
Period
2007–2018
In brief

Blackstone bought Hilton at the top of the 2007 market, watched the equity get marked down heavily in the financial crisis, restructured the debt, pivoted the business towards fees, and ended up with what is widely cited as the most profitable buyout ever.

  1. C1.1Snapshot
  2. C1.2The business and the thesis
  3. C1.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C1.4What went wrong
  5. C1.5What went well
  6. C1.6Outcome
  7. C1.7Lessons for deal teams

§C1.1Snapshot

Real deal. Figures are rounded from public reporting and are approximate. Check primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsor Blackstone (real estate and private equity funds)
Announced / closed July 2007 / October 2007
Enterprise value About USD 26bn
Funding About USD 20.5bn debt, about USD 5.6bn equity
Implied equity cushion Roughly 21% of the price
Exit route IPO December 2013, then staged sell-downs to 2018
Outcome Widely reported profit of about USD 14bn
Verdict Good, but only after surviving a near-miss

§C1.2The business and the thesis

Hilton Hotels owned, managed and franchised hotels under brands including Hilton, Hampton, Embassy Suites, DoubleTree and Conrad. It had three quite different economic engines in one company:

  • Owned real estate. Capital-heavy, cyclical, but valuable land and buildings.
  • Management contracts. Fees for running hotels other people own.
  • Franchising. Royalties on revenue for letting owners use the brand and booking system.

Blackstone's thesis was that the fee businesses were undervalued inside a real-estate-heavy listed company, that the brand pipeline could grow globally with little capital, and that a large owned portfolio gave hard-asset support for a lot of debt. Blackstone also owned other hotel businesses and knew the sector well.

§C1.3Entry and deal structure

The deal was priced at the peak of the pre-crisis credit boom, and it shows in the structure.

Sources USD bn Uses USD bn
Debt (mortgage, mezzanine, corporate loans) 20.5 Purchase of equity and refinancing 26.1
Blackstone equity 5.6
Total 26.1 Total 26.1

Around four-fifths of the price was borrowed. A large share of the debt was secured on the owned hotels, with layers of mezzanine debt above it. That is a structure that works well while hotel revenue grows and becomes dangerous quickly when it falls.

§C1.4What went wrong

The timing could hardly have been worse. The deal closed months before the financial crisis. US hotel revenue per available room fell sharply in 2009, as business travel and conferences were cut. Highly fixed hotel operating costs meant profits fell much faster than revenue.

Blackstone marked its Hilton equity down steeply, by around 70% at the low point, according to press coverage at the time. With roughly USD 20bn of debt against collapsing earnings, the equity was close to worthless on a mark-to-market basis and several maturities were approaching.

§C1.5What went well

Three things turned it around.

  1. A debt restructuring from a position of relative strength. In 2010 Blackstone negotiated with lenders who did not want to own a hotel company in a recession. It bought back about USD 2bn of debt for about USD 800m, a large discount, and lenders converted a further USD 2bn or so into preferred equity. Debt fell to around USD 16bn and maturities were pushed out.
  2. New management and a leaner centre. Chris Nassetta became CEO in late 2007. He cut corporate overhead, moved headquarters from Beverly Hills to Virginia, and pushed a consistent performance culture across the brands.
  3. An asset-light growth engine. Growth came mainly from new franchised and managed hotels built with other people's capital, especially internationally. Every new room added fee income without adding debt. The development pipeline grew to one of the largest in the industry.

The cycle also recovered, which matters. Operational work gets you the rebound. It does not guarantee one.

§C1.6Outcome

Hilton relisted on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2013, one of the largest hotel IPOs on record. Blackstone then sold down in stages. In 2017 Hilton spun off its owned real estate into a separate listed REIT and its timeshare business into another company, leaving a fee-driven hotel manager and franchisor valued at a much higher multiple. Blackstone sold its final shares in 2018.

Measure Approximate figure
Equity invested (original plus 2010 injection) USD 6.4bn
Reported total profit USD 14bn
Implied multiple of money About 3x
Hold period About 10.5 years

A crude single-exit calculation on those figures gives an IRR in the low teens. The true figure was higher because a large share of the proceeds came from 2013 onwards rather than at the end. The lesson in the numbers: an enormous absolute gain can come with only a solid annualised return when the hold is long.

§C1.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Capital structure decides whether you survive long enough to be right. Covenant-light terms and long-dated maturities gave Blackstone time. A tighter structure would likely have handed Hilton to its lenders.
  • Negotiate restructurings early. Lenders facing losses will often accept a discount to avoid owning the asset.
  • Separate what the market values differently. Splitting owned real estate from the fee business re-rated the company.
  • Absolute profit and IRR tell different stories. Quote both when you describe a deal.

In brief

A fictional UK mid-market deal. A fragmented, regulation-driven services market, a platform bought at 9x, fourteen small bolt-ons bought at 6x, real integration work, and an exit at 12x. The value bridge shows exactly where 4.7x came from.

  2. C2.2The business and the thesis
  3. C2.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C2.4What went well
  5. C2.5What went wrong
  6. C2.6Outcome
  7. C2.7Lessons for deal teams

§C2.1Snapshot

Fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Aldermoor Capital, UK mid-market buyout fund
Business Electrical, fire-safety and lift inspection for commercial buildings
Entry 2016 at 9.0x EBITDA of £10.0m, EV £90.0m
Exit 2021 to a large sponsor at 12.0x EBITDA of £25.0m, EV £300.0m
Equity in / out £49.0m / £230.0m
Returns 4.7x MOIC, about 36% IRR
Verdict Good

§C2.2The business and the thesis

Harbourline carried out statutory inspections that building owners are legally required to commission: electrical installation checks, fire-alarm servicing and lift examinations. Demand is driven by regulation rather than the economy. About 80% of revenue repeated each year.

The market was highly fragmented. Hundreds of small regional firms with £0.5m to £1.5m of EBITDA served local customers. National facilities managers wanted one provider covering the whole country. That gap was the thesis:

  1. Buy a well-run regional leader as the platform.
  2. Acquire small operators at low multiples, because small businesses sell cheaply.
  3. Integrate them onto one scheduling system, one brand and one sales team.
  4. Sell a national, larger, lower-risk business at a platform multiple.

§C2.3Entry and deal structure

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (9.0x £10.0m) 90.0 Unitranche loan (4.5x) 45.0
Transaction fees 4.0 Aldermoor equity 44.0
Management rollover 5.0
Total 94.0 Total 94.0

The unitranche came with an uncommitted accordion: extra debt for acquisitions, subject to a leverage test on a pro-forma basis. Management rolled £5.0m and received a management incentive plan on top. Returns below are shown on total equity before incentive-plan dilution.

§C2.4What went well

  • Disciplined bolt-on pricing. Fourteen acquisitions added £9.0m of EBITDA for £54.0m in total, an average of 6.0x. £34.0m came from the accordion and £20.0m from the company's own cash.
  • Integration before the next deal. The team paused acquisitions for six months in 2018 to move every business onto one job-scheduling system. Engineer utilisation rose and overlapping depots closed. That delivered £2.0m of cost synergies.
  • Organic growth. Platform EBITDA grew 7% a year, from £10.0m to £14.0m, helped by cross-selling fire and lift work to electrical customers.
  • A better business to own. No customer was above 3% of revenue at exit, and national contracts made up a growing share. A buyer could underwrite it with confidence.

§C2.5What went wrong

  • Two early bolt-ons lost their founders within a year, and with them some key customer relationships. Aldermoor moved to longer earn-outs and retention packages for later deals.
  • One acquisition in 2019 had weak safety record-keeping. Remediation cost £0.6m and a regulator warning was a reputational scare. Compliance diligence became a standard workstream.
  • Leverage rose rather than fell, from 4.5x to 2.8x only because EBITDA grew so fast. Net debt itself increased.

§C2.6Outcome

Exit EBITDA build £m
Platform EBITDA at entry 10.0
Organic growth 4.0
Acquired EBITDA 9.0
Integration synergies 2.0
Exit EBITDA 25.0

Exit EV = 12.0x × £25.0m = £300.0m. Net debt at exit was £70.0m, leaving £230.0m of equity. MOIC = 230 ÷ 49 = 4.7x. Over five years that is 4.691/5−1≈36%4.69^{1/5} - 1 \approx 36\%4.691/5−1≈36%.

The value bridge explains the £181.0m equity gain:

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (25.0 − 10.0) × 9.0x entry multiple 135.0
Multiple expansion (12.0 − 9.0) × £25.0m exit EBITDA 75.0
Change in net debt £45.0m at entry to £70.0m at exit (25.0)
Entry fees (4.0)
Total equity gain 181.0

The £9.0m of acquired EBITDA was bought at 6.0x and sold at 12.0x. That arbitrage alone was worth £54.0m.

§C2.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Buy-and-build works in fragmented, non-cyclical markets where small firms trade at a genuine discount to scaled platforms.
  • Arbitrage is only real if integration earns the higher multiple. A buyer paying 12x wants one business, not fourteen.
  • Watch the net debt line. Growing EBITDA can hide rising absolute debt.
  • Earn-outs and retention protect people businesses. In services, the customers often follow the founder.

Case C3/Case studies

Alliance Boots: A FTSE 100 Take-Private and a Strategic Exit

GoodReal deal13 min read

£11.1bn take-private funded with about £9bn of debt, exited to Walgreens in two steps

Sponsor
KKR with Stefano Pessina
Sector
Pharmacy retail & pharmaceutical wholesale
Period
2007–2015
In brief

KKR and Alliance Boots' largest shareholder took a FTSE 100 company private weeks before the credit crunch. Defensive earnings carried the debt through the crisis, and a two-stage sale to Walgreens produced a strong return.

  1. C3.1Snapshot
  2. C3.2The business and the thesis
  3. C3.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C3.4What went well
  5. C3.5What went wrong
  6. C3.6Outcome
  7. C3.7Lessons for deal teams

§C3.1Snapshot

Real deal. Figures are rounded from public reporting and are approximate. Check primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsor KKR, alongside executive deputy chairman Stefano Pessina
Closed June 2007
Price About £11.1bn, the first FTSE 100 company taken private by a PE firm
Funding About £9bn of debt
KKR's own equity About £1.22bn
Exit Walgreens bought 45% in 2012 and the rest by the end of 2014
Outcome KKR and partners were reported to be on course to almost triple their money
Verdict Good

§C3.2The business and the thesis

Alliance Boots was formed in 2006 by merging Boots, the UK high-street health and beauty retailer, with Alliance UniChem, a pan-European pharmaceutical wholesaler led by Pessina.

The thesis rested on three points.

  • Defensive cash flows. Prescriptions and everyday health products hold up in downturns. That supports heavy borrowing better than most retail.
  • An owner-operator partner. Pessina already owned a large stake and ran the combined group. Rolling his stake into the deal aligned the main manager with the sponsor.
  • Room to improve. Boots had under-performed as a listed company. Merger integration, procurement savings and international expansion were all underway.

§C3.3Entry and deal structure

The consortium won after a competitive bidding process. About £9bn of the funding was debt, arranged by a large bank syndicate at the peak of the market. The equity came from KKR's funds and balance sheet, Pessina's rolled shares, and co-investors.

The debt was large even for a defensive business. The banks were left holding much of it when the credit markets froze weeks after closing, and had to sell it later at a loss.

§C3.4What went well

  • Earnings held up. Trading proved resilient through the 2008–2009 recession, as the thesis predicted. That kept the company comfortably able to pay its interest.
  • Operational delivery. Integration of the merged group, buying savings on a much larger scale, and growth of the Boots own brands, including No7, all improved profits.
  • International expansion. The wholesale arm grew in new markets, making the group more attractive to a global buyer.
  • An elegant exit. In 2012 Walgreens paid about USD 6.7bn in cash and shares for 45%, with an option to buy the rest. It exercised that option in 2014 and the combined group became Walgreens Boots Alliance. A staged sale let the sponsors realise part of the value early and keep upside through Walgreens shares.

§C3.5What went wrong

  • Timing and syndication. Closing just before the credit crunch left lending banks with losses. That did not hurt the equity directly, but damaged relationships.
  • Tax and public scrutiny. The group moved its headquarters to Switzerland and benefited from interest deductions on its debt. It faced criticism in the UK over how little tax it paid.
  • The legacy after exit. Boots in the UK later struggled under Walgreens ownership, with pharmacy funding cuts and store closures. This came after the sponsor's exit, but it is a reminder that a good sponsor return does not settle whether a business was strengthened.

§C3.6Outcome

KKR invested about £1.22bn of equity in 2007. At the time of the 2012 Walgreens deal, KKR and its partners were widely reported to be on course to almost triple their money. Much of the consideration came as Walgreens shares, so the final result also depended on the Walgreens share price after 2014.

§C3.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Defensive earnings are the best protection against bad timing. Alliance Boots and Energy Future Holdings closed in the same year. One business held its earnings and the other did not.
  • A strategic buyer can pay for what a financial buyer cannot. Walgreens valued global purchasing scale and international expansion.
  • Staged exits can bridge valuation gaps. An option structure let both sides agree a deal when a full sale might have stalled on price.
  • Reputation is part of the return. Tax and job questions can follow a deal long after exit.

Case C4/Case studies

Northgate Packaging: Carve-Out Done Properly

GoodFictional12 min read

Neglected division bought cheaply, stood up alone, restructured, sold to a trade buyer at 3.0x

Sponsor
Calderstone Partners (fictional)
Sector
Industrial packaging
Period
2014–2018
In brief

A fictional corporate carve-out. The parent's EBITDA overstated standalone profits, the TSA ran late and the IT cutover went badly, yet procurement, plant consolidation and pricing work still delivered 3.0x in four years.

  1. C4.1Snapshot
  2. C4.2The business and the thesis
  3. C4.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C4.4What went well
  5. C4.5What went wrong
  6. C4.6Outcome
  7. C4.7Lessons for deal teams

§C4.1Snapshot

Fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Calderstone Partners, European mid-market fund
Business Rigid plastic containers for food and chemicals, seven UK plants
Seller A listed industrial group exiting non-core businesses
Entry 2014, EV £120.0m: 6.0x reported EBITDA, 7.5x standalone EBITDA
Exit 2018 trade sale at 9.0x EBITDA of £28.0m, EV £252.0m
Equity in / out £70.0m / £212.0m
Returns 3.0x MOIC, about 32% IRR
Verdict Good

§C4.2The business and the thesis

Northgate was a steady but neglected division. The parent had starved it of capital and management attention for a decade. Plants were under-used, raw-material buying was done separately at each site, and price increases lagged resin costs.

Carve-outs often sell cheaply because the seller wants a clean, fast exit and few buyers can handle the complexity. Calderstone's thesis was that the discount paid for the complexity was larger than the cost of solving it.

§C4.3Entry and deal structure

The first job was to get the true earnings. Inside the parent, Northgate received shared services, such as IT, finance, HR and insurance, below their real cost.

EBITDA bridge £m
EBITDA as reported within the parent 20.0
Standalone costs to replace group services (4.0)
Standalone EBITDA 16.0

The headline price of 6.0x looked cheap. On standalone EBITDA it was 7.5x, a fair price. The sponsor underwrote the deal on the lower number.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value 120.0 Term loan B (4.0x standalone) 64.0
Transaction fees 6.0 Calderstone equity 70.0
One-off separation costs 8.0
Total 134.0 Total 134.0

A transitional services agreement (TSA) let Northgate keep using the parent's IT and payroll for 18 months while it built its own.

§C4.4What went well

  • Procurement. Buying resin centrally across all plants, with indexed contracts, saved £3.0m a year.
  • Footprint. Closing two of seven plants and moving volume to the others saved £4.0m a year, after £10.0m of one-off restructuring costs.
  • Pricing. New contracts included resin pass-through clauses, adding £2.0m. Margins stopped swinging with oil prices.
  • Volume growth. With capital finally available, new lines for chemical customers added £3.0m.
  • Management. A new CFO and operations director joined in the first 100 days. The divisional MD stayed and was given real authority for the first time.

§C4.5What went wrong

  • The TSA overran by nine months, costing £2.0m more than planned.
  • The IT cutover disrupted invoicing. For two months many invoices went out late, debtor days rose sharply, and the company drew £5.0m on its revolving credit facility to cover the cash gap.
  • A plant closure cost a customer. One food customer disliked the move to a more distant plant and left, taking £1.0m of EBITDA.

None of these was fatal, because the plan had cash buffers and the core levers were in management's control.

§C4.6Outcome

Exit EBITDA was £28.0m: £16.0m standalone, plus £3.0m procurement, £4.0m footprint, £2.0m pricing and £3.0m volume, net of the lost customer already reflected in volume. A European packaging group paid 9.0x, valuing Northgate at £252.0m. Net debt was £40.0m, so equity was £212.0m.

MOIC = 212 ÷ 70 = 3.0x. Over four years, 3.031/4−1≈32%3.03^{1/4} - 1 \approx 32\%3.031/4−1≈32%.

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (28.0 − 16.0) × 7.5x standalone entry multiple 90.0
Multiple expansion (9.0 − 7.5) × £28.0m 42.0
Debt paydown £64.0m at entry to £40.0m at exit 24.0
Entry fees and separation costs (14.0)
Total equity gain 142.0

§C4.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Price carve-outs on standalone EBITDA. The seller's reported figure hides real costs.
  • Budget more time and cash for separation than the plan says. TSAs and IT migrations almost always run late.
  • Operational levers inside management's control are the safest value creation. None of this deal's upside needed a market recovery.
  • Strategic buyers pay for fixed businesses. A cleaned-up, focused asset fitted a trade buyer's network and earned a higher multiple.

Kestrel Software: Great Operations, Average Return

AverageFictional11 min read

EBITDA more than doubled, but paying 20x and selling at 14x left 1.8x

Sponsor
Wrenfield Equity (fictional)
Sector
Vertical software (SaaS)
Period
2017–2022
In brief

A fictional software buyout. Management more than doubled EBITDA, yet the entry multiple from a hot auction and a 2022 valuation reset absorbed most of the gain. The value bridge shows how multiple compression cancels operational success.

  1. C5.1Snapshot
  2. C5.2The business and the thesis
  3. C5.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C5.4What went well
  5. C5.5What went wrong
  6. C5.6Outcome
  7. C5.7Lessons for deal teams

§C5.1Snapshot

Fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Wrenfield Equity, technology-focused buyout fund
Business Software for residential property managers: rent collection, maintenance, compliance
Entry 2017 at 20.0x EBITDA of £10.0m, EV £200.0m, about 5.0x ARR of £40.0m
Exit Late 2022 to another sponsor at 14.0x EBITDA of £22.0m, EV £308.0m
Equity in / out £146.0m / £260.0m
Returns 1.8x MOIC, about 12% IRR
Verdict Average: above the hurdle, well below the fund's target

§C5.2The business and the thesis

Kestrel sold subscription software to letting agents and property managers. Customers rarely left, because switching meant migrating tenant records and retraining staff. At entry:

Metric Value
Annual recurring revenue (ARR) £40.0m
ARR growth 20%
Gross revenue retention 93%
Net revenue retention 108%
EBITDA margin 26%

The thesis was to keep growth at 15–20%, raise prices, add payments and insurance modules to lift revenue per customer, and expand margins as the business scaled.

§C5.3Entry and deal structure

The sale ran as a competitive auction with six bidders. Wrenfield won by paying 20.0x EBITDA.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (20.0x £10.0m) 200.0 Recurring-revenue loan (1.5x ARR) 60.0
Transaction fees 6.0 Wrenfield equity 146.0
Total 206.0 Total 206.0

The recurring-revenue loan was sized on ARR rather than EBITDA, a common structure for software. At 6.0x EBITDA it looked high, but lenders were comfortable with the customer stickiness. The equity cheque was large: 71% of the total.

§C5.4What went well

  • Operational delivery. ARR reached £75.0m. EBITDA more than doubled to £22.0m.
  • Payments module. Collecting rent through Kestrel created a new revenue stream worth £6.0m of ARR by exit.
  • Pricing. Annual price rises of 5–7% stuck, with little extra churn.
  • Resilience. Covid barely touched the business. Rent still had to be collected.

§C5.5What went wrong

  • Growth slowed. ARR growth fell from 20% to 11% as the easy customers were already won. Net revenue retention slipped to 104%.
  • A costly replatforming. The old code base could not scale. Rebuilding it took two years and cost £15.0m of R&D, which held back margins and delayed new modules.
  • The market re-rated. In 2022 rising interest rates cut software valuations sharply. Buyers that would have paid 20x in 2021 offered 14x a year later.
  • Holding on did not help. Waiting for multiples to recover would have lengthened the hold and cut IRR further, while the fund needed to show realisations to raise its next fund.

§C5.6Outcome

Exit EV = 14.0x × £22.0m = £308.0m. Net debt at exit was £48.0m, so equity was £260.0m.

MOIC = 260 ÷ 146 = 1.8x. Over five years, 1.781/5−1≈12%1.78^{1/5} - 1 \approx 12\%1.781/5−1≈12%.

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (22.0 − 10.0) × 20.0x entry multiple 240.0
Multiple compression (14.0 − 20.0) × £22.0m (132.0)
Debt paydown £60.0m at entry to £48.0m at exit 12.0
Entry fees (6.0)
Total equity gain 114.0

Management created £240.0m of value by growing earnings. Multiple compression took back more than half of it.

§C5.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Your entry multiple is a bet on the exit multiple. Paying 20x assumes someone else will pay something similar later.
  • Model a multiple-compression case. An exit at 14x should have been a standard downside test, not a surprise.
  • Low leverage limits the downside, but also the upside. A 71% equity cheque protected the deal but diluted returns.
  • Check the technology in diligence. A proper code and architecture review would have found the replatforming need and priced it in.

Ashworth Foods: When a Dividend Recap Flatters the IRR

AverageFictional11 min read

Flat EBITDA and a supermarket price war; a recap lifted IRR but cut MOIC

Sponsor
Belvoir Capital (fictional)
Sector
Food manufacturing
Period
2012–2019
In brief

A fictional chilled ready-meals supplier squeezed by its supermarket customers. Nearly all the return came from paying down debt, and a year-three dividend recap raised IRR while lowering the multiple of money.

  1. C6.1Snapshot
  2. C6.2The business and the thesis
  3. C6.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C6.4What went well
  5. C6.5What went wrong
  6. C6.6Outcome
  7. C6.7Lessons for deal teams

§C6.1Snapshot

Fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Belvoir Capital, UK mid-market fund
Business Chilled ready meals, mostly supermarket own-label
Entry 2012 at 7.0x EBITDA of £18.0m, EV £126.0m
Dividend recap Year 3: £40.0m of new debt paid out to shareholders
Exit 2019 to a food group at 7.0x EBITDA of £19.0m, EV £133.0m
Equity in / total returned £58.0m / £107.0m
Returns 1.8x MOIC, about 12% IRR
Verdict Average

§C6.2The business and the thesis

Ashworth made ready meals for two of the big four UK supermarkets. It was efficient, had modern factories and a strong food-safety record. Belvoir's thesis was to win a third supermarket, launch a premium branded range and use scale to cut costs.

The obvious risk sat in the customer list: the top two customers were 70% of revenue. The investment committee accepted it because the relationships were long-standing and switching suppliers of chilled food is hard.

§C6.3Entry and deal structure

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (7.0x £18.0m) 126.0 Senior debt (4.0x) 72.0
Transaction fees 4.0 Belvoir equity 58.0
Total 130.0 Total 130.0

§C6.4What went well

  • Cash generation. Strong cost control and tight working capital meant the business paid down debt steadily every year.
  • An early dividend. By year three EBITDA had reached £21.0m and leverage had fallen. Belvoir borrowed another £40.0m and paid it out as a dividend. The fund had got back 69% of its money within three years.
  • Food-safety record. No product recalls in seven years kept both key customers loyal.

§C6.5What went wrong

  • A supermarket price war. From 2014 the discounters Aldi and Lidl grew fast. The big supermarkets pushed price cuts down to suppliers. With 70% of revenue in two customers, Ashworth had no negotiating power.
  • The third customer never came. A long tender was lost on price.
  • Input-cost inflation. After the 2016 fall in sterling, imported ingredients and packaging became more expensive. Contracts did not allow price increases to be passed on quickly.
  • The branded range failed. Marketing spend of £5.0m produced little lasting revenue.

EBITDA went from £18.0m at entry, to £21.0m in year three, down to £17.0m in year five, and recovered only to £19.0m by exit. After seven years, the business earned barely more than when it was bought.

§C6.6Outcome

Exit EV = 7.0x × £19.0m = £133.0m. Net debt at exit was £66.0m, leaving £67.0m of equity. Adding the £40.0m dividend, Belvoir received £107.0m for its £58.0m.

MOIC = 107 ÷ 58 = 1.84x. The IRR on cash flows of −58 in year 0, +40 in year 3 and +67 in year 7 is about 12%.

What if there had been no recap?#

Assume the £40.0m had stayed in the company, saving interest at 6% for four years, about £10.0m. Exit net debt would have been about £16.0m and equity about £117.0m.

With recap Without recap
Total proceeds £107.0m £117.0m
MOIC 1.84x 2.02x
IRR 12.3% 10.6%

The recap raised IRR by returning cash early, but lowered the multiple because the extra debt cost interest. Which matters more depends on the fund: IRR drives carry and league tables, while multiple is the money LPs actually receive.

Where the return came from#

Driver Calculation £m
EBITDA growth (19.0 − 18.0) × 7.0x 7.0
Multiple change 7.0x to 7.0x 0.0
Cash generation used to repay debt and fund the dividend (72.0 + 40.0) − 66.0 46.0
Entry fees (4.0)
Total gain including the dividend 49.0

Almost the whole return came from cash generation, not from building a better business.

§C6.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Customer concentration is a risk to margins, not just revenue. Large customers may stay, but they will take your profit.
  • Check whether contracts let you pass on cost increases. Ask how fast and how fully.
  • Always show IRR and MOIC together. Recaps and early distributions can move them in opposite directions.
  • Deleveraging alone gives average returns. Top-quartile deals need earnings growth or a better multiple.

Case C7/Case studies

Debenhams: A Great Sponsor Return, a Weakened Business

MixedReal deal12 min read

Over 3x in under three years for the sponsors; the company later failed under its debts and leases

Sponsor
CVC, TPG and Merrill Lynch Private Equity
Sector
Department store retail
Period
2003–2006 (company collapsed 2019–2021)
In brief

A £1.7bn take-private returned more than three times the sponsors' equity within three years, helped by property sales and cost cuts. The business went back to the stock market carrying more debt and rent, and eventually closed. A case study in who a return is good for.

  1. C7.1Snapshot
  2. C7.2The business and the thesis
  3. C7.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C7.4What went well, for the sponsors
  5. C7.5What went wrong, for the business
  6. C7.6Outcome
  7. C7.7Lessons for deal teams

§C7.1Snapshot

Real deal. Figures are rounded from public reporting and are approximate. Check primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors CVC Capital Partners, TPG and Merrill Lynch Private Equity
Closed Late 2003
Price About £1.7bn
Sponsor equity About £600m
Exit Stock market relisting in May 2006
Sponsor outcome Reported at more than three times their equity in under three years
Company outcome Administration in 2019, all stores closed by 2021
Verdict Mixed: excellent for the sponsors, poor for the business long term

§C7.2The business and the thesis

Debenhams was one of the UK's largest department store chains, with prime town-centre and shopping-centre sites, many of them owned. The sponsors saw three sources of value.

  • Property. Owned stores could be sold to property investors and rented back, releasing cash tied up in buildings.
  • Cost and working capital. Stock levels, supplier terms and central costs all had room to tighten.
  • A quick relisting. A leaner, higher-margin business could be sold back to public investors at a good price.

§C7.3Entry and deal structure

The consortium won a contested bid, paying about £1.7bn with about £600m of equity. The rest was debt. The plan was a short hold, so cash extraction and a fast exit were central from the start.

§C7.4What went well, for the sponsors

  • Sale and leaseback. Stores were sold to property companies and leased back on long leases. The cash raised helped fund large returns to the owners.
  • Tighter operations. Stock was cut, suppliers were paid more slowly and costs were reduced. Reported margins improved.
  • A fast, successful exit. Debenhams was refloated in 2006 at a value similar to what the sponsors paid, but they had already taken out large sums. The three firms were reported to have made more than three times their £600m in under three years.

§C7.5What went wrong, for the business

  • Rent replaced ownership. After the leaseback, the company paid rent on buildings it used to own, often on long leases with upward-only rent reviews. Those costs were fixed whatever happened to sales.
  • More debt at relisting. The company went back to the stock market with far more debt than before the buyout.
  • Under-investment. Cutting capital spending improved short-term cash flow but left stores looking tired as online shopping grew.
  • A weak public-market start. The share price fell well below the IPO price within about two years, after profit warnings. Investors who bought at the IPO lost money.

Debenhams struggled for years afterwards. Leases and debt left little room to invest as shoppers moved online. It went into administration in 2019, with lenders taking control. Covid closures finished it off. All stores closed by 2021, and online retailer Boohoo bought the brand name.

§C7.6Outcome

Perspective Result
Sponsors Reported more than 3x their equity in under three years
IPO investors Large losses as the share price fell
Company Weaker balance sheet, higher fixed costs, eventual failure
Employees Many thousands of jobs lost when the business closed

It is too simple to blame the 2003 buyout alone for a collapse sixteen years later. Online shopping, many other owners' decisions and Covid all played a part. But the deal left the company less able to adapt: less property to borrow against, higher fixed rents, and more debt.

§C7.7Lessons for deal teams

  • Sale and leasebacks create debt-like costs. Rent is a fixed claim on cash flow. Count leases when you judge leverage, as the IFRS 16 accounting rules now require.
  • A quick flip moves risk to the next owner. If you are the buyer of a sponsor-backed IPO, ask what was taken out and what was cut.
  • Returns and business health can diverge. Judge a deal by what it did to the company as well as the multiple of money.
  • Reputation matters to fundraising. Deals like this shaped public and political views of private equity for years.
