§C8.1Snapshot

Fictional case, built to show the mechanics cleanly. All figures are illustrative.

Item Detail
Sponsor Hartwell Capital, mid-market buyout fund
Business 60 mid-price gyms in UK towns and cities
Entry 2018 at 9.0x "adjusted" EBITDA of £25.0m, EV £225.0m
Additional equity £20.0m equity cure in 2020
Outcome 2023 debt-for-equity swap; lenders take 90% of the company
Sponsor returns 0.0x: £114.0m lost
Verdict Bad

§C8.2The business and the thesis

Corrigan ran mid-price gyms with pools and classes. Membership had grown steadily. The plan was to open 20 new clubs in five years, raise prices, and cut costs through central buying and digital sign-up.

§C8.3Entry and deal structure

The sale process marketed adjusted EBITDA of £25.0m. The sponsor's own quality-of-earnings review told a different story.

EBITDA bridge £m QoE view
Reported EBITDA (before IFRS 16) 21.0 Supported
Run-rate profit from 8 recently opened clubs 2.5 Optimistic: assumes mature membership levels immediately
"One-off" pre-opening and launch marketing 1.5 Recurring while the company keeps opening clubs
Adjusted EBITDA 25.0 Supportable figure closer to 21.0–22.0

In a competitive auction, Hartwell paid 9.0x the adjusted number. On reported EBITDA, that was 10.7x.

Uses £m Sources £m
Enterprise value (9.0x £25.0m) 225.0 Unitranche (5.5x adjusted EBITDA) 138.0
Transaction fees 7.0 Hartwell equity 94.0
Total 232.0 Total 232.0

A further £40.0m capex facility funded new clubs. The covenant allowed net leverage up to 7.0x, measured on adjusted EBITDA before rent was treated as a financing cost.

The leverage nobody headlined#

Corrigan paid about £28.0m a year in rent on long leases. Under IFRS 16 those leases were worth about £250m as liabilities. Counting them, true lease-adjusted leverage at entry was well above 15x. A business with high fixed rent, high staff costs and high energy costs has very little room when revenue falls.

§C8.4What went wrong

  • The add-backs did not appear. 2019 EBITDA was £22.0m against a plan of £28.0m. New clubs matured slowly, and some took members from nearby Corrigan clubs.
  • Budget competitors. Low-cost 24-hour gyms opened near a third of the estate, pulling price sensitive members away.
  • Covid closures. Clubs were shut for much of 2020 and 2021. EBITDA was negative £6.0m in 2020. Rent still had to be paid or negotiated.
  • An equity cure. To avoid a covenant default in 2020, Hartwell put in £20.0m of new equity. Lenders agreed a covenant holiday and let interest roll up instead of being paid in cash.
  • An energy shock. In 2022, heating pools and running air conditioning became far more expensive. EBITDA recovered only to £14.0m.

By the end of 2022 net debt had grown to £190.0m, from drawing the capex facility and rolled-up interest. Leverage was 13.6x, before counting leases.

§C8.5Outcome

In 2023 the lenders and the sponsor agreed a restructuring.

Item Result
Debt Cut from £190.0m to £100.0m
Lenders Took 90% of the equity in exchange for the debt written off
Management 10% through a new incentive plan
Hartwell Nothing. Its £94.0m plus the £20.0m cure were lost

Some weaker clubs were closed and several landlords agreed rent cuts as part of the process.

§C8.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Price on EBITDA the QoE supports. An auction does not make weak add-backs real.
  • "One-off" costs that repeat every year are not one-off. Pre-opening costs are normal for a business that keeps opening sites.
  • Count leases as leverage. Rent-heavy businesses carry much more fixed obligation than debt alone suggests.
  • An equity cure should be a decision, not a reflex. Before putting in more money, ask whether it saves the investment or only delays losing it.
  • Stress-test with a real shock. A three-month revenue collapse is a useful test for any high fixed-cost business.

Case C9/Case studies

Toys "R" Us: Debt That Left No Room to Adapt

BadReal deal12 min read

USD 6.6bn buyout with more than USD 5bn of debt; about USD 400m a year in interest; liquidated in 2018

Sponsor
KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado Realty Trust
Sector
Specialty retail
Period
2005–2018
In brief

Three sponsors bought the toy retailer with heavy debt. Interest costs of around USD 400m a year absorbed cash that could have modernised stores and online sales, while Amazon, Walmart and Target took share. A failed IPO, bankruptcy and liquidation followed.

  1. C9.1Snapshot
  2. C9.2The business and the thesis
  3. C9.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C9.4What went wrong
  5. C9.5Outcome
  6. C9.6Lessons for deal teams

§C9.1Snapshot

Real deal. Figures are rounded from public reporting and are approximate. Check primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors KKR, Bain Capital and Vornado Realty Trust
Closed July 2005
Price About USD 6.6bn
Funding More than USD 5bn of debt, about USD 1.6bn of sponsor equity
Interest burden About USD 400m a year by 2017
Exit attempt IPO filed in 2010, withdrawn in 2013
Outcome Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2017; US stores liquidated in 2018
Verdict Bad

§C9.2The business and the thesis

Toys "R" Us was the leading specialist toy retailer in the US, with a large international business and the Babies "R" Us chain. Its share had been falling for years as discount retailers used toys to bring shoppers into their stores.

The sponsors' thesis combined three things:

  • Real estate value. The company owned many of its stores. Vornado, a property investor, brought expertise in extracting value from that estate.
  • Babies "R" Us. A growing, profitable format with loyal customers.
  • Operational improvement. Better stock control, store formats and pricing to fight back against discounters.

§C9.3Entry and deal structure

Most of the price was borrowed and placed on the company's balance sheet. Store property was held in separate property companies, with the operating business paying rent to them.

Item Approximate figure
Purchase price USD 6.6bn
Debt More than USD 5bn
Sponsor equity USD 1.6bn

Toy retail is highly seasonal. A large share of annual profit comes in the weeks before Christmas, while debt and rent must be paid all year round. That makes high leverage riskier than headline annual EBITDA suggests.

§C9.4What went wrong

  • Interest crowded out investment. Paying around USD 400m a year of interest left little for store upgrades, technology or e-commerce. Rivals were investing heavily in all three.
  • The market moved online. Amazon grew quickly in toys. Walmart and Target used toys as loss-leaders. Toys "R" Us could not compete on price or convenience.
  • A failed exit. An IPO was filed in 2010, but weak results and market conditions meant it was withdrawn in 2013. Without an exit, the sponsors could not reduce the debt through a sale.
  • Refinancing became harder. Each year the company needed to refinance large debt maturities. Suppliers, worried about being paid, started demanding cash upfront before the 2017 holiday season.

§C9.5Outcome

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2017 with around USD 5bn of debt. A weak holiday season followed. In 2018 the US business was liquidated rather than restructured, and more than 30,000 jobs were lost. The UK business collapsed the same year.

Party Result
Sponsor equity USD 1.6bn effectively lost
Sponsors' fees and interest received Reported at about USD 464m over the hold, according to an advocacy group's analysis
Employees More than 30,000 jobs lost; severance became a public controversy
Creditors Large losses

The fees partly offset the sponsors' losses. That became a central part of the public debate about the deal.

§C9.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Leverage and disruption do not mix. A business losing share to structural change needs cash to adapt. Heavy debt takes that option away.
  • Seasonality multiplies leverage risk. Judge debt against the weakest part of the year, not just annual EBITDA.
  • Property value is not the same as operating strength. Owning stores gave security for lenders, but did not make the retail business competitive.
  • Always have a second exit route. When the IPO window closed, there was no clear plan B.

Case C10/Case studies

TXU / Energy Future Holdings: The Biggest LBO and a One-Way Bet

BadReal deal13 min read

USD 45bn buyout betting on high gas prices; shale gas collapsed them and about USD 8bn of equity was wiped out

Sponsor
KKR, TPG and Goldman Sachs Capital Partners
Sector
Power generation & utilities
Period
2007–2014
In brief

The largest leveraged buyout ever was, underneath, a bet that natural gas prices would stay high. The US shale boom pushed them sharply down, cut power prices in Texas, and left a business with around USD 42bn of debt in bankruptcy.

  1. C10.1Snapshot
  2. C10.2The business and the thesis
  3. C10.3Entry and deal structure
  4. C10.4What went wrong
  5. C10.5Outcome
  6. C10.6Lessons for deal teams

§C10.1Snapshot

Real deal. Figures are rounded from public reporting and are approximate. Check primary sources before quoting them externally.

Item Detail
Sponsors KKR, TPG and Goldman Sachs Capital Partners, with co-investors
Closed October 2007
Enterprise value About USD 45bn including debt, the largest LBO in history
Sponsor equity About USD 8bn
Outcome Chapter 11 in April 2014 with roughly USD 42bn of debt
Sponsor returns Equity wiped out
Verdict Bad

§C10.2The business and the thesis

TXU was the largest power company in Texas. The company, renamed Energy Future Holdings after the buyout, had three parts:

Business What it did Economic profile
Luminant Coal, lignite and nuclear power stations Profits depend on wholesale power prices
TXU Energy Selling electricity to homes and businesses Competitive retail
Oncor Regulated transmission and distribution network Stable, regulated returns

The core of the thesis was simple. In the Texas power market, gas-fired plants usually set the wholesale electricity price. TXU's coal and nuclear plants cost much less to run. When gas was expensive, power prices were high and TXU earned wide margins. In 2007 gas prices were high and had been rising. The sponsors bet they would stay that way.

§C10.3Entry and deal structure

The buyout was financed mostly with debt placed on the generation and retail businesses. Oncor was ring-fenced: regulators required it to be kept legally separate so its customers were protected if the rest of the group failed.

To win public support, the sponsors also agreed to cancel most of TXU's plans to build new coal plants.

§C10.4What went wrong

  • The shale gas revolution. New drilling techniques unlocked huge US gas supplies. Benchmark US gas prices fell from above USD 13 per million British thermal units in mid-2008 to below USD 2 in 2012.
  • Power prices followed. Cheap gas pushed Texas wholesale electricity prices down. Luminant's margins collapsed, and much of the company's debt depended on those margins.
  • Hedges ran out. Hedges on gas prices protected earnings for the first few years, but they were set to expire and could not be renewed at the old prices.
  • Recession cut demand. Lower industrial power use added to the pressure.
  • Buying time made the hole deeper. Debt swaps and maturity extensions from 2009 to 2013 delayed default, but interest kept accumulating.

Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway bought about USD 2bn of the company's bonds early on. Buffett later called the purchase a major mistake.

§C10.5Outcome

Energy Future Holdings filed for Chapter 11 in April 2014 with roughly USD 42bn of debt, one of the largest non-financial bankruptcies in US history.

Party Result
Sponsors and co-investors About USD 8bn of equity lost
Generation and retail creditors Took ownership; the business became Vistra Energy in 2016
Oncor Protected by the ring-fence; later sold to Sempra Energy in 2018

§C10.6Lessons for deal teams

  • Know what you are really betting on. Strip away the complexity and this was a leveraged bet on the price of natural gas.
  • Never put high leverage on a single uncontrollable variable. Operational improvement could not offset a structural fall in the commodity price.
  • Stress-test the thesis itself, not just the plan. The key question was: what if gas prices halve and stay low? The answer was bankruptcy.
  • Hedges buy time, not safety. They protect near-term cash flow but expire.
  • Size and prestige do not reduce risk. The biggest deal, backed by the most experienced sponsors, still failed on its central assumption.
